In general, an inverse relationship exists between a given energy system’s maximum rate of ATP production (i.e., ATP produced per unit of time) and its capacity (i.e., the total amount of ATP produced over time). The phosphagen system is capable of achieving the highest rate of ATP production, while fat oxidation through the oxidative system has the greatest capacity of ATP production. As a result, the phosphagen energy system primarily supplies ATP for high-intensity activities of short duration (e.g., 100 m sprint), the glycolytic system for moderate- to high-intensity activities of short to medium duration (e.g., 400 m dash), and the oxidative system for low-intensity activities of long duration (e.g., marathon). The duration of the activity also influences which energy system is used. Athletic events range in duration from 1 to 3 seconds (e.g., snatch and shot put) to more than 4 hours (e.g., long-distance triathlons and ultramarathons). If an athlete makes a best effort (an effort that results in the best possible performance for a given event), the time considerations shown in table 3.2 are reasonable (48, 79, 126, 146, 149). At no time, during either exercise or rest, does any single energy system provide the complete supply of energy. During exerc

chapterTitle: Bioenergetics of Exercise and Training
text: Substrate Depletion and Repletion Energy substrates—molecules that provide starting materials for bioenergetic reactions, including phosphagens (ATP and CP), glucose, glycogen, lactate, free fatty acids, and amino acids—can be selectively depleted during the performance of activities of various intensities and durations. Subsequently, the energy that can be produced by the bioenergetic systems is reduced. Fatigue experienced during many activities is frequently associated with the depletion of phosphagens (66, 89) and glycogen (21, 79, 92, 133). Importantly, performance is rarely limited by the depletion of substrates such as free fatty acids, lactate, and amino acids. Consequently, the depletion and repletion pattern of phosphagens and glycogen following physical activity is important in exercise and sport bioenergetics. Phosphagens Fatigue during exercise appears to be at least partially related to the decrease in phosphagens (i.e., ATP and CP). Phosphagen concentrations in muscle are more rapidly depleted as a result of high-intensity anaerobic exercise compared to aerobic exercise (66, 89). CP can decrease markedly (50%-70%) during the first stage of high-intensity exercise of short and moderate duration (5-30 s) and can be almost completely depleted as a result of very intense exercise to exhaustion (86, 93, 97, 110). Muscle ATP concentrations may decrease only slightly (34) or may decrease up to 50% to 60% (145) of the pre-exercise levels during experimentally induced f

chapterTitle: Bioenergetics of Exercise and Training
text: energy sources, such as glycogen and free fatty acids. Postexercise phosphagen repletion can occur in a relatively short period, with complete ATP resynthesis occurring within approximately 3 to 5 minutes, and CP being fully resynthesized within 8 minutes (75, 89). Note that half of the CP stores are replenished in 30 seconds, allowing for repeated maximal contractions interspersed with brief rest intervals. While repletion of phosphagens is largely accomplished as a result of aerobic metabolism (75), glycolysis can contribute to recovery after high-intensity exercise (29, 40). The effects of training and supplementation on resting concentrations of phosphagens is an ongoing area of investigation. Aerobic endurance training may increase resting concentrations of phosphagens (49, 99) and decrease their rate of depletion at a given absolute submaximal power output (33, 99) but not at a relative (percentage of maximum) submaximal power output (33). Although researchers have reported indications of increased resting concentrations of phosphagens (12, 127), short-term (eight weeks) studies of sprint and six months of resistance or explosive training have not shown alterations in resting concentrations of phosphagens (11, 16, 147, 150). However, total phosphagen content can be larger following sprint training due to increases in muscle mass (150). Resistance training has been shown to increase the resting concentrations of phosphagens in the triceps brachii after five weeks of trai

chapterTitle: Bioenergetics of Exercise and Training
text: suggests that both anaerobic training, including sprinting and resistance training (16, 106), and aerobic endurance training (64, 65) can increase resting muscle glycogen concentration with concomitantly appropriate nutrition. The rate of glycogen depletion is related to exercise intensity (137). Muscle glycogen is a more important energy source than liver glycogen during moderate- and high-intensity exercise. Liver glycogen appears to be more important during low-intensity exercise, and its contribution to metabolic processes increases with duration of exercise. Increases in relative exercise intensity of 50%, 75%, and 100% of maximal oxygen uptake result in increases in the rate of muscle glycogenolysis (the breakdown of glycogen) of 0.7, 1.4, and 3.4 mmol · kg−1 · min−1, respectively (133). At relative intensities of exercise above 60% of maximal oxygen uptake, muscle glycogen becomes an increasingly important energy substrate; the entire glycogen content of some muscle cells can become depleted during exercise (132). Relatively constant blood glucose concentrations are maintained at very low exercise intensities (<50% of maximal oxygen uptake) because of low muscle glucose uptake. However, as exercise duration increases beyond 90 minutes, blood glucose concentrations fall but rarely below 2.8 mmol/L (2). Long-duration exercise (>90 min) at higher intensities (>50% of maximal oxygen uptake) may result in substantially decreased blood glucose concentrations as a result of l

text: Very high-intensity, intermittent exercise, such as high-intensity resistance training, can cause substantial depletion of muscle glycogen (decreases of 20%-60%) with relatively few sets (low total volume) (100, 126, 146, 148). Although phosphagens may be the primary limiting factor during resistance exercise with high resistance and few repetitions or few sets, muscle glycogen may become the limiting factor for resistance training with larger volumes of work accumulated using many sets and repetitions (126). This type of exercise could cause selective muscle fiber glycogen depletion (more depletion in type II fibers), which can also limit performance (50, 126). As with other types of dynamic exercise, the rate of muscle glycogenolysis during resistance exercise depends on intensity (i.e., the greater the intensity, the faster the rate of glycogenolysis). However, it appears that when the total work performed is equal, the absolute amount of glycogen depletion is similar, regardless of the resistance training session’s intensity (69, 126). Repletion of muscle glycogen during recovery is related to postexercise carbohydrate ingestion. Repletion appears to be optimal if 0.7 to 3.0 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight is ingested every 2 hours following exercise (56, 137). text: Capacity Following Endurance Training Hendrickse and colleagues (77) tested the hypothesis that superimposing endurance training in both older and younger highly resistance-trained men would lead to an increase in fiber oxidative capacity and a decrease in fiber size. Eight highly resistance-trained younger (mean age = 28 years) and seven older (mean age = 67 years) men participated in a 10-week cycle endurance-training program consisting of five 6-minute intervals at 75% max heart rate (HRmax) separated by 4-minute intervals at 90% HRmax, superimposed on their usual resistance training program of at least 4 sessions per week (2 upper body, 2 lower body). Before and after the 10 weeks of training, V̇ O2max, body fat percentage, an MRI of the upper leg, the maximal voluntary isometric contraction torque (MVC) of the knee extensor muscles, and a vastus lateralis muscle biopsy were taken. While there were expected differences in anatomical cross-sectional area of the thigh muscles, following training no relative difference was observed between younger and older men for V̇ O2max per kilogram body mass. The imposed endurance training equally increased the succinate dehydrogenase (a Krebs cycle enzyme) activity in both younger and older participants and significantly increased the number of capillaries around type I fibers. text: Bioenergetic Limiting Factors in Exercise Performance Factors limiting maximal performance (22, 49, 79, 88, 104, 156) must be considered in the mechanisms of fatigue experienced during exercise and training. Understanding the possible limiting factors associated with a particular athletic event is required when one is designing training programs to achieve a physiological adaptation that seeks to delay fatigue and possibly enhance performance. Table 3.4 depicts examples of various limiting factors based on depletion of energy sources and increases in muscle hydrogen ions, although other potential factors have been postulated. Glycogen depletion can be a limiting factor both for long-duration, low-intensity exercise supported primarily by aerobic metabolism and for repeated, high-intensity exercise supported primarily by anaerobic mechanisms. Of importance to resistance training, sprinting, and other primarily anaerobic activities is the effect of metabolic acidosis on limiting contractile force (53, 79, 116, 117, 125). Several other factors have been implicated in the development of muscle fatigue and may limit exercise performance, including increased intracellular Pi, ammonia accumulation, increased ADP, and impaired calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (4, 5, 131, 156, 160). text: Oxygen Uptake and the Aerobic and Anaerobic Contributions to Exercise Oxygen uptake (or consumption) is a measure of a person’s ability to take in oxygen via the respiratory system and deliver it to the working tissues via the cardiovascular system, and the ability of working tissues (predominantly skeletal muscle) to use oxygen. During low-intensity exercise with a constant power output, oxygen uptake increases for the first few minutes until a steady state of uptake (oxygen demand equals oxygen consumption) is reached (figure 3.9) (7, 85). FIGURE 3.9 Low-intensity, steady-state exercise metabolism: 75% of maximal oxygen uptake (V̇ O2max). EPOC = excess postexercise oxygen consumption; V̇ O2 = oxygen uptake. At the start of an exercise bout, however, some of the energy must be supplied through anaerobic mechanisms because the aerobic system responds slowly to the initial increase in the demand for energy (62, 155). This anaerobic contribution to the total energy cost of exercise is termed the oxygen deficit (figure 3.9) (85, 109). After exercise ceases, oxygen uptake remains above pre-exercise 211

text: levels for a period of time that varies according to the intensity and length of the exercise. Postexercise oxygen uptake has been termed the oxygen debt (85, 109), recovery O2 (109), or the excess postexercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) (22). The EPOC is the oxygen uptake above resting values used to restore homeostasis to the pre-exercise condition (141). Only small to moderate relationships between the oxygen deficit and the EPOC have been observed (13, 77); the oxygen deficit may influence the size of the EPOC, but the two are not equal. The possible factors affecting the EPOC are listed in the sidebar Excess Postexercise Oxygen Consumption Is Intensity, Duration, and Mode Dependent (17, 21, 22, 58, 109). Excess Postexercise Oxygen Consumption Is Intensity, Duration, and Mode Dependent Excess postexercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) refers to the prolonged increase in V̇ O2 that may be observed for hours after exercise (58). The greatest EPOC values are found when both exercise intensity (i.e., >50%-60% V̇ O2max) and durations (i.e., >40 min) are high. Performing brief, intermittent bouts of supramaximal exercise (i.e., >100% V̇ O2max) may induce the greatest EPOC with lower total work. There is interindividual variability for EPOC in response to a given relative exercise stimulus. The effects of aerobic exercise modes on EPOC are unclear. chapterTitle: Bioenergetics of Exercise and Training
text: Metabolic Specificity of Training Appropriate exercise intensities and rest intervals can permit the “selection” of specific primary energy systems during training for specific athletic events (22, 109, 157). Few sports or physical activities require maximal sustained effort to exhaustion or near- exhaustion, such as competitive middle-distance sprints (400 m to 1,600 m). Most team sports and training activities produce metabolic profiles that are very similar to those of a series of high-intensity, constant- or near-constant-effort exercise bouts interspersed with rest periods, such as American football, basketball, and hockey. In this type of exercise, the required exercise intensity (work performed) that must be met during each exercise bout is much greater than that which can be sustained using aerobic energy sources alone. Increasing aerobic energy efficiency and capacity through primarily long, slow aerobic endurance training while simultaneously compromising or neglecting anaerobic energy efficiency and anaerobic capacity training is of little benefit to athletes in these sports (84, 111). For example, it would be of little benefit for a baseball player to run many long, slow miles during training rather than focusing on exercises that can concurrently improve anaerobic power and capacity using time efficient interval training. The use of appropriate exercise intensities and rest intervals (i.e., work-to-rest ratios) allows for the “selection” of specific primary energ

text: Interval Training Interval training is a method that emphasizes bioenergetic adaptations for a more efficient energy transfer within the metabolic pathways by using predetermined intervals of exercise and rest periods (i.e., work-to-rest ratios). Theoretically, properly spaced work-to-rest intervals allow more work to be completed at higher exercise intensities with the same or less fatigue than during continuous training at the same relative intensity. An early paper by Christensen and colleagues (31) compared the total running distance, average oxygen uptake, and blood lactate concentration during continuous running for 5 minutes and interval running totaling 30 minutes with 2:1, 1:1, and 1:2 work-to-rest ratios. Subjects were assigned a continuous running intensity (speed) that would result in fatigue within 5 minutes. At that fast pace during the continuous run, the subjects were able to complete 0.81 miles (1.3 km) before exhaustion. However, by using 2:1, 1:1, and 1:2 work-to- rest ratios and the same running intensity for a total duration of 30 minutes, the subjects were able to complete 4.14 miles (6.66 km), 3.11 miles (5 km), and 2.07 miles (3.33 km), respectively, all while working aerobic capacity in a manner similar to that in the continuous running condition. Therefore, much more distance can be accomplished at higher intensities with interval training; this concept has been established for over 45 years (31). A series of short-term (two-week) interval training s

text: to influence the efficacy of using interval training for metabolic adaptations. Few studies provide results that can be used to generate definitive guidelines for choosing specific work-to-rest ratios. One such study, however, reported aerobic and anaerobic metabolic variables, total work, and time-to-exhaustion differences between two different work-to-rest ratios in elite cyclists (119). The cyclists performed two intermittent protocols that included either a 40:20- second or a 30:30-second work-to-rest interval to exhaustion at a fixed work rate. The 40:20-second work-to-rest ratio resulted in significantly reduced total work and time to exhaustion while producing higher metabolic values (V̇ O2max, lactate concentration, ETC). In contrast, the 30:30-second work-to-rest ratio provided sustained but slightly lower metabolic values for a considerably longer period of time. Another study manipulated the work variable via intensity and duration of the work-to-rest ratios. Wakefield and Glaister (154) reported a greater amount of time above 95% V̇ O2max during running at an intensity of 105% of V̇ O2max versus 115% of V̇ O2max with a work duration of 30 seconds rather than 20 and 25 seconds (rest = 20 s). When one is determining the proper work-to-rest ratio for athletes, knowledge of the time intervals, intensity of work, and recovery periods for each of the energy systems is critical to maximizing the amount of work that can be accomplished for a given exercise intensity. High-intensity interval training typically incorporates either running- or cycling-based modes of exercise and is an efficient exercise regimen for eliciting cardiopulmonary (23) and metabolic and neuromuscular (24) adaptations. In fact, Buchheit and Laursen (23) stated that HIIT “is today considered one of the most effective forms of exercise for improving physical performance in athletes” (p. 314). The authors (24) indicate, however, that the intensities and durations of the active and recovery portions of each work bout are the most important factors to consider. To optimize HIIT training adaptations for athletes, HIIT sessions should maximize the time spent at or near V̇ O2max. In comparison to more general interval training, during HIIT specifically, the cumulative duration and intensity of the active portions of the work bouts should equate to several minutes above 90% of V̇ O2max (24). The benefits of a HIIT protocol designed to repeatedly elicit a very high percentage of V̇ O2max are primarily the result of the concurrent recruitment of large motor units and near-maximal cardiac output (6). Thus, HIIT provides a stimulus for both oxidative muscle fiber adaptation and myocardial hypertrophy. Additional HIIT adaptations include increases in V̇ O2max, proton buffering, glycogen content, anaerobic thresholds, time to exhaustion, and time-trial performance. text: Combining Training Modalities Some suggest that aerobic endurance training should be added to the training of anaerobic athletes to enhance recovery, because it is postulated that recovery relies primarily on aerobic mechanisms. In contrast, it is postulated that anaerobic resistance training should be added to aerobic endurance training because it can aid in preventing soft tissue injuries. However, when considering the metabolic specificity of training, thought should be given to whether the practitioner is programming combination training, cross-training, or concurrent training. These are related but distinctly different concepts when seeking to achieve metabolic specific training adaptations. Broadly, combination training refers to any training program that includes a mix of different types of exercises or activities. It does not necessarily imply a specific structure or timing, just that various exercise modalities are combined to achieve overall fitness improvements. For example, an 800-meter runner may include sessions of long, slow distance aerobic work alongside more event-specific distances and efforts. In contrast, cross-training deliberately involves incorporating different types of exercise with the same underlying metabolic adaptation profile (i.e., enhancing aerobic capacity), without overstressing the primary activity muscles (e.g., including rowing in a program for a runner), often with the aim of complementing the main sport performance. In comparison, concu

text: performance capabilities could be due to an interference in anaerobic energy production capabilities due to aerobic endurance training (153). Additionally, combined anaerobic and aerobic endurance training can reduce gains in muscle girth (36, 128), maximum strength (36, 76, 128), and speed- and power-related performance (44, 73). Even though the exact mechanism for this interference phenomenon is unknown and whether there is any threshold limit, it has been suggested that combination training and, more specifically, concurrent training may increase training volume to a level that may result in overtraining in comparison to aerobic and anaerobic training alone. Hickson and colleagues (82) provide evidence that concurrent training that includes progressive endurance running and cycling and heavy resistance training may produce a plateau effect and, ultimately, a decrease in strength gains. Specifically, it was reported that the concurrent training program of heavy resistance training combined with an endurance program provided significant improvements in squat strength during the first seven weeks of the program, followed by a two-week plateau and then a decrease in squat strength during the final two weeks of the program. The results provided evidence that continual strength gains may be inhibited with progressive concurrent endurance training such as running and cycling. Other mechanisms that have been suggested to hinder the development of strength when combined with endura

chapterTitle: Bioenergetics of Exercise and Training
text: was no reduction in V̇ O2max over the 12 weeks in runners who participated in resistance and plyometric training. Furthermore, the concurrent training improved performance measures such as maximal strength, peak running velocity, and 3-kilometer (1.7 miles) time trial compared to endurance training alone. Thus, in highly trained runners it appears that strength training can improve performance while not hindering metabolic parameters (V̇ O2max). Although oxidative metabolism is important for increased postexercise V̇ O2, lactate removal, and PCr restoration from heavy anaerobic exercise (e.g., resistance training and sprint training) (135), care must be used in prescribing aerobic endurance training for anaerobic sports. In this context, it should be noted that specific anaerobic training can stimulate increases in aerobic power and enhance markers of recovery (54). Thus, it appears that extensive aerobic endurance training to enhance recovery from anaerobic events is not necessary and may be counterproductive in most strength and power sports. 222

chapterTitle: Bioenergetics of Exercise and Training
text: Conclusion Training programs with increased productivity can be designed through an understanding of how energy is produced during various types of exercise and how energy production can be modified by specific training regimens. Which energy system is used to supply energy for muscular contraction and to perform work is determined primarily by the intensity of exercise and secondarily by the duration of exercise. Metabolic responses and training adaptations are largely regulated by exercise characteristics (e.g., intensity, duration, and recovery intervals). How these responses and adaptations occur following physical activity forms the basis for metabolic specificity of exercise and training. This principle allows for enhanced athletic performance through the implementation of improved training programs. text: hormonal benefits for health and performance. The endocrine system interacts with the nervous, immune, and musculoskeletal systems to create a network vital for health and athletic performance. Hormones regulate cellular activities, including muscle synthesis, recovery, and overall physiological well-being, by balancing anabolic and catabolic processes. Strength and conditioning professionals must understand the endocrine system to design training programs that enhance performance, recovery, and injury prevention. This knowledge allows for manipulating hormonal responses to exercise, supporting adaptations, and preventing overtraining. The system’s interplay has far-reaching effects on athletic performance and broader health concerns such as metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular health. 228

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Historical Perspective on Interest in the Endocrine System The significance of the endocrine system in strength and conditioning gained prominence with the rise of anabolic drug use in the 1940s and 1950s (7, 58). Fahey and colleagues were the first to investigate how resistance exercises affected endogenous hormone concentrations, specifically testosterone, across different sexes, ages, and training statuses, paving the way for ongoing research into hormonal responses to resistance exercise and training (23). In 1988, a series of reviews were published from the first symposium on the physiology of resistance exercise and training at the American College of Sports Medicine’s annual meeting. As part of that symposium set of papers, Kraemer (97) overviewed the sparse number of studies that had been done on the various hormonal responses to resistance exercise and training. This stimulated a line of hormonal research that continues today to explore further the mechanisms behind these acute responses and training adaptations (46). Now the body of literature consists of thousands of studies on this topic. 229

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Endocrine Terminology, Functions, and Mechanisms Grasping the effects of resistance exercise on hormonal responses requires a solid understanding of endocrine system terminology. While the learning curve is significant, becoming familiar with this language is vital for effectively translating scientific insights into practical training strategies. Hormones, the chemical messengers or signal molecules, are synthesized, often stored, and released into the blood by endocrine glands and certain other cells (figure 4.1, table 4.1). Neurons also synthesize, store, and secrete neurotransmitters, which may perform hormonal functions, a study known as neuroendocrinology—exploring interactions between the nervous and endocrine systems. Typically, endocrine glands are prompted to release hormones by a chemical signal received by receptors on the gland or by direct neural stimulation. For example, the adrenal medulla, the inner part of the adrenal gland, releases the hormone epinephrine in response to sympathetic neural stimulation from the brain (68, 74, 87, 129). Meanwhile, the outer layer of the adrenal cortex produces and releases cortisol when stimulated by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the pituitary gland (75, 78, 90). Once released, these hormones travel in the bloodstream to specific receptors located on the surface (for peptide hormones) or inside the target tissue cells (for steroid and thyroid hormones) (4, 5, 6, 8, 22, 39), facilitating a targeted and efficient resp

text: Understanding Signaling Concepts Different types of workouts trigger specific, complex cellular endocrine signaling processes, thus highlighting the importance of the selection for each of the five acute program variables and then the total amount of work performed in a workout (70) for the endocrine response. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) primarily directs protein synthesis, but the regulation and expression of DNA affect many other cellular functions and the synthesis of various molecules essential for life. Hormonal signaling processes begin when glands release hormones during, or in anticipation of, a resistance exercise workout. These hormones then bind to specific receptors in muscle cells and other cells. This binding initiates a cascade of responses, generally resulting in altered cellular metabolism or DNA transcription modulation, which can affect protein synthesis. It is essential to know that every cell and many subcellular organelles have genomic and non-genomic receptors, and this is where the hormone signals its message to make proteins. Here is a simplified breakdown of the signaling process for skeletal muscle: 1. Stimulating the muscle. Resistance exercise activates muscles, prompting a hormonal response. 2. Hormonal response. Hormones are released and travel to muscle cells. 3. Hormone–receptor interaction. Hormones bind to specific receptors in the cell membrane of muscle cells (peptide hormones) or inside the muscle cells (steroid hormones), signaling the n

Regular training uses this muscle development and repair mechanism, which is essential for developing lean muscle mass and athletic performance. 235

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Functions of the Endocrine System in Resistance Exercise and Training The major functions of the endocrine system can be classified into the following key hormonal actions: Anabolic responses (to build up). Hormones such as testosterone, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and growth hormone play critical roles in muscle growth and repair. Permissive actions (to allow). Hormones such as insulin and thyroid hormones enable critical metabolic and physiological activities by enhancing nutrient uptake and promoting essential chemical reactions in muscles, thereby supporting muscle growth and overall metabolic functions. Catabolic processes (to break down). For example, cortisol helps manage energy during stress but can hinder muscle growth if not properly managed through adequate rest and recovery. This emphasizes the balance needed in training regimens. Types of Hormonal Release Mechanisms Hormones are typically released into the bloodstream via the classic endocrine pathway after gland stimulation. Hormones can also operate through intracrine, autocrine, and paracrine mechanisms, which do not rely on the bloodstream. Intracrine and autocrine actions involve hormones either binding to internal receptors within their producing cell or being released to bind to surface receptors on the same cell. An example of this is insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF- 1) and its splice variant mechano growth factor (MGF), which muscle fibers produce in response to mechanical stress or interacti

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Binding Proteins Hormones are often transported in the blood by various binding proteins (4, 6), which serve as a temporary storage location and protect the hormones from degradation, thereby extending their lifetime in the body (called the half-life). It is important to note that hormones typically exert their effects only when they are released, and thus are “free,” from these proteins. However, some binding proteins, such as sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG), which binds testosterone and estrogen, can initiate cellular responses themselves by activating pathways, including the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) pathway (29). These interactions are crucial for understanding endocrine regulation and continue as an area of study (101). Target Cells and Tissues Hormones influence a wide array of cells by interacting with receptors throughout the body (1, 2, 57, 59, 62, 63). While our focus is on skeletal muscle tissue, it is important to recognize that resistance exercise–induced hormone release also affects bone, other connective tissues, the kidneys, the liver, immune cells, and neural tissues, including the brain. Interestingly, not only do these target cells in the different tissues adapt to the exercise stress, but their receptors also gain a positive adaptive effect with training. 237

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Importance of Recruitment of Muscle Tissue Henneman’s size principle shows that as the resistance increases (i.e., heavier loads), more and larger muscle fibers are recruited to meet the increased force demand. This principle outlines the recruitment order of motor units—from smaller, slow-twitch fiber motor units to larger, fast-twitch fiber motor units. The heavier the resistance, the greater the number and size of motor units recruited in a muscle to produce force (77). While anabolic and catabolic hormones maintain homeostatic balance by interacting with all cells, stress causes hormonal changes that reflect the body’s need to meet new metabolic demands and recovery needs. However, only recruited motor units adapt to the training stimulus and are affected by the endocrine system’s increase in anabolic hormones, likely due to the increased activation of more receptors. Interestingly, and of importance, increased catabolic hormone responses to stress or distress can affect all tissues even if not recruited for exercise performance. A catabolic state is highly detrimental for an athlete, especially when cortisol levels remain chronically elevated. Combined with the presence of reactive oxygen species (free radicals) generated by the body’s inflammatory response, this condition significantly impairs recovery and hampers performance (77). 238

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Muscle as the Target for Hormone Interactions Resistance exercise and training leads to muscle remodeling through a complex network of metabolic and cellular signals. This process involves muscle fiber damage, an inflammatory response, and the breakdown of damaged proteins, ultimately synthesizing new proteins integrated into muscle structures. The inflammatory phase, which involves the immune system, including T and B cells, is significantly influenced by hormonal activity, emphasizing the role of neuroendocrine immunology in understanding how the nervous, endocrine, and immune systems interact in muscle adaptation (77). Hormones regulate the balance between protein synthesis and degradation, playing a critical role in muscle adaptation after resistance exercise. They stimulate the production of contractile proteins like actin and myosin, as well as structural proteins such as titin, which are essential for muscle function. Anabolic hormones, including insulin, insulin-like growth factors (IGFs), testosterone, and GH, are particularly vital because they drive tissue growth and counteract the effects of catabolic hormones like cortisol and progesterone, which can lead to protein degradation. Furthermore, hormones like thyroid hormones play a supportive, permissive role, facilitating the actions of other hormones. The potentially negative effects of cortisol in recovery, such as inhibiting immune cell activity and disrupting pathways like the Akt/mechanistic target of rapamyci

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Role of Receptors in Mediating Hormonal Changes The effectiveness of hormonal signals depends entirely on the presence of hormone-specific receptors on or in the target cells. This ensures that each hormone only affects its intended cells and tissues (those that express the specific receptors). Such specificity is crucial for maintaining precise hormonal regulation within the body. Since many hormones cannot directly cross the cell membrane, they rely on binding to membrane receptors that cause secondary messengers to transmit signals internally, including reaching the DNA in the cell’s nuclei. These receptors, located either in the cell membrane for polypeptide hormones or within the cytosol for steroid and thyroid hormones, allow various cells, from muscle fibers to immune and brain cells, to respond to hormonal signals. A fundamental principle in endocrinology, often described through the lock-and-key model (24), explains how a hormone (the key) must precisely match a receptor (the lock) to trigger a response (figure 4.2). However, this model oversimplifies the complexity of hormone–receptor interactions. For example, cross-reactivity allows receptors to engage with hormones other than their primary matches, and allosteric binding can modify how a receptor responds to its primary hormone (such as blocking binding to the receptor and thus signaling). Additionally, receptors might have allosteric sites where nonhormonal substances can enhance or reduce the hormonal response.

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Adaptation Limits and Receptor Sensitivity When a muscle fiber has reached its capacity for protein incorporation, or when a chronically elevated concentration of a hormone causes overstimulation, receptors may become desensitized or unresponsive—a condition known as receptor downregulation; a classic example of this phenomenon is insulin resistance, which can be caused by chronically elevated circulating insulin concentrations. The reduced signal from the hormone following overstimulation signifies a reduced ability of the hormone to interact with its receptor or downregulation of the number of receptors, which can effectively stop further cellular responses and adaptations (37, 122). As such, receptors can adjust their affinity for binding, and the number of available receptors can vary. These changes affect cellular adaptation as significantly, if not more, as changes in hormone concentrations. For example, heavy resistance overtraining can lead to a downregulation of beta-2 receptors, affecting their interaction with epinephrine and reducing muscle contractile force (37). Exploring how receptor characteristics alter in response to training and affect muscle adaptation is key to understanding the complex interactions between hormones and exercise. 241

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Categories of Hormones Hormones can be classified into three main categories based on their molecular structure: steroid, peptide (or polypeptide), and amine hormones. Steroid Hormone Interactions Steroid hormones, including cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol produced by the adrenal cortex and/or gonads, can diffuse across cell membranes due to their lipophilic (fat-soluble) nature. They engage with specific receptors inside the cell to form a hormone– receptor complex (H-RC). This complex undergoes a conformational change, activates, and pairs with another H-RC. It then moves to the nucleus, interacts with the DNA, and promotes the transcription process for specific proteins by “unzipping” DNA and identifying regulatory elements of the targeted gene (18, 117). The resulting mRNA is then translated by ribosomes in the sarcoplasm into the intended proteins. The steroid hormone–induced protein synthesis process is depicted in figure 4.3. Testosterone’s influence on muscle cells encompasses more than its genomic effects. In addition to the primary nuclear receptor, a membrane receptor for testosterone has also been described in detail (128). Such a membrane receptor allows testosterone to affect the cell through rapid and nongenomic interactions (i.e., those that do not involve DNA transcription in the nuclei) within various other cellular compartments. These interactions play a crucial role in muscle adaptation, recovery, and growth by facilitating the production of essentia

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: comprehensive grasp of steroid hormones’ impact on muscle biology (91). Polypeptide Hormone Interactions Polypeptide hormones are composed of chains of amino acids and include hormones such as GH and insulin. Due to their non-lipophilic nature, polypeptide hormones cannot cross the cell membrane, and, therefore, their effects are mediated by secondary messengers within the cell. When these hormones bind to their membrane receptor, they cause a conformational change that allows the receptor to transmit the hormonal signal inside the cell. This transmission initiates a cascade of signaling events that, among others, can affect metabolic activities, influence DNA transcription, or kick-start mRNA translation at the ribosome. For example, insulin activates a pathway that results in glucose transporters (specifically GLUT4) migrating from the cytosol to the cell membrane, enhancing the cell’s uptake of glucose (45). This is crucial for managing blood glucose levels and cellular substrate availability for ATP production. 244

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Amine Hormone Interactions Amine hormones are indeed synthesized from amino acids, including those derived from tyrosine (such as epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine) and tryptophan (such as serotonin), and primarily exert their effects by binding to membrane receptors. These hormones typically act through secondary messenger systems, similar to polypeptide hormones. For example, epinephrine and norepinephrine interact with G protein-coupled receptors to initiate signaling cascades involving cAMP or other secondary messengers. 247

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Training-Mediated Hormonal Responses and Mechanisms Electrical, chemical, and hormonal signals are transmitted from the brain, active muscles, and other tissues to various endocrine glands, preparing the body’s physiological systems for the demands of the workout (20, 23, 28, 32, 35, 49, 75, 80, 81). Heavy resistance training over months to years significantly enhances musculature size, strength, and power, mediated partly through adaptive hormonal responses (47, 50, 70, 73, 76, 88, 95). These adaptations arise from increased levels of anabolic hormones such as testosterone, growth hormone, and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF- 1) that acutely rise during exercise and remain elevated after exercise. Additionally, resistance exercise leads to an upregulation of hormone receptors in muscle tissues, which increases the muscle’s sensitivity to these hormones and enhances protein synthesis and muscle hypertrophy. The structural changes in muscle and neural adaptations contribute to increased strength and power, including improvements in the rate of force production and alterations in muscle fiber recruitment patterns. Resistance training also positively affects bone density and the strength of connective tissues, supporting increased muscular strength and overall physical performance. One critical pathway in muscle protein synthesis activated by resistance training is the mammalian target of the rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, which is crucial for muscle growth. These complex interacti

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Interpreting Hormonal Changes in Peripheral Blood Understanding exercise effects on the body goes beyond physical observations; it includes reading studies that monitor biochemical changes such as hormone fluctuations in blood, muscle, and surrounding fluids (114). These changes provide insights into the body’s stress response and adaptation to exercise. However, interpreting these changes can be complex, because hormone levels in the blood are just one aspect of a broader hormonal response that also includes neural and nutritional factors such as being fasted or not and if proteins and carbohydrates are ingested around a workout. Increases in blood hormone levels generally indicate enhanced release from endocrine glands, potentially boosting hormone–receptor interactions in target tissues. Yet the actual impact depends on the state and quantity of the receptors—whether they are primed to bind hormones and initiate crucial processes involved in protein synthesis, including activating pathways such as mTOR (11, 13, 14, 66). Conversely, decreases in hormone levels might suggest increased tissue uptake, faster hormone breakdown, or reduced secretion. Several physiological factors, including circadian rhythms, fluid volume changes, tissue clearance rates, venous pooling, and interactions with binding proteins, also influence observed circulating hormone concentrations after exercise. These factors determine the hormone’s efficacy in interacting with receptors and triggering cellu

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: maximal amounts of motor units and enhance receptor binding. However, such workouts’ relatively low metabolic demands typically result in only modest, if any, increases in blood concentrations of testosterone, IGF-1, and growth hormone. Nevertheless, slight hormonal changes, combined with paracrine and autocrine signaling, are generally sufficient to effectively signal via receptors and other molecular pathways within tissues in the neuromuscular system to stimulate growth and repair. Conversely, a workout that involves 8RM to 10RM resistances, short rest periods of 1 to 2 minutes, and a higher volume of work produces greater metabolic demands on the body. The metabolic stress is evidenced by significant increases in blood lactate and a surge in both anabolic and catabolic hormones. These hormonal changes signal skeletal muscle receptors effectively, even with the recruitment of fewer motor units using lighter resistances. Periodization strategies that incorporate a range of different resistances over time ensure effective muscle activation across various workout styles, where hormones help mediate changes. Such workout design variations reflect the complex nature of exercise-induced hormonal activation and its contribution to adaptive changes in the body. Hormone responses in the blood are tightly linked to the characteristics of the resistance exercise protocol. 251

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Adaptations in the Endocrine System From Resistance Training Resistance training affects muscles and connective tissues and significantly affects the other physiological systems, including the endocrine system. This type of training also trains the endocrine glands, with the gland’s involvement dependent on the demands of the motor units activated during exercise. The endocrine system’s adaptations to resistance training include changes in the following: Hormone synthesis and storage Hormone transport via binding proteins Clearance and degradation rates of hormones Fluid shifts from blood to tissues during exercise Hormone–receptor binding affinity The number of tissue receptors Glandular cell changes The intensity of signals sent to cell nuclei by hormone– receptor complexes Cellular interactions influencing muscle protein production Hormones are secreted to maintain homeostasis, regulating physiological functions during both the acute stress of a workout and chronic stress from long-term training, which activates these homeostatic mechanisms (17, 33, 34, 41, 49, 56, 125, 126, 130). These adaptations might lead to subtle changes in resting hormone levels, demonstrating the dynamic responsiveness of the endocrine system to physical training. 252

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Primary Anabolic Hormones in Muscle Development Key anabolic hormones that drive muscle tissue growth and remodeling include testosterone, growth hormone, and insulin-like growth factors (IGFs), with additional roles played by insulin and thyroid hormones (25, 26, 27, 28, 38, 91). Testosterone’s Role in Muscle Adaptation Testosterone, the primary androgen affecting skeletal muscle, and dihydrotestosterone, which acts mainly on sex-linked tissues, play crucial roles in the body. While circulating testosterone levels indicate anabolic activity, the actual binding of testosterone to its receptor is vital for stimulating muscle growth. Binding to androgen genomic and non-genomic receptors activates various signaling pathways that enhance gene expression for muscle hypertrophy and suppress those involved in protein degradation. Therefore, increased testosterone levels due to increased motor unit activation indicate metabolic demands beyond homeostatic conditions and are associated with enhanced receptor binding (124, 133). Testosterone also indirectly affects muscle growth by promoting the release of growth hormone from the pituitary, which influences muscle protein synthesis. This hormone’s relationship with growth hormone is either permissive or synergistic in promoting protein synthesis (103). Furthermore, testosterone affects the nervous system by interacting with neuron receptors, altering neurotransmitter amounts, and influencing structural protein changes within muscle cell

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: bind to intracellular androgen receptors, directly influencing DNA transcription. Testosterone also binds to membrane receptors, enabling rapid intracellular effects like calcium release (21, 131). Understanding the varied impacts of testosterone and its interaction with exercise conditions reveals how differential forces on cell membranes during resistance training or feedback mechanisms to the brain can alter cellular actions and receptor interactions (18). Despite increases in testosterone concentrations during high- intensity aerobic endurance exercise, significant hypertrophy does not typically occur. The lack of hypertrophy may be due to oxidative stress, which can lead to reduced type I muscle fiber size to optimize oxygen transport distances to mitochondria. High-intensity endurance training, including intervals performed alone, has been shown to lead to decreases in type I muscle fibers (88). Influence of Sex Hormones Testosterone, while primarily recognized as a male sex hormone, also plays a significant role in women, who naturally have only about 5% to 10% of the circulating testosterone levels found in men due to the absence of testes. Research on testosterone responses in women following resistance exercise has yielded mixed results. Most studies have not shown a notable acute increase in total testosterone after workouts; if increases are observed, they are generally small (15, 23, 51, 56, 81, 134). However, some studies note these increases specifically in fre

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: While women have lower baseline testosterone levels, exercise can still influence their hormone levels. Moreover, individual variations exist among women, with some producing higher concentrations of adrenal androgens. A study comparing active women with inactive controls found differences in baseline testosterone levels, indicating that regular exercise might influence these levels (15). Despite these findings, other research has not consistently demonstrated changes in serum testosterone concentrations in women with training (23, 51, 56, 81, 134), highlighting the complexity of hormonal responses to resistance exercise in women. While testosterone levels in women are lower, the dynamic interaction between testosterone, SHBG, DHT, and androgen receptors facilitates significant responses to resistance exercise. These interactions can include muscle mass and strength increases, essential for physical health and metabolic function. The response of androgen receptors to even small increases in testosterone and the compensatory role of other androgens like DHT emphasize the complex but critical nature of androgens in female physiology and resistance exercise. An interplay between free and total testosterone is critical for optimizing exercise outcomes. Free testosterone, which represents only 0.5% to 2% of total testosterone, is vital for direct interaction with muscle tissues. Younger men generally exhibit higher postexercise increases in free testosterone compared to older men,

text: Exercise-Induced Responses Men’s testosterone levels are generally highest in the morning and gradually decrease throughout the day. However, this does not mean that morning workouts are more effective than afternoon workouts. The effectiveness of exercise depends more on the availability of hormone receptors in both men and women, which is not directly linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. Exercise can trigger increases any time, with the overall response related to intensity, volume, and rest periods between sets (17, 23, 44, 48, 81, 134). However, the magnitude of the testosterone’s response is, as with all hormones, dependent on where blood is sampled in the hormone’s circadian cycle (e.g., testosterone is higher in the morning than in the late afternoon), and thus, it is important to understand where a measure of a hormone was made and if the study has a resting control for the time of day to determine the magnitude above resting levels accurately. Its circadian cycle is important for the interpretation of the results of a study. Most studies have used the morning time frames. Testosterone dynamics in young males, particularly those under 18, are influenced significantly by puberty, affecting their responses to exercise. Prepubescent boys produce minimal testosterone, which limits exercise-induced hypertrophy. Adolescent males can enhance serum testosterone levels through exercises that engage large muscle groups like squats and deadlifts, using heavy resistance of 85%

Such data demonstrate that the improvements were more likely driven by neural factors augmented by hormonal changes rather than significant muscle growth. Over time, factors such as training duration and experience play critical roles in hormonal adjustments. For instance, a notable study by Häkkinen and colleagues (49) observed small but significant increases in resting serum testosterone levels over two years among elite weightlifters, alongside increases in follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone, which are crucial in regulating testosterone production. Testosterone also supports the development of the nervous system and enhances neural adaptations necessary for strength gains, particularly in highly trained athletes (51, 52). Additionally, training sessions that acutely elevate testosterone levels have been linked to more remarkable resistance training ad

Yet the androgen receptors in trained women rapidly respond to the available testosterone after exercise (111, 133). Nutritional strategies, particularly consuming proteins and carbohydrates before a workout, have been shown to upregulate skeletal muscle androgen receptor content, emphasizing the importance of preworkout nutrition (93). While most exercise studies have evaluated fasted states, interestingly, as pre- and post-protein and carbohydrate supplementation are used, a reduction in the testosterone values is observed, most likely due to the greater uptake by the muscle for use. 259

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Growth Hormone Growth hormone (GH) is produced in the pituitary gland by somatotroph cells, divided into two types based on their secretion patterns and the forms of GH. Band 1 somatotrophs generate the smaller, newly synthesized 22 kD molecular weight isoform of GH, a 191 amino acid polypeptide. Conversely, band 2 somatotrophs produce aggregates of these smaller isoforms (e.g., two 22 kD units combining to form a 44 kD molecule), which are considered older and are potential GH storage forms (61). These aggregates can be released into the bloodstream, interacting with specific tissue receptors. For instance, aggregated GH binds to receptors in the tibial growth plate to stimulate bone growth. These different molecular weight variants target various tissues, including bone, muscle, liver, and immune cells, influencing glucose use, protein synthesis, lipolysis, collagen synthesis, and enhancing immune cell function. The presence of different GH isoforms in the blood can only be distinguished through various assays, with most studies focusing on the smaller 22 kD isoform using immunoassays. This focus has shaped much of our current understanding of GH’s role and function in the body, but the aggregated forms of GH might have greater biological potency and importance (61, 91). Figure 4.6 outlines the basic feedback mechanisms regulating the production of GH isoforms, highlighting the complex control the pituitary gland exercises over GH secretion. 260

text: FIGURE 4.6 Diagram of the basic growth hormone cybernetics and interactions. Remember that GH will be secreted from two different types (I and II) of anterior pituitary somatotrophs, each releasing different molecular weight isoforms. Resistance exercise increases the 22 kD isoform in both men and women. It is sensitive to the amount of total work performed and the rest period duration used because these affect the demands on the glycolytic energy system and H+ ion production; drops in pH are a key stimulator of 22 GH release (41, 54). Women have been shown to have higher resting values of the 22 kD isoform of GH than men in the early follicular phase of the menstrual cycle (81). GH levels in women tend to be higher during the menstrual cycle’s follicular phase than in the luteal phase. During the follicular phase, which occurs from the beginning of menstruation until ovulation, estrogen levels rise, and this hormonal environment is associated with increased GH secretion. While GH is present throughout the entire cycle, its secretion is generally more pronounced during this phase due to the influence of estrogen, which stimulates GH production. Additionally, oral contraceptive use can influence women’s acute GH response to exercise (84). Specifically, women who used oral contraceptives exhibited a blunted or reduced GH 261

text: response compared to those not using oral contraceptives. Figure 4.7 (79, 83) demonstrates the response patterns of GH to low- and high-volume exercise workouts in which exercise response patterns to different workouts are similar in men and women. The body’s response to GH varies with resistance exercise, and understanding these responses is crucial for optimizing training outcomes. Initially observed in studies from the late 1970s to early 1990s, resistance training can acutely elevate GH levels in the blood, particularly through exercises involving large muscle groups and high intensity (100, 123, 130). Research has shown that the type of workout—especially the intensity, volume, and rest periods— significantly affects acute GH responses (75, 83). Short rest periods combined with moderate resistance tend to produce higher GH spikes compared to longer rest periods. While resting concentrations are not typically affected by training, the ability to do more total work or tolerate greater increases in H+ ions and resultant pH decreases allows for greater peak GH concentrations in recovery. While general responses are similar to those in men, subtle differences exist due to factors such as the menstrual cycle and hormonal contraception, affecting GH levels and their response to exercise. Yet the impact on training appears minimal (79, 81, 85). Resistance training affects the various molecular or aggregate forms of GH, with evidence showing that high-intensity workouts lead to i

text: Insulin-Like Growth Factors and Binding Proteins IGFs, primarily IGF-1 and IGF-2, are small polypeptides crucial for various anabolic processes in the body, including cellular growth, development, and metabolism. These growth factors are structurally similar to insulin and originate from larger precursor molecules modified posttranslationally to become active. IGF-1, the most researched, is predominantly synthesized in the liver in response to stimulation by 22 kD GH (16, 22, 27, 91). Besides GH, IGF synthesis is also influenced by thyroid hormones and testosterone (137, 138, 139, 140). IGFs perform several functions, including enhancing protein synthesis, increasing amino acid transport across cell membranes, and stimulating growth in tissues such as muscle and bone. In the bloodstream, IGFs are mostly bound to proteins, with only about 2% in the free (unbound) form; same as for other hormones, the binding proteins regulate IGF activity and availability. These binding proteins are critical in modulating the growth-promoting actions of the IGFs (91). Additionally, IGFs stimulate the secretion of their binding proteins within muscle cells, influencing cellular sensitivity to IGFs (105). IGF binding proteins (IGFBPs) are a group of proteins that regulate the bioavailability and activity of IGFs. There are six main types of IGFBPs (IGFBP-1 to IGFBP-6) found in humans, each with distinct binding affinities, tissue distributions, and biological functions. IGFBPs can inhibit or enh

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: IGF Responses to Exercise The role of IGFs extends to exercise response, where resistance exercise particularly influences their production and activity. Mechanical stress from resistance exercise triggers muscle fibers to produce IGF-1 locally, which then acts to stimulate muscle growth and repair. This local production is often more critical than the circulating levels of IGF-1, which may not consistently change with resistance exercise (109, 113). The response of IGF-1 to heavy resistance exercise can vary, influenced by the initial levels of IGF-1 before training and the response of GH. Studies indicate that lower baseline IGF-1 levels typically lead to increases after exercise, whereas higher baseline levels may result in no change or even decreases (W.J. Kraemer, unpublished data). Nutritional status, including caloric intake and restriction, also significantly modulates resting and exercise-induced IGF-1 concentrations (55, 92). In women, resistance training has increased total IGF-1 levels and decreased IGF-binding protein-1 during workouts, suggesting exercise-specific adaptations in the IGF system (43). The IGF superfamily’s complex response patterns to training involve mechanisms such as IGF type, release, transport, and receptor interactions, along with interactions with other anabolic hormones targeting similar outcomes such as protein synthesis. However, highly trained men and women both showed increases in IGF-1 concentrations, but women demonstrated values hig

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Training Adaptations and IGF and Binding Proteins The full scope of training-induced IGF-1 adaptations across different tissues continues to be a significant area for research (91, 112). Training adaptations from resistance exercise influence IGF levels and their interactions at the cellular level. Resistance training enhances the activation and expression of IGF-1 receptors, boosting the signaling pathways essential for cell growth and survival. However, the full scope of how different training regimens affect IGF levels, particularly the balance between local (muscle) and systemic (circulating) IGF, remains a rich area for research. As noted in a study by Hatfield and colleagues, in highly resistance-trained men and women (i.e., squat 1RM: 2.1 ± 0.4 and 1.7 ± 0.6 × body mass, respectively), training affects the resting and acute responses of IGF-1 and IGFBPs (54). Thus, IGF-1 and binding proteins have training-related adaptations in their response patterns for production, release, binding, and interactions with cellular targets (42, 54, 91, 112, 121). Continued research is needed to better understand the complex dynamics of IGFs in response to resistance training, including the specific effects of exercise on different forms of IGF and their binding proteins. This research will help optimize training strategies and potentially inform therapeutic interventions targeting muscle health and performance (102, 106). 266

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Adrenal Gland, Cortisol, and Its Role in Resistance Exercise The adrenal gland is integral to the body’s adaptation to stress, particularly during and after exercise. Structurally, it consists of two main components: the medulla and the cortex, each responding to stress in distinct ways. The adrenal medulla, the inner core of the gland, is directly stimulated by the autonomic nervous system during acute stress. It rapidly secretes catecholamines such as epinephrine and norepinephrine, alongside dopamine and specific enkephalin- containing polypeptides like peptide F, which are implicated in immediate stress responses and immune enhancement (129). The adrenal cortex is stimulated by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary gland to produce and release cortisol. Cortisol has critical roles in modulating inflammation and managing metabolic responses to stress. As such, cortisol is regulated on a systemic level by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and locally within tissues by enzymes such as 11β-hydroxy- steroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) to maintain glucocorticoid balance (25, 27, 99). Cortisol is crucial for sustaining energy during prolonged stress by facilitating glucose availability through selective glucose sparing and mobilization, gluconeogenesis, and fat and protein catabolism. However, prolonged elevation of cortisol levels—if not returned to baseline within 24 hours—can adversely affect the body, because cortisol in this context is consi

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: phases, vital for post-exercise muscle remodeling and overall recovery (30). Cortisol is critical in energy balance, immune regulation, and vascular integrity within skeletal muscle. It aids in increasing energy availability and modulating immune activity during exercise. After exercise, cortisol helps reduce inflammation and muscle damage, but sensitivity to cortisol decreases within 24 hours to protect against prolonged exposure. Athletes show a refined capability to convert cortisol to cortisone, protecting tissues during exercise stress. However, overtraining can impair this conversion process, potentially inhibiting anabolic activities like muscle growth by reducing IGF-I synthesis (27, 30, 91). Despite its reputation as a catabolic hormone, cortisol is essential for carbohydrate metabolism, particularly when muscle glycogen stores are low (25, 27, 99). It plays a role in converting amino acids to carbohydrates, increasing proteolytic enzymes, inhibiting protein synthesis, and suppressing glycogenesis and immune function (30, 91). Cortisol levels increase in response to resistance training, particularly with high intensity or volume involving large muscle masses. The acute hormonal response prepares the body for future physical demands and aids recovery. The resistance exercise cortisol response differs some between men and women. Men generally experience higher increases in cortisol from certain types of training protocols, such as high-volume workouts, whereas women ra

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: detrimental, acute increases assist in muscle remodeling by helping clear damaged proteins. Adaptations to resistance training also include enhanced cortisol conversion efficiency, reflecting a physiological adaptation to regular, intense exercise (75, 127). Resistance exercise protocols using high volume, large muscle groups, and short rest periods increase serum cortisol values (88). Though chronic high concentrations of cortisol may have adverse catabolic effects, acute increases still contribute to remodeling muscle tissue and maintaining blood glucose. 269

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Catecholamines and Their Role in Resistance Exercise and Training Catecholamines, primarily epinephrine but also including norepinephrine and dopamine, are secreted by the adrenal medulla and play a crucial role in enhancing strength and power during resistance training. These hormones facilitate the fight-or-flight response by acting as central motor stimulators and peripheral vascular dilators, enhancing enzyme activity and calcium release in muscles (89). Notably, higher catecholamine release before and during intense resistance sessions has been linked to sustained force output, emphasizing their importance in maintaining performance (32). Physiological Functions of Catecholamines Catecholamines enhance resistance training outcomes by doing the following: Increasing force production through central mechanisms and boosting metabolic enzyme activity Accelerating muscle contraction rates Raising blood pressure Enhancing energy availability and muscle blood flow through vasodilation Augmenting the secretion rates of other anabolic hormones such as testosterone Acute and Training-Induced Responses The acute response to high-intensity, short-rest resistance exercises typical in bodybuilding—characterized by increased levels of norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine during the session and brief recovery periods—illustrates catecholamines’ role in meeting the physical demands of such protocols (86). Epinephrine levels also correlate with lactate concentrations, reflecting its

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: metabolic stress responses. Importantly, adrenal responses to stress are critical until the stressor is removed, with endogenous opioid peptides like proenkephalins from the adrenal medulla playing roles in immune system modulation crucial for recovery (129). Continuous high stress without varied training can lead to delayed recovery and, eventually, adrenal exhaustion, reducing the adrenal medulla’s ability to secrete catecholamines effectively. Training Adaptations and Long-Term Impacts Heavy resistance training enhances an athlete’s capacity to secrete more epinephrine during maximal efforts (87). Consistent training may decrease epinephrine responses to single sessions, such as a bench press workout (44). This adaptation suggests that regular training can modulate catecholamine responses, reducing their surge during familiar tasks to maintain a more balanced hormonal environment conducive to ongoing strength gains and recovery. Understanding the role of catecholamines in resistance training helps in designing programs that optimize hormonal responses to enhance strength, hypertrophy, and overall athletic performance. Catecholamines’ ability to interact with other hormones underscores their pivotal position in the endocrine response to resistance exercise, highlighting the importance of managing exercise intensity, volume, and recovery to maximize beneficial hormonal interactions. Training protocols must be varied to allow the adrenal gland to engage in recovery processes

text: How Can Athletes Manipulate the Endocrine System With Resistance Exercise? General Concepts The more muscle fibers recruited for an exercise, the greater the extent of the potential remodeling process in the whole muscle. Only muscle fibers activated by resistance training are subject to adaptation, including hormonal adaptations to stress. To Increase Serum Testosterone Concentrations Serum testosterone concentrations have been shown to increase acutely by using these methods independently or in various combinations: Large muscle group exercises (e.g., deadlift, power clean, squat) Heavy resistance (85% to 95% 1RM) Moderate to high volume of exercise, achieved with multiple sets or multiple exercises Short rest intervals (30-60 s) To Increase 22 kD Growth Hormone Concentrations Growth hormone levels have been shown to increase acutely with use of either of these methods or both in combination: Use workouts with higher lactate concentrations and associated acid–base disruptions; that is, use high intensity (10RM, or heavy resistance) with three sets of each exercise (high total work) and short (1 min) rest periods. Supplement diet with carbohydrates and protein before and after workouts. To Optimize Responses of Adrenal Hormones Use high volume, large muscle groups, and short rest periods to expose the body to adrenergic stress. Be careful to vary the training protocol and the rest period length from short to long over time. Provide days of complete rest, and use lower-volume

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Other Hormonal Considerations in Resistance Training A variety of hormones contribute to normal bodily functions and adaptively respond to resistance training, including insulin, thyroid hormones, and beta-endorphin. These hormones play roles in growth, repair, pain relief, and managing exercise stress, though research on their specific adaptations to resistance training is limited (15, 26, 27, 28, 51, 64, 71, 75, 82, 98). For healthy individuals, significant chronic changes in the resting concentrations of insulin and thyroid hormones are generally not observed due to tight homeostatic control. However, resistance training has been noted to improve insulin sensitivity, possibly reflecting only the acute effects of recent exercise sessions (10). Thyroid Hormones Thyroid hormones, particularly triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4), play a significant role in both acute and chronic responses to resistance exercise and training. Immediately following resistance exercise, T3 levels generally remain unchanged, while T4 levels might spike briefly and then decrease during subsequent rest periods (65, 107). This acute response suggests a temporary adjustment to meet the immediate metabolic demands of exercise. In the context of long-term resistance training, transient reductions in T3 and T4 levels can occur, which typically normalize after several months (3, 116). These fluctuations indicate an initial adaptation phase in which the thyroid axis adjusts to the increased demands of

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Specifically, T3 enhances protein synthesis by increasing the transcription of genes involved in muscle hypertrophy and repair. Additionally, T4’s conversion to T3 in peripheral tissues ensures a steady supply of active hormones to meet ongoing metabolic needs. Thyroid hormones also help regulate lipolysis and glucose metabolism, which are essential for providing the necessary energy substrates during and after resistance exercise. By modulating these processes, thyroid hormones help maintain energy balance and facilitate recovery. Furthermore, thyroid hormones interact with other endocrine responses during resistance training. For example, they can enhance the action of GH and IGF-1, both of which are vital for muscle growth and repair. This synergistic effect amplifies the overall anabolic environment, promoting more effective muscle adaptation and strength gains. Thus, thyroid hormones are integral to immediate and long-term resistance exercise adaptations. They ensure metabolic homeostasis, support energy production, enhance protein synthesis, and interact with other hormones to facilitate muscle growth and repair. Understanding their role highlights the complex hormonal interplay required for effective training adaptations and overall metabolic regulation. Insulin The insulin response to resistance exercise and training is crucial to metabolic regulation and muscle adaptation. Physiologically, resistance exercise induces an acute increase in insulin sensitivity, which en

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: control and reduced risk of type 2 diabetes (96, 107). Furthermore, the increased muscle mass from long-term resistance training enhances basal metabolic rate and glucose disposal, stabilizing insulin levels and improving metabolic efficiency (115, 119). Thus, the insulin response to resistance exercise supports immediate energy needs and recovery after exercise and contributes to long- term metabolic health and disease prevention. 276

chapterTitle: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training
text: Conclusion The endocrine system’s interaction with the nervous, immune, and musculoskeletal systems forms a complex network crucial for optimizing health and athletic performance. Hormones coordinate a wide range of cellular activities, influencing muscle synthesis, recovery, and overall physiological well-being. The dynamic balance between anabolic hormones, which promote muscle growth, and catabolic hormones, responsible for muscle breakdown and energy mobilization is vital for responding effectively to resistance training. Strength and conditioning professionals need a deep understanding of the endocrine system’s functions to design effective training programs that maximize performance and minimize injury risks. This knowledge enables the manipulation of hormonal responses to both acute exercise and chronic training adaptations, enhancing recovery and preventing overtraining. The subtle interplay among various bodily systems and hormones has significant implications beyond athletic performance, affecting conditions such as metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular health. By leveraging insights from the endocrine system, coaches and athletes can achieve peak performance and support long-term health. This overview highlights the sophisticated yet orderly system that mediates the body’s responses to resistance exercise, emphasizing the critical role of the endocrine system in sport science and overall health management.
