The most significant change in cardiovascular function with long- term (6-12 months) aerobic endurance training is the increase in maximal cardiac output, resulting primarily from improved stroke volume; maximal heart rate generally remains unaltered or may even decrease slightly. Because maximal heart rate may remain unaltered or actually decrease slightly with prolonged training (95), perhaps as a result of increased parasympathetic tone (13), the size of the left ventricle (both chamber volume and wall thickness) and the strength of contractions (increased contractility) are the key to increasing stroke volume with maximal as well as submaximal exercise. Consequently, a significantly lower heart rate in response to a standardized submaximal level of work is another hallmark of aerobic endurance training. Furthermore, heart rate increases more slowly in trained athletes than in sedentary people for a given workload (38, 108). Another notable change that comes with aerobic endurance training is the peripheral cardiovascular adaptations at the level of the arterioles and capillaries within the muscles (108). Incre

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: muscle fiber capillary density has been observed in response to aerobic endurance training and is a function of the volume and intensity of training. In addition to delivering oxygen, nutrients, and hormones, the capillary circulation provides the means for removing heat and metabolic by-products. Subsequently, increasing capillary density decreases the diffusion distance for oxygen and metabolic substrates, enabling an improved exchange during subsequent aerobic endurance training and performances (88). The implication of the abovementioned changes is that they increase an aerobic endurance athlete’s ability to improve his or her maximal oxygen uptake, which is of paramount importance for optimal aerobic endurance performance. The reason for this is that a close relationship exists between maximal cardiac output and maximal oxygen uptake, the latter being the product of maximum cardiac output and arteriovenous oxygen difference (108). More simply, an increase in maximal oxygen uptake means more oxygen is delivered to and extracted by the working muscles, thereby providing an increase in exercise intensity and ultimately performance. While not related to aerobic endurance performance outcomes, it is also worth noting that a common cardiovascular adaptation following aerobic endurance training is a lower resting heart rate. The normal discharge rate of the sinoatrial (SA) node ranges from 60 to 80 times per minute. Aerobic endurance training results in a significantly slower d

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: endurance–trained athletes have also been found to have an accelerated heart rate recovery after exercise (13). This is important to know for athlete training and monitoring purposes. Respiratory Adaptations Pulmonary ventilation generally does not limit aerobic exercise and is either unaffected or only moderately affected by training (8, 32). While the respiratory system can accommodate the demands of high-intensity aerobic endurance exercise for the majority of athletes, evidence suggests that in some highly trained aerobic endurance athletes, such total body aerobic endurance exercise may exceed the respiratory system’s functional capacity and affect the ability to transport oxygen to locomotor musculature (2). Furthermore, the ventilatory adaptations observed appear to be highly specific to activities that involve the type of exercise used in training; that is, adaptations observed during lower extremity exercise primarily occur as a result of lower extremity training (108). If exercise training focuses on the lower extremities, thereby reducing lactate levels and carbon dioxide production from lactate buffering as training adaptations take place, one will not likely observe ventilatory adaptation during upper extremity activities, where no training adaptations have taken place (108). Training adaptations include increased tidal volume and breathing frequency with maximal exercise. With submaximal activity, breathing frequency is often reduced and tidal volume is increase

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: aerobic training in disciplines such as cycling and running can lead to beneficial adaptations in movement economy through improvements in motor recruitment. Chronic aerobic training can result in increased muscle coactivation, enhanced leg stiffness, and a greater ratio of eccentric-to-concentric muscle activity, enabling athletes to use stored elastic energy more efficiently, reducing the metabolic cost of exercise (73a). Supporting research has shown that trained cyclists and runners exhibit less variability in muscle activity between pedal strokes and strides, respectively, as well as shorter durations of muscle activity compared to their novice counterparts (21a). Furthermore, multisport athletes, such as triathletes, demonstrate more extensive and variable muscle coactivation, along with less modulation and refined patterns of muscle activity during cycling and running when compared to single-sport athletes (21a, 21b) reflecting interference with neuromuscular adaptations from multisport training. Muscular Adaptations One of the fundamental adaptive responses to aerobic endurance training is an increase in the aerobic capacity of the trained musculature. This adaptation allows the athlete to perform a given absolute intensity of exercise with greater ease. More impressively, after training, an athlete can exercise at a greater relative intensity of a now-higher maximal aerobic power. Thus, measuring an athlete’s maximal oxygen uptake only before and after aerobic endura

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: Consequently, the onset of blood lactate accumulation (OBLA) (see chapter 3) occurs at a higher percentage (up to 80%-90%) of the trained athlete’s aerobic capacity. The muscular component of an aerobic endurance training program involves submaximal muscle contractions extended over a large number of repetitions with little recovery. Therefore, the relative intensity is very low, and the overall volume is very high. This manner of training encourages relative increases in aerobic potential that are similar in type I and type II fibers (167). Compared to type II fibers, type I fibers have a higher preexisting initial aerobic capacity, to which the increase in aerobic potential from training is added (53). Thus, type I fibers possess an oxidative capacity greater than that of type II fibers both before and after training. However, it should be noted while aerobic endurance training has been found to encourage relative increases in aerobic potential that are similar in type I and type II fibers (167), such training has also been found to reduce type I and type II fiber size while maintaining or improving the functional ability of the fibers (157). After 13 weeks of marathon running training, a reduction of 20% in muscle fiber size in both fiber types was found, while strength in both fiber types was maintained and actually increased by 18% in type IIa fibers following a three-week taper (157). Little evidence shows that type II fibers change into type I fibers as a result of aer

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: aerobic endurance exercise, for example, a hybrid I/IIa fiber could transform to a type I fiber (110). This scenario was highlighted by Trappe and colleagues (157), who examined the impact of aerobic endurance training on muscle fiber adaptations in runners participating in a 16-week marathon training study including a 3- week taper and marathon. The results showed approximately a 50% decline in the percentage of hybrid fibers and an increase in the percentage of type I fibers in the gastrocnemius muscle. While our understanding of how hybrid fibers in humans adapt to various training environments is still evolving, we do know that hybrid fibers in aerobic endurance runners are influenced by training volume, and the content of hybrid fibers (i.e., distribution of MHC isoforms) differs between longer- versus shorter-distance runners (80). Further, the abovementioned conversions following aerobic endurance training, whether within fiber type or from hybrid fibers, results in a more oxidative phenotype of the muscle that contributes to improved aerobic endurance performance. At the cellular level, muscular adaptations to aerobic exercise include an increase in the size and number of mitochondria (68) and increased myoglobin content (26, 64). Myoglobin is a protein that transports oxygen within the cell. Mitochondria are the organelles in cells that are responsible for aerobically producing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) via oxidation of pyruvate and lactate (the products of glycol

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: intensity (71). The training induced an increase in fat use attributed to the increase in fat-metabolizing enzymes and greater mitochondrial respiratory capacity within the exercising muscles (108). Bone and Connective Tissue Adaptations The selection of different forms of aerobic exercise has met with some success in bringing about improvements in bone mass. Aerobic programs that are the most successful in stimulating bone growth involve more intense physical activities such as running and high- intensity aerobics (12, 17). Running promotes bone growth more effectively than other types of aerobic exercises such as cycling and swimming. This is due to the repetitive high-impact loading that occurs during running, in which the body experiences forces several times its own weight. In contrast, cycling and swimming are weight- supported activities that place minimal strain on the skeletal system, resulting in less stimulation for bone growth (150). In fact, non- weight-bearing aerobic exercise can reduce bone density, particularly in areas not used to produce locomotion. For example, in a study comparing athletes who were runners, cyclists, or both, it was reported that individuals who were runners had greater total and leg bone mineral density when compared to non-exercising control participants, while cyclists had a reduced lower spine bone mineral density than the non-exercising control group, and those in both groups had greater total and arm bone mineral density compared to

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: The key to the success of aerobic exercise in stimulating new bone formation is that the activity must be significantly more intense than the daily activities the person normally engages in so as to exceed the minimum threshold intensity, as well as at a cyclical strain to exceed the minimum and strain frequency for bone growth (12). The intensity of the activity must systematically increase in order to continually overload the bone. Eventually, it may become difficult to overload bone through aerobic exercise when the oxygen transport system rather than limitations of the musculoskeletal system restricts the progression to new exercise intensity. Bone responds to the magnitude and rate of external loading. Therefore, to enhance the stimulus to the musculoskeletal system, it is also necessary to increase the rate of limb movement. Using high- intensity interval training techniques is one method of providing a greater osteogenic stimulus while still providing the benefits associated with aerobic exercise (14, 39). Another method to increase the musculoskeletal system stimulus is to combine aerobic endurance training with resistance training, a known stimulus for improving bone mass (107), in what is commonly referred to as concurrent training (146) (refer to chapter 21 for more information). In mature adults, the extent to which tendons, ligaments, and cartilage grow and become stronger is proportional to the intensity of the exercise stimulus, especially from weight-bearing a

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: during weight bearing is likely essential to maintain tissue viability (148). Aerobic exercise, particularly running, has received a lot of research attention due not only to the health benefits it can provide but also because of suggestions that habitual running can have a negative impact on joints like the knees and hips, increasing the risk of cartilage damage and osteoarthritis. While mixed or inconclusive findings on the impact of running on knee health have been reported (154), a study evaluating thousands of non-elite male and female runners across the life span (ages from 12 to over 50) reported that running did not increase the odds of knee pain or symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (97). Similarly, a study has reported that running does not increase the risk of symptomatic knee osteoarthritis compared to non-running activities (98). In individuals without preexisting osteoarthritis, running does not appear to harm the knees (98). Moreover, some research suggests that running may even offer protection against general knee pain (29). This protection may be associated with the improved periarticular strength, not to mention proprioception that comes with the running motion (98). In studies of elite aerobic endurance-trained athletes, the results are similar to those of lesser-trained runners. For example, in a study of over 2,000 former elite athletes, it was found that those from a power and mixed-sports background (e.g., soccer, basketball, track and field) had an incre

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: expectancy, thus explaining the later onset of osteoarthritis, if it does occur (90). While these studies did not highlight any notable differences in the outcomes between the elite and non-elite running athletes, it has been suggested that the level of exposure may be a risk factor for knee osteoarthritis (98), as a result of the duration, intensity, and frequency of training. Endocrine Adaptations Just as endocrine responses to resistance training are needed for muscle development (87), the changes in hormone production that contribute to the body’s adaptation to aerobic exercise are equally important (45, 46, 82, 108, 113). Testosterone, insulin, insulin-like growth factors (IGF-1), and growth hormone affect the integrity of muscle, bone, and connective tissue as well as assist in maintaining metabolism within a normal range (40, 41, 84, 85, 158). The endocrine adaptations following aerobic endurance training vary according to the level of exercise intensity and duration, with some hormonal responses increasing while others decrease, as outlined in the following. High-intensity aerobic training augments the absolute secretion rates of many hormones in response to maximal exercise, although trained athletes have attenuated hormonal responses to submaximal exercise (103). However, the hormonal response of trained athletes is similar to an untrained person when performing aerobic endurance exercise at the same relative submaximal exercise intensity (108). The greater hormonal

text: activity and its influence on energy supply. Over the course of a season, high-level male aerobic endurance runners’ basal concentrations of certain hormones (e.g., testosterone and insulin) may change and be more sensitive to variances in training parameters such as intensity and distance run each week than hormones such as cortisol (1). Further, these responses may also be influenced by energy availability, with basal testosterone concentrations decreasing for athletes who ran a greater number of miles and had low energy availability (1). Additionally, research on elite rowers has demonstrated that certain hormones (testosterone and cortisol) may be more sensitive to changes in training volume than hormones such as growth hormone (129). Also worth noting is that low energy availability can affect the degree of protein involvement in aerobic endurance exercise, particularly during bouts of long duration (94). Therefore, consideration must be given over the course of a season as to how the training variables are manipulated and energy supplies are affected, not to mention how an athlete recovers (i.e., type of recovery strategies employed including nutrition), because these factors will determine the endocrine response as well as the adaptations experienced during and after training. An important point related to all this information is what is known as relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S). For more detail, see chapter 11. Aerobic training, especially running, is often

Consequently, these protein pathways can also be influenced by exercise–nutrient interactions, especially in the early stages of recovery after exercise, hence the importance of post-exercise recovery nutrition that incorporates the ingestion of high-quality proteins in addition to carbohydrates (145). 354

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training Much research has been done on training adaptations associated with aerobic endurance exercise (5, 15, 20, 34, 42, 65, 66, 161). Aerobic metabolism plays a vital role in human performance and is basic to all sports, if for no other reason than recovery (156). Metabolically, the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain are the main pathways in aerobic energy production. Aerobic metabolism produces far more ATP energy than anaerobic metabolism and uses fats, carbohydrates, and (minimally) proteins as fuel sources for generating ATP. Many sports involve interactions between the aerobic and anaerobic metabolic systems and thus require appropriate training. For example, soccer, lacrosse, basketball, field hockey, and ice hockey involve continuous movement (and thus constant aerobic demand) mixed with bursts of sprint and power activities. Proper conditioning of the aerobic system is vital to the athlete’s ability to sustain such activity and adequately recover within and between exercise sessions. What Improvements in Performance Result From Aerobic Exercise? The body systems affected by aerobic exercise include musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, and respiratory. Adaptations include the following: • Respiratory system. Decreased submaximal respiration rate (37). • Cardiovascular system. Decreased heart rate for fixed submaximal workloads (131) associated with increased stroke volume and cardiac output. Blood (plasma) volume is also increased

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: • Aerobic power (maximal oxygen uptake). Arguably the most significant change in physiological variables with aerobic exercise training is an increase in maximal oxygen uptake (V̇ O2max), the criterion index of cardiovascular fitness. The V̇ O2max is determined in part by genetics and by the training program undertaken by the athlete. Elite athletes may show minor changes in V̇ O2max with training (5%-10%), while untrained individuals may increase V̇ O2max by as much as 20% (67, 75). A high V̇ O2max coupled with increased lactate threshold allows enhanced performance for running sports as well as sports requiring intermittent sprinting (soccer, basketball, and other team sports). • Lactate threshold. Aerobic training increases the absolute lactate threshold, allowing the highly trained individual to work at both a higher relative and absolute percentage of his or her V̇ O2max than a less-trained individual. This increased tolerance of lactate translates into a variety of performance outcomes; these include running at a higher percentage of V̇ O2max for a race (resulting in reduced time), covering more distance during a game, enhanced recovery for second-half performance, and working at higher exercise intensities throughout an event. The importance of having a high lactate threshold can be seen in the following example. Two individuals can have the same V̇ O2max, perhaps 50 mL · kg−1 · min−1; however, if one has a lactate threshold of 80% of V̇ O2max (i.e., threshold occurs a

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: may have a higher propensity for fiber shifting and other factors such as the tapering or other phase of training may affect these shifts (125, 102). From a performance standpoint, these metabolic and fiber changes result in a more efficient use of aerobic energy production. • Exercise economy. The economy of exercise is mostly a function of biomechanics and technique, which are influenced by the athlete’s metabolic, cardiovascular, and neuromuscular efficiency and training (7). Two aerobic endurance athletes may have the same maximal oxygen uptake and lactate threshold yet not show the same performance outcomes. The athlete with better economy would be able to race at a higher target pace or power for the same amount of energy consumption, likely resulting in a better performance, even though the two athletes have the same V̇ O2max and lactate threshold (23). Every athlete needs a basic level of aerobic endurance—if not for performance, for health reasons—that can be achieved using a wide variety of training modalities and programs (see chapter 21 for more information). Apart from the stereotypical submaximal aerobic training methods, another method that can produce significant gains in aerobic fitness (e.g., increased V̇ O2max, lactate threshold) is interval training (16, 42, 92). One of the most measured adaptations to aerobic endurance training is an increase in maximal oxygen uptake associated with an increase in maximal cardiac output (15, 31, 65, 161). As the intensity

text: capillary densities, and improved enzyme activity. It may be that experienced athletes do not experience further increases in their V̇ O2max through chronic aerobic endurance training but that their performance improves due to enhanced exercise economy (15, 66). The intensity of training is one of the most important factors in improving and maintaining aerobic power. Short, high-intensity bouts of interval sprints can improve maximal oxygen uptake if the interim rest period is also short. A repeated sprint-sequence interval session can generally be defined as at least two short bouts of ≥10 seconds with a short recovery period of ≤60 seconds; however, this will depend on the athletes’ goals (50). Callister and colleagues (20) demonstrated that long rest periods used with sprints improve sprint speed without significant increases in maximal aerobic power. Therefore, longer training sessions with higher amounts of rest between exercise bouts result in less improvement in aerobic capacity. The use of shorter recovery periods between high-intensity training intervals has been shown in various studies to improve various skeletal muscle metabolic processes, resulting in improved aerobic endurance performance (48). Aerobic endurance training is generally associated with alterations in body composition, assuming appropriate nutritional intake. Aerobic endurance training usually decreases the relative percentage of body fat but has little or no significant effect on fat-free mass. Lon

text: External and Individual Factors Influencing Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training A variety of external and individual factors can influence both the acute responses and the chronic adaptations of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to exercise. The effects of altitude, heat, hyperoxic breathing, smoking, vaping, and blood doping (external factors), as well as genetic potential (individual factor), are briefly described in this section. Altitude At elevations greater than 3,900 feet (1,189 m), acute physiological adjustments begin to occur to compensate for the reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere (61). Figure 6.1 presents the adjustments to altitude hypoxia that are immediate and longer term. Two adjustments that occur early in the acclimatization process are particularly important. First, there is an increase in pulmonary ventilation (hyperventilation) at rest and during exercise. This increase in ventilation is primarily the result of increased breathing frequency. With longer stays at high elevation, however, increased tidal volume also contributes to augmented ventilation. Stabilization of ventilation is dependent on the level of altitude and the duration at altitude (77). Second, in the early stages of altitude exposure, cardiac output at rest and during submaximal exercise increases, due primarily to increases in heart rate (61, 108). Submaximal heart rate and cardiac output can increase 30% to 50% above sea-level values, and stroke volume is

Within 10 to 14 days at a given altitude, heart rate and cardiac output begin to return to normal values because of the longer-term acclimatization response of increased red blood cell production. Thus, with acute exposure to altitude, hyperventilation and increased submaximal cardiac output are rapid and relatively effective responses to offset the challenges of the reduced partial 362

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: pressure of oxygen. However, despite these adjustments, during this acute period, arterial oxygen saturation decreases and results in decreases in maximal oxygen uptake and aerobic performance at altitudes above 3,900 feet (1,189 m). Acclimatization changes revert in about one month after return to sea level. As indicated in figure 6.1, chronic physiological and metabolic adjustments that occur during a prolonged altitude exposure include increased formation of hemoglobin (generally 5%-15% increase, although higher values have been reported) and red blood cells (30%-50% increase), increased diffusing capacity of oxygen through the pulmonary membranes, maintenance of the acid–base balance of body fluids by renal excretion of HCO3− and through hyperventilation, and increased capillarization. All these adaptations generally improve tolerance of the relative hypoxia at medium and high altitudes (58, 61, 108) and may result in nearly sea-level exercise capacities with adequate acclimatization. A minimum of three to six weeks is needed to adapt at moderate altitude (2,200 to 3,000 ft [608 to 914 m]). However, reduced performance, compared to sea level, is generally expected with altitude exposure regardless of the period of acclimatization. Heat Acclimatization The physiologic responses to aerobic exercise depend on the environmental conditions in which an athlete is exercising. Consequently, high environmental temperatures and humidity cause significant alterations to heart rate, oxygen uptake, minute ventilation, and blood lactate responses and, ultimately, performance due to interactions between the environmental conditions and an athlete’s thermoregulatory systems (117). If these environmental conditions are hot and dry or warm/hot and humid and produce a sufficient level of heat stress, performance can be impaired due to a cascade of thermoregulatory responses including an increase in sweat rate and blood flow to the skin to facilitate greater heat transfer to the environment. Such a process is in competition with increasing skeletal muscle blood flow to meet the metabolic demands of active muscle (54) and thus restrains blood flow 364

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: availability for oxygen and nutrient delivery and metabolic by- product removal in exercising muscle. If this process continues long enough without sufficient fluid intake, dehydration can result, further compounding the issue and putting the athlete under greater physiological and thermoregulatory stress, leading to further compromised performance (54). However, repeated exposure over a long period of time (often referred to as natural exposure) to a hot environment can result in thermoregulatory and physiological adaptations referred to as heat acclimatization, which can improve an athlete’s heat tolerance (10). An athlete can undertake heat acclimation protocols (often referred to as artificial exposure) to expose the body to such hot environments, thereby raising core and skin temperatures and increase sweating to elicit the same adaptations (124). The body undergoes a number of well-known chronic thermoregulatory and physiological changes during the heat acclimatization process. These adaptations include an earlier onset of sweating in conjunction with an increase in sweat rate and evaporative cooling, a reduction in resting and exercising skin and core body temperature, an expansion in plasma volume and hence an increase in blood volume, a reduction in resting and exercising heart rate, and a reduction in gastrointestinal distress (49). The benefit of these physiological adaptations is that the athlete not only has an improved heat tolerance ability via an improved thermoregulatory system, but such adaptations have also been found to improve time-trial performance (57, 99) and improve maximal oxygen uptake and power output at lactate threshold (99). Additionally, the athlete’s perception of effort and level of thermal comfort have also been found to be improved following heat acclimation (49). However, in a review by Rahimi and colleagues (130) of the physiological responses to heat acclimation across 11 randomized controlled trials with 215 participants, it was reported that heat acclimation was effective for improving time-trial 366

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: performance as well as reducing time-trial heart rate and maximal heart rate, despite there being no beneficial effect on maximal oxygen uptake, core or mean skin temperature, plasma volume, or blood lactate, nor meaningful effects on rating of perceived exertion or thermal comfort. The differences between studies and whether improvements were observed with respect to heat acclimation may be related to the environmental conditions (i.e., warm or hot, dry or humid), intensity of the exercise used, the acclimation protocols that the athletes were exposed to, and the initial level of athlete acclimation, all of which determine the degree of thermoregulatory and physiological adaptations (124). Heat acclimation adaptations start to occur quickly once exposed to the hot environment and continue for the duration of the process. However, it needs to be noted that heat acclimation adaptations do not all occur at the same rate, with some occurring more quickly than others and some (e.g., sweat rate) continuing as the acclimation period continues (124). The time course of the physiological adaptations to heat acclimation are outlined in figure 6.3. The physiological changes to the thermoregulatory system start to occur very quickly, commencing from the first day of exposure (124) and continuing over subsequent days, with the majority of the adaptations (~75%) reported to occur within the first four to six days (121). Unfortunately, heat acclimation–induced thermoregulatory and physiolo

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: coincide with the rate of adaptation; that is, those that adapted quickly also decay quickly (122). Typically, full heat acclimation adaptations are expected to be lost after a month if there is no repeated exercise heat stress (128). It also appears that the loss of adaptations may be affected by the level of exercise undertaken after heat acclimation. Consequently, it is recommended that athletes maintain their training in the days after heat acclimation to assist retaining their thermoregulatory and physiological adaptations (128). It has also been reported that the heat acclimation adaptations may remain longer for those athletes acclimatized in dry, hot environments compared to humid, hot environments (121). Unfortunately, little research has been conducted on the transferability of adaptations between different hot environments (e.g., hot and dry to warm and humid). However, in one of the few studies to investigate this aspect of heat acclimation, it was found that cross-adaptation from one environment to the other is achievable (56), an important point worth noting for athletes who train and compete in different hot environments. 368

Two other factors to consider with respect to heat acclimation are the influence of the level of aerobic fitness and biological sex. There is evidence to suggest that athletes who have a higher level of aerobic fitness have a greater ability to exercise in the heat due to the ability to tolerate higher core body temperatures (124) and may also better retain their heat acclimation adaptations (121). With respect to sex, differences are observed in the physiological responses to exercise in the heat between males and females. Females have been found to experience greater increases in body temperature in the heat due to a lower total body sweat response when compared to males (43). This difference in sweat rate is attributed to a smaller increase in sweat rate for a given increase in body temperature (i.e., lower thermosensitivity) (43). It has also been observed that while both females and males respond to short- term heat acclimation protocols, females may require a slightly longer protocol to establish thermoregulatory and cardiovascular stability (111). 369

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: With this information in mind, strength and conditioning professionals need to consider the type of heat acclimation protocol that they will employ, the proximity of the heat acclimation protocol to the athlete’s competition, and the training status and sex of the athlete with whom they are working, in order to maximize the potential benefits from the acclimation environment to the competition environment. More information on heat acclimation protocols and the different types and considerations when implementing such protocols are outlined in chapter 21. Altitude or Heat: Which Training Protocol Should an Athlete Undertake? Before answering this question, it is important to understand how the two types of training protocols differ in terms of adaptations. Heat acclimation training has become popular with aerobic endurance athletes, often as an alternative to altitude training due to less expense and easier access to hot versus altitude training environments. While evidence suggests that heat acclimation can improve maximal oxygen uptake in thermoneutral (164) and hot environments (99, 163) as well as performance in thermoneutral (112) and hot environments (57, 99), the changes are not due to the same physiological mechanisms brought about by altitude training (hypoxic exposure). Training at altitude causes exposure to a hypobaric-hypoxic environment and a reduction in an athlete’s arterial oxygen content, which sets off a sequence of events starting with an increase in the am

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: targets changes in the thermoregulatory system via increases in core body temperature, which in turn brings about a reduction in central venous pressure and renal perfusion and subsequent increase in aldosterone secretion (6). The result of this process is a sudden and large expansion in plasma volume, which in turn increases stroke volume and hence is proposed to improve maximal aerobic capacity and subsequent aerobic endurance performance (6). A graphical representation of the proposed physiological mechanisms of altitude training and heat acclimation training and their subsequent effect on aerobic endurance exercise performance is provided in figure 6.4. In view of the potential benefits to both altitude and heat training as outlined above, one might think that completing both forms of training together would provide an athlete with the best of both worlds—that is, erythropoiesis from hypoxia stimulation and plasma volume expansion from heat acclimation. Unfortunately, the answer is not that simple, for altitude training can evoke an acute reduction in plasma volume, which is in contrast with the expansion of plasma volume experienced with heat acclimation (118). In addition, the time course of adaptations to altitude (hypoxic exposure) and heat acclimation appears to be different, with hypoxia exposure generally requiring slightly longer exposure times compared to heat acclimation (60). Research has been conducted to investigate the efficacy of combining the two forms of

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training

The results of these studies suggest that even though the physiological adaptations to altitude and heat training may be different, hypoxic exposure does not provide any additional benefit above and beyond heat acclimation as it relates to exercise performance in the heat, nor does it impair heat acclimation. In light of these research findings, which training protocol (altitude or heat) should an athlete complete? In answering this question, it is important to remember two points. First, nonhematological adaptations are directly related to the stresses of the training environment, and second, the nonhematological adaptations to both altitude and heat are specific to the environment in which the athlete will compete (118). Or put another way, what is going to have the biggest impact on the athlete’s performance on race day, altitude or heat? For example, if an athlete was preparing for a marathon to be held at an altitude of 2,500 to 3,000 meters (8,202-9,843 ft), the answer would be altitude, because the athlete would notice the change in atmospheric pressure at that altitude if he or she were from a sea-level environment. However, if the athlete was preparing for a marathon at sea level but in a warm to hot and humid environment and notably above his or her temperate, dry training environment, he or she would be best served by undertaking a heat acclimation protocol. chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: Hyperoxic Breathing Breathing oxygen-enriched gas mixtures (hyperoxic breathing) during rest periods or following exercise can result in short-term improvements in oxygen transport, lactate metabolism, power output, and work tolerance when compared to normoxic breathing (21). In contrast, studies examining the systematic supplementation of hyperoxic breathing during aerobic endurance training over time show contradictory results and overall small benefits (21). Hyperoxic breathing has been proposed to increase the amount of oxygen carried by the blood and therefore increase the supply of oxygen to working muscles and reduce central fatigue (21). However, the breathing of ambient air at sea level by healthy people results in arterial hemoglobin oxygen saturation between 95% to 98%. Thus, the potential for hyperoxic breathing during rest periods or following exercise has yet to be fully elucidated (58, 126). Smoking and Vaping Relatively little research is available regarding smoking and exercise performance, possibly because athletes and active individuals may tend to avoid smoking for fear of impairing performance or increasing disease risk (100, 123). However, based on the available evidence, it is clear that smokers experience lower oxygen uptake, impaired heart rate responses to exercise, and a decrease in muscular endurance compared with nonsmokers (9, 91). Smokers experience impairments in lung function and are at increased risk for chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: bronchial tree due to the irritation of smoke; and paralysis of the cilia on the surfaces of the respiratory tract by nicotine, which limits the ability to remove excess fluids and foreign particles, causing debris to accumulate in the respiratory passageways and adding to the difficulty of breathing. Thus, even the light smoker may feel respiratory strain during exercise and experience a reduction in the level of performance (58, 108). Carbon monoxide, a component of cigarette smoke, is associated with an impaired hemodynamic response to exercise and increased catecholamine release. Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity for hemoglobin than does oxygen. The resulting carboxyhemoglobin (carbon monoxide and hemoglobin) reduces the amount of oxygen that can be carried by hemoglobin and thus reduces the oxygen that can be provided to the working muscles. The reduction in oxygen- carrying capacity may reduce maximal exercise capacity, and submaximal cardiovascular responses may increase in an effort to provide adequate oxygenated blood to the working muscles. The increased catecholamine release increases heart rate and blood pressure. Vaping refers to the act of inhaling an aerosol often containing nicotine and flavoring through a device, commonly known as an e- cigarette or vape pen, which heats a liquid to generate vapor without the combustion associated with traditional cigarette smoking. Vaping is currently the most common modality of nicotine consumption in young people, with

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: prospective cohort study has examined the link between vaping and long-term adverse respiratory outcomes. This is further complicated by the large spectrum of vaping options including various flavors, additives, and nicotine concentrations. However, in vaping products that contain nicotine (over 99% of products), the nicotine-stimulated catecholamine release can activate receptors in the heart and result in an increased heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac contractility and workload and, in the long term, can result in changes in cardiovascular physiology and the development of heart failure and other associated chronic health issues (133). Studies examining short-term side effects of vaping report inflammation and cellular damage in the lungs, leading to decreased lung capacity and impaired gas exchange (22, 151), which may in turn affect performance and recovery times during exercise. However, whether these changes are maintained over the long term and after vaping cessation is still yet to be established. Studies also demonstrate that both acute and subacute vaping can exacerbate both asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and induce physiological changes in the airways and immune system (159), which can negatively affect performance and recovery in athletes. Very few studies have examined the effect of vaping directly on aerobic endurance exercise. text: Blood Doping The practice of artificially increasing red blood cell mass (blood doping) as a means to improve athletic performance has been criticized as unethical and as one that poses serious health risks to the athlete (120). Nonetheless, research has suggested that this practice can improve aerobic exercise performance and may enhance tolerance of certain environmental conditions (138). Blood doping can be accomplished through infusion of an individual’s own red blood cells or those from someone else, or through administration of EPO, which stimulates red blood cell production. Infusion of red blood cells rapidly increases red blood cell mass but for just a few weeks (116), whereas EPO takes longer to cause an increase in red blood cell production but the effect lasts as long as EPO is administered (138). In either case, it is theorized that increasing red blood cell mass increases the blood’s ability to carry oxygen and thus increases oxygen availability to working muscles. Maximal oxygen uptake has been demonstrated to increase by up to 11% with either red blood cell infusion or EPO administration (138, 139). At standardized submaximal workloads, blood doping has also been associated with decreased heart rate and blood lactate as well as higher pH values (138). The effects of blood doping suggest the potential for diminishing the impact of various environmental conditions. The effects of altitude appear to be lessened with blood doping, although as altitude increases, t

chapterTitle: Adaptations to Aerobic Training
text: little aid relating to the response to heat of those who are not acclimatized (138). Much less is known about blood doping with respect to cold stress, and although some theoretical benefit has been suggested, this practice could conceivably increase health risks (138). The health risks associated with blood doping further complicate the controversy surrounding this practice. Theoretically, high hematocrit levels may increase risks for embolic events such as stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism. Increased arterial blood pressure, flu-like symptoms, and increased plasma potassium levels may present themselves with EPO use (139). Finally, there is risk associated with infusion or transfusion, although in most cases the risk is relatively small (139). Genetic Potential The upper limit of an individual’s genetic potential contributes significantly to the absolute magnitude of the training adaptations. The magnitude of change also depends on the current training status of the individual. Each biological system adaptation, such as that of the cardiovascular system, has an upper limit, and as the athlete gets closer to that upper limit, smaller and smaller gains are observed. For example, in some elite competitions (e.g., swimming), small gains in performance may be the difference between the gold medal and 26th place. Thus, in an event in which tenths or hundredths of a second make a big difference, it may be worth the extra training time to ga

text: Detraining Detraining is defined as the partial or complete loss of training- induced adaptations in response to an insufficient training stimulus (114, 115). Detraining is governed by the principle of training reversibility, which states that whereas physical training results in several physiological adaptations that enhance athletic performance, stopping or markedly reducing training induces a partial or complete reversal of these adaptations, compromising athletic performance. A distinction needs to be made with regard to cessation of training that results in a reversal of adaptations and tapering. Tapering is the planned reduction of volume of training (usually in duration and frequency but not intensity) that occurs before an athletic competition or a planned recovery microcycle. This type of reduction in training is designed to enhance athletic performance and adaptations. Aerobic endurance adaptations are most sensitive to periods of inactivity because of their enzymatic basis. The exact cellular mechanisms that dictate detraining changes are unknown, and further research is needed to clarify the underlying physiological alterations. Two review articles (114, 115) address the factors that contribute to aerobic performance, most importantly V̇ O2max and the factors determining V̇ O2max (cardiac output and arteriovenous oxygen difference) and the impact of detraining. text: Proper exercise variation, intensity, maintenance programs, and active recovery periods can adequately protect against serious detraining effects (36). 380

text: Conclusion Aerobic endurance exercise produces many acute cardiovascular and respiratory responses, and aerobic endurance training produces many chronic adaptations. This information can be of particular value for developing the goals of a conditioning program and can provide a basis for clinical evaluation and the selection of parameters to be included in such an evaluation process. Knowledge of cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, muscular, bone and connective tissue, and endocrine system responses to aerobic endurance training can help the strength and conditioning professional understand the scientific basis for aerobic conditioning and the adaptations to expect and monitor during training. Adaptations to specific types of exercise stimuli take place in the body. Optimal adaptations reflect careful design, implementation, and performance of strength and conditioning programs. chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: CHAPTER 7 AGE-RELATED DIFFERENCES AND THEIR IMPLICATIONS FOR RESISTANCE TRAINING Rhodri S. Lloyd, PhD, Sylvia Moeskops, PhD, and Avery D. Faigenbaum, EdD After completing this chapter, you will be able to understand the merits of adopting a long-term approach to the development of athleticism for child and adolescent populations; evaluate the evidence regarding the safety, effectiveness, and importance of resistance exercise for youth populations; describe the effects of aging on musculoskeletal health and performance; explore the trainability of older adults and the benefits of exercise, including resistance training in aging populations; and explain why adaptations to resistance exercise vary greatly among these distinct populations. Resistance exercise has been proven to be a safe and effective method of conditioning for individuals with various needs, goals, and abilities. Resistance training is also recognized as a fundamental 384

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: component of long-term athletic development that helps to support lifelong participation in sport and recreational physical activity from childhood to the more senior years of life (137). In light of its many benefits for all individuals, resistance exercise for youth (137) and older people (76) has received increasing public and medical attention. However, when designing and evaluating resistance training programs, strength and conditioning professionals need to understand the implications of age-related differences in body composition, muscular performance, trainability, and injury risk to facilitate individualized exercise prescription. For the purposes of this chapter, resistance exercise is defined as a specialized method of conditioning whereby an individual is working against a wide range of resistive loads to enhance health, fitness, and performance. This term should be distinguished from the sport of weightlifting, in which individuals attempt to lift maximal amounts of weight in competition, specifically in the clean and jerk and snatch exercises. The term childhood refers to a period of life before the development of secondary sex characteristics (e.g., pubic hair and reproductive organs), and the term adolescence refers to the period between childhood and adulthood. For ease of discussion, the term youth or young athlete refers to both children and adolescents. The terms older and senior include men and women over 65 years of age. Athleticism reflects the ability

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: Youth Populations The National Strength and Conditioning Association considers long- term athletic development as the development of athleticism over time, with an aim to enhance physical fitness, reduce injury risk, and improve mental and physical health and well-being (137). The concept of regularly participating in activities that enhance athleticism is relevant for people of all ages. However, over the past two decades, there has been a growing focus on long-term athletic development programs, particularly for youth populations (137). Athletic development models that encompass multiple modes of training have been proposed previously in the literature. For example, Lloyd and Oliver (141) proposed the youth physical development (YPD) model, which provides training guidelines for males and females (figure 7.1a and 7.1b). The YPD model is based on the notion that all components of fitness are trainable at all stages of development, and therefore training programs should be multifaceted in nature to develop multiple dimensions of athleticism. Crucially, the model promotes a consistent focus on the simultaneous development of muscle strength and motor skill competency, which provide the foundations for overall athleticism (137). The model also supports children engaging in some form of physical activity and preparatory conditioning early in life to take advantage of the heightened neuroplasticity associated with early childhood development (88). Similarly, training prescription

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: model focuses on bespoke elements of athletic development, several notable commonalities exist between models: (a) Children should be exposed to a wide range of training activities that target motor skill development and muscular strength, (b) training should begin simple and become more advanced as children progress through the various stages of development, and (c) training should be generic to start with and then become more specialized over time as workloads and training exposure increase. Collectively, strength and conditioning programs effectively promote the development of athleticism in both children and adolescents (141). In particular, leading international consensus (17, 137, 139, 215) and seminal meta-analytical data (132, 134) have indicated the effectiveness of resistance training in enhancing multiple components of fitness in youth populations. While the effectiveness of resistance training in youth is unequivocal, it is important for strength and conditioning professionals to understand how the fundamental principles of growth, maturation, and development can affect training adaptations, confound interpretation of testing or monitoring data, and can influence the development and evaluation of safe and effective resistance training programs. Because youth sports training has become more intense and complex (21), anatomical, physiological, and psychosocial factors that may be associated with acute and chronic injury also need to be considered. The Growing Child

text: and a child transitions to young adulthood. During puberty, changes also occur in body composition and the performance of physical skills, with such changes varying markedly between individuals. 388

text: FIGURE 7.1 The youth physical development model for (a) males and (b) females. Font size refers to importance; light blue and light red boxes refer to preadolescent periods of adaptation; dark blue and dark red boxes refer to adolescent periods of adaptation. FMS: fundamental movement skills; MC: metabolic conditioning; PHV: peak height velocity; SSS: sport-specific skills; YPD: youth physical development. Adapted by permission from R.S. Lloyd and J.L. Oliver, “The Youth Physical Development Model: A New Approach to Long-Term Athletic Development,” Strength and Conditioning Journal 34, no. 3 (2012): 61-72. Chronological Age Versus Biological Maturation Because of considerable variation in the rates of growth and development, it is not particularly accurate to define a stage of maturation or development by age in months or years, which is known as chronological age. Children do not grow at a constant rate, and there are substantial interindividual differences in physical development at any given chronological age. For example, a group of 14-year-old children can have a height difference as great as 9 inches (23 cm) and a weight difference up to 40 pounds (18 kg), while an 11-year-old girl may be taller and more physically skilled than an 11-year-old boy. These differences correspond to variations in the timing, tempo, and magnitude of maturation (142). The onset of puberty can vary from 8 to 13 years in girls and from 9 to 15 years in boys, with girls beginning puberty approxi

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: that physical training delays or accelerates growth or maturation in boys and girls (70). Further, the osteogenic benefits of physical activity, specifically weight-bearing activities that generate compressive forces, are essential for skeletal remodeling and growth (228). The gold standard for determining biological maturation is skeletal age assessment. This technique involves trained radiographers comparing X-rays or radiographs of a child against standard reference radiographs to determine the extent of ossification of the bones of the left wrist (93, 201, 217-219). Ossification refers to the process of laying down new bone material by cells called osteoblasts. While skeletal age provides the most accurate and reliable form of assessing maturity, concerns with cost, specialist equipment, time constraints, and the need for specific radiographic expertise make the method unrealistic for most practitioners working with youth. Furthermore, strength and conditioning professionals are not qualified to determine sexual age as an indicator of maturation, given the invasive nature of this assessment. For most practitioners, the most realistic and feasible means of estimating biological age is from somatic assessments (142). Somatic age reflects the degree of growth in overall stature or smaller subdimensions of the body (e.g., limb length). Measures of growth (e.g., standing height and seated height) are relatively easy to collect, are noninvasive, and require minimal equipment. T

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: observed age at PHV (184); this appears to be a valid alternative for classifying maturity status when compared to longitudinal growth curve analysis (166). Using age, height, weight, and mid-parental height, a child’s eventual adult height can be estimated, and their current height can then be determined as a percentage of predicted adult height (125). For example, a 13-year-old boy who is 165 centimeters (5 ft 5 in) tall, 60 kilograms (132 lb) in weight and whose mother and father are 160 centimeters (5 ft 3 in) and 185 centimeters (6 ft 1 in), respectively, would be estimated at approximately 90% of their predicted adult height. In some cases, it may be appropriate to measure somatic growth every three months (142). More frequent measures could be taken to create a rolling average and a smoother growth curve; however, this is not always feasible. For most settings, taking measurements every three months is likely more practical. This interval should be long enough to prevent practitioners from misinterpreting small growth changes caused by measurement inconsistencies. However, as a child nears their peak height velocity (PHV), it may be wise for practitioners to measure more frequently, such as monthly. This increased frequency is due to the rapid growth rate associated with this developmental stage. The adolescent growth spurt ensues approximately 88% to 95% of predicted adult height, and longitudinal data indicate that PHV occurs at approximately 91% to 92% of predicted

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: the pubertal growth spurt (170, 225). Strength and conditioning professionals may need to adjust training programs (e.g., reinforce high-quality movement patterns, target flexibility restrictions, correct muscle imbalances, or decrease the volume or intensity [or both] of training) during these periods of rapid growth. If a young athlete complains of pain or discomfort during a growth spurt, the strength and conditioning professional should also consider the possibility of an overuse injury rather than labeling these complaints “growing pains” and, in consultation with the child’s parents or guardians, should refer the child to a medical practitioner. Notwithstanding the influence of growth and maturation, training programs should be tailored to accommodate individual differences in ability and previous training experience, particularly when prescribing exercise for children in the weight room. It might be suitable for an early-maturing, experienced, and technically competent 13-year-old girl to be exposed to more advanced forms of training, whereas a late-maturing 16-year-old boy with no training history and low levels of technical competency may not be ready for the demands of heavy resistance exercise and require more introductory training approaches. Therefore, while a given training program will have an intended adaptation (e.g., strength and power development), a child’s technical competency (i.e., how well they move) in addition to their training age (i.e., the length

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: these needs. For example, a strength and conditioning professional will typically need to use different interpersonal skills to coach an inexperienced child with low technical competency and low levels of self-confidence, versus an experienced and highly competent adolescent who simply lacks motivation. Two children of the same chronological age can differ biologically by up to five years, which underlines the importance of accounting for maturation in the design of individualized training programs. Muscle and Bone Growth As children grow, muscle mass steadily increases. At birth, approximately 25% of a child’s body weight is muscle mass, and by adulthood this percentage increases to about 40% (146). During puberty, marked increases in hormonal concentrations (e.g., testosterone, growth hormone, and insulin-like growth factor) in boys result in a discernible increase in muscle mass and widening of the shoulders, whereas in girls an increase in estrogen production causes increased body fat deposition, breast development, and widening of the hips (59). Although muscle mass in girls continues to increase during adolescence, the increase occurs at a lower rate than in boys due to differences in their hormonal profiles (146). Throughout this time, the increase in muscle mass in both sexes is due to the hypertrophy of individual muscle fibers rather than hyperplasia (146). Peak muscle mass occurs between the ages of 16 and 20 years in females and between 18 and 25 years in males un

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: FIGURE 7.2 Bone formation, which takes place as a result of growth and development. Most bone formation occurs in the diaphysis (primary ossification center), which is the central shaft of a long bone, and in the growth cartilage (secondary ossification center), which is located at three sites in the child: the epiphyseal (growth) plate, the joint surface, and the apophyseal insertions of muscle–tendon units. When the epiphyseal plate becomes completely ossified, the long bones stop growing (figure 7.2). Although bones typically begin to fuse during early adolescence, girls generally achieve full bone maturity about two to three years before boys. The actual age varies considerably, but most bones are fused by the early 20s. A particular concern in children is the vulnerability of the growth cartilage to trauma and overuse (106). Injuries to the growth cartilage may disrupt the bone’s blood and nutrient supply and result in permanent growth disturbances (e.g., skeletal undergrowth, skeletal overgrowth, or malalignment of bone). Trauma from falls or excessive repetitive stress that may result in a ligament tear in an adult may produce an epiphyseal plate fracture in a child. Because the peak incidence of epiphyseal plate fractures in children occurs at around the time of PHV, it seems that a preadolescent child may be 395

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: at less risk for an epiphyseal plate fracture than an adolescent child experiencing the growth spurt (156). It has been suggested that the epiphyseal plates of younger children may be stronger and more resistant to shearing-type forces, which may be the cause of injuries to the growth cartilage (156). Growth cartilage in children is located at the epiphyseal plate, the joint surface, and the apophyseal insertions. Damage to the growth cartilage may impair the growth and development of the affected bone. However, the risk of such damage can be reduced with appropriate exercise technique, sensible progression of training loads, and suitable instruction by qualified strength and conditioning professionals. Developmental Changes in Muscular Strength As muscle mass increases throughout preadolescence and adolescence, so does muscular strength. In fact, the growth curves for strength are similar to those for body mass (59). In boys, peak gains in strength typically occur about 1.2 years after PHV and 0.8 years after peak weight velocity, with body weight being the clearer indicator (146). This reflects the adage that children “stretch out before they fill out”; that is, they experience growth in height before gaining muscle mass. This pattern also suggests that during periods of rapid growth, muscle increases first in mass and later in its ability to express and attenuate high levels of force. This is reflected by meta-analytical data that show adolescents were able to attain incre

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: and a general plateau in the natural strength development of girls during adolescence (139, 146). On average, peak strength is usually attained by age 20 in untrained women and between the ages of 20 and 30 in untrained men (146). An important factor related to the expression of muscular strength in children is the development of the nervous system. If myelination of nerve fibers (motor neurons) is absent or incomplete, fast reactions and skilled movements cannot be successfully performed, and high levels of strength and power are impossible. As the nervous system continues to develop with age, children improve their performance in skills that require coordination, balance, agility, speed, strength, and power. Since the myelination of many motor neurons is incomplete until sexual maturation, children should not be expected to respond to training in the same way or to reach the same skill level as adults until they reach full neural maturity (127). However, children are well placed for skill development given the heightened neuroplasticity associated with childhood. This stage of development involves the process of pruning and strengthening of the synaptic pathways (88), which, with the appropriate environment and activities, enable children to refine motor control strategies and enhance skill acquisition. International consensus proposes that all youth should be exposed to training programs that provide an opportunity to develop a broad range of fitness components to build we

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: concomitantly instead of developing them in a hierarchical, sequential manner. Because physiological functions are more closely related to biological age than to chronological age, at any given time an early- maturing child will likely have an advantage in measures of athleticism (e.g., absolute strength) if compared against a later- maturing child of the same sex with less muscle mass. Clearly, physical differences in body proportions can affect the execution of resistance exercises. For example, short arms and a large chest cavity offer a biomechanical advantage in upper body pressing exercises, whereas conversely, long legs and a long torso are a disadvantage in squatting movements. These anthropometric factors have implications for strength and conditioning professionals who are attempting to standardize fitness tests or develop a resistance training program for a group of boys and girls who vary greatly in physical size. It should be noted that whether in a testing or training environment, the practitioner should use child-size resistance machines or exercises using body weight, medicine balls, elastic bands, dumbbells, or barbells. In situations where practitioners are coaching groups of young athletes, they typically will need to account for variation in technical competency, maturity status, and training experience to provide a training session that is individualized wherever possible. When coaching large groups of children with low coach-to-athlete ratios, individual

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: chronological-age peers with more advanced biological maturity. Although late maturers tend to eventually catch up to the early maturers as they proceed through adolescence, young athletes should realize that many factors, including motivation, coaching, and innate ability, contribute to success in sport. Importantly, when coaching youth populations, especially young children (e.g., 5-7 years of age), training environments should attempt to foster task- oriented views of success (e.g., application of effort, learning something new) rather than an ego-oriented view (e.g., simply winning or beating others). While not an exhaustive list, previous literature has noted that athletic development programs should seek to cultivate a growth mindset, self-determined motivation, perceived competence, confidence, and resilience as key psychological attributes in young athletes (175). Youth Resistance Training Clinicians, coaches, and exercise scientists now agree that resistance exercise is a safe and effective method of conditioning for children (13, 56, 65, 71, 127, 139, 215). An increasing number of boys and girls are participating in resistance training activities, and major sports medicine organizations support children’s participation in a range of resistance exercise modes, provided that the programs are appropriately designed and supervised by qualified professionals (21, 56, 139, 215). National standards and grade-level outcomes for physical education include guidelines and reco

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: the very first time. Children should begin resistance training at a level that is commensurate with their physical and technical abilities, maturity level, and individual goals (141). Adult programs and training philosophies should not be superimposed on younger populations. In such instances, the intensity and volume of training are often too severe, and the recovery between training sessions is inadequate to enable training adaptation to take place. When introducing children to resistance training activities, it is always better to underestimate their physical abilities and gradually increase the volume and intensity of training than to exceed their abilities and risk injury or long-term negative health outcomes. Responsiveness to Resistance Training in Children A plethora of research now shows both children and adolescents can make meaningful improvements in a wide range of athletic qualities in response to different modes of resistance training (59, 141). Much of the early controversy surrounding youth resistance training stemmed from the issue of children’s trainability (i.e., children’s responsiveness to the stimulus of resistance exercise) due to early studies failing to demonstrate a strength increase in preadolescents who participated in a resistance training program (49). Although the lack of significant findings in these studies could be explained by methodological shortcomings, such as short study duration or inadequate training volume or intensity, the results fr

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: intensity and volume of training are adequate (48, 63, 135, 138, 197). Children as young as age five have benefited from developmentally appropriate resistance training (3, 121), and a variety of training modalities have proven to be effective (139). While gains in a maximum strength range of approximately 10% to 90% have been reported in the literature (15), strength gains of roughly 30% to 40% are typically observed in untrained preadolescent children following short-term (8-20 weeks) resistance training programs (56, 139). However, following the initial adaptation period, the rate of change in strength gains will be attenuated as youth adapt to the training program, thus highlighting the need for continued, progressive training. Meta-analytical data have shown that resistance training interventions realize larger gains in muscle strength and power when programs exceed 23 weeks in duration (134). Longer-term training programs afford more opportunities for children to learn and develop skills but also enable children to be exposed to higher intensities of training in a safe and progressive manner. Lesinksi and colleagues (134) also indicated that strength gains were greater when young athletes were exposed to higher relative intensities (>80% 1RM). Similar notions apply to other fitness components, with data showing larger gains in jump height in response to moderate- to high-intensity resistance training (212) and greater gains in peak oxygen uptake (V̇ O2peak) when enduran

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: specific needs, abilities, and aspirations of the individual. Children who participate in resistance training programs are likely to undergo periods of reduced training or inactivity due to program design factors, extended travel plans, busy schedules, injury, involvement in multiple sports, or decreased motivation. This temporary reduction or withdrawal of the training stimulus is called detraining. In children, unlike adults, the evaluation of strength changes during the detraining phase is complicated by the growth- related strength increases during the same period. Nevertheless, data indicate that training-induced strength gains in children are impermanent and tend to return to untrained control group values during the detraining period (55, 69). In one report, participation in physical education classes and organized sports throughout an eight- week detraining period did not maintain the preadolescents’ training- induced strength gains (69). In another study comparing the effects on children of one and two days per week of resistance training, participants who resistance trained only once per week averaged 67% of the strength gains of participants who resistance trained twice per week (63). While increased training frequency is related to a greater strength training effect in youth (15), this finding must be considered in light of lifestyle factors (e.g., nutrition and sleep) and other commitments that youth or young athletes may have (e.g., competitive playing schedule,

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: effects of a two-year strength training program on strength (123), speed (208), and change-of-direction speed (124) in youth soccer players in Germany. Using a linear periodized training approach (i.e., four weeks of technique block, eight weeks of hypertrophy emphasis block, and eight weeks of strength emphasis, all of which repeated twice), young athletes ranging from 11 to 19 years of age were able to make substantial increases in squat strength (123), which also translated to improvements in speed (208) and change-of-direction- speed (124) performance. Notwithstanding the clear benefits of resistance training, combined resistance training (i.e., strength training and plyometrics) has been shown to be more effective than strength training in isolation (193). Previous research has investigated the effects of 28 weeks of combined resistance training versus combined resistance training with weightlifting on physical fitness (187) and established lower limb injury risk factors (188) in adolescent boys. Notably, both training groups were able to realize improvements in physical fitness (i.e., strength, power, speed), movement competency (i.e., resistance training skills battery quotient), and lower limb jump- landing mechanics (i.e., tuck jump assessment) irrespective of program content; however, the percentage improvement in movement competency was greater when weightlifting progressions were included in the combined resistance training program. Interestingly, the first 14 wee

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: gymnastics training (160). The study adopted a linear periodized approach to training with a large proportion of time devoted to general preparatory training. The gains in athleticism reported exceeded those of both of a gymnastics-only and a non-gymnastics control group. Interestingly, this study demonstrated a temporal response to training, like the findings of Pichardo and colleagues (187). Significant improvements were observed in different physical attributes over time. After four months, isometric absolute peak force and standing broad jump showed notable increases. By seven months, improvements were seen in countermovement jump height, modified reactive strength index, and drop jump height. Finally, at the 10-month mark, enhancements were noted in peak sprint speed, spring-like behavior, and vaulting vertical takeoff velocity. This study underscores the benefits of long-term engagement in strength and conditioning and that some adaptations take time to materialize, especially in less mature children. Changes in muscle hypertrophy can significantly contribute to training-induced strength gains in adolescents and adults, yet it is unlikely that muscle hypertrophy is primarily responsible for training- induced strength gains (at least up to 20 weeks) in preadolescents (179, 197). Although some findings do not agree with this suggestion, preadolescents appear to experience more difficulty increasing their muscle mass through a resistance training program due to inadequate

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: improvements in motor skill performance, and the coordination of the involved muscle groups could be partly responsible for training- induced strength gains in preadolescents (197). One cannot state without qualification, however, that resistance training does not result in muscle hypertrophy in preadolescents, because it is possible that longer study durations, higher training volumes, and more precise measuring techniques (e.g., computerized imaging) may be needed to uncover potential training-induced muscle hypertrophy in youth who are following a resistance training program. Researchers have reported novel data showing that prepubertal female gymnasts significantly improved muscle thickness (as measured by 2D ultrasound) in addition to measures of isometric peak force and stretch-shortening cycle function following exposure to a 10-month neuromuscular training intervention (161). While muscle thickness is not a direct measure of muscle size or volume, it has been positively correlated with muscle anatomical cross-sectional area (77). The data from Moeskops and colleagues (161) indicate that some change in muscle architecture might be possible even in prepubertal children when they are exposed to long-term neuromuscular interventions. During and after puberty, training-induced gains in strength are typically associated with gains in muscle hypertrophy and architecture (85, 195) due to hormonal influences and ongoing neural adaptations (86). Although lower levels of testost

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: with resistance training. Neurological factors, as opposed to hypertrophic factors, are primarily responsible for these gains. In addition to increasing muscular strength, muscular power, and muscular endurance, regular participation in a youth resistance training program has the potential to influence many other health- and fitness-related measures (84, 132, 139). Resistance exercise may favorably alter selected anatomic structures (128, 223), psychosocial parameters (25, 147), and academic outcomes (200) in youth. In addition, ongoing participation in resistance training has been found to reduce injuries in sport and recreational activities (186, 224) and improve motor skills and powerful sporting movements (14, 40, 177).
