text: From a clinical perspective, it has been reported that muscular fitness is associated with lower obesity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular risk among children and adolescents (43, 84). Of note, meta-analytical data indicate that resistance training can reduce body fat in children and adolescents who are overweight or obese (153). The grades for indicators of youth physical activity around the world are low, which suggests a widespread crisis of physical inactivity (6). Children who are obese or those who lead sedentary lives (e.g., who take a bus to school and watch television or play computer games after school and on weekends) are not ready for 1 to 2 hours of sport training four or five days a week. Current global findings based on a pooled analysis of 3,663 population-representative studies with 222 million children, adolescents, and adults found the burden of obesity has increased and the age of onset of obesity has decreased in most countries (39). Specific to the United States, data from 2013 to 2016 show that 17.8% (95% confidence interval [CI], 16.1%-19.6%) of American youth aged 2 through 19 years were obese and the prevalence of severe obesity was 5.8% (95% CI, 4.8%-6.9%) (174), and the prevalence of many cardiovascular disease risk factors are projected to increase over the next 30 years (118). Although the treatment of childhood obesity is complex, it seems that obese youth enjoy resistance training because it is not aerobically taxing and provides an oppor

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: might benefit the most are the ones who are less fit to begin with. This notion underlines the importance of practitioners understanding and advocating for long-term athletic development as a fundamental concept for all youth (137). While resistance training does not affect the genotypic maximum, it probably has a favorable influence on growth at any stage of development, as long as appropriate guidelines are followed (70). In fact, regular participation in an exercise program that includes resistance training and weight-bearing physical activities has been shown to enhance bone mineral density in children and adolescents (50, 221). In support of these observations, it has been reported that elite adolescent weightlifters who regularly train with heavy weights while performing multijoint exercises display levels of bone density well above values of age-matched controls (41, 180). These findings may be especially important for girls who are at an increased risk for developing osteoporosis later in life, a clinical condition characterized by low bone mass and an increased susceptibility to fractures (231). Every year, millions of physical activity–related injuries occur during leisure time and sport participation among children and adolescents (23, 196), and it has been estimated that more than 50% of overuse injuries sustained by children could be prevented with simple approaches including coaching education, preparatory conditioning, delayed specialization, adequate time off

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: young soccer players has been shown to decline throughout a competitive season (143) and that injury incidence fluctuates during different phases of the season (e.g., immediately after returning from annual holiday periods) (198, 226), it is prudent for youth to look beyond resistance training as a preseason activity and instead continue to engage in a modified and periodized resistance training program throughout the competitive season and during the postseason and off-season to reduce the risk of subsequent injury. The goal should be for all children and adolescents to engage in long-term, periodized athletic development programs (inclusive of resistance exercise) rather than short-term programs to enhance physical fitness and reduce the risk of injury. Early sport specialization is defined as children engaging in intensive, year-round (>8 months) training and/or competition in a single sport, typically beginning during the prepubertal years (131). Traditional early specialization sports included gymnastics, dance, and swimming; however, there is a growing trajectory of youth opting to specialize in other sports at younger ages (21). In many cases, early sport specialization results in young athletes accumulating weekly training volumes that exceed recommended guidelines (21, 202). Even though some coaches argue that early sport specialization is the key to success, this notion has been challenged in the literature (21, 114, 131). Notably, meta-analytical data from 51 studi

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: overtraining and potential burnout (22, 47). Additionally, it seems that late specialization and involvement in a variety of sports and activities during the younger years may be better related to sporting success at a later age (21, 72, 78, 96, 159). Although the total elimination of youth sport injuries is an unrealistic goal, the addition of resistance training as part of a long-term athletic development program may better prepare the young athlete to handle the duration and magnitude of unanticipated forces that develop in practice and game situations (65, 106), whether or not they have specialized. Because of individual differences in growth, maturation, and stress tolerance, resistance training intensity, volume, and rate of progression need to be carefully prescribed since this form of training adds to the chronic repetitive stress placed on the developing musculoskeletal system. Proper progression and program variation will optimize gains, prevent boredom, and reduce the stress that can lead to overtraining. This will be particularly effective when practitioners use reliable data to help inform decision-making around program design, and this evidence-informed approach will also work well with those young athletes who have specialized (163). Additionally, well-planned recovery strategies (e.g., proper cool- down, postexercise meal or snack, and adequate sleep) can help to maximize training adaptations. Potential Risks and Concerns Appropriately prescribed youth resistance training programs are relatively safe when compared with other sports and activities in which children and adolescents regularly participate (139, 181). Paradoxically, it seems that the forces placed on the joints of young athletes during sport participation may be far greater, and more difficult to anticipate, than those generated from resistance training programs (65). The belief that resistance training is dangerous for children is not consistent with the needs of children and the documented risks associated with this type of training. Children and adolescents have been injured in the weight room; however, such injuries are more likely to be accidental (98, 169) and typically occur in cases in which the levels of supervision and instruction, technical competency, and training loads are inappropriate (65). This highlights the need for strength and conditioning professionals to heed safety guidelines when working with younger populations. Although epiphyseal plate fractures have been reported in adolescents who were resistance training, these reports were case studies and typically involved the performance of heavy overhead lifts in unsupervised settings (97, 203, 207). An epiphyseal plate fracture has not been reported in any prospective youth resist

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: guidelines and procedures, the risk of an epiphyseal plate fracture is minimal. Dispelling the Myths of Youth Resistance Training A wealth of evidence proves children and adolescents can safely and effectively engage in resistance training to promote improvements in physical fitness, reduce the risk of sport-related injury, and enhance measures of health and well-being. However, there still remain certain unfounded myths among some health professionals that may deter youth from engaging in resistance training (67). Resistance training stunts bone growth. False! Resistance training stimulates bone remodeling and strengthens bone, muscular tissue, and connective tissue during childhood and adolescence. Resistance training is unsafe for children. False! With correct technique, appropriate loading, and high-quality instruction, resistance training is a safe method of training for all youth. Resistance training is only for young athletes. False! Resistance training promotes positive physical and psychosocial adaptations in all youth, regardless of whether they participate in competitive sports. Children need to wait until puberty to realize the benefits of resistance training. False! Research clearly shows that young children can make meaningful gains in physical fitness following resistance training. Children should be psychologically mature enough to understand and follow instructions. Young girls and boys will become “bulky.” False! Studies have shown that resistance training d

A pretraining medical examination is not mandatory for apparently healthy children; however, all participants should be screened for any injury or illness that may limit or prevent safe participation in a resistance training program (215). The goals of youth resistance training programs should not be limited to increasing muscular strength but should also include teaching children about their bodies, promoting an interest in physical activity, teaching weight room etiquette, and having fun. It seems likely that children who enjoy participating in physical activities and sport are more likely to be active later in life (220). Two important areas of concern in the development of youth resistance training programs are the quality of instruction and rate of progression. Strength and conditioning professionals must have a thorough understanding of youth resistance training guidelines, an ability and willingness to demonstrate proper exercise technique, and the requisite pedagogical skills to speak with children at a level they understand (59, 137, 139). Professionals should deemphasize competition between participants and focus on proper technique instead of the amount of weight lifted. To optimize any training program, practitioners should conduct an initial assessment of the individual’s characteristics (i.e., physical, technical, psychosocial) and the demands of the sport or physical activity in which he or she participates, commonly known as a needs analysis. With this information collated, practitioners can then adopt an appropriate assessment battery on relevant measures of physical performance and injury risk, in addition to estimations of maturity status. Similarly, consideration should be given to the long- term aspirations of the child prior to finalizing the training program. Of course, it should be recognized that the level of sophistication and rigor of the needs analysis and assessment process is context specific; completing this preliminary work is far easier for a practitioner working one on one with a small number of children in a private facility compared to another teacher or coach working in a high school setting that is responsible for the programming of hundreds of school-aged children. Regardless of the situation, it is important to have some understanding of the current training status of the child to know how to construct the program. However, strength and conditioning professionals should recognize that such approaches might place the child at heightened risk of injury due to the cumulative fatiguing effects of multiple repetitions on technical form. In order to obtain a surrogate measure of muscular strength without the use of repetition maximum schemes, practitioners could use field-based measures of different jump protocols (e.g., vertical jump or long jump) or handgrip strength, measures that have been significantly correlated to 1RM values in youth (29, 157). Irrespective of the strength testing protocol used, the child or adolescent must be able to demonstrate and maintain correct technical competency throughout the entire test under the watchful eye of a qualified professional. Advanced multijoint exercises such as the snatch and clean and jerk can be incorporated into a child’s program at the appropriate time (i.e., after foundational strength and technique progressions have been completed), but the primary focus, especially early in a resistance training program, should be on developing motor skill competency and muscle strength (168, 194). The athletic motor skill competencies (AMSC) have been proposed to represent the foundational movements that underpin all athletic movements (figure 7.4; 194). text: Youth Resistance Training Guidelines Each child should understand the benefits and risks associated with resistance training. Competent and caring strength and conditioning professionals should design and supervise training sessions based primarily on the desired training adaptation and technical competency but also with consideration to growth and maturation. The exercise environment should be safe and free of hazards, and the equipment should be appropriately sized to fit each child. Dynamic warm-up exercises, movement challenges, and opportunities for exploratory play should be performed before resistance training. When appropriate, static stretching exercises should be performed after resistance training. Carefully monitor each child’s tolerance to the exercise stress. Begin with light loads to allow appropriate adjustments to be made. Increase the resistance gradually (e.g., 5%-10%) as technique and strength improve. Depending on individual needs and goals, different set × repetition combinations (e.g., 3 × 5) can be performed on a variety of single- and multijoint exercises (and those targeting the strengthening of the core musculature). Advanced multijoint exercises, such as the snatch and clean and jerk, may be incorporated into the program, provided that appropriate loads are used and technical proficiency remains a key outcome. text: Older Adults The number of men and women over the age of 65 continues to rise, and more opportunities for participation in sports ranging from marathon running to weightlifting are available to older athletes. While the cardiovascular endurance and muscular strength of older competitors or masters athletes are truly exceptional, even the most highly trained athletes experience some decline in performance after age 30 (83, 107). For example, competitive weightlifting ability has been shown to decline with age at a rate of approximately 1% to 1.5% per year until approximately age 70, after which a more dramatic decrease occurs (152). Older individuals who do not engage in physical activity typically see greater decrements in several physical performance measures and increase their risk of debilitating injury (95, 182). Strength and conditioning professionals should understand the physiological changes that occur with aging and the associated trainability of older individuals. In addition, the potential health risks associated with physical activity for older individuals need to be considered. Age-Related Changes in Musculoskeletal Health Significant changes in body composition with advancing age can lead to the development of physical functional impairments and injury. The well-documented loss of bone and muscle with age not only makes activities of daily life such as getting out of a chair and opening a window more difficult but also increases the risk for falls, fractures, an

text: density between −1 and −2.5 standard deviations (SD) of the young adult mean, whereas osteoporosis is defined by a bone mineral density below −2.5 SD of the young adult mean (119). These conditions, which result in bones with less density and strength, are serious concerns for older people (particularly women) because they heighten the risk of skeletal fracture and poor bone health (2). The slow but progressive loss of bone with age has been linked to physical inactivity and to hormonal, nutritional, mechanical, and genetic factors (7, 11). Computed tomography has revealed that after age 30 there is a decrease in the cross-sectional areas of individual muscles, along with a decrease in muscle density, reductions in tendon compliance, 419

text: and an increase in intramuscular fat (2, 110). These changes seem to be a predictable consequence of advancing age and seem to be most pronounced in women (110). The observed muscle atrophy with aging appears to result from physical inactivity and a gradual and selective denervation of type II muscle fibers (136, 192, 237). Decreased muscle mass results in a loss of muscle strength. In one report, 40% of women aged 55 to 64 years, 45% of women aged 65 to 74 years, and 65% of women aged 75 to 84 years were unable to lift about 10 pounds (4.5 kg) (115). The reduction in the size and number and the gradual denervation of muscle fibers (100, 192) and the age-related changes in motor unit morphology and properties (108, 204) also lead to a decrease in the ability of a muscle to generate power (i.e., exert force rapidly); in fact, power recedes at a faster rate than muscle strength with aging (79). Since everyday activities require a certain degree of power production, a decrease in the ability of muscles to produce force rapidly may adversely affect the ability of older adults to safely perform activities such as stair climbing and walking. Factors that may contribute to the age-related decline in muscle strength and power include reductions in muscle mass, nervous system changes, hormonal changes, poor nutrition, and physical inactivity (16, 112). The functional consequences of these age-related changes are significant because the magnitude and rate of change influence the age at

A direct result of these losses is a decrease in functional independence and an increased risk of falls and fractures. Age-Related Changes in Neuromuscular Function Seniors are at an increased risk of falling, which can lead to serious health, psychosocial, and economic consequences that negatively affect overall quality of life. Specifically, falls can result in pain syndromes, joint dislocations, skeletal fractures, limitations on daily functional activities, and a reduction in self-confidence (95, 211). Falls can also lead to permanent disability, institutionalization, and fatalities (46). Intrinsic factors that lead to increased risk of falls in seniors include decrements in muscle strength and power (190), reaction time (2), and impaired balance and postural stability (205). Muscle activity before (preactivation) and immediately following (cocontraction) contact with the ground is an important mediator of braking and dynamic stabilization in both

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: limb using fast stretch reflexes to better prepare the limb for ground contact. Cocontraction is a motor control strategy that dynamically stabilizes the joint; however, due to the simultaneous activation of both the agonist and antagonist muscle groups crossing the same joint, net joint moments and agonistic force outputs are reduced (236). Research shows that seniors rely on increased levels of muscle cocontraction as a compensatory mechanism to offset their increased balance difficulties and to minimize postural sway (171). Research also highlights that reduced mechanical power output when walking (especially during the push-off phase) of is one of the biomechanical aging features of gait (45). Intuitively, this literature would suggest that older adults should use a variety of training modes specifically designed to offset these natural reductions in neuromuscular function. Such methods include low-intensity plyometrics, strength training, balance and dynamic stabilization exercises, and proprioception training to develop the ability to react more efficiently with the ground (92, 95, 189). Physical activity interventions can be effective in improving neuromuscular function and preventing falls in seniors (95, 112, 222). However, simply increasing physical activity will not prevent falls on its own. Rather, seniors must engage with, and adhere to, multidimensional, periodized programs that incorporate elements of both resistance and balance training (76, 112, 222). Further

Notably, maximal aerobic power decreases with age in adults as a consequence of various physiological changes that accompany aging; for example, muscle mass and strength decreased (130) and fat mass increases (129), with men showing a more rapid decline than women (233). On average, when women and men are matched by age, the aerobic power values of women range from 73% to 85% of the values of men (229); however, the general physiological response to training in later life is equivocal between men and women (4, 183). The differences in aerobic power may be caused by several factors, including women’s higher percentage of body fat and lower blood hemoglobin values and men’s larger heart size and blood volume (24, 34). Notwithstanding the importance of a varied training program, the relative importance and potency of resistance training in increasing muscular strength, muscular power, and bone mineral density, while counteracting the age-related declines in contractile function and muscle atrophy, in addition to its many other health benefits for seniors, cannot be overlooked (76). Resistance Training for Older Adults Aging does not appear to enhance or reduce the ability of the musculoskeletal system to adapt to resistance exercise, and as a training mode, resistance training can be an efficacious tool against the declines associated with sarcopenia (28). Resistance training can also improve mobility and enhance physical functioning that enable seniors to perform activities of daily living (ADL) and preserve independence (76). Furthermore, data also show that muscular strength is an important factor for reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer mortality, and all-cause mortality (87, 164). Resistance training provides a highly effective means of attenuating physiological changes associated with aging, improving physical function, and decreasing the risk of chronic health conditions. Responsiveness to Resistance Training in Older Adults A great deal of attention has focused on strategies to improve the musculoskeletal health of older men and women. Because of the deconditioned state of many seniors, desirable changes in muscle strength and function can result from a variety of resistance training protocols, particularly during the first few weeks of training (82). Previously sedentary older men have more than doubled knee extensor strength and tripled knee flexor strength following a 12- week resistance training program (80), and similar observations have been made in older women after 12 weeks of resistance training (33). In a seminal study, the ability of very old men and women (87- 96 years old) to improve muscular strength was demonstrated following only eight weeks of resistance training (73). Meta- analytical data has indicated that in a sample of more than 800 seniors

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: scale (117). Collectively, resistance training appears to be an effective means to mitigate age-related dynapenia (76). Improvements in gait speed, stair-climbing ability, balance, and overall spontaneous activity have also been associated with training- induced strength gains in older populations (145). Declines in muscle power are associated with disability and the ability to perform ADL, particularly in females (112), and the need to minimize age-related deficits in muscle power is an important part of exercise prescription for seniors (76, 112). Evidence indicates that resistance training specific to power development may help optimize functional abilities in older adults (2, 92, 178) and that power training may be as effective as traditional resistance training in developing muscle architecture and neuromuscular activation properties of the lower limb (230). In some instances, it has been suggested that high- velocity power training has a greater influence on the ability to produce explosive force than traditional progressive resistance training (92, 191). For example, Fielding and colleagues (74) showed that older adults who completed high-velocity resistance training made greater gains in peak power and similar gains in maximum strength compared to seniors who trained at slower velocities over a 16-week training period. Similar results were reported by Reid and colleagues (199); in that study, older adults who completed a high- velocity, high-power resistance training

Meta-analytical data have indicated that resistance training is also an effective treatment to improve body fat mass and for muscle strength and performance in seniors diagnosed with sarcopenia (35). Resistance training has also been shown to have an important effect on energy balance in older adults, as evidenced by an increase in the resting metabolic rate of men and women who resistance train (26). It is noteworthy that dietary modifications (a change in total food intake or selected nutrients) in addition to resistance training promotes a greater hypertrophic response than resistance training alone in older men (154). Although the response of bone to resistance exercise is influenced by a complex interaction of many variables (e.g., hormonal status, activity history, and nutrition), it has been reported that resistance exercise has a positive effect on bone health in older men and women (103, 173). Regularly performed resistance training can offset the age-related declines in bone health by maintaining or increasing bone mineral density (BMD). text: Collectively, these studies show the transient nature of neuromuscular adaptations and underline the importance of viewing resistance training as a lifelong commitment. Resistance training may also reduce the risk of osteoporotic fractures by improving dynamic balance, muscle mass, and overall level of physical activity (2). While resistance exercise undoubtedly can improve bone health in older adults, the interaction of exercise with hormonal and nutritional factors influences the degree of benefit of the exercise program. Furthermore, bones retain the beneficial effects of exercise only as long as training is continued. During periods of inactivity, bone density tends to revert to preexercise levels (111). Older men and women can make significant improvements in strength, power, mobility, and functional ability in response to periodized and progressive resistance training. Aerobic, resistance, and balance exercise are all beneficial for older adults, but only resistance training can increase muscular strength, muscular power, and muscle mass. Program Design Considerations for Older Adults Resistance training is currently recognized as an important component of a well-rounded fitness program for older adults (2, 76, 112). Because age-related losses of musculoskeletal strength, power, and mass may be almost universal, programs designed to maintain or improve musculoskeletal health in older adults should be implemented. Even though older populations retain the capacity to adapt to increased levels of physical activity, safe and effective exercise guidelines must be followed. Before participation in an exercise program, seniors should complete a medical history and risk factor questionnaire (76). Potential limitations and possible restrictions for physical activity can be ascertained from this information. In some cases, physician clearance is required before the initiation of a moderate or vigorous exercise program (76)—for example, in cardiac rehabilitation patients or cancer survivors. Any questions regarding a participant’s medical status (e.g., heart disease, hypertension, arthritis, osteoporosis, or diabetes mellitus) should be answered by a health professional. After this information has been obtained, a preprogram evaluation to document baseline measurements and assess responses to specific exercise modalities should be performed. Although a treadmill exercise test is often used to evaluate cardiovascular responses to aerobic exercise, a strength test (preferably on the equipment used in training) should be performed to assess responses to resistance exercise and aid in the exercise prescription. Evidence suggests that resistance training can be safe for seniors when individuals adhere to appropriate training guidelines (2, 76, 112). On the other hand, poorly designed programs can be potentially hazardous. For example, failing to provide sufficient rest periods between sets and between different exercises, programming exercises that are technically too challenging, or increasing the intensity of exercise (typically the external load against which the individual is working) all increase the likelihood of resistance training–related injury. Like the situation with youth populations, the resistance training stimulus should not be increased at the expense of technical competency for older adults. Untrained seniors who begin resistance training should start at a relatively low exercise intensity and volume, and the exercise prescription should be individualized (76). During the early stages of a resistance training program for older adults, investing in education, reducing anxieties, and building confidence are key outcomes to promote long-term engagement. text: Dispelling the Fears of Resistance Training for Older Adults Despite the publicized benefits of resistance exercise for older adults, misperceptions remain about the notion of lifting weights. Literature has noted the phenomenon of a “fear of resistance exercise,” which can lead to older adults demonstrating avoidance behavior to resistance exercise due to apprehension, anxiety, or a lack of confidence (4). Similarly, a lack of awareness or understanding can be a barrier to older adults participating in resistance exercise, which underlines the importance of correct education and the promotion of individualized approaches (31, 109). To dispel the fears of resistance training, certain key messages should be promoted to older populations: Resistance training can cause injury to the musculoskeletal system in older adults. False! When programs are technique focused, individualized, and designed and delivered by appropriately qualified professionals, resistance training is a safe and effective mode of training for older adults and can promote positive adaptations in both muscle and bone (76). Resistance training is not safe for older adults with cardiovascular or musculoskeletal contraindications. False! Resistance training can easily be modified to accommodate for such contraindications. Initially training at lower volumes and intensities, avoiding the Valsalva maneuver, reducing ranges of motion, and simplifying exercise variants are some of the ways in which prescription can ac

chapterTitle: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: mass, strength, and power are important for performing ADLs and physical independence. A resistance training program for older men and women should vary in volume and intensity throughout the year to lessen the likelihood of overtraining and ensure that progress is made throughout the training period. Because recovery from a training session may take longer in older populations, a training frequency of two or three sessions per week is recommended, at least during the initial adaptation period (76, 112). Strength and conditioning professionals should be sensitive to the concerns of individuals and be able to modify a training program based on the person’s health history and individual goals. With competent instruction and support from friends, older men and women can gain confidence in their ability to resistance train, which may be enough to ensure good adherence to the program. However, since a majority of older adults do not currently engage in resistance training activities (54, 122, 213), professionals may initially need to increase awareness of the fitness benefits associated with resistance exercise, address the concerns that seniors may have about participating in a resistance training program, and adapt the exercises and intensity to the needs of the participants. Safety Recommendations for Resistance Training for Older Adults Older adult participants should be prescreened, since many older people suffer from a variety of age-related medical conditions. If necessary,

text: Older adults should use a resistance intensity that does not excessively overload the musculoskeletal system. Participants should avoid performing the Valsalva maneuver during resistance training to avoid an abnormal increase in blood pressure. Older adults should be allowed 48 to 72 hours of recovery between exercise sessions. They should perform all exercises within a range of motion that is pain free. As with any individual engaging with resistance training, older adults should receive individualized exercise instruction from qualified instructors. Researchers have reported that social support, access to qualified fitness professionals, improving the ability to complete daily activities, and decreasing the fear and likelihood of falls are some of the motivators for older adults consistently engaging in resistance and balance exercise. An additional consideration related to resistance training in older men and women is appropriate nutrition. The quality and quantity of a person’s food intake (or perhaps selected nutrients) may mean the difference between losing and gaining muscle mass. It seems that adequate amounts of protein are essential for muscle hypertrophy in older people (126, 151). Furthermore, inadequate intakes of macronutrients (fat, protein, and carbohydrate) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) are associated with potential negative health consequences, including fatigue, compromised immune function, and delayed recovery from injury. text: Conclusion Based upon the available research, resistance training can be a safe and effective method of conditioning for males and females of all ages and abilities. The potential benefits are multifactorial, including positive effects on a variety of physical performance variables (e.g., strength and power), health markers (e.g., body composition and cardiac function), and psychosocial development (e.g., self-image, confidence, well-being). Moreover, regular participation in a resistance training program can reduce the risk of sport- and physical activity–related injuries in athletes and nonathletes of all ages and abilities and promote independent living in seniors. Though the fundamental principles of resistance training are similar for people of all ages, there are unique concerns specific to youth and senior populations. Knowledge of age- and maturity-related differences is essential to the development and evaluation of safe and effective resistance training programs. Strength and conditioning professionals should be aware that individual responses to resistance exercise may vary greatly and should be sensitive to the individual needs of all participants. Over the past few decades, coaches, clinicians, and exercise scientists have added to our understanding of age- and maturity- related differences and their implications for resistance exercise. text: CHAPTER 8 SEX-RELATED DIFFERENCES AND THEIR IMPLICATIONS FOR RESISTANCE TRAINING N. Travis Triplett, PhD, and Nicole Dabbs, PhD After completing this chapter, you will be able to discuss sex-related differences in physical characteristics and muscular function and the implications for resistance training in females; recognize common injuries and conditions in females; discuss responses and adaptations to resistance training in females; and understand resistance training recommendations for females. Strength and conditioning professionals need to understand sex- related differences in physical characteristics, body composition, and physiological responses to resistance exercise when designing and evaluating resistance training programs for females. An understanding of these differences and the areas of concern that are unique to female athletes can help to optimize performance and decrease the risk of sport-related injuries. 438

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: Implications of Resistance Training for Females Females who regularly participate in resistance training activities can improve their health, reduce their risk of degenerative diseases (e.g., osteoporosis) and their injury rates, and enhance their overall sporting performance. Whereas in the past females may have questioned the value of resistance training or even avoided this type of exercise due to social stigma, evidence clearly indicates that females are capable of tolerating and adapting to the stresses of resistance exercise and that the benefits are substantial (93). Furthermore, to enhance health and fitness and reduce injury rates, it is now suggested that resistance training be an essential component of any exercise or training program that females follow (127, 128, 167). Physical Changes in Early Adulthood While differences in growth and development between boys and girls are covered in chapter 7, a few physical developmental changes continue into early adulthood. On average, females mature earlier than males (105), and most measures of female growth and maturation are complete by around age 18. Some exceptions include the growth plates, which typically close by the age of 20, and peak bone density (around age 30) (105). However, neither of these are undeveloped enough to result in a higher risk of injury from training, including activities such as high-intensity or high-load plyometrics (2, 122). The brain also continues to develop throughout the 20s, but most of

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: benefits beyond improvements in athletic performance due to improved reaction time and cognitive processing include a reduction in the risk of falls later in life (2). During puberty the production of estrogen in girls increases fat deposition and breast development, whereas testosterone production in boys increases bone formation and protein synthesis. Though estrogen also stimulates bone growth, boys have a longer growth period and commence puberty at a later stage, and therefore adult men tend to achieve greater overall stature than adult women (2). On average, adult females tend to have more body fat, less muscle, and lower bone mineral density than adult males. Furthermore, females tend to be lighter in total body weight than males. Anthropometric measurements of adults indicate that males tend to have broader shoulders relative to their hips and females tend to have broader hips relative to their waist and shoulders. The broader shoulders in males can support more muscle tissue and can also provide a mechanical advantage for muscles acting at the shoulder. Although some female athletes have lower fat percentages than untrained males, extremely low body fat percentages in females may be associated with adverse health consequences (124, 125). Maintaining skeletal muscle mass and bone mineral density is important for both athletic performance and health. Without a sustained resistance training program, muscle mass and bone density begin a pattern of decline in the mid-30s,

text: A key focus of any resistance training program for a female should be to maintain muscle mass and bone mineral density, both of which are important for athletic performance and overall health. Pregnancy Pregnancy occurs only when pubertal sexual development is complete and prior to menopause (average age between 12-51 years). There are significant and specific physiological and anatomical changes that occur during each of the trimesters of pregnancy and postpartum periods, which can affect physical training and performance (table 8.1). Multiple professional organizations have recommendations for physical activity and exercise during pregnancy (20, 21, 26, 123, 188). All of the published guidelines promote exercise as a minimal- risk activity that has benefits for most females during pregnancy, with some modifications to programming and specific exercises required as pregnancy progresses due to normal anatomic and physiologic changes that occur. These guidelines are presented in table 8.2. For pregnant females, program design variables (exercise selection, frequency, intensity, and duration) should be based on the baseline level of fitness of the athlete immediately prior to the confirmation of pregnancy. Resistance training at a moderate intensity during pregnancy has many benefits including improved blood sugar levels and improved insulin usage, as well as improved feelings of energy and reduction of fatigue (181). text: Anterior Cruciate Ligament It is important for strength and conditioning professionals to be aware of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries in female athletes, particularly in sports such as soccer, lacrosse, and basketball (3, 4). According to a number of reports, ACL injuries occur in greater absolute frequencies in males (122), but in comparable sports female athletes’ relative rate of ACL injuries is two times higher than those reported for male athletes (3, 4, 78, 86, 114). Although it is possible that the increasing absolute number of knee injuries simply reflects an increase in participation by females in organized sport, others have suggested causative factors. It is possible that the high muscular resistance and knee torque during high-load landing and rapid change-of-direction movements may cause microdamage or strain on the ACL over time, increasing the risk for injury for all athletes (12, 187). However, female athletes may have other factors contributing to an increase in the rate of ACL injury, such as anatomical, biomechanical, and external factors. Anatomical factors, such as femoral notch size reducing tensile strength, greater tibial slope increasing strain, and ligament laxity (45, 74, 98, 163), may contribute to heightened ACL injury risk in females. However, it is believed that the most significant contributing factor is a neuromuscular deficiency, which ultimately leads to abnormal biomechanics such as increased dynamic knee valgus upon contact with

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: agility, and balance training that is designed and delivered by a strength and conditioning professional critical to reducing the risk of ACL injuries (6, 51, 79, 183). Additional clinical trials are needed to determine the best method for reducing the incidence of ACL injuries in female athletes and improving adherence to these training protocols. Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is a broad term used for pain arising from the patellofemoral joint, also known as runner’s knee or jumper’s knee (24). Female athletes are more than two times more likely to have incidences of PFPS compared to male athletes (25). PFPS has been shown to be attributed to the hip mechanics in female athletes before puberty, and modified mechanics in the knee may be related to PFPS throughout development in female athletes (60). Strength and conditioning professionals should focus on lower extremity biomechanics, exercise technique, imbalances, and weaknesses with any athlete experiencing PFPS to improve outcomes. The National Athletic Trainers’ Association has a position statement that provides guidance to practitioners on how to manage patellofemoral pain in athletes, including use of bracing, taping, or other modifications (24). Bone Stress Injuries Bone stress injuries, including stress fractures, have regularly been shown to occur at a higher rate in female athletes than in male athletes (34, 153). The accumulation of repetitive stress, bone stress injuries frequent

text: risk factors could be identified through a screening process for bone stress injuries, such as vitamin D levels and early sport specialization (1, 180). Continuing to prescribe exercises that are osteogenically stimulating and alerting workload through periodization may assist in reducing bone stress injuries for female athletes. Concussions A concussion, or mild traumatic brain injury, is an impact to the head or body that causes the brain to move rapidly back and forth in the skull, which disrupts normal brain function (73). Female athletes are at an increased incidence of sport-related concussions in some sports (soccer, basketball, softball), with hockey having the highest incidence of concussions compared to male athletes in similar sports (35, 41, 133). Female athletes have been shown to have twice the rate of contact with equipment and surfaces compared to male athletes. However, player-to-player contact has been shown to be similar in both female and male athletes for causing concussions (32, 97). Other factors, such as biomechanical and hormonal differences, may lead to a greater susceptibility of concussions in female athletes (109, 151, 161). Female athletes experience longer recovery time with prolonged symptoms after a concussion compared to male athletes (32, 41, 109, 161). text: How Can Female Athletes Reduce Their Injury Risk? To help female athletes reduce their injury risk, strength and conditioning professionals should do the following: Recommend preparticipation screening by a sports medicine physician. This should include identification of risk factors for injury along with musculoskeletal testing. Encourage female athletes to participate in a year-round conditioning program that includes resistance, plyometric, speed and agility, and flexibility training. The conditioning program should meet the specific needs of each athlete and should progress in a periodized fashion that allows for training adaptations to continually manifest. Ensure that females learn, and can repeatedly demonstrate, correct movement mechanics (e.g., jumping, landing, twisting, and cutting) within a variety of environments. Precede every exercise session with a general dynamic warm-up and a specific warm-up using movements that resemble those involved in the activity and that target the activation of key muscle groups (e.g., posterior chain muscle groups). Provide augmented feedback within training sessions to optimize skill transfer and enhance biomechanics related to injury. Mental Health Mental health has gained increasingly more attention in athletes with a focus on sport organizations and practitioners to take a holistic approach when training athletes (33, 57, 77, 149). Athletes are exposed to additional mental health risk factors (77, 149), and female athletes in pa

text: Research also suggests that elite female athletes are twice as likely to self-report symptoms of depression than male athletes (63), which may inhibit health and performance. In 2021, 40% of collegiate female athletes reported experiencing overwhelming anxiety compared to 22% in collegiate male athletes (189). Early detection of mental health issues is critical, and strength and conditioning practitioners should understand symptoms and how these issues arise and should promote and provide environments that support an athlete’s mental health, prevention, and treatment team and strategies of mental health disorders. Sleep A majority of athletes receive less-than-age-appropriate sleep levels, and a loss in sleep for athletes is a known risk factor for increased injury risk (15, 16, 157). Female collegiate athletes may be particularly likely to have low sleep durations that are consistent with sleep deprivation (<7 h/night), in association with daytime sleepiness and dysfunction (30, 69). Sleep quantity (113, 116) and quality have been shown to be lower after training and competition in female athletes (134, 136). Education on sleep hygiene for athletes, coaches, and support practitioners has been shown to address some barriers preventing good sleep quality and thus has been shown to improve sleep in athletes (115, 135). Improving sleep quality and quantity is critical for optimal recovery (178). Pelvic Floor Dysfunction Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) is a term used to identify v

text: exertion (22, 150). It has been reported that UI in female athletes occurs 5 times more compared to male athletes, and 2.7 times more compared to sedentary females (42, 150, 164, 172). Female athletes have an overall 27% prevalence of UI compared to male athletes, and a 36% prevalence of UI compared to sedentary females (42, 150, 164, 172). Participating in sport has been reported to be one of the main causes of UI in female athletes, with high-impact and high- loading sports increasing incidence of SUI. UI may be due to the imbalance of contraction strength and an increase in abdominal pressure that results in deformation of the connective tissue (99, 107). Programs should include prevention, lifestyle modifications, pelvic floor strengthening, biofeedback, and pharmacological interventions. Female athletes should be taught how to properly engage their pelvic floor muscles and abdominal wall muscles, and in some cases may need to see a physical therapist that specializes in PFD. With proper education and pelvic floor treatment, females can recover from UI (46, 55). How Can Females Improve Their Health Outcomes? chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: Training Responses and Adaptations Before resistance training programs can be properly designed, understanding the physiological responses to a resistance training session and adaptations to regularly performing a resistance training program are critical. The main body systems involved are the musculoskeletal, metabolic, and endocrine systems, which have varying levels of response and adaptation differences between males and females. These differences can affect how programming priorities are set, which is important for obtaining the optimum training results. Musculoskeletal Resistance training offers a multitude of benefits for females, including the attenuation of age-related declines in bone mineral density (89). Specifically, the stress from the mechanical loading applied via resistance training directly increases the magnitude of skeletal remodeling and therefore bone mass. Resistance training can increase bone mineral density in various skeletal regions of the body (89). It is also known that higher intensities of resistance training promote greater degrees of osteogenesis (103) and that preadolescence is an opportune time to participate in weight-bearing and other loaded activities in order to enhance bone mineral density (65, 80). Through participation in a resistance training program, females can also experience muscle hypertrophy. When sophisticated techniques (e.g., computed tomography) are used to accurately measure changes in muscle cross-sectional area, relative

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: may be less than in males. A genetic disposition to develop a large muscle mass may also be a contributing factor (166). Metabolic The metabolic system is a key system in physical activity, and understanding its function is necessary to understanding the acute responses and training adaptations of the other body systems. While the metabolic system operates similarly in males and females, some differences exist that relate to the amount and type of muscle mass, which can affect the magnitude of training-related adaptations. However, there is a lack of research comparing males and females of similar training backgrounds, as well as in high-level athletes, which limits the understanding of the metabolic system and how it adapts in female athletes. Anaerobic Energy The biochemical pathways that provide short-term energy include ATP-PCr and glycolysis. While all muscle fibers can produce energy with all types of biochemical pathways, the faster muscle fibers that have a greater capacity for force production have a greater amount of the substrates (phosphocreatine, glycogen) and enzymes needed for the nonoxidative biochemical pathways (see chapter 3). On average, males have a slightly higher proportion of these faster (type II) muscle fiber types (84, 165). While both males and females have the capacity to undergo muscle hypertrophy with various types of anaerobic training, as previously indicated, the level of absolute hypertrophy attained by males will exceed that of females, res

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: electron transport chain, and lipid oxidation), which continuously supply energy at rest and for lower intensity activities (62). The oxidative pathways depend on the cardiorespiratory system’s ability to supply oxygen and remove metabolic wastes, and research reviews have presented differences in males and females under various conditions (9, 29, 96, 186). Female endurance athletes have been shown to be more fatigue resistant during prolonged events, despite having overall lower aerobic capacity (V̇ O2max) relative to body size and slower performance times than males (17, 48). This is thought to be due to muscle fiber type distribution (165), with females having a greater proportion of type I oxidative fibers on average. Females therefore oxidize a greater amount of fat and a lesser amount of carbohydrate and protein (40, 170). This finding is supported by Cardinale (2018), who determined that females have close to 33% greater mitochondrial respiration than males. These differences may present an advantage to female athletes in most types of endurance activities, including ultraendurance events (174). Training adaptations in the aerobic energy pathways differ in magnitude between males and females with regard to the cardiovascular system in particular (145), which affects oxygen delivery to the muscle tissue and subsequent oxidative energy production. text: Endocrine The endocrine system is responsible for regulating physiological responses and adaptations to the various stressors encountered, including physical activity. In response to strength training and conditioning, the endocrine system regulates muscular repair and growth (58, 95) as the various anabolic and catabolic mechanisms triggered by the endocrine system affect the ability of skeletal muscle to generate force and to adapt to training (95). The immediate, or acute, endocrine response to a training session traditionally has been thought to be a greater catalyst for muscle tissue growth and remodeling than the chronic changes in resting hormonal concentrations (94). While a large number of hormones perform a myriad of functions within the human body, a much smaller number affect muscle responses to training, and even fewer have been the focus of research in athletic females. The primary hormones to have known influence on muscle and strength development, which have been studied in females, include testosterone, the growth hormone family, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and cortisol. It is also important to understand general function of the hormones involved in the menstrual cycle, because they can influence training and performance in female athletes and are found in much higher concentrations than in males. text: resistance exercise, females do not exhibit significant elevations in testosterone concentrations (95, 177). However, with prolonged training, some acute elevations in testosterone have been observed in females (137). These increases are likely due to a combination of factors including a decreased rate of degradation, evidenced by lower measures of metabolites of testosterone breakdown (49). Therefore, in females, testosterone likely still has an important role in the development of absolute muscular size, strength, and power with resistance training and may also be an important indicator of the trainability of an individual (67, 68). Growth Hormones and Growth Factors Growth hormones (GH) have a primary role in muscle tissue remodeling and repair but do not function alone, because muscle protein synthesis is triggered with the growth factor known as IGF-1. In females, it has been demonstrated that resting concentrations of GH are higher than in males (92) and with chronic training, GH levels at rest are lower in females compared to males (171), which could indicate a greater sensitivity to the hormone, but research is lacking. After chronic resistance training, circulating GH rises similarly in females and males. Following an acute resistance exercise bout in females, circulating GH concentrations increase two- to fourfold (66, 83). text: Cortisol Cortisol is an important hormone that helps regulate blood glucose levels as well as inflammation. Cortisol rises in anticipation of exercise and sport competition in order to prepare the body for the upcoming psychological and metabolic demands (118, 140). This anticipatory rise has been shown to be greater in trained females than in sedentary females (47). The cortisol response to acute exercise is greatest in resistance exercise protocols that result in higher levels of GH (91) and blood lactate (90). Several investigations have demonstrated that in comparison to males, the cortisol response to acute exercise is attenuated in females (58, 66, 140). This is thought to be due to higher cortisol sensitivity in females (156) or the impact of female sex hormones on modulating activity of the sympathetic nervous system, adrenal glands, and hypothalamus-pituitary axis (175). Training influences the magnitude of the cortisol response in females. Elite female athletes do not exhibit an anticipatory rise in cortisol before exercise (47) but do exhibit higher cortisol secretion and different patterns of secretion (158). In addition, female sex hormones (estradiol and progesterone) may lower cortisol responsivity, thereby potentially altering the effects of cortisol over the menstrual cycle (104). Immune factors modulate glucocorticoid sensitivity (59), accounting for differences observed in female athletes. The Menstrual Cycle Females experience the menstrual cycle during ad

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: training program. Therefore, it is important that practitioners have a general understanding of the menstrual cycle and its physical effects. In brief, two primary hormones are released from the ovaries during the menstrual cycle, estradiol and progesterone. During the initial half of the cycle, menstrual bleeding occurs and then estradiol peaks and drops. Progesterone rises and peaks during the second half of the cycle, and there is a second but lesser peak of estradiol. By the end of the cycle, both estradiol and progesterone drop to their lowest levels (figure 8.1). Estradiol In menstruating adult females, the primary form of estrogen is estradiol, which has been shown to directly affect the structure and function of muscle, tendon, and ligaments, as well as contribute to muscle mass and strength (37). Estradiol appears to have a more protective effect on skeletal muscle (100) by attenuating the amount of damage. To do this, estradiol may decrease postexercise membrane disruption, act as an antioxidant, act as a membrane stabilizer, and mediate inflammatory cell infiltration (53, 141). In addition, estradiol may influence contractile properties of skeletal muscle and muscle protein turnover (71). This supports muscle mass development by promoting protein synthesis over degradation and enhancing sensitivity of the response to resistance training (71, 72). chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: Resistance Training Considerations With resistance training, the primary goal is to improve strength and power. When comparing training-induced changes in muscular strength between sexes, it is important to distinguish between absolute and relative measures. Sex-related differences in hypertrophy and muscle mass (106, 132, 143) indicate that absolute muscle strength in females is lower than in males (108, 117), whereas males’ greater absolute strength is primarily achieved by larger muscle fiber size (117, 146, 160). The absolute lower body strength of females is generally closer to male values compared to the absolute values for upper body strength (10, 82, 84, 117). Sex- related differences in body composition, anthropometric characteristics, and distribution of fat-free mass can partly explain these sex-related differences, which are apparent in recreationally trained individuals as well as highly trained athletes (14). When considered on a relative basis, sex-related differences in muscular strength are greatly reduced. Females have similar number of muscle fibers as males, and strength is similar when normalized to muscle volume (113, 117). Differences in hypertrophy between males and females may be due to a variety of factors such as endocrine and genetics because they relate to regulating muscle mass (184), whereas factors such as muscle cross-sectional area and enzyme activity may contribute to strength and performance differences (85, 131, 162). Because the average m

text: Sex-related differences in power output are similar to those for muscular strength. Measurements comparing power outputs of female athletes relative to lean body mass were reported to be similar for lower body power and still presented differences for upper body power when compared to male athletes (10, 61). Although the data are equivocal, sex-related differences in the rate of force development (147, 148) and the recruitment differences in muscle activation where females express lower levels of type IIa fibers’ percent of myosin heavy chain isoform content (138, 139) could partly explain these findings. During progressive overload and targeted training, female athletes experience substantial power and strength increases similar to male athletes (64). In a recent study, maximal strength and vertical jump height were increased in collegiate volleyball players by using a combination of traditional resistance training exercises and weightlifting variations at various loads in addition to volleyball practice, over the course of about 2.5 years of training (88). Other research supports plyometrics in female basketball players and other velocity-based resistance training in cyclists to improve strength, power, and muscle hypertrophy (36, 119). It has also been reported that adding heavy strength training to a female athlete’s endurance training increased muscle strength, performance, and size without affecting endurance running performance or running economy (176). text: The most recent evidence on menstrual cycle and performance from meta-analyses did not conclude any systematic relationship between performance and menstrual cycle phase in trained female athletes (38, 50, 111, 112). Other considerations are necessary to consider, such as varying menstrual cycle symptoms among female athletes and the effect on their sleep and recovery during all stages of the menstrual cycle (110). Consequently, the current evidence does not support modifying prescription of resistance training based on a female athlete’s menstrual cycle phase. 461

chapterTitle: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training
text: Conclusion Evidence indicates that resistance exercise can be a safe and effective method of training for female athletes of all ages and abilities. The potential benefits are multifactorial, including positive effects on a variety of physical performance variables (e.g., strength and power), health markers (e.g., body composition and cardiac function), and psychosocial development (e.g., self-image and confidence). Moreover, regular participation in resistance training programs can better prepare female athletes to increase performance and decrease risk of injury. Though the fundamental principles of resistance training are similar for people of both sexes, there are unique considerations specific to female athletes. Knowledge of sex-related differences is essential to the development and evaluation of safe and effective resistance training programs. Strength and conditioning professionals should be aware that individual responses to resistance exercise may vary greatly independent of sex and should be sensitive to the individual needs of all participants. Over the past few decades, coaches, clinicians, and exercise scientists have added to our understanding of sex-related differences and their implications for resistance exercise. Their work has quantified the impact of resistance training on female athletes and has provided the foundation for recommendations about the design of strength and conditioning programs. Statler, Andrea M. DuBois, Bradley D. Hatfield, and Evan B. Brody to this chapter. chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: random, and variable practice and how to use these schedules to facilitate skill acquisition and learning; and understand different types of instructions and feedback and their application in a practice and performance setting. Excellence in athletic performance is the result of sound skill and physical training accompanied by optimal rest and recovery cycles and appropriate diet. The role of sport psychology is to help athletes achieve more consistent levels of performance at or near their physical potential by carefully managing their physical resources through appropriate psychological strategies and techniques. By understanding these strategies and techniques, strength and conditioning professionals can better design sport-specific and even position-specific training programs with the ultimate goal of maximizing performance. After introducing foundational concepts, we address how one’s mind, through cognition, can influence physical performance, and then we describe the ideal performance state—the ultimate goal of every athlete. In part, this state is marked by psychological and physiological efficiency (i.e., employing only the amount of mental and physical energy required to perform the task). We discuss the primary psychological influences—motivation, attention, and arousal—on skill acquisition and performance, citing several theories of how these phenomena can change psychomotor learning and athletic performance. chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: Role of Sport Psychology An athlete is someone who engages in a social comparison (i.e., competition) involving psychomotor skill or physical prowess (or both) in an institutionalized setting, typically under public scrutiny or evaluation. The essence of athletic competition involves comparing oneself to others and putting ego and self-esteem on the line in a setting that is bound by rules and regulations. The psychologically well-prepared athlete is characterized by efficiency of thought and behavior. Efficiency is typically associated with skilled performance, when actions are fluid and graceful, which conserves energy. The concept can also be extended to psychological activity; an efficient athlete adopts a task-relevant focus, not wasting attention on task- irrelevant processing such as worrying, catastrophizing, or thinking about other things such as critical external observers such as a coach or audience. Sport psychology is a multifaceted discipline, drawing on constructs of exercise science and psychological principles, that seeks to understand the influence of behavioral processes and cognitions on sport performance. Sport psychology is typically classified as a scientific field of study within sports medicine and has three major goals: Measuring psychological phenomena Investigating the relationships between psychological variables and performance Applying theoretical knowledge to improve athletic performance By applying the information gained through an awareness o

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: them for effective performance. Throughout this chapter we introduce a structure for understanding the interrelationships not only between the mental skills themselves but between the mental skills and the physical, technical, and tactical skills being developed in the weight room and on the practice field. Note, however, that these skills can only be truly effective if they are understood, practiced, and applied in a performance setting. Like the physical, technical, and tactical constructs described throughout the rest of this book, mental skills also need to be taught, practiced, integrated into performance, and evaluated for effectiveness. 468

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: Ideal Performance State The ideal performance state has been studied from a number of perspectives. Williams and Krane (68) listed the following characteristics that athletes typically report about this state: Absence of fear—no fear of failure No thinking about or analysis of performance (related to the motor stage of automaticity) A narrow focus of attention concentrated on the activity itself A sense of effortlessness—an involuntary experience A sense of personal control A distortion of time and space, in which time seems to slow In a sense, this ideal performance state seems to represent everything that applied sport psychology programs attempt to promote. There is an absence of negative self-talk, a strong feeling of efficacy, and an adaptive focus on task-relevant cues. An important aspect is that the athletes trust in their skill and conditioning levels and just let it happen, without interference from negative cognitive processes. Kobe Bryant, a premier player in the National Basketball Association, described being in this state, saying, When that happens, you really do not try to focus on what’s going on because … you could lose it in a second. Everything becomes one noise—you don’t hear this or that; everything’s just one noise—you’re not paying attention to one or the other.… You just really try to stay in the present and not let anything break that rhythm. Again, as long as you just kind of stay there, you become oblivious to everything that’s going on. You don’t

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: Bryant’s comments richly reinforce many of the concepts discussed throughout this chapter. It is important to remember that his mental state rested largely on a sound physical training program and on a history of performance success. Bryant exhibited phenomenal physical prowess, arduously running sprints, training on the court, and lifting weights in the off-season. Combined with superior performance on the basketball court, such preparatory physical effort contributed greatly to his focused, confident psychological state. 470

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: Energy Management: Arousal, Anxiety, and Stress In order for athletes to perform effectively, they need to learn how to best manage their mental and physical energy levels. Athletes who waste energy through worry, anger, frustration, or anxiety experience a greater likelihood of distraction and decreased self- confidence, and they have less physical energy for when performance is most important (20). Thus, the ability to maintain self-control and manage energy reserves in a performance environment is a critical skill for any performer. Mental energy is generated, maintained, depleted, and refreshed via our emotions. Emotions are temporary feeling states that occur in response to events and that have both physiological and psychological components (19). These emotions affect mental and physical energy and therefore can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on human performance. Emotions such as excitement can be beneficial to performance, causing us to feel motivated, which elevates self-confidence and reinforces commitment levels. However, emotions can be detrimental when an athlete is overexcited or underexcited (e.g., too amped up or too flat) or when an athlete loses control of his or her emotions and ceases to function effectively in a performance environment (e.g., an athlete who cannot control his or her anger or frustration). Training athletes to tap into their emotions to generate or elevate energy, while maintaining a sense of control over those emotions, is a

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: Arousal The training environment provides a host of new and unfamiliar experiences that create multiple opportunities to test oneself and be evaluated for effectiveness. Because of this, athletic performance is frequently affected by arousal, anxiety, and stress. These terms are often used interchangeably; however, in reality, they are different elements within the same construct. Arousal is simply a blend of physiological and psychological activation in an individual and refers to the intensity of motivation at any given moment (64). For example, a psyched-up athlete may experience tremendous mental activation characterized by positive thoughts and a strong sense of control, whereas a flat athlete could experience minimal activation characterized by wandering thoughts and feelings of boredom. Arousal is always present in an individual to some degree, on a continuum ranging from being deeply asleep, or comatose, to highly excited; but in and of itself it is not automatically associated with pleasant or unpleasant events. It is simply a measurement of activation, and as such can be indexed by such metrics as heart rate, blood pressure, electroencephalography (EEG), electromyography (EMG), and catecholamine levels, or with self-report instruments such as the activation–deactivation checklist (63). The optimal arousal required for efficient performance depends on several factors that are discussed later in the chapter. Anxiety Anxiety is a subcategory of arousal in that it is a

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: The term anxiety is often confusingly used to refer to both a stable, enduring personality construct and a more short-term, changeable mood state. These are, in fact, different constructs within the emotional state of anxiety. State anxiety refers to a subjective experience of apprehension and uncertainty accompanied by elevated autonomic and voluntary neural outflow and increased endocrine activity (57). State anxiety is a generally negative experience, but its effects on athletic performance can be positive, negative, or indifferent, depending on such factors as the athlete’s skill level and personality and the complexity of the task to be performed. State anxiety is distinct from but related to trait anxiety, a personality variable or disposition relating to the probability that one will perceive an environment as threatening. In essence, trait anxiety acts as a primer for the athlete to experience state anxiety (58). Trait anxiety also affects the appropriate level of arousal for a given individual. People with high levels of trait anxiety tend to flood attentional capacity with task-irrelevant cognitions, such as thoughts of failure, catastrophe, or ego-oriented concerns. During a complex decision-making task, these attentionally demanding cues could compromise an athlete’s selective attention. The athlete with low trait anxiety may handle higher levels of pressure with decreased thoughts of task failure. State anxiety is the actual experience of apprehension and uncontr

chapterTitle: Psychological Foundations of Performance
text: is racing, and negative thoughts intrude. This lack of physical and psychological efficiency is typically initiated by uncertainty about a present or anticipated event. At least three important factors are usually present: A high degree of ego involvement, in which the athlete may perceive a threat to self-esteem A perceived discrepancy between one’s ability and the demands for athletic success A fear of the consequences of failure (such as a loss of approval from teammates, coach, family, or peers) Because these constructs of anxiety and arousal are complex and interrelated, figure 9.1 provides a summary of the interrelationships of arousal, state anxiety, and trait anxiety and the cognitive and somatic components of anxiety. 474
