text: During the weeks before the test, athletes should engage in enough training to establish a baseline of fitness in the activity being tested. Strength and conditioning professionals should be aware that responses to exercise in the heat are highly individual. Avoid testing under extreme combinations of heat and humidity. Figure 13.2 illustrates the combinations of temperature and humidity at which heat injury risk is present. Using temperature limits of at least 5 °F (3 °C) below those listed is recommended, especially on sunny days, to provide a safety margin and enable better test performance. On days when the temperature has exceeded or is expected to exceed the recommended limits, indoor facilities should be used if available, or testing should be conducted during morning or early evening hours when temperatures are acceptable. The athletes, especially those coming from cool climates, should be acclimated to the heat and humidity for at least one week before testing. Start with short workouts and progress to workouts of longer duration. Athletes should make sure they are well hydrated in the 24-hour period preceding aerobic endurance testing in the heat. A good indication of adequate hydration is a plentiful volume of clear urine (refer to chapter 10 for more detailed preexercise hydration guidelines). Salt tablets should generally be avoided. Athletes should be encouraged to drink during exercise in the heat. Plain water is most appropriate for exercise up to 1 hour in du

chapterTitle: Principles of Test Selection and Administration
text: evacuated (or both). Selection and Training of Testers Test administrators should be well trained and should have a thorough understanding of all testing procedures and protocols. The testing supervisor should make sure that all novice personnel perform and score all tests correctly, as in timing sprint speed with a stopwatch or determining a 1RM back squat. It is essential that all testers have sufficient practice so that the scores they obtain correlate closely with those produced by experienced and reliable personnel. The testers should be trained to explain and administer the tests as consistently as possible. Test reliability is impaired, for example, if one test administrator provides considerable verbal encouragement to a group of athletes while another tester provides no verbal encouragement to another group. Administrators should have a checklist of materials needed for testing and written test protocols to refer to if questions arise during the testing process. Recording Forms Scoring forms, whether paper based or digital, should be developed before the testing session and should have space for all test results and comments. Factors such as environmental conditions should be documented. The specific details of setup for the testing should also be noted. For example, for a 1RM squat, the tester can note the pin height that was used for the barbell. This allows test time to be used more efficiently and reduces the incidence of recording errors. Test Format A well-orga

chapterTitle: Principles of Test Selection and Administration
text: Test planning must address such issues as whether athletes will be tested all at once or in groups and whether the same person will administer a given test to all athletes. The main consideration here is the number of athletes that are being tested. It is preferable to have the same person administer a given test if time and schedules permit, because this eliminates the issue of interrater reliability. If this is not feasible, the test supervisor can allow simple, well-defined tests (e.g., counting correct push-ups) to be administered by different testers and tests requiring schooled judgment (as of proper form in the squat) to be scored by the most skilled and experienced personnel. As a rule, each tester should administer only one test at a time, especially when the tests require complex judgments. It is permissible to have one tester alternate between two testing stations to avoid wasting time as athletes get ready. However, the tester must focus on only one test at a time. Planning and practicing the testing sessions beforehand will go a long way toward ensuring an efficiently run testing session. Testing Batteries and Multiple Testing Trials When time is limited and the group of athletes is large, duplicate test setups may be employed to make efficient use of testing time. For example, when one is conducting the 300-yard (274 m) shuttle, two test courses can be set up (16). A tester can administer up to two nonfatiguing tests in sequence to an athlete as long as test rel

chapterTitle: Principles of Test Selection and Administration
text: (21). When administering a test battery (e.g., one in which wrestlers perform maximal repetition pull-up and push-up tests for assessment of local muscular endurance), tests should be separated by at least 5 minutes to prevent the effects of fatigue from confounding test results (also see the following section, Sequence of Tests). Sequence of Tests Knowledge of exercise science can help determine the proper order of tests and the duration of rest periods between tests to ensure test reliability. The fundamental principle with test sequencing should be that one test should not affect the performance of a subsequent test. This should allow for optimal performance in each test and also allows for valid comparisons with previous testing results. For example, a test that maximally taxes the phosphagen energy system requires 3 to 5 minutes of rest for complete recovery (6, 12), whereas a maximal test of the anaerobic glycolytic energy system requires at least 1 hour for complete recovery (10). Therefore, tests requiring high-skill movements, such as agility tests, should be administered before tests that are likely to produce fatigue and confound the results of subsequent tests. A logical sequence, although there are some variations, is to administer tests in this order: 1. Nonfatiguing tests (e.g., height, weight, flexibility, skinfolds and girth measurements, vertical jump) 2. Agility tests (e.g., T-test, 5-10-5 test, 5-0-5 test, Illinois test) 3. Maximum power and strength tests

An effort should be made to administer fatiguing anaerobic capacity tests and aerobic tests on a different day than the other tests. However, if performed on the same day, these tests should be performed last, after an extended rest period. It is important that test sessions be conducted at the same time of day to avoid fluctuations in physiological responses due to differences in circadian rhythm (33). It is also recommended that tests be conducted indoors, which will allow for climate and testing surfaces to remain more consistent. The order of tests should be designed in such a way that the completion of one test does not adversely affect performance in subsequent tests. Preparing Athletes for Testing The date, time, and purpose of a test battery should be announced in advance to allow athletes to prepare physically and mentally. To maximize test reliability, athletes should be familiar with test content and procedures. Athletes should also be in a state of readiness to perform. Athlete readiness has been defined as “the state of being fully prepared to train and perform physically

The instructions should cover the purpose of the test, how it is to be performed, the amount of warm-up recommended, the number of practice attempts allowed, the number of trials, test scoring, criteria for disallowing attempts, and recommendations for maximizing performance. The instructions that are given to the athletes need to be clear and concise because this will increase the reliability and objectivity of the test (25). As an important supplement to reading test instructions aloud, the test administrator or a competent assistant should demonstrate proper test performance when possible. The athletes should be given opportunities to ask questions before and after the demonstration. The test administrator should anticipate questions and have answers prepared. It is important to motivate all athletes equally rather than giving special encouragement to only some. Whenever possible, tell athletes their test scores immediately after each trial to motivate them to perform better on subsequent trials (2). Reliability of testing improves with pretest warm-up (2). An appropriately organized warm-up consists of a general warm-up followed by a specific warm-up. Both types of warm-ups include body movements similar to those involved in the test. chapterTitle: Principles of Test Selection and Administration
text: Conclusion Tests and measurements can be used to assess athletic talent, identify physical capacities in need of improvement, provide reference values to evaluate the effectiveness of a training program, and set realistic training goals. To optimize test quality, testers must understand and consider validity and reliability. Test selection involves consideration of the physiological energy systems required by the sport; movement specificity; and the athletes’ experience, training status, age, and sex. Testers must also consider environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and altitude before administering tests. Strength and conditioning professionals must always remain conscious of potential health risks during testing and attentive to signs and symptoms of possible health problems that require medical referral. Testers must be carefully selected and well trained, and the testing session must be well planned and organized using the appropriate testing sequence. Consistent and effective preparation of athletes for testing is essential. Heikkinen, PhD, Jo Clubb, MS, and John McMahon, PhD The authors would like to acknowledge the significant contributions of Michael McGuigan, Everett Harman, and John Garhammer to this chapter. After completing this chapter, you will be able to discern the best ways to measure selected parameters related to athletic performance; administer field tests appropriately; evaluate and analyze test data and make normative comparisons; understand appropriate statistics; and combine the results of selected tests to generate an athletic profile. As discussed in chapter 13, the strength and conditioning professional—often referred to as the tester in this chapter—who has a broad understanding of exercise science can effectively choose and use tests and measurements to make training program decisions that help athletes optimize their physical preparation and maximize their potential. To do this effectively, the tester must administer tests correctly, analyze test data accurately (or understand how test data have been analyzed if the tester is not responsible for this, such as when using proprietary software), and then combine the results of selected tests to generate an athletic profile. This chapter covers these basic aspects of testing performance-related parameters and provides comprehensive age- and sport- specific descriptive and normative data for selected tests. 764

text: Measuring Parameters of Athletic Performance Athleticism incorporates many physical abilities, some of which are much more amenable to training than others. Such abilities may be called general components of athletic performance—that is, abilities that enable effective responses to the various physical demands of a specific sport or event. This section focuses on how each component can be tested and highlights relevant issues. Maximum Muscular Strength (Low-Speed Strength) Maximum muscular strength tests can be split into dynamic or isometric demands; those that involve relatively low movement speeds reflect low-speed muscular strength. In this case, muscular strength is related to the force a muscle or muscle group can exert in one maximal effort while maintaining proper form, and it can be quantified by the maximum weight that can be lifted once (the 1-repetition maximum [1RM]) in exercises such as the bench press or back squat, or the maximum force that can be exerted at a particular isokinetic velocity (5, 6, 45, 72, 100, 101, 103, 109, 124). Because 1RM tests do not require expensive equipment and reflect the kind of dynamic ability necessary in sport, they are the maximal strength tests of choice for most strength and conditioning professionals. In general, 1RM tests are administered after the athlete has warmed up by performing a few sets of the test exercise with submaximal loads, beginning with a relatively light load. The first attempt is usually with approximately

text: Anaerobic or Maximum Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) High-speed muscular strength or maximal anaerobic muscular power (or anaerobic power) is related to the ability of muscle tissue to exert high force while contracting at a high speed. Tests of strength and power are of very short duration, are performed at maximal movement speeds, and produce very high-power outputs. High-speed maximal muscular power tests are often called (maximal) anaerobic power tests. Scores on high-speed muscular strength tests include the 1RM of explosive exercises (e.g., the power clean, snatch, push jerk), the height of a vertical jump, and the time to sprint up a staircase (e.g., Margaria-Kalamen test) (69, 100, 103, 124, 126). Because explosive exercise tests take about 1 second while low-speed maximal strength tests generally require 2 to 5 seconds to complete, phosphocreatine and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) stored in the active muscle(s) are the primary energy sources for both types of tests. Maintaining correct technique or form is also important when measuring anaerobic power for both performance validity and safety reasons. Most maximal muscular strength tests involve relatively slow movement speeds and therefore reflect low-speed strength. Assessment of high-speed muscular strength can involve measuring the 1RM of explosive resistance training exercises or the height of a vertical jump. Power output reflects the interplay between force and velocity. The height of a jump is a function o

Load-Velocity Profile Velocity-based training (VBT) using commercially available technology has become an increasingly popular method for measuring bar speed and displacement during the performance of individual resistance training exercises. These technologies allow testers to measure the intensity of an exercise using bar velocity as a metric rather than simply using percentages of a 1RM (15, 156). These methods are based on the inverse relationship between bar speed and the weight lifted. Specifically, as the absolute weight on the bar increases, a linear decrease in bar velocity is typically recorded. Using this knowledge, strength and conditioning professionals can create an individualized load–velocity profile by performing a series of sets performed with progressively increasing loads (i.e., 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 90% of 1RM) (156). The creation of the load– velocity profile has been suggested to be useful for evaluating and prescribing exercise intensity during resistance training programs and has also been suggested to be a useful tool for estimating or monitoring the 1RM. When the load–velocity profile is created from a series of increasing loads as a percentage of the 1RM with the back squat exercise (figure 14.1) a linear relationship exists between load and velocity (14). Agility Agility traditionally has been considered the ability to stop, start, and change the direction of the whole body rapidly (134, 143). Agility consists of two main components: speed in changing direction and cognitive factors (134). The definition of agility has been revised to take into account the perceptual qualities, and it is now considered “a rapid, whole-body, change of direction or speed in response to a sports-specific stimulus” (134, 143). Agility testing therefore involves tests of change of direction with a cognitive component, such an anticipation and reaction. Tests such as the T-test, the 5-0-5 test, the 5-10-5 test (also known as the pro agility test), and the L-drill (also known as the 3-cone drill) are used to assess change of direction. Speed Speed is movement distance per unit of time and is typically quantified as the time taken to cover a fixed distance. The time taken to sprint from a stationary start over a short distance such as 10 yards or meters reflects acceleration, whereas longer sprints such as 40 yards (37 m) would measure maximum speed (163). Assessing movement patterns can reveal indicators of injury susceptibility in young athletes. Well-established screening tools such as the functional movement screen (FMS), tuck jump assessment (TJA), landing error scoring system, and drop jump assessments are commonly used for this purpose (123). Additionally, tailored movement screening protocols have been devised specific to particular sports, aiming to pinpoint injury risks, performance limitations, or even talent identification opportunities. Tailored training programs can be developed by strength and conditioning professionals to target specific individual needs, including addressing movement limitations. Multiple movement screens assess parts of the AMSC spectrum, but consensus has not been reached regarding which are most appropriate for a given cohort. One narrative review (122) included 10 movement screens, including but not limited to the FMS, TJA, resistance training skills battery (RTSB), and back squat assessment (BSA). Interested readers are directed to the review by Pullen and colleagues (122) for more detailed information on the methodologies, reliabilities, and strengths and limitations of each of these tests when selecting the screening test that is the most appropriate for the environment. 771

text: Implementing movement screens can be complex due to variations in implementation practices, criteria, grading, and movement analysis. Understanding reliability of screen implementers is critical, although both novice and expert raters can achieve substantial reliability (104). Recording movements for retrospective analysis after testing is recommended, because it allows raters to review video footage, pause, slow down, and rewatch to accurately assess movements. The number of repetitions performed and how they are graded are crucial. Due to ongoing brain maturation, youth exhibit higher movement variability, and performance regressions can coincide with growth spurts (54, 68). Therefore, movement screens should assess each repetition for consistency. Some screens, such as the FMS and RTSB, use a best repetition technique, which limits the assessment of movement consistency. Others, like the TJA, use a sum-of-repetition scoring system, capturing movement variability. Considering total body versus segmental analysis is also important because total body approaches like the FMS may miss specific deficiencies or compensations, whereas segmental analysis provides detailed insights (123). Flexibility Flexibility can be defined as the range of motion about a body joint (13). Typical devices for measuring flexibility include manual and electric goniometers, which measure joint angle, and the sit-and-reach box, which is used to evaluate the combined flexibility of the lower back and hi

With a trained and competent tester, the skinfold measurement technique is the most valid and reliable (r = 0.99) means for assessing body fatness that is generally available to the strength and conditioning professional and is preferable to body circumference methods (95). Other methods available to strength and conditioning professionals include bioimpedance devices and total body plethysmography, although dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is often labeled as a gold standard. The skinfold method uses calipers that measure the thickness of a double layer of finger-pinched skin and subcutaneous fat. A good skinfold measurement device should squeeze the fold of skin and fat with constant pressure regardless of the amount of tissue being measured (41, 69, 120). Circumference methods may be added, because they are relatively quick and simple and can yield important chronic disease risk information. For example, waist circumference can assess abdominal fat, and a high waist circumference is associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and certain types of cardiac disease (69). text: Monitoring Protocols, Procedures, and Equipment When selecting tests for athletic assessment, it is crucial to consider the protocols, procedures, and equipment necessary to effectively implement them. Every athletic environment is unique, requiring careful consideration to optimize these aspects for specific settings. Protocols are systematic plans outlining guidelines to achieve specific objectives. In athlete testing, they provide a comprehensive framework within which procedures are developed, setting standards for consistency, reliability, and validity (as explained in detail in chapter 13). A monitoring protocol represents the overarching strategy for conducting performance assessments, detailing the overall approach for tracking an athlete’s physical capacities and specifying test types and frequencies throughout the season. Using Artificial Intelligence to Analyze Testing Data Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a potentially transformative tool in sport. Yet there is still much confusion, apprehension, and skepticism about the value of AI. AI is defined as “the ability of a digital computer to perform tasks commonly associated with intelligent beings … such as the ability to reason, discover meaning, generalize, or learn from past experience” (31). Within AI, machine learning (ML) is the ability of computer machines to learn from and develop data without human input or interaction. These approaches offer various advantages to sport, including automating or se

In this position the knee angle should be approximately 120 degrees and 145 degrees, and the hip angle should be approximately 125 degrees and 150 degrees (62). The force plate should always be set up on a stable surface (ideally in the same location each time) and the force zeroed with nothing on the plates immediately before the athlete tests. Jumping with the use of an arm swing can also be tested and is referred to as an Abalakov jump. Either way, consistency should be used and each jump should be tracked as to whether it was performed with (Abalakov) or without an arm swing. 4. During the jump, the dominant arm reaches upward while the nondominant arm moves downward relative to the body. 4. Procedure 1. The test procedures are essentially the same as for the vertical jump, except that the countermovement is removed. Begin with the athlete standing on a calibrated, zeroed force platform. (Note: The squat jump and vertical jump with countermovement can also be tested using a switch or contact mat system (figure 14.9) [158], which estimates jump height [51] but cannot measure force outputs.) 2. The athlete descends into a squat position (knee angle approximately 110 degrees) and holds this position for 2 to 3 seconds before jumping vertically, keeping hands fixed on hips. 3. The takeoff and landing positions, as well as jumping strategy, should be the same for each trial. Specifically, the tester should ensure there is no countermovement (dip) at the start of the jump, both through visual observation and, where a force plate is used, by assessing the force–time curve. 4. The best of three trials is recorded. The ratio of the vertical jump height with countermovement to squat jump height can be calculated as the eccentric utilization ratio (99). 5. text: 10 DROP JUMP Equipment A box that may vary in height from 8 to 16 inches (20-40 cm) Floor with good traction Measurement equipment such as force plates (with corresponding software on laptop or tablet), switch mats, optoelectronic systems, and smartphone applications Personnel One tester/recorder Procedure 1. When performing a drop vertical jump, the athlete should step out before free-falling from as close as possible to the height of the box rather than stepping down (i.e., lowering) or jumping off (i.e., rising) the box. Box height selection for an athlete can vary but is typically 20 centimeters (8 in.), 30 centimeters (12 in.), or 40 centimeters (16 in.) (figure 14.11a). The higher the box, the greater the plyometric demand. When using a device that is not flush with the ground or base of the box when conducting the drop vertical jump test, such as when using a switch mat, the strength and conditioning professional should measure the box height from the top of the box to the top surface of the switch mat. 2. The athlete steps out from the box and lands on the floor, force plate, or switch mat (figure 14.11b) and, as quickly as possible, jumps again (figure 14.11c). Drop jumps should be performed with the athlete attempting to jump with a short ground contact time while still aiming to jump as high as possible. text: 11 REBOUND JUMP Equipment Floor with good traction Measurement equipment such as force plates (with corresponding software on a laptop or tablet), jump mats, optoelectronic systems, and smartphone applications Personnel One tester/recorder Procedure 1. Rebound-based vertical jumps require the athlete to jump from a preceding vertical jump. When performing a rebound vertical jump, the athlete should first complete a maximal-effort vertical countermovement jump followed by either a predetermined number of rebound vertical jump repetitions or a predetermined set duration (e.g., 10 seconds). Rebound vertical jumps from a ground-start position have been performed with single or multiple repetitions, including the 10-5 repeated jump test (64), which requires 10 maximal vertical rebound jumps following the initial maximum countermovement jump. 2. All styles of rebound vertical jump should be performed with the athlete attempting to jump with a short ground contact time while still aiming to jump as high as possible. A short ground contact time is achieved by limiting flexion of the ankles, knees, and hips while in contact with the ground by adopting high leg stiffness (high force with shallow range of motion). 3. As per the drop jump, the most reported performance variables following rebound vertical jump testing are jump height, ground contact time, and reactive strength index (calculated as jump height divided by ground contact time). For the 10-5 repeated jump test, the best 5 re

The purpose of this test is to observe how many times the athlete can jump over the box in a left to right fashion over a duration of 90 seconds. The athlete begins on top of the box and then jumps down laterally to one side before jumping back up to the top of the box again. The athlete then repeats this procedure in the opposite direction. Each time the athlete reaches the top of the box counts as 1 repetition. 2. The athlete must leave the ground with two feet and touch the top of the box with two feet before jumping down to the other side. The athlete is not permitted to step up onto the box. 3. This is repeated for as many times as the athlete is able to during the 90-second duration of the test. The tester should record the number of hops taken with proper form over the course of the test. The arms are at the sides, resting on the floor, with the fingers touching a 4-inch-long (10 cm) piece of masking tape positioned perpendicular to the fingers. A second piece of masking tape is situated parallel to the first tape at a distance determined by the age of the athlete (4.7 inches [12 cm] for those younger than 45 and 3.1 inches [8 cm] for those 45 or older). 2. text: 19 YMCA BENCH PRESS TEST Equipment A barbell, weight plates, two safety locks, and enough total weight to assemble an 80-pound (36 kg) or a 35-pound (16 kg) load (including safety locks) Flat bench press bench (preferably with an upright rack to hold the barbell) Metronome Personnel One spotter/recorder Procedure 1. Instruct the athlete in proper technique for the flat barbell bench press as described in chapter 16. 2. Allow the athlete to perform a specific warm-up of 5 to 10 repetitions with a light to moderate load. 3. The spotter/recorder stands at the head end of the bench throughout the test to help raise the bar on a failed attempt and to help the athlete place the bar back on the rack. 4. Set the resistance at 80 pounds (36 kg) for males and 35 pounds (16 kg) for females. 5. Set the metronome cadence at 60 beats/min to establish a rate of 30 repetitions per minute (one beat up, one beat down). 6. The athlete grips the bar at shoulder-width, lifts the bar off the rack, and extends the elbows. Then, in time with the metronome, the athlete repeatedly lowers the bar to the chest and raises it up again to full elbow extension, until the athlete can no longer keep up with the metronome. The movement should be smooth and controlled, with the bar reaching its highest and lowest position with each beat of the metronome. The athletes continue running for as long as they can maintain the increasing speed as indicated by the auditory signals. 8. The termination of the test is indicated by the inability of an athlete to maintain the required pace for two trials. A warning is given the first time the start or turning line is not reached. 9. The athlete stands in the center of a grid with eight lines (120 cm [47 in.]) extending out at 45-degree increments as shown in figure 14.27 (115, 126). 2. The athlete maintains a single-leg stance facing in one direction while reaching with the contralateral leg as far as possible for each taped line, touching the farthest point possible and 811

text: then returning to the bilateral position. Within a single trial, the athlete remains facing in the beginning direction and the stance leg remains the same, with the other leg doing all of the reaching. 3. The distance from the center of the star to the touch position is measured. 4. The starting direction and support leg are chosen randomly. Three trials are performed for each condition and averaged. 5. A 15-second rest is allowed between each reach. 6. Trials are discarded if the athlete does not touch the line, lifts the stance foot from the center grid, loses balance, or does not maintain start and return positions for 1 full second. 7. Athletes should be given a minimum of four practice trials before being tested (103). 8. It has been suggested that testing the anteromedial, medial, and posteromedial positions is sufficient for most situations (66). text: Procedure 1. Tape the measuring stick or tape measure to the floor. Place one piece of tape about 24 inches (61 cm) long across the measuring stick and at a right angle to it at the 15-inch (38 cm) mark. 2. Have the athlete warm up with nonballistic exercises involving the hamstrings and lower back (e.g., by walking rapidly for 3-5 min); performing several repetitions of flexing forward from a standing, knees-extended position, reaching toward the toes, then reaching upward toward the ceiling (all without jerking); jogging in place while trying to kick the heels into the upper thighs from behind; and finishing with standing toe-touching or similar stretching on the floor. 3. Have the athlete sit shoeless with the measuring stick between the legs with its zero end toward the body, the feet 12 inches (30 cm) apart, the toes pointed upward, and the heels nearly touching the edge of the taped line at the 15-inch (38 cm) mark (figure 14.28a). 4. The athlete slowly reaches forward with both hands as far as possible on the measuring stick, holding this position momentarily. To get the best stretch, the athlete should exhale and drop the head between the arms when reaching. Be sure the athlete keeps the hands adjacent to each other and does not lead with one hand. The fingertips should remain in contact with the measuring stick (figure 14.28b). The tester may hold the athlete’s knees down, if necessary, to keep them straight. text: 1. The athlete holds the wooden dowel overhead with the shoulders fully flexed and with elbows locked. The grip should be twice shoulder-width using biacromial width as the reference measurement point for shoulder width. Biacromial width is the distance between the widest bony points at the superior portion of both shoulders. The feet are approximately shoulder- width apart, with toes pointing forward or slightly out (figure 14.29a). 2. The athlete then squats down; the initial action is flexion of the hips and knees. The heels remain in contact with the floor at all times. 3. The lowering continues until the crease of the hips is below the top of the knee. 4. text: 35 SKINFOLD MEASUREMENTS Equipment Skinfold calipers Flexible tape measure Marking pen Personnel One tester, one recorder Procedure (Obtaining a Skinfold Measurement) 1. Skinfold measurements should be made on dry skin, before exercise, to ensure maximum validity and reliability (70). The number of sites and equations should be selected based on the population tested (see table 14.35 near the end of the chapter). 2. Grasp the skin firmly with the thumb and index finger to form a fold of skin and subcutaneous fat. 3. Place the caliper prongs perpendicular to the fold 0.5 inch to 1 inch (approximately 1-2 cm) from the thumb and index finger. 4. Release the caliper grip so that its spring tension is exerted on the skinfold. 5. Between 1 and 2 seconds after the grip on the caliper has been released, read the dial on the caliper to the nearest 0.5 millimeter. 6. Obtain one measurement from each test site, and then repeat all test sites for a second trial. If the measurements do not differ by more than 10%, average the two measurements to the nearest 0.5 millimeter. Otherwise, take one or more additional measurements until two of the measurements are within 10%, and average those two measurements to the nearest 0.5 millimeter. Procedure (Measuring the Selected Site and Calculating the Body Fat Percentage) 1. There are specific equations for estimating body density (Db) (then, in turn, percent body fat [%BF]) for different populations. First, select the equation appropriate for the

chapterTitle: Administration, Scoring, and Interpretation of Selected Tests
text: Calf—a vertical fold along the medial side of the calf, at the level of maximum calf circumference (figure 14.30h) 3. Using the appropriate population-specific equation from table 14.35, calculate the estimated body density from the skinfolds (61). 4. Enter the body density into the appropriate population-specific equation from table 14.36 near the end of the chapter to calculate the percent body fat from the body density (69). 5. Note that there are no universally accepted norms for body composition. When strength and conditioning professionals assess an athlete’s body composition, they must account for a standard error of the estimate (SEE) and report a range of percentages that the athlete falls into. Note that the minimum SEE for population-specific skinfold equations is ±3% to ±5%. Therefore, if a 25-year-old male athlete’s body fat is measured at 24%, there is a minimum of a 6% range (21%-27%). text: Statistical Evaluation of Test Data Once the proper test or tests have been chosen and administered and the scores collected, the next step may include any or all of the following: (1) analysis of the data to determine the change in performance of the individuals or group over the training period (weeks, months, or years); (2) analysis of the individual or group’s performance relative to that of similar individuals or groups tested in the past; (3) analysis of the relationship of each athlete’s scores to those of the group; and (4) comparison of individual scores to local, state, national, or international norms. An important outcome of repeated performance testing is evaluation of both the improvement of individual athletes and the overall effectiveness of the physical conditioning program as determined by changes in test scores (103). A difference score is the difference between an athlete’s score at the beginning and end of a training period or between any two separate testing times. The percent change is another measure that can be used. However, evaluating the effectiveness of a training program merely by degree of improvement has two major limitations. First, athletes who begin the training period at a higher training status will not improve as much as untrained athletes who perform poorly at the beginning of training (i.e., the principle of diminishing returns). The window of adaptation for the various physical capacities is typically greater for less well-trained athl

chapterTitle: Administration, Scoring, and Interpretation of Selected Tests
text: Mode—the score that occurs with the greatest frequency. If each numerical score appears only once, there is no mode. If two or more scores are tied for greatest frequency, all of the similar scores are modes. The mode is generally regarded as the least useful measure of central tendency. Variability The degree of dispersion of scores within a group is called variability. Two common measures of variability are the range and the standard deviation. The range is the interval from the lowest to the highest score. The advantage of the range is that it is easy to understand; the disadvantage is that it uses only the two extreme scores and so may not be an accurate measure of variability (145). For example, the range could be the same for a group of widely dispersed scores as for a group of scores that are narrowly dispersed except for one deviant score. The standard deviation is a measure of the variability of a set of scores about the mean. The formula for the standard deviation of a sample is as follows: SD=∑(x−x¯)2n−1 (14.1) where Σ refers to a summation, x is a score, x is the mean of the scores, and n is the sample size (number of scores). A relatively small standard deviation indicates that a set of scores is closely clustered about the mean; a large standard deviation indicates wider dispersion of the scores about the mean. The standard deviation is most useful when the group of scores is “normally distributed,” forming the bell-shaped curve shown in figure 14.32 (26, 67). T

text: FIGURE 14.33 Z-score column chart representing standardized test scores across different fitness tests for an individual athlete. The zero represents the team average. Percentile Rank An individual’s percentile rank is the percentage of test takers scoring below that individual. As in calculation of the median, percentile ranking requires arranging scores ordinally (lowest to highest). For example, if an athlete is ranked in the 75th percentile, 75% of the group produced scores below that athlete’s score. Norms based on large samples are sometimes expressed in evenly spaced percentiles. Several examples of percentile rank tables are shown in the tables near the end of the chapter. Inferential Versus Magnitude Statistics The use of inferential statistics allows one to draw general conclusions about a population from information collected in a population sample. For example, if a boys’ 9th-grade gym class is put through a battery of tests and it is assumed that the class (sample) is representative of all the 9th- grade boys in the school (the population), the results of these tests can be used to make inferences about the population as a whole. A basic assumption of inferential statistics is that the sample is truly representative of the population (27). Magnitude statistics can provide a more useful approach for practitioners because it allows for interpretation of the clinical significance of fitness testing (75). To describe and evaluate the magnitude of change in a fitness

text: Effect size is a statistic that can be useful for calculating group performance following a training program or comparing between groups of athletes (42). The effect of the training program can be calculated as the difference or change in the mean score as a proportion of the pretest standard deviation (equation 14.3). ES = (x posttest − x pretest) / SD pretest (14.3) For example, a group of athletes had a pretraining mean bench press 1RM of 104.5 kilograms (standard deviation of 5.7 kg), and after a 12-week training intervention the mean bench press is 111.7 kilograms. The calculated effect size would be equal to (111.7 − 104.5) / 5.7 = 1.26. Several scales have been provided to compare the magnitude of the effect (28, 103, 127), but reference values for small (0.2), moderate (0.6), large (1.2), and very large (2.0) can be a useful starting point for practitioners (42, 75). For the example just given, this would mean that the strength and conditioning professional would interpret the effect size of 1.26 as meaning that the training program had a large effect. Developing an Athletic Profile To determine the sport-specific training status of an athlete, the strength and conditioning professional can combine the results of selected tests to generate an athletic profile, which is a group of test results related to sport-specific abilities that are important for quality performance in a sport or sport position. text: Conclusion Motor abilities and body composition variables that can be improved through strength and conditioning programs include maximum muscular strength, maximum muscular power, anaerobic capacity, local muscular endurance, aerobic capacity, agility, speed, flexibility, girths, percent body fat, and lean body mass. Performance testing can be used to evaluate basic motor abilities as well as the improvement of individual athletes over time and the overall effectiveness of a physical conditioning program. Numerous tests are available to measure sport-specific physical capabilities and training status. Strength and conditioning professionals can either use existing normative data to evaluate athletic performance or develop their own normative data. Statistical measures of central tendency, variability, percentile rank, smallest worthwhile change, effect size, and standard scores are useful for evaluating physical abilities and the improvement of a group as well as the individuals within the group. chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: CHAPTER 15 PERFORMANCE PREPARATION, MOBILITY, AND FLEXIBILITY Ian Jeffreys, PhD After completing this chapter, you will be able to identify the components and benefits of a preperformance preparation routine; structure effective preperformance preparation routines (warm- ups); identify the factors that affect flexibility; use flexibility exercises that take advantage of proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation; and select and apply appropriate static and dynamic stretching methods. This chapter is devoted to two key areas: performance preparation (warming up) and training for flexibility. While these two areas often have been linked, it is important to differentiate between the two, because they have distinctly different key functions. A warm-up is designed to prepare an athlete for performance either in an upcoming training session or competition and where the goal is to 854

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: optimize performance while potentially lessening the risk of injury. Flexibility training, on the other hand, aims to increase the range of motion around a joint, normally through the use of different forms of stretching. The first part of this chapter looks at the aims of a warm- up and suggests appropriate structures and protocols for designing effective warm-ups, and the second part discusses factors that affect flexibility and the use of different stretching protocols to enhance flexibility. 855

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: Performance Preparation—The Warm- Up A warm-up period is now almost universally accepted as an integral part of any training session or competition (10), yet until recently there was surprisingly little published research to support the practice (65) and even less on the optimal structure and content of a warm-up (48). Essentially, the overarching goal of a warm-up is to prepare an athlete mentally and physically for exercise or competition (45). A period of preparation is needed because a body at rest is unprepared for optimal performance. A period of warming up facilitates the instigation of a range of acute physiological responses that enable the body to cope with the specific demands being placed on it (65). Taken together, these acute responses not only enable the body to cope with these acute demands but also facilitate responses that can potentially optimize subsequent performance. While these processes occur across a number of body systems, they typically can be divided into temperature-related effects and non–temperature-related effects (10). Temperature-related effects include an increase in muscle temperature, core temperature (62), enhanced neural function, and the disruption of transient connective tissue bonds (30), while non– temperature-related effects can include increased blood flow to muscles, an elevation of baseline oxygen consumption, and postactivation potentiation (10). While passive warm-up techniques (e.g., external heating of the muscles) may be abl

text: activity undertaken, the positive effects on performance are thought to include the following: Enhanced muscle fiber contraction frequency, conduction, and relaxation velocity of both agonist and antagonist muscles (45) Improvements in the rate of force development and reaction time (3) Improvements in muscle force output, especially at higher velocities (30) Lowered viscous resistance in muscles and joints (30) Improved oxygen delivery due to the Bohr effect, whereby higher temperatures facilitate oxygen release from hemoglobin and myoglobin (see chapter 6 for more details) (62) Increased blood flow to active muscles through vasodilation (62) Enhanced metabolic reactions (30) facilitating energy transduction including faster ATP turnover, especially in anaerobic pathways (4) An increased psychological preparedness for performance (10) While the number of quality studies investigating the impact of warm-up on performance is surprisingly low, more than 80% of the published research has demonstrated a positive effect on performance (37, 40). These performance improvements include enhancement of endurance performance (both aerobic and anaerobic), improvements in performance on physical tasks such as jumping, and in actual sporting performance (37). text: As stated previously, a body at rest is unprepared for activity, and in this way a warm-up can be considered a process of preparation for the upcoming performance. The conventional advice is that a warm-up should consist of a period of aerobic exercise, followed by some form of stretching, and ending with a period of activity similar to the upcoming activity (36). A traditional warm-up program typically involves two key phases. The first is a general warm-up period (48), which may consist of 5 minutes of low-intensity aerobic activity such as jogging, skipping, or cycling. The aim of this phase is to increase heart rate, increase and redistribute blood flow, increase deep muscle temperature, increase respiration rate, and decrease the viscosity of joint fluids (28). This phase historically has been followed by a period of general static stretching that aims to replicate the ranges of motion required for the upcoming activity, although this has been largely superseded by dynamic stretching protocols (48). In the traditional approach, following the general warm-up is the specific warm-up period, which incorporates movements similar to the biomechanical movement patterns of the athlete’s sport. This phase should also include rehearsal of the skills to be performed (97). The whole warm-up should progress gradually and provide sufficient intensity to increase muscle and core temperatures without causing fatigue or reducing energy stores (62). text: Targeted and Structured Warm-Ups Activities undertaken within warm-ups using this structure of general and specific warm-ups vary considerably. Consequently, although athletes may be performing an appropriately structured warm-up, this cannot ensure that the warm-up itself adequately addresses the key variables required to optimize subsequent performance (36). Effective planning needs to carefully consider the specific requirements of the subsequent performance and how the warm-up can ensure that any necessary responses are elicited. Additionally, the needs and capacities of the athletes should be considered and be planned according to any specific logistical and environmental factors. It is also important that planning delineates between warm- ups used before competition and the more ubiquitous warm-ups used within a training session, because the ultimate objectives of both can be quite different. Whereas the key objective in a precompetition warm-up is to maximize performance in that competition, the training warm-up, as well as optimizing acute performance, can contribute to performance in other productive ways and across a wider range of timescales (49). Subsequently, the planning process for these is different. Strength and conditioning professionals should plan warm-ups incorporating short-, medium-, and long-term considerations that will contribute to the overall development of the athlete. In recent times, the use of structured and standardized warm-up systems such as the FIFA 11 has become more prevalent and emphasizes medium- and longer-term planning, often with the goal of injury reduction through the sequenced development of physical characteristics associated with a reduction in injury risk (2, 5, 33). The results of these have been encouraging and demonstrate the potential for longer term planning of warm-ups to contribute to athletic development (2, 5). However, despite the success of this approach, uptake has been surprisingly low; a potential reason for this has been the standardized structure in which activities are preprescribed that does not allow for flexible application (2). Whereas structures such as the FIFA 11 are preprescribed, it is likely that a range of potentially effective warm-ups exist (89) and that these need to be able to adapt to specific situations and over time as the needs of the athletes change (89). The first phase of the RAMP protocol involves activities that raise the level of key physiological parameters while also focusing on enhancing the skill level of the athletes. While at first glance this phase could be considered analogous to the general warm-up, having the aim of elevating body temperature, heart rate, respiration rate, blood flow, and joint fluid viscosity via low-intensity activities, it is the latter focus on skill development that is very different. Here, unlike traditional general warm-up activities, the focus is not on generic aerobic exercises to elicit the required physiological responses but instead to use activities that simulate the movement patterns of the upcoming activity and develop the movement patterns or skill patterns the athlete will need to deploy within the sport. In this way, the session, from the outset, is specifically targeted at key movement patterns and skill capacities that contribute to longer term development, as well as providing for the required physiological effects of the activity (48). This also assists in the psychological preparation of the athlete for practice or competition because the session constantly addresses components that relate to performance. See table 15.1 for a full example of a RAMP protocol. Debate persists as to whether static stretching should be used within warm-up, and at present the evidence is equivocal. Some reviews of the literature on the effect of static stretching on performance question the practice (82, 83, 97), suggesting that it can compromise muscle performance (53). Studies have demonstrated negative effects of static stretching on performance in a range of parameters such as force production (9, 23-26, 27, 31, 75), power performance (21, 92, 96, 97), running speed (35), reaction or movement time (8), and strength endurance (70). It has been suggested that this may be associated with a reduction in the stiffness of the musculotendinous units caused by a change in intramuscular viscoelastic properties (5, 40) or to a reduction in efferent neural input to the muscles (40). However, other studies show no decrement in performance, and a more recent review by Kay and Blazevich (52) concludes that there is clear evidence that short-duration static stretching has no detrimental effect on subsequent performance unless stretches are held for greater than 60 seconds. Additionally, if static stretching is used, research suggests that following it with a period of more intense activity may offset any potential decrements in performance (6). However, as highlighted previously, effective warm-up planning should not be focused solely on short-term considerations but should also consider longer term outcomes, and this provides a different perspective to the debate. Because no consistent link has been shown between stretching and injury prevention (43, 44, 74, 85, 89), the focus in warm-ups should shift to performance. Exercises should be designed to contribute to preparation for the upcoming session but also enhance the athlete’s overall movement capacities. Exercises that encourage the athlete to develop and use key movement patterns are ideal activities within this phase of the warm-up (51). The use of a range of exercises built around these key movement patterns provides all of these key advantages while also providing an opportunity to address any specific movement issues an athlete may demonstrate (51). Additionally, this approach helps maintain the temperature-related benefits of the raising phase of the warm-up (51). Also, any distance measured in yards can be the same in meters; precision is not necessary. What is crucial to note at this point is that while the first two phases have moved the body from a state of rest to a more prepared state, it is still unprepared for maximal performance, especially in activities that require high levels of force or speed application. This is why a warm-up must include a progressive sequence of exercises that increase the intensity of activity up to a level that will be experienced in the upcoming activity or sport; this is the potentiation phase. While this third phase, potentiation, could be considered as analogous to the specific warm-up, crucially its focus on the progressive intensity of activities is different. The quality of muscle contraction depends on its contractile history, and there exists a staircase or treppe effect, where consecutive contractions result in a net increase in contractile force (47, 60). This contractile history makes the motor neuron more sensitive to action potentials, allowing muscle to be activated with decreased neural input (47). This phase therefore deploys sport-specific or fitness capacity–specific (e.g., speed and agility exercises) activities that demonstrate a staged increase in intensity until the athlete is performing at the intensity required for the subsequent

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: to the upcoming session yet can also address the longer-term requirements of the athlete (48). With effective planning, this phase of the warm-up can be a key part of a training session, presenting an ideal opportunity to work on aspects of performance such as plyometrics, speed, and agility (51). Effective planning of this phase can allow considerable training time to be spent on key components of fitness without an overall increase in training duration (51). Indeed, it is this phase that ultimately determines the optimal length of the warm-up, because the potentiation phase can become a key part of the session, allowing the delivery of elements such as speed training and agility training; in these instances, the entire warm-up will be longer but will progress almost seamlessly to the main session. Central Nervous System Preparatory Exercises The potentiation phase of the warm-up is predicated on the history- dependent nature of muscle force production and involves a progressive series of exercises up to the intensity of the upcoming activity. This typically uses exercises similar to those in the main activity (e.g., a series of sprints before a football session). However, this history dependence also raises an important question: If a series of activities up to maximal intensity can elicit an enhanced neural output (e.g., enhanced motor unit recruitment or enhanced rate coding) and facilitate performance, can the use of augmented activities enhance this even further? text: The potential for residual force enhancement through CNS stimulation has been attributed to a range of physiological mechanisms, including the phosphorylation of myosin light chains, pennation angle changes in a muscle, recruitment of higher threshold motor units, and enhancement of the H-wave amplitude (91). It has also been suggested that PAPE could be attributed to an increase in the quantity of neurotransmitters released and their efficiency, resulting in enhanced muscle contractions together with an elevation in excitation potentials across synaptic junctions at the spinal cord (40, 91). However, no definitive answer emerges as to the mechanisms by which PAPE is elicited, and with so many potential contributory mechanisms, it is expected that there will be great variation in both the optimal stimulus and the probable response of an individual to any protocol. This potential individuality of response is made more probable by the fact that the preconditioning activity does not only have the potential to generate PAPE; it also has the potential to generate fatigue (the fitness fatigue theory). This balance between potentiation and fatigue must always be kept in mind when designing PAPE-based activities— indeed, throughout the design of a warm-up. A range of modalities have been purported as having the potential to stimulate PAPE, including resistance training exercises, variable resistance exercise, isometric contractions, resisted sprinting, and assisted sprinting (72), wi

text: Across all protocols, the evidence to support the use of PAPE exercises is equivocal, with great variation on most modalities. Here the interaction of potentiation and fatigue will always be a challenge; for example, the activities that may generate the greatest potentiation are also those that are likely to result in the greatest fatigue. Definitive conclusions are made even harder by the variation in the warm-up used in the studies and whether the positive results are as much a result of an effective potentiation phase rather than evidence of PAPE. To further challenge the application of the phenomenon, it appears that the effects are also highly individual and relate to the interaction of a range of factors, such as the type of stimulus, the intensity of the stimulus, the volume of the stimulus, the time duration between stimulation and application, and the individual characteristics of the athlete. As a result, definitive guidelines on the application of PAPE in any warm-up (see the sidebar) should be considered tentative at best. Much of the current research has focused on the acute application of CNS preparation. However, some research suggests that the positive effects of a bout of high-intensity exercise may last significantly longer than the windows that have been explored to date—perhaps up to 48 hours. Here consideration needs to be placed not just on what modality generates the greatest potential enhancement but also on what can be effectively applied into warm-up routines. chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: Guidelines and Precautions for CNS Preparatory Exercises The stimulatory effect is likely greater with well-trained athletes with high speed and power capacities. Resistance-based protocols likely have the greatest potential for gain but also the greatest potential for fatigue. Plyometric and resisted sprint-based exercises may have lower potential but be more accessible for use in warm-ups. Higher intensities will likely generate greater potentiation but also greater fatigue and thus require greater recovery times. The closer the similarity between the preconditioning activity and the main activity, the higher the likely transfer to enhanced performance. The effects of all protocols will be highly variable and should be prescribed on an individual basis. Some athletes may not benefit from CNS stimulation. The logistical challenges of implementing protocols may outweigh any potential benefits. Any decision should be based on a wide and comprehensive cost-benefit analysis. 872

text: Flexibility Flexibility is defined as the range of motion (ROM) that occurs about a joint. Flexibility can be expressed statically and dynamically. Static flexibility refers to the range of possible movement about a joint (28) and its surrounding muscles during a passive movement (40). Static flexibility requires no voluntary muscular activity; an external force such as gravity, a partner, or a machine provides the force for a stretch. Dynamic flexibility, on the other hand, refers to the available ROM during active movements and therefore requires voluntary muscular actions. Dynamic ROM is generally greater than static ROM. However, the relationship between static and dynamic ROM has historically been questioned and still remains largely unresolved, especially in relation to the fact that a normal range of motion cannot guarantee normal movement (19), indicating that ROM alone cannot determine the quality of any movement. Therefore, the direct transfer between measures of static flexibility and sport performance cannot be determined. In determining the role flexibility can play in performance, it is important to look at the nature of the sport or activity being undertaken. Given that performance in the majority of sports is dynamic in nature, it is advised to look beyond the role of flexibility as a static quality and instead consider its contribution as a dynamic quality (66). Here, the concept of mobility introduced earlier can be a more enlightening term than flexibility,

text: Flexibility and Performance Given the lack of a direct link between flexibility and movement capability, optimizing flexibility in relation to the specific activity rather than simply maximizing flexibility should be the focus of training (68). Clearly, the direct effects of flexibility on performance therefore depend on the types of activity undertaken, and it is always important to remember that the most flexible athlete is not always the most successful (84). Given that different sports and activities have specific requirements for ROM, it is likely that optimal levels of flexibility exist for each activity, with these related to the specific movements required within the particular sport or activity, together with the reduction of any potential injury risk that may present if an athlete lacks a specific ROM (93). As well as a consideration of the ROM itself, it is also important that the strength and conditioning professional keep in mind the kinetic and kinematic patterns required within the ROM, because this will also dictate the types of development methods used. The development of greater ROM should be linked with the requirements for enhancing performance, and this often involves the need to apply force over the required ROM and the ability to assume the key technical positions required for the sport. In some instances, greater ROM can be seen as the missing link in the athlete’s power program, because the ability to apply force over a greater ROM can increase impuls

text: it is important to note that both inflexibility and hyperflexibility can increase injury risk (77, 89). For example, in contact sports, an excessive ROM at the shoulder or a laxity in the ligaments of the knee may predispose the athlete to injury in contact situations. Additionally, general flexibility imbalances between joints, which could increase injury risk, must be considered (87, 88). Factors Affecting Flexibility A number of anatomical and training-related factors affect flexibility. Training cannot alter some factors, such as joint structure, age, and sex. However, others can be manipulated and thus are important considerations in the design of flexibility development programs. A long-term program of stretching can have cumulative positive effects ranging from enhanced flexibility to enhanced strength (80). Strength and conditioning professionals should consider each athlete’s unique combination of factors and sport requirements when recommending flexibility development exercises and programs. Joint Structure The structure of a joint determines its ROM (64). Ball-and-socket joints, such as the hip and shoulder, move in all anatomical planes and have the greatest ROM of all joints (64). The wrist is an ellipsoidal joint (an oval-shaped condyle that fits into an elliptical cavity), primarily allowing movement in the sagittal and frontal planes; its ROM is significantly less than that of the shoulder or hip (64). In contrast, the knee is a modified hinge joint, with move

text: flexibility between young men and women may be due in part to structural and anatomical differences and the type and extent of activities performed. Older people undergo a process called fibrosis, in which fibrous connective tissue replaces degenerating muscle fibers (57). This is likely due to inactivity and a tendency to use less of the available ROM during movement. Just as older people can improve strength, they can improve flexibility with appropriate exercise. Muscle and Connective Tissue A range of body tissues can influence flexibility. For example, factors such as muscle tissue, the musculotendinous unit (MTU), tendons, ligaments, fascial sheaths, joint capsules, and skin may limit ROM (28). The relative contributions of these to increased flexibility, both acutely and chronically, remain unclear and reflect the relative impacts of elasticity and plasticity (93). Elasticity refers to the ability to return to original resting length after a passive stretch, while plasticity refers to the tendency to assume a new and greater length after a passive stretch. Stretching exercises can positively affect connective tissues by taking advantage of their plastic potential, although the relative importance of each tissue type and the differences between individual responses remains unclear (12). text: Neural Control The control of an athlete’s ROM is as much determined by central and peripheral nervous system inputs as by structural elements (66); see chapter 1 for more detail. This system includes both afferent and efferent mechanisms, resulting in both reflexive and conscious activities that ultimately control the ROM an athlete is able to attain (see the Proprioceptor sidebars on pages 376 and 378). A key aspect of an effective flexibility program is the capacity to positively affect this system, allowing for elicitation of a greater ROM. Resistance Training A comprehensive and proper resistance training program may increase flexibility (69) and also assist in the development of force capacity through the enhanced ROM. Effective strength training protocols should be seen as an important adjunct to a stretching program (78). However, this comes with two provisos. The first proviso is that heavy resistance training with limited ROM during the exercises may decrease ROM (28). To prevent loss of ROM, an athlete should perform exercises that develop both agonist and antagonist muscles (16) and should exercise through the full available ROM of the involved joints. Muscle Bulk The second proviso is that a significant increase in muscle bulk may adversely affect ROM by impeding joint movement. An athlete with large biceps and deltoids, for example, may experience difficulty in stretching the triceps (28), causing difficulty in performing exercises such as racking a power clean

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: the need for extreme joint mobility, but similarly, where ROM is crucial, the potential negative effects of muscle bulk should be considered and training programs planned accordingly. Activity Level An active person tends to be more flexible than an inactive one, although it is important to note that it is not activity level alone that improves flexibility but also the type of activity that influences flexibility (76). Stretching exercises, or exercises requiring the body to move through a full ROM, are essential if joint flexibility is to be maintained or increased. Similarly, resistance training, especially using full ranges of motion, can be an effective stimulus to maintain or increase ROM, and both men and women have successfully increased their flexibility as an outcome of properly designed resistance training programs (69). Proprioceptor: Muscle Spindles The muscle spindles are located within intrafusal muscle fibers that run parallel to extrafusal muscle fibers; they monitor changes in muscle length (40). During a rapid stretching movement, a sensory neuron from the muscle spindle innervates a motor neuron in the spine. The motor neuron then causes a muscle action of the previously stretched extrafusal muscle fibers; this is the stretch reflex. Stimulation of the muscle spindle and the subsequent activation of the stretch reflex should be avoided during stretching, because motion will be limited by the reflexive muscle action. text: Types of Stretching Stretching techniques typically fall into three broad categories: static, dynamic, and precontraction (73). Static Stretching The static stretching approach requires the movement of a body segment to a point in the ROM where resistance to further movement is experienced (i.e., the end position). This stretching action can be performed either actively or passively. An active stretch occurs when the person stretching supplies the necessary forces to enable the end position to be reached. During the sitting toe touch, for example, the athlete contracts the abdominal muscles and hip flexors to flex the torso forward to stretch the hamstrings and low back. A passive stretch occurs when a partner or a stretching machine provides external force to cause or enhance a stretch. A static stretch involves a slow and constant movement toward the end position, which is then held for 10 to 30 seconds (66). This duration is thought to cause an acute viscoelastic relaxation response, facilitating relaxation and concurrent elongation of the stretched muscle (34). Because it is performed slowly, static stretching does not elicit the stretch reflex of the stretched muscle (71); therefore, the likelihood of injury is less than during ballistic stretching (71). In addition, static stretching is easy to learn and has been shown to effectively improve ROM (38). Although injury to muscles or connective tissue may result if the static stretch is too intense, there are no real disad

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: gradually increases the intensity of the stretch by leaning forward until he or she feels mild discomfort in the hamstrings or lower back. The athlete holds this position for 10 to 30 seconds and then slowly returns to an upright sitting position. The stretch is static because it is performed slowly and the end position is held without movement. Dynamic Stretching Dynamic stretching is a broad term used to describe actions that involve active motions where a performer moves actively in a controlled and moderate paced manner through a typically large ROM (66). Often this approach is used as a type of functionally based stretching exercise that uses sport-generic and sport-specific movements to prepare the body for activity (48). Dynamic stretching —sometimes referred to as mobility drills (3)—places an emphasis on the movement requirements of the sport or activity rather than on individual muscles. This type of exercise can closely duplicate the movement requirements of a sport or activity (48); for example, a walking knee lift stretch mimics the knee lift of a sprinter. The ability to actively move a joint through a ROM is generally far more sport specific than the ability to statically hold a stretch. Advantages of dynamic stretching include the ability to promote mobility and to replicate the movement patterns and ROM required for sport activities. As a consequence, dynamic stretches, as outlined in the discussion of warm-up, are increasingly the preferred method of increas

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: When one is designing a dynamic stretching program, the starting point should be a careful analysis of the major movement patterns within the given sport as well as an analysis of fundamental movement patterns that can facilitate performance and the ROM required within these movements. One can then select exercises that replicate those movements via a series of dynamic stretches. In this way, it is possible to achieve a highly specific flexibility program. Dynamic stretching also provides the opportunity to combine movements (48). This gives the strength and conditioning professional a large number of combinations that can be used to provide variety in the warm-up. Athletes can perform dynamic stretching exercises either for a series of repetitions in the same place (e.g., 10 lunges) or for a series of repetitions to cover a given distance (e.g., lunge for 15 m [16 yd]). Regardless of the method chosen, each drill should start at an appropriate ROM and gradually increase this during subsequent repetitions or sets. Additionally, the speed of movement can also be increased but always under a high level of control. For example, athletes can perform the knee lift exercise over a distance of 15 meters, starting at a walk and building to a skip in subsequent repetitions. In a dynamic stretch that mirrors a sport skill—such as a sprinter’s knee lift drill—it is important that the stretch also emphasize the key skill factors required for the movement so that the most important mechan

text: sequenced, may injure muscles or connective tissues, especially when there has been a previous injury (20). Ballistic stretching usually triggers the stretch reflex that does not allow the involved muscles to relax, which may limit ROM, so the strength and conditioning professional should monitor this during the session. For example, consider the sitting toe touch performed as a ballistic stretch rather than a static stretch. The athlete sits on the ground with knees extended, lower extremities together, and upper body perpendicular to the legs. The athlete reaches quickly toward the ankles, bounces at the end position, and immediately returns to a near-vertical upper body position. With each repetition, the end position extends farther than in the preceding repetition. Ballistic stretching has been shown to be as effective as static stretching in enhancing ROM (58) and could play a role in a flexibility development program (22). However, care must be taken to ensure that the athlete is appropriately prepared for this type of exercise acutely and chronically, and special care should be taken when a previous injury has been reported. Dynamic and ballistic stretches may appear similar; however, a number of key differences significantly alter the effects of these activities such that dynamic stretching avoids the potential negative effects associated with ballistic stretching. Dynamic stretching avoids bouncing and is performed in a more controlled manner than ballistic stretchi

text: increasing flexibility. PNF techniques are usually performed with a partner and involve both passive movement and active (concentric and isometric) muscle actions. PNF stretching has been purported as being superior to other stretching methods for increasing flexibility (81), possibly because it activates the sensory receptors in the agonist and antagonist muscles (56), although evidence for this has not been consistently shown (38, 56). Additionally, PNF stretching can often be impractical because most of the stretches require a partner and some expertise. During a PNF stretch, three specific muscle actions are used to facilitate the passive stretch. Both isometric and concentric muscle actions of the antagonist (i.e., the muscle being stretched) are used before a passive stretch of the antagonist to achieve autogenic inhibition (see the Proprioceptor: Golgi Tendon Organs sidebar on this page). The isometric muscle action is referred to as hold and the concentric muscle action as contract. A concentric muscle action of the agonist, called agonist contraction, is used during a passive stretch of the antagonist to achieve reciprocal inhibition. Each technique also involves passive, static stretches that are referred to as relax. When using static contractions, these should be held for approximately 3 to 6 seconds at no more than 20% of maximum voluntary contraction, with the first repetition generally giving the greatest benefit. One or two sessions per week are recommended (8

chapterTitle: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility
text: simultaneously contracts the muscle opposing the muscle that is being passively stretched. Here the tension in the contracting muscle stimulates the GTO and causes a simultaneous reflexive relaxation of the stretched muscle. There are three basic PNF stretching techniques: hold-relax (15, 18), contract-relax (15), and hold-relax with agonist contraction (18). The techniques are completed in three phases. With each of the three techniques, the first phase incorporates a passive prestretch of 10 seconds. The muscle actions used in the second and third phases differ for the three techniques; the second and third phases give each technique its name. The following sections use the hamstring stretch to describe the three techniques; figures 15.1 and 15.2 show the starting positions for the athlete and the partner. Hold-Relax The hold-relax technique begins with a passive prestretch that is held at the point of mild discomfort for 10 seconds (figure 15.3). The partner then applies a hip flexion force and instructs the athlete, “Hold and do not let me move the leg.” The athlete holds and resists the movement so that an isometric muscle action occurs and is held for 6 seconds (figure 15.4). The athlete then relaxes, and a passive stretch is performed and held for 30 seconds (figure 15.5). The final stretch should be of greater magnitude due to autogenic inhibition (i.e., activation of the hamstrings). 885
