text: Core Stability and Balance Training Methods There is increasing interest in training the core in an attempt to improve overall health, rehabilitate from injuries, and enhance athletic performance (14). To target core stability and balance, interventions ranging from traditional ground-based free weight exercises to training on unstable devices have been advocated in the applied literature. Anatomical Focus The term core is commonly used in the popular media and in some training journals (13) to refer to the trunk or, more specifically, the lumbopelvic region of the body (151). However, interpretation of the scientific literature appears to make an accurate or consistent definition of the core tenuous at best (13, 153). Typically, the anatomical core is defined as the axial skeleton and all the soft tissues with proximal attachments that originate on the axial skeleton (13, 14). It is important to note that the appendicular skeleton includes the pelvic and shoulder girdles, while the soft tissues include the articular cartilage and fibrocartilage, ligaments, tendons, muscles, and fascia (13). Ultimately, the soft tissues act to generate forces (concentric muscle actions) and resist motion (eccentric and isometric muscle actions). The muscles that are typically associated with the core allow for the transference of torques and angular momentum during the performance of integrated kinetic chain activities, such as kicking or throwing (111, 151). In fact, Willardson (151) suggest

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: throwing or hitting distances, vertical jump performance, and horizontal jump performance. Isolation Exercises Isolation exercises typically consist of dynamic or isometric muscle actions designed to isolate specific core musculature without the contribution of the lower and upper extremities (14). For example, common exercises performed to isolate the core are the prone plank (118) and side plank (140). Evidence shows that these types of isolated exercises can increase muscle activation, which has been suggested to result in improvements in spinal stability and a reduction of injuries (94). While evidence suggests that these types of activities result in improvements in performance in untrained individuals and those recovering from an injury, support is limited for the idea that these types of training activities translate to improvements in sport performance (81, 109, 151). While Lou and colleagues (81) have reported a positive transfer between the effects of core training on basketball-related performance, several other authors have reported that isolated core training is not very effective at improving sport performance (14, 109, 151). Additionally, according to Behm and colleagues (14) and Willardson (151), there is strong evidence that ground-based free weight exercises (e.g., squat, deadlift, push press, snatch, and exercises that involve trunk rotation) offer a greater benefit to actual sport performance compared to isolated core training. Ground-based free weight act

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: Ground-based free weight activities appear to offer similar or, in most cases, greater activation of the core musculature when compared to traditional isolation exercises designed to engage the core. Machines Versus Free Weight Exercises When free weight training methods are compared to machine-based training methods, each has advantages and disadvantages (14, 49, 58, 107, 128). With regard to machine-based training, the stability provided by the machine may result in a better ability to target specific muscle groups, which may be useful when targeting hypertrophy (120), but in the context of sport performance, muscle rarely if ever functions in such an isolated fashion (14). With regard to the stabilizer muscles, it is generally accepted that activation of these muscles is greater during free weight training when compared with machine-based training (48). In partial support of this belief, Anderson and Behm (6) state that the activity of the back stabilizers was 30% lower during a Smith machine squat when compared to a free weight squat. Additionally, there is scientific support for the contention that machine-based strength gains exert a negligible or a possible detrimental effect on the muscle activation pattern in athletic movements (6, 20, 97). However, if instability is increased via performance of ground-based free weight training on unstable surfaces or devices, greater decrements in force production, the rate of force development, and power outputs have been noted (3

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: Free weight ground-based exercises offer the ideal combination of specificity and instability, especially when one is focusing on strength and power development. Instability Devices Instability-based exercises are typically considered those that are performed on unstable surfaces or devices commonly found in strength and conditioning facilities. The increased popularity of training on instability devices seems to have stemmed from their use by physiotherapists in the rehabilitation process. These devices are used to promote postural disequilibrium or imbalance requiring a greater stabilizing function of the core musculature (14, 151). If perturbations are applied during use of these devices, a balance challenge can occur that requires activation of the core musculature in order to induce postural adjustments to remain upright (27). Numerous instability devices are available to the strength and conditioning professional; the most common are the Swiss, physio, and Pezzi gymnastics balls (14). Other instability options include hemispherical physioballs with one inflated dome side and a flat rubber side, inflatable disks, wobble boards, balance boards, foam tubes, and various foam platforms. Natural surfaces such as sand can also create scenarios that introduce instability into an athlete’s movement pattern, creating an increased balance challenge that results in increased core muscle activation. Many strength and conditioning professionals believe that performing instability exe

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: overall power output (33) may be less than 70% of what can be achieved when the exercise is performed under stable conditions. Additionally, there can be a significant reduction in the rate of force development that is achieved during the exercise (84). Training with a reduced force production, power output, and rate of force development may not be the most advantageous method for preparing athletes, because these factors have a large impact on many aspects central to successful sport performance. Overall, performance of resistance exercises on unstable devices by athletes results in muted performance improvements when compared to training on stable devices (29, 126, 161). The lack of performance benefit noted in the literature might be expected based on the lack of dynamic correspondence between exercises performed on unstable surfaces and sporting activities (45, 129). Additionally, the ineffectiveness of training on unstable surfaces may also be related to the principle of diminishing returns, because it is very likely that trained athletes require a much greater adaptive stimulus in terms of force production, movement velocity, and rate of force development to realize performance gains than can be provided by instability exercise devices (14, 79). Therefore, the performance of static balance activities on instability devices may be considered an introductory training step to improve balance and core stability before the implementation of dynamic or explosive ground- based

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: When used in the rehabilitation setting, unstable devices have been shown to reduce low back pain and improve the efficiency of the soft tissues that stabilize the knee and ankle joints (13, 14). Since several muscles related to the knee joint originate in the lumbopelvic region, the core of the body could be considered an important contributor to the prevention of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries (99). In fact, several studies provide evidence that using instability devices may reduce the likelihood of ACL injuries, especially after rehabilitation from an ACL injury (100). For example, Fitzgerald and colleagues (40) reported that activities that challenge the rehabilitating athlete using perturbations stimulated by tilt boards, roller boards, and other balance devices make a successful return to competitive sport activities five times more likely. Historically, it is often suggested that the addition of balance training to traditional training methods results in a reduction in ACL injuries (24). However, in a systematic review, Grimm and colleagues (46) contest this contention and suggest that these types of interventions do not reduce ACL injury risk. In contrast, ground- based free weight activities seem to have a more balanced effect, leading to improvements in performance while increasing core strength and balance abilities. text: Variable-Resistance Training Methods Resistance training practices include three methods for applying overload to the body: constant external, accommodating, and variable resistance (41, 88). The most common method for applying resistance during training is to use a constant external load, which is best represented by traditional resistance training methods (e.g., free weights). In this scenario, the external load remains constant throughout the range of motion, better represents real-life activities, and allows for a more realistic skeletal muscle coordination and movement pattern (54, 88, 106). On the other hand, accommodating resistance (sometimes referred to as semi-isokinetic resistance applications) generally allows for the speed of movement or isokinetic resistance to be controlled throughout a range of motion (88, 128). Stone and colleagues (128) suggest that these types of devices have poor external validity. Additionally, these devices are unlikely to provide an adequate training stimulus when compared to more traditional methods such as those involving constant-loaded free weight movements, particularly when those movements are performed with multijoint movement patterns. With traditional resistance training exercise, the external load remains constant, but the forces exerted by the muscle vary in accordance with the mechanical advantages associated with the joints involved in the movement (17, 41, 130). In order to combat the changing mechanical advantages and ine

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: resistance at the bottom of the squatting motion and increase resistance as the athlete ascends from the bottom position. Another consideration is that during the concentric effort of a movement, a large portion of time is spent decelerating (41). Overall, it has been suggested that variable-resistance methods may be able to match the changes in joint leverage (164), overcome the mechanical disadvantages associated with specific joint angles (35, 123, 124, 146), and provide for compensatory acceleration (123, 124). With the use of a variable-loaded resistance model, the methodology most commonly seen in modern strength and conditioning facilities is the application of chains or rubber bands (41, 89, 133). The combination of chains or bands with traditional free weight resistance training methods has been shown to alter the loading profile typically seen during these constant-loaded activities (41, 66). Specifically, the chains or bands allow for the resistance to be varied across the range of motion achieved during the activity. With use of a variable-loaded resistance model, the most common methodology used in modern strength and conditioning facilities is the application of chains or rubber bands. Chain-Supplemented Exercises One increasingly popular method of applying variable resistance is the addition of chains to traditional resistance training activities such as the bench press or back squat (8, 17, 59, 88, 145). Specifically, these studies used a method in which the chain was suspended from the bar without touching the floor until the athlete had reached the lowest position in the squat or until the bar had reached chest height in the bench press (7, 10). While some research seems to support this methodology, much more research is needed to explore the various methods of applying chains to traditional resistance training methods. Determining Resistance With Chains The resistance provided by chains is largely dictated by the structure, density, length, and diameter of the chain and must be quantified before the chain is used in a resistance training setting. Additionally, the number of links in a chain will affect the amount of resistance provided by the chain (17, 89). To quantify the loading provided by chains, Berning and colleagues (17) developed a practical chart that related chain link diameter and length to the resistance load provided by the chain. McGuigan, “Forms of Variable Resistance Training,” Strength and Conditioning Journal 31, no. 1 (2009): 60 Determining the Load to Use With Chains To determine the load used with chains, the absolute chain resistance at the top and at the bottom portion of the movement are summed and then averaged. For example, if athletes wanted to train at a 5-repetition maximum (5RM) load in the bench press, they would first determine the 5RM load without the chains. Then, if their 5RM is 120 kilograms (265 lb), they would subtract the average chain resistance from this load. If at the bottom position the load is 0 kilograms and at the top the chain load is 11.1 kilograms (24.5 lb), the average is 5.55 kilograms (12.2 lb). Thus, the athlete would add 114 to 115 kilograms (251.3-253.5 lb) to the barbell to achieve the appropriate loading. text: Ways to apply chains include letting them touch the floor from the fully extended position during the movement (17) or hanging them from lighter chains (figure 17.1), which allows them to touch the floor only on reaching the lowest portion (figure 17.2) of the movement pattern (i.e., bottom of the squat or at chest level during the bench press) (8, 10). Baker (8) suggests that the second method may affect the velocity of movement in three distinct ways. First, the total barbell–chain complex comes into play only at the top of the movement (i.e., extend portion) when the chain links have been lifted off the floor. At the bottom of the movement, the links are in full contact with the floor, providing a reduction in load and allowing the athlete to accelerate the barbell at a faster rate. Second, it is possible that a within-repetition postactivation potentiation effect may occur in response to a greater neural activation. Specifically, when the chains pile on the floor and the mass of the barbell decreases, a greater neuromuscular activation may occur, allowing for an enhancement in movement velocity. Finally, it is possible that the decreasing resistance at the bottom portion of the movement may cause a more rapid stretch–shortening cycle. The links of the chains are draped over the lighter supporting chains, such that the chain does not contact the floor until the barbell reaches chest height. Resistance Band Exercises The use of resistance bands to augment traditional barbell resistances has become increasingly popular among strength and conditioning professionals (8, 39, 77, 138, 145). There is some research support for the use of resistance bands combined with 1107

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: traditional resistance training exercises (5, 104, 127, 146). For example, Wallace and colleagues (146) suggest that using bands to substitute 35% of the total load during a back squat can acutely increase peak power by approximately 13%. Additionally, Baker and Newton (9) suggest that the use of bands may result in a postactivation potentiation effect within each repetition. Support for this contention comes from the work of Stevenson and colleagues (127), who demonstrated that the use of bands to account for 20% of the training load resulted in an acute increase in the concentric rate of force development when compared to a constant-loaded condition. While these data seem to suggest that the addition of bands to traditional resistance training methods may offer some benefit, especially to power or rate of force development (66), some research contests these findings (35, 115). For example, Ebben and Jensen (35) report no differences in integrated electromyography and mean ground reaction forces when resistance bands are used to apply 10% of the total loading during squats. Currently, minimal research on the use of resistance bands, especially longitudinal studies, has been conducted to determine whether the acute effects noted by some authors translate into superior strength and power gains over time. However, there is some evidence that the use of resistance bands during an off-season strength training program performed by Division 1AA football players induces a greater in

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: bands is important because it can exert an impact on their overall stiffness, density, yield, and tensile strength (82, 88, 89, 138). Ultimately, the tension (resistance) generated by a resistance band is determined by the overall stiffness of the band and the extent to which the band is stretched (deformation) (89, 165). Specifically, based on Hooke’s law, the tension generated by a band is equal to its stiffness (k) multiplied by the deformation (d): Tension = Stiffness (k) × Deformation (d) As the band is stretched (i.e., increased deformation), the amount of tension placed on the band linearly increases. However, several studies suggest that resistance bands exhibit both curvilinear and linear deformation regions (5, 89, 105). When using bands in conjunction with traditional free weight training exercises such as the bench press or back squat, the strength and conditioning professional must be aware that there can be a 3.2% to 5.2% difference between two supposedly equal bands that could result in an 8% to 19% difference in mean tension between the bands (89). A basic length–tension relationship can be seen in table 17.2, and tension can be predicted based on the length of the band with the use of a prediction equation. Application of an Accentuated Eccentric Load The prescription of training loads during resistance training typically employs the use of a constant load that is lifted during the eccentric and concentric portions of the resistance training exercise. This practice creates a unique loading problem because it is well documented that muscles are stronger during eccentric (i.e., lengthening) versus concentric (i.e., shortening) muscle actions, resulting in what is referred to as an eccentric strength deficit (figure 17.5) (51, 91). In fact, depending on the exercise, up to 50% more force can be produced during eccentric muscle actions when compared to concentric muscle actions (34, 53, 64, 70, 143). As 1112

text: such, the use of constant loads during resistance training results in a lower relative load being used during the eccentric phase of the movement when compared to the concentric phase (144). One variable resistance training strategy that addresses this differential is the use of accentuated eccentric loading (AEL), which is sometimes referred to as augmented eccentric loading (95, 132). With this loading strategy, an additional load is applied during the eccentric phase of the movement and then removed during the concentric phase of the movement. For example, an eccentric muscle action can be overloaded during a countermovement jump by holding dumbbells and releasing them 1113

text: before the initiation of the vertical jump (122). Alternatively, if the athlete’s 1RM bench press is 120 kilograms (265 lb), the eccentric phase of the movement could be performed with 100% of the concentric 1RM (i.e., 120 kg [265 lb]) and the load can be reduced to 60% of 1RM (i.e., 72 kg [159 lb]) during the concentric phase of the exercise (32). Typically, this is accomplished with the use of weight releasing devices, often referred to as a weight releaser (91, 95). Benefits Associated With Accentuated Eccentric Loading The primary benefits associated with the use of AEL occur as a result of an overload applied during the eccentric phase of a resistance training or jumping exercise (91). Relatively little research has explored the chronic application of AEL, but due to the greater mechanical tension (43) and work (142, 143) during the eccentric phase, some researchers have suggested that AEL would be useful when targeting hypertrophy. While this rationale is sound, based on the available research increases in muscle size associated with AEL are comparable to traditional training methods (78, 119). It is, however, plausible that AEL results in architectural changes, such as the elongation of the muscle fascicles, allowing for higher shortening velocities which could affect strength and power performance (91). Additionally, the application of AEL tactics may have further benefits to enhancing strength and power performance by inducing changes to the neuromuscular system (144

text: Programming and Accentuated Eccentric Loading When implementing AEL as part of a periodized resistance training program it is important that the strength and conditioning professional remember that AEL is an advanced training tactic that is used to exploit the established benefits of eccentric overload training (131). As such, this training tactic should be used with caution, and it is important that the athlete’s resistance training experience and strength levels are considered when determining the exercises that AEL is implemented with and the loads used during both the eccentric and concentric phases of the movement (91). Accentuated eccentric loading (AEL) is an advanced training tactic and should be reserved for athletes with extensive resistance training experience. When programming AEL exercises the magnitude of the eccentric load is generally considered as either being submaximal (i.e., <100% of concentric 1RM), maximal (i.e., 100% of concentric 1RM), or supramaximal (i.e., >100% of concentric 1RM) (91, 143). The decision about which eccentric load to apply is likely mitigated by the targeted performance outcome and by the athlete’s training experience and their relative strength levels, with stronger athletes likely experiencing greater benefits from training with AEL tactics (91). One approach for implementing submaximal AEL is to apply this loading tactic with kettlebells, dumbbells, or elastic bands while performing plyometric exercises (e.g., countermovement, box

When programming AEL, three basic strategies can be implemented: using AEL on every repetition contained within the set, only applying AEL on the first repetition of the set, or using AEL on the first repetition of a cluster set (figure 17.8) (51). When AEL is applied on every repetition of a set the set must be structured with a cluster set format (i.e., 15-40 s interrepetition rest) so that the weight releaser can be reapplied after every repetition (figure 17.8a). The rest interval applied should be structured to account for the time needed to reapply the weight releaser and to re-rack and un-rack the bar. Alternatively, the AEL can be applied on the first repetition of the set, which allows the repetitions contained in the set to be performed in a continuous manner with enhanced 1117

text: Nontraditional Implement Training Methods Traditionally, resistance training interventions used in most modern strength and conditioning facilities have relied heavily on barbells, dumbbells, and various resistance training machines. More recently, strength and conditioning professionals have begun to incorporate nontraditional implements to potentially improve training specificity and to add greater variation to the preparation of athletes. Nontraditional implements can include items that are typically associated with strongman training such as tires, logs, kettlebells, stones, weighted sleds, and other weighted implements (59). Strongman Training Strongman implement training has recently seen an increase in popularity as a proposed tool for enhancing sport performance (15, 87, 116, 147, 159, 166). Some of the most common strongman exercises are tire flipping, log (or keg) lifting, farmer’s walks, and sled pushes and pulls. While research on these types of exercises is limited, some evidence suggests that they can be used to introduce a high-intensity stimulus resulting in an elevated blood lactate response (16, 73, 166). Additionally, it has been suggested that these types of exercises create a greater degree of instability that effectively challenges the athlete in different ways compared to traditional resistance training activities (87). Recent systematic reviews on the biomechanics of strongman have critiqued the research methodologies employed (63) as well as the resul

While both groups tended to report improvements in strength and functional performance measures (0.2%-7%), no significant differences were observed between groups. This would indicate that strongman training can be equally as effective as traditional training and that its use might provide additional variety and interest to highly experienced resistance- trained athletes who may benefit from more variations in their training stimulus. Heavy sled pulls have also been the focus of some training studies (96, 157). For example, the training study by Winwood and colleagues (157) attempted to match strongman to traditional resistance training exercises. One example was the use of heavy sled pulls with 85% of the athlete’s 1RM back squat for 3 sets of 25 meters (27 yd). Morin and colleagues (96) have also compared eight weeks of heavy sled sprint training (10 × 20 m [22 yd] sprints per session with 80% of body mass) to a control group performing unresisted sprinting on sprinting performance. Heavy sled training produced a range of moderate effect size improvements in horizontal force production and 5-meter (5 yd) sprint performance, with effect sizes indicating that heavy sled training had small to moderate benefits when compared to traditional sprinting. Further, a meta- analysis including 13 studies demonstrated the effectiveness of resisted sled training with a range of loads (5%-80% body mass) for improving acceleration (up to 10 m [11 yd]) but

Due to the potentially more awkward and unpredictable nature of strongman training compared to traditional resistance training, muscle activation and injury risk may also differ substantially between these training approaches. McGill and colleagues (87) quantified trunk and hip muscle activity and kinetics across the farmer’s walk, suitcase carry (unilateral farmer’s walk), yoke walk, tire flip, log lift, keg lift, and stone lift. While all of these movements required exceedingly high levels of activation of certain trunk and hip muscles and produced large spinal loads, these biomechanical characteristics exhibited considerable between-exercise variation. Such results suggest that each of these strongman exercises impose somewhat unique challenges on the trunk and hip musculature, suggesting that the inclusion of a variety of strongman exercises may be useful to better develop spinal stability across a range of movement situations. Regarding injury risk, the somewhat unique challenges imposed by different strongman exercises (87) may be consistent with the views of 213 strongman athletes who felt that certain exercises (tire flip, yoke walk, and stone lift) were more dangerous and likely to contribute to injury risk when compared to other strongman exercises (158). text: Tire Flipping Tire flipping typically employs truck or heavy-equipment tires that can be modified via placement of an extra load in the center to address individual strength needs (59, 147). The selection of the appropriate tire size depends on numerous factors that the strength and conditioning professional must consider when designing a specific program for an athlete. Thought must be given to the tire’s dimensions, including the height, width, and weight (21). A key consideration is the tread on the tire; worn treads are more difficult to grip, and pronounced treads potentially contain cuts, debris, or exposed metal that could put the athlete at risk for injury (21, 147). The most common injury associated with the tire flip is biceps tears (158), which may occur when the hands slip on the tire. To mitigate this injury risk, it is generally recommended that the tires used should be dry and have sufficient tread to allow the athlete to maintain grip and properly execute the exercise (21). Additionally, it is important that the tire is selected based on the individual athlete’s strength levels and that the movement is performed with appropriate exercise technique so that injury risk is minimized. Three basic techniques have been used to describe tire flip techniques: the sumo, the backlift style, and shoulders-against-the- tire technique (21, 147). The sumo and backlift styles are somewhat similar in that the feet are placed close to the tire, but they differ on the width of

text: Limited research has investigated tire flipping techniques (73, 162). Keogh and colleagues (73) primarily quantified the phases and temporal characteristics most related to successful (fast) completion of 2 sets of 6 repetitions of a 232-kilogram (511 lb) tire flip, separated by 3 minutes’ rest. The phases of the movement were broken down into a first pull, second pull, transition, and push, somewhat similar to the clean and jerk. Results suggested that minimizing time during the second pull and push phases was most associated with faster flips, suggesting that the tire flip may be used as an alternative to exercises such as clean and jerk to develop total body power. To optimize this development of total body power, the athlete should emphasize a powerful triple extension of the lower extremities to generate sufficient momentum for the tire to continue to rotate upward and forward before the push phase. This will also require the selection of appropriately sized tires that allow this rapid triple extension and transition to the push phase so that each repetition is performed relatively quickly (~3-4 s). When this occurs, athletes often have to round their back and position their knees close to their chest in order to initiate the movement. Log Lifting One of the classic exercises that is a part of strongman training is the log lift, which is essentially a version of the clean and overhead press. Other traditional lifting movements can also be performed with logs, such as cleans, presses, jerks, rows, squats, deadlifts, and lunges (59, 108, 156). Logs are typically made from metal and designed to have weight added to them while offering a midrange grip support to accommodate a neutral grip position (108). Weight is typically added with the use of traditional plates, which eliminates much of the need for having a variety of logs (59). text: Weighted Carries Strongman competitions commonly involve a range of weighted carries including the farmer’s walk, yoke walk, or sandbag or keg carries, with regular gym programs potentially also involving Zercher carries (using a barbell held across the elbows on the upper abdominals) or unilateral carries in which the load is held overhead or by one hip (i.e., suitcase carry). A primary advantage of these exercises is that they often involve horizontal motion and unilateral ground contact and require coordinated activity of many muscles of the body. Weighted carries may therefore develop total body and trunk stability, grip strength (for farmer’s walks) as well as the ability to produce high levels of anterior–posterior and vertical impulse to initiate propulsion and to be able to absorb these forces on impact at heel strike (163). These exercises therefore may mimic performance in a range of occupational and sporting demands (62, 87) or create substantial metabolic demands that can be exploited in a metabolic or anaerobic conditioning circuit (55, 163). The following exercises are common weighted carries. Farmer’s walk: The farmer’s walk requires the athlete to hold a load at the sides in each hand while walking forward (87, 147). The farmer’s walk can be performed with static loads (e.g., farmer’s bar handles or a heavy dumbbell) or variable loads (e.g., water-filled objects) (147). Regardless of the type of load used, the farmer’s walk offers a unique activation pattern o

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: walking. Keogh and colleagues (71) identified that compared to slower trials, the fastest trials had significantly greater stride length and rate and reduced ground contact time. Yoke walk: The yoke walk is another common strongman event whereby a heavy frame is carried on the shoulders of the athlete over a set distance. As McGill and colleagues (87) observed significantly greater spinal compression forces during the performance of the yoke walk when compared to six other strongman events, it is likely that this exercise has the potential to challenge and improve core stability. However, it must be performed with appropriate loads and technique to reduce the risk of injury, especially since Winwood and colleagues (154) reported that 213 strongman athletes ranked this exercise as the second most dangerous strongman lift in terms of injury risk. Similar to the farmer’s walk (71), faster yoke walks were characterized by increased stride length and stride rate, lower limb range of motion, and reduced ground contact time (61). Based on the impulse–momentum relationship, it would appear that weighted carries (e.g., farmer’s and yoke walks) require the production of high levels of anterior–posterior and vertical forces over short contact times, perhaps suggesting some potential to improve horizontal motion such as acceleration sprinting or initiating body contact in tackling or blocking opponents in contact or combat sports. Unilateral carries: Unilateral carries with the load positioned overhead (e.g., kettlebell or dumbbell) or at the hip via a kettlebell, dumbbell, or farmer’s handle (suitcase carry) impose a unique frontal plane challenge to the athlete (87). These carries may be advanced total body exercises that will improve lateral trunk flexor muscles (e.g., obliques and quadratus lumborum) and scapular control, thereby allowing better lateral stabilization of the spine than more traditional exercises such as dumbbell side bends or side planks. Technique Tips for Weighted Carries Irrespective of where the load is positioned on the body, the athlete should look to move in a similar way to normal walking. For example, during the carrying component of the exercise, the athlete should retain a predominantly neutral and vertical spinal position with no substantial hyperextension, flexion, or lateral spinal flexion. The athlete should use loads that challenge his or her desired walking speed, step length, step rate, and ground contact time but are still within his or her ability to maintain core and total body stability. In order to achieve this, the athlete will need to concentrate on keeping the loads in the same relative position to his or her center of mass throughout the carry. text: handle on it (28). In Western literature the term kettlebell is used to refer to a weighted implement consisting of a ball with a handle, which is probably better termed a kettleball (28). Along with the increasing interest in the use of kettlebell training has been an increase in the amount of scientific inquiry into the efficacy of using these implements with athletes and general populations. The majority of the scientific evidence supporting the use of kettlebells highlights their potential usefulness as a tool for general physical or fitness development (38, 65). In these studies, the most common exercise employed is the kettlebell swing, which can be performed with either one or two hands (65, 87, 137). While kettlebell swings appear to have a positive impact on cardiovascular fitness, it is important to note that this activity does not offer the same level of cardiovascular benefit as treadmill running or more traditional aerobic exercise (65). Currently, limited research explores the efficacy of kettlebell training as a strength development tool. When used with clinical and recreationally trained populations, kettlebell training has been reported to increase muscular strength levels compared to no training (68, 103). Additionally, when a battery of kettlebell exercises (i.e., swings, goblet squats, accelerated swings) is performed across a six-week training intervention, there appears to be an increase in muscular strength and vertical jump performance in recreationall

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: preparation exercise and that more traditional training methods such as weightlifting are more effective for developing maximal strength and jumping performance capacity. However, further scientific research is needed to develop a better understanding of the role that kettlebells may be able to play in the development of athletes. Types of Kettlebells When working with kettlebells, one must consider the type of kettlebell, of which there are two: the cast iron (figure 17.9) and the sport kettlebell (figure 17.10) (28). The cast iron, or fitness, kettlebells are cast from iron and range in size depending on their weight. The sport or competition kettlebells are made from steel and have universal design and measurements. Specifically, the size of the kettlebell does not change regardless of the weight, and the various weights are indicated by different colors (28). Besides the structural differences in the size and dimensions of the cast iron and sport kettlebell, the other difference is that the cast iron kettlebell is less expensive and probably more prevalent in strength and conditioning facilities. Handle diameter: 35 mm (1.4 in.) Considerations for Selecting Kettlebells The first major consideration in the selection of a kettlebell is the type of load provided. The two basic types of kettlebells are the fixed and the adjustable (28). With fixed-loaded kettlebells, such as cast iron or competition kettlebells, the load stays constant; thus, a set of kettlebells, which range across several loads, is required in order to provide training variety. Adjustable kettlebells are either plate loaded or shot loaded. In actuality, a plate-loaded kettlebell is simply a handle that is attached to weight plates and is not really a kettlebell even though it is classified as one (28). In contrast, a shot-loaded kettlebell is a hollow version of the more traditional kettlebell. Historically, these kettlebells were filled with sand, water, lead, and even mercury (28). If this type of kettlebell is only partially filled, the shot moves around in the ball, causing an increased training stressor. While popular in the early 20th century, especially with circus strongmen such as the famous Arthur Saxon and Eugen Sandow, this type of kettlebell is not popular in contemporary strength and conditioning. 1131

text: The second consideration relates to the handle, because it is the major interface between the athlete and the kettlebell. With cast iron kettlebells, the handle diameter changes slightly as the weight increases. For example, a 20-kilogram (44 lb) or heavier kettlebell has a handle between 33 (1.3 in.) and 35 (1.4 in.) millimeters; a smaller kettlebell may have a smaller handle diameter. Additionally, to facilitate the types of exercises that use kettlebells, the spacing between the handle and the top of the ball is standardized in good kettlebells. Typically, the space between the bottom of the handle and the top of the ball is 55 millimeters (2.2 in.), and the length of the handle is 186 millimeters (7.3 in.) (28). With regard to handle surface, some kettlebells come with smooth painted handles; others have polished steel handles, which have no paint and are basically bare metal. The polished steel handle tends to allow for a better grip because it holds chalk better and does not get as slippery as painted or polished handles do when athletes sweat on them (28). The performance of this exercise involves placing the end of a standard Olympic barbell (i.e., 20 kg [44 lb]) into a metal cylinder that is attached to a standard squat rack or stand-alone base attachment through a universal joint (4). text: Additionally, the landmine device can be used to perform a variety of exercises including the landmine row (80), Romanian deadlift (RDL) (85), squat (26, 114), press (135), and squat to press (69). While these exercises have become commonly implemented as part of the resistance training practices of many athletes (4), there is a paucity of scientific research exploring the actual physiological impact and efficacy of these exercises. As such, significantly more research is warranted to understand the unique training stimulus provided by landmine exercises. Sled Training In addition to the training studies incorporating sleds as a part of the conditioning program, several studies have examined the acute responses to sled exercise (72, 150, 152, 160). Keogh and colleagues (72) sought to describe the spatiotemporal characteristics of the heavy sled pull, using six resistance-trained subjects with experience in the heavy sled pull. Participants performed 3 25-meter (27 yd) sets of sled pulls with 171.2 kilograms (377 lb), with 3 minutes of rest between sets. Several significant differences were observed between the acceleration (the start through 5 m [5 yd]) and maximum velocity (20-25 m [22-27 yd]) phases, with average velocity, step length, swing time, and a range of segment and joint angles being significantly greater in the maximum velocity than acceleration phase. The fastest trials also had significantly greater step length, swing times, and trunk and knee angles at certain

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: significantly decreased and blood lactate significantly increased (peaking at 12.4 mmol/L immediately after) for a period of 1 hour, with no significant changes in creatine kinase at any time point. Testosterone and cortisol tended to increase at 15 minutes after (significant only for testosterone), with no significant changes in the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio observed. Such results suggest that concentrated sled pull exercises can produce profound metabolic fatigue and short-term hormonal augmentation with no muscle damage. The relatively quick recovery and lack of muscle damage (perhaps due to the concentric-dominant nature of this exercise) may indicate that lower and upper body sled exercises could be a key component of a resistance training program when athletes’ recovery abilities are particularly challenged, such as when they are performing large volumes of concurrent training or competing several times per week. Winwood and colleagues (160) and Williams and colleagues (152) have examined the potential of moderate to heavy sled pulls to produce a postactivation potentiation enhancement (PAPE) sprinting effect in adult semi-elite rugby (75%-150% body mass) and adolescent high school soccer players (loads producing a velocity decline of 40%-50% that equated to 66%-70% body mass), respectively. text: Unilateral Training When employing training methods, one can use unilateral or bilateral training interventions. These types of training methods can be performed with the upper body or lower body, depending on the targeted outcomes. Common lower body unilateral training exercises include lunges, step-ups, and the single-leg squat, which is sometimes referred to as the Bulgarian split squat. This exercise isolates one leg and is typically used in the preparation of athletes from numerous sports. Typically, these types of exercises are integrated into training programs with varying degrees of emphasis (86) in an attempt to reduce bilateral asymmetries (75) or as a rehabilitation tool (37). They are often used to reduce a bilateral deficit, where asymmetries in force production are observed between unilateral and bilateral movements (67). It has also been demonstrated that bilateral movements exhibit a bilateral facilitation in which voluntary activation of the agonist muscle group increases (12, 117). Trained or stronger individuals tend to exhibit a bilateral facilitation, while untrained, injured, or weaker athletes exhibit a bilateral deficit (14). Therefore, based on the bilateral facilitation response, trained individuals should not use unilateral methods as the primary strategy to develop strength. text: Conclusion In designing strength and conditioning interventions, one can use a variety of methods to apply overload. The use of alternative methods and nontraditional implements is increasing in popularity. When choosing to implement these methods, strength and conditioning professionals should consider the benefits and weaknesses of these types of training interventions. Additionally, the level of the athlete dictates whether use of these methods is warranted. For example, a novice athlete or untrained individual may derive a large benefit from doing bodyweight or core stability exercises. Conversely, the trained or elite athlete may experience greater gains with traditional ground-based free weight exercises. With the advanced athlete, the use of variable resistance may also allow for a greater training stimulus to be applied to traditional training methods. If choosing to employ alternative methods or nontraditional element–based training methods, strength and conditioning professionals must always ensure that they teach proper exercise techniques as well as constantly monitor their athletes to ensure that a safe training environment is maintained. text: 2 SIDE PLANK Starting Position Lie on the floor on the left side. Position the left elbow underneath the left shoulder with the left forearm perpendicular to the body. text: Strongman Exercises 9 TIRE FLIP Starting Position Begin facing the tire with the feet hip- to shoulder-width apart. Squat down and lean into the tire so that the chin and the anterior deltoids are resting on the tire and the feet are positioned back far enough to maintain a neutral spine position. Keeping the arms outside the knees and the elbows fully extended, grasp the tire with a supinated grip. All repetitions begin from this position. Upward Movement Phase Begin by extending the knees and hips and plantar flexing the ankles while pushing the tire forward. Move forward explosively toward the tire by taking two or three steps. Continue this movement until the body is aligned in a 45-degree angle to the tire. Consider flexing the hip and knee of one leg fully to drive the knee upward and toward the tire. text: the shoulders. The log can either be cleaned and pressed each repetition or cleaned once and pressed for multiple repetitions. Starting Position Stand with the feet placed between hip- and shoulder-width apart with the toes pointed forward or slightly outward. Squat down with the hips lower than the shoulders, and grasp the log with a closed, neutral grip. Place the hands on the log handles with the arms slightly outside of the knees and the elbows fully extended. Place the feet flat on the floor, and position the log in front of the shins and over the balls of the feet. All repetitions begin with the back in a neutral spine position, scapulae depressed and retracted, head in line with the vertebral column, and shoulders over or slightly in front of the log. Upward Movement Phase: First Pull Lift the log off the ground by extending the hips and knees. Keep the torso-to-floor angle constant; do not let the hips rise before the shoulders. Keep the elbows extended and the shoulders over or slightly ahead of the log. Upward Movement Phase: Transition As the log passes the knees, pull the log into the body by dropping into a full squat position while ensuring the elbows are about shoulder height and positioned slightly behind or above the hands. Briefly pause in this position with the log on the thighs. Upward Movement Phase: Second Pull Forcefully jump upward by extending the hips and knees and plantar flexing the ankles. 1149

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: Ensure the log is kept close to the body throughout this phase, whereby it essentially rolls up the upper body toward the shoulders. Upward Movement Phase: Catch After the lower body has fully extended, pull the body under the log and rotate the arms around under the log, similar to the catch in the power clean. Simultaneously flex the hips and knees to a quarter- or half- squat position. Rack the log across the front of the clavicles and anterior deltoids. Preparation Phase: Dip Flex the hips and knees at a slow to moderate speed to move the log in a straight path downward. Continue the dip to a depth not to exceed a quarter squat. Keep the feet flat on the floor, the torso erect, and the upper arms directly under the log. Upward Movement Phase: Drive Immediately on reaching the lowest position of the dip, reverse the movement by forcefully and quickly extending the hips and knees and then the elbows to move the log overhead. Downward Movement Phase Lower the log by gradually reducing the muscular tension of the arms to allow a controlled descent of the log to the shoulders. Simultaneously flex the hips and knees to cushion the impact of the log on the shoulders, and then return the log to the floor. If sufficient drop pads are available, it is possible to drop the log from overhead to the floor. chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: Assume a position under the yoke with the bar positioned on top of the upper trapezius muscles, with the feet positioned underneath the hips and the rest of the body symmetrically positioned under the frame. This should look something similar to the starting position of a partial barbell back squat, except that the hands are positioned on the vertical bars around lower chest height. Liftoff and Walking Phase After strongly bracing the spine, forcibly push the feet into the ground while pushing the elbows and hands forward into the vertical bars to better stabilize the yoke. While continuing to brace the spine and push the elbows and hands forward, adopt a walking movement pattern in which the spine remains vertical; initially focus on performing a series of short and relatively fast steps. While accelerating, increase the length of steps and further reduce ground contact times. Ending Position After completing the set distance, flex the hips, knees, and ankles to lower the frame carefully to the ground. Maintain a strong braced spinal position to minimize the risk of impact injury. chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: The sandbag can be positioned lengthways in the intended direction of the carry or positioned across the body. Due to the width of the sandbag, it may be necessary to rotate the hips outward, with the elbows inside the knees. Wedge the fingers under the sides of the sandbag so that the hands act as hooks under each side of the sandbag. Liftoff Position After strongly bracing the spine and ensuring a strong grip on the sandbag, forcibly push the feet into the ground and row the sandbag into your chest. If the sandbag is quite heavy, transition into a full squat position. However, if the sandbag is light to moderately heavy, it may be possible to bypass the full squat position and, via forceful hip extension, stand up from this position and initiate the carrying phase. Full Squat Position As the sandbag approaches the chest at the end of the liftoff phase, drop the hips rapidly into a deep squat position so that the sandbag is tightly held against the chest and resting on the upper thighs. Once secure and balanced in this position, initiate the concentric phase of the squat movement by vigorously extending the hip and knee joints while continuing to strongly pull the sandbag into the chest. Arms may be kept on the side of or above the sandbag, depending on personal preference. Carrying Phase From here, adopt a walking movement pattern, initially focusing on performing a series of short, fast steps, which will increase total body balance and stability. text: 14 FORWARD SLED PUSH AND PULL Starting Position (Push) Stand behind the sled and position the hands on the vertical bars of the prowler at a comfortable height, typically somewhere between hip and knee height in a standing position. (Note: The lower the hands are positioned on the prowler, the more likely this will result in a horizontal trunk and shin position, which will increase the ability to apply propulsive horizontal forces and accelerate the sled.) Keep the hands closer to the shoulders and elbows near the hips (shown) or extend the arms forward in front of the body (not shown), depending on personal preference. 1157

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: If the load is heavy, it is advisable to start with the two feet positioned together (not shown) to maximize the ability to apply horizontal force to initiate movement of the heavy sled. If the load is lighter, it is possible to start in an alternate split stance (shown) to better replicate a sprint starting position. Forward Pushing Phase While bracing the spine, initiate a stepping pattern that initially focuses on performing a series of short, relatively fast steps, which will increase the ability to apply horizontal forces to the ground. While building up speed, increase the length of the steps and further reduce ground contact times. The ability to apply propulsive horizontal forces to the ground can be optimized by ensuring the front foot is positioned behind the hip throughout the entire pushing phase. Starting Position (Pull) Stand in front of the sled and attach the sled to the body via a chest and shoulder harness (shown) or hold separate handles in each hand (not shown). Regardless of the attachment method to the sled, assume a position in which the trunk and shin are close to horizontal (not shown), which will increase the ability to apply propulsive horizontal forces and accelerate the sled. This can be best achieved by placing the hands on the ground (not shown) if connected via a harness to the sled or by leaning forward (not shown) if holding handles in each hand. If the load is heavy, it is advisable to start with the two feet positioned together (not shown)

text: Other Alternative Exercises 16 BACK SQUAT WITH BANDS Band Placement Loop the ends of long elastic bands around the band pegs of each side of a power rack. If the rack does not have band pegs, 1162

Take the other ends of the bands and place them over the ends of the bar so they rest against the outside of the weight plates on either side. Extend the hips and knees to lift the bar off the supporting pins or ledge, and take one or two steps backward. Position the feet shoulder-width apart or wider, even with each other, and the toes pointed slightly outward. Stand with an erect torso by positioning the shoulders back, tilting the head slightly back, and protruding the chest up and out to create a neutral or slightly arched back. All repetitions begin from this position. Downward Movement Phase Begin the exercise by flexing the hips and knees slowly and under control while keeping the torso-to-floor angle relatively constant. Maintain a

text: 17 ACCENTUATED ECCENTRICALLY LOADED BENCH PRESS Note: This exercise requires the use of weight releasers, which allow additional load to be applied during the eccentric phase of the movement. The spotting technique used is identical to that outlined for the bench press in chapter 16. Set-up Prior to the athlete initiating the movement the spotter should load the barbell with the appropriate weight and the weight releasers are attached to the barbell. It is important that the weight releasers are loaded correctly and placed evenly on the barbell so that they release at the completion of the downward movement phase without disrupting the athlete’s normal movement pattern. As a general rule, the weight releasers should be set so that they disengage from the barbell approximately 2 to 4 inches (5-10 cm) before the completion of the downward movement (51). Starting Position Lie in a supine position on a bench in the five-point body contact position. Place the body on the bench so that the eyes are below the racked barbell. Grasp the barbell with a closed, pronated grip slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Signal the spotter for assistance in moving the barbell off the supports. Position the barbell over the chest with the elbows fully extended. All repetitions begin from this position. Downward Movement Phase 1165

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: Lower the barbell under control to reduce the movement of the weight releasers. The weight releasers will disengage from the barbell about 2 to 4 inches (5-10 cm) before touching the chest at approximately nipple level. Keep the wrists stiff and the forearms perpendicular to the floor and parallel to each other. Maintain the five-point body contact position. Upward Movement Phase Push the barbell upward and very slightly backward as fast as possible until the elbows are fully extended. Keep the wrists stiff and the forearms perpendicular to the floor and parallel to each other. Maintain the five-point body contact position. Do not arch the back or raise the chest to meet the bar. At the end of the set, signal the spotter for assistance in racking the bar. Keep a grip on the bar until it is racked. text: 19 SINGLE-ARM LANDMINE ROW Setup and Starting Position While standing facing away from the axis of rotation of the landmine barbell, assume a hip-width stance with the unfixed side of the barbell just outside of the working-side leg with the toes behind the barbell sleeve. While maintaining a 25- to 45-degree knee angle, hinge at the hips until able to grasp the end of the barbell with one hand while the elbow is extended and reaching downward. In this position the forward trunk inclination should be roughly 30 to 60 degrees relative to the ground. This trunk angle should remain constant throughout the movement (80). Upward Movement Phase The upward movement phase (i.e., concentric phase) is initiated from the starting position and ends at the top position where the barbell reaches the greatest angle relative to the floor and contacts the torso. Throughout this motion remain stationary with an approximately neutral axial alignment while simultaneously retracting the shoulder girdle, extending the glenohumeral joint, and flexing the elbow to pull the barbell along the natural arc of the landmine barbell device (80). Downward Movement Phase Allow the shoulder girdle to protract, the glenohumeral joint to flex, and the elbow to extend simultaneously to return to the starting position (80). Note: As part of a balanced training program, this movement is performed on both sides of the body. MAJOR MUSCLES INVOLVED 1169

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: Stand facing the axis of rotation of the landmine barbell with a slight forward lean, while assuming a shoulder-width stance with the knees slightly flexed and grasping the end of the bar with one hand. The bar should be positioned about 4 to 6 inches (10.2-15.2 cm) away from the shoulder of the arm that is holding the bar (135). The other arm is held out to the side of the body and used for balance during the exercise. Downward Movement Phase Begin the exercise by flexing the hips and knees slowly and under control while keeping the torso-to-floor angle relatively constant. Maintain a flat-foot position with the knees aligned over the feet as they flex. Continue flexing the hips and knees until the thighs are parallel to the floor, the torso begins to round or flex forward, or the heels begin to rise off the floor. Upward Movement Phase Extend the hips and knees while keeping the torso-to-floor angle relatively constant. Keep the torso erect, shoulders back, and chest up and out. Keep the heels on the floor and the knees aligned over the feet. Continue extending the hips and knees; as the fully-standing position is reached, press the bar up and slightly forward until the elbow of the arm holding the bar is fully extended; full knee and elbow extension should be attained at about the same time. Return to the Starting Position Keeping the lower body and torso stationary, slowly lower the bar in a controlled manner until it is returned to the starting position. 1171

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training
text: 21 TWO-ARM KETTLEBELL SWING Starting Position Stand with feet flat and placed between hip- and shoulder-width apart with the toes pointed straight ahead, straddling a kettlebell. Squat down with the hips lower than the shoulders and grasp the kettlebell with a closed, pronated grip. Place the hands on the kettlebell with index fingers touching or close together, inside of the legs, keeping the elbows fully extended. Position the body with the back in a neutral spine position, shoulders retracted and depressed, feet flat on the floor, and eyes focused straight ahead or slightly upward. Maintain a neutral spine or normal lordotic position while flexing the hips and knees to approximately a quarter-squat position, with the kettlebell hanging at arm’s length between the thighs. All repetitions begin from this position. Backward Movement Phase Begin the exercise by flexing at the hips to swing the kettlebell between the legs. Keep the knees in a moderately flexed position with the back neutral and the elbows extended. Keep swinging the kettlebell backward until the torso is nearly parallel to the floor and the kettlebell is past the vertical line of the body. Forward and Upward Movement Phase When the backward swing reaches its end point, reverse the movement by extending the hips and knees to move the kettlebell in an upward arc. 1174

chapterTitle: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: Principles of Anaerobic Exercise Prescription Resistance training programs for athletic populations require attention to the principles of specificity, overload, progression, variation, reversibility, and individualization. One of the most basic concepts to incorporate in all training programs is specificity. The term, first suggested by DeLorme in 1945 (39), refers to the method whereby an athlete is trained in a specific manner to produce a specific adaptation or training outcome. In the case of resistance training, specificity refers to aspects such as the muscles involved, the muscle action (e.g., concentric, eccentric, and isometric), and the movement velocity and coordination (i.e., movement pattern; this does not mean replicating specific sporting movements), but it does not always reflect the combination of all these aspects. Importantly, it does not mean that all aspects of the training must directly mimic that of the sporting skill. For example, a squat movement is relevant to the vertical jump because it involves overcoming resistance in a similar movement pattern (e.g., combined knee and hip flexion followed by forceful knee and hip extension) and engages muscles (i.e., predominantly the knee and hip extensors) that are involved in the vertical jump, yet the speed of movement and force application are disparate between the squat and vertical jump. Sometimes used interchangeably with specificity is the acronym SAID, which stands for specific adaptation to imposed d

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: athlete. Without an overload stimulus, even an otherwise well-designed program greatly limits an athlete’s ability to make improvements. The obvious application of this principle in the design of resistance training programs involves increasing the loads assigned in the exercises, especially if the primary training goal is to improve maximal strength. Other more subtle changes include altering the number of training sessions per week (or per day in some instances) or increasing training volume by adding exercises or sets, which may preferentially stimulate a hypertrophic response (96, 143). Alternatively, varying exercise choice, modifying rest periods between sets and exercises, or any combination of these can result in an overload. The basis of the overload principle is to provide the body with a unique training stimulus to facilitate the development of the desired adaptations. Although an overload stimulus is typically thought of as an increase of a given training variable (e.g., load, volume, velocity), a reduction in these variables may also provide the opportunity for adaptation to take place. For example, a reduction in intensity (i.e., relative load) allows for an increase in the speed of a movement, thus facilitating the development of rapid force production characteristics (i.e., speed–strength). Alternatively, a reduction in training volume while maintaining (or increasing) intensity during a deload week may lead to an enhancement in performance (figure 18.1) if a

As the volume load increases across the first three weeks; some accumulation of fatigue occurs. Only once there is a reduction in volume load, during the deload week, does the increased performance manifest. If a training program is to continue producing higher levels of performance, the intensity or volume (i.e., overload) of training must continue to provide a unique stimulus. Progression, when applied properly, with loading or volume being sequential and specific to the desired adaptive response, promotes long- term training benefits. Although it is customary to focus only on the resistance used (i.e., intensity), one can progressively increase training volume by raising the number of weekly training sessions, adding more drills or exercises to each session, increasing the number of sets performed, or changing the type or technical requirements of the drills or exercises. For example, an athlete may progress from the front squat and clean grip shoulder shrug to learning the hang power clean and eventually the power clean through the use of a sequential application of various training exercises that segment the key positions associated with the lift (21). A key factor governing how training progression is applied is that it must be based on the athlete’s training needs and training status and it needs to be introduced systematically and gradually

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: Variation within resistance training programs focuses on removing linearity by manipulating overload and specificity to promote the desired adaptations. For example, strength and conditioning professionals may introduce variation into a training program by modifying volume, intensity, set configuration, rest periods, and exercise selection to provide a novel overload stimulus. These modifications to a training program may help reduce training monotony while also potentially reducing fatigue and providing a range of training stimuli. Regarding training intensity, strength–power characteristics have been developed within training programs that include more variation compared to prescribing constant repetition ranges with a greater or fewer number of sets and training or not training to failure (121, 195, 196). Moreover, it has been suggested that maximal and rapid force production may be improved to a greater extent using a combination of heavy and light training intensities compared to performing only one loading method (68, 118, 189). Strength and conditioning professionals can add variation to a training program at both the macro and micro level in several ways. At the macro level, implementing a periodized training plan may help develop specific fitness characteristics (e.g., hypertrophy, strength, and power) at different times throughout the training year. This in turn may provide athletes with a variety of training stimuli and potentially enhance the adaptations in subseq

text: loading is prescribed for longer than six weeks (186). Involution related to poor fatigue management may be the product of nonfunctional overreaching without the inclusion of proper recovery, however (54, 55). While the loss of fitness characteristics could be mitigated by incorporating retaining loads (i.e., small percentage of overall training volume focused on maintaining a desired characteristic) (42), it is important that strength and conditioning professionals understand the difference between retaining loads and the minimal effective dose needed to maintain or develop a fitness characteristic. The training goals and needs of each athlete are unique and should therefore command a training program suited specifically for them; this training principle is termed individualization. Athletes competing in different sports, the same sport, or in different events come with different genetic characteristics and training histories that affect how they respond to various training stimuli. As such, strength and conditioning professionals should always avoid a cookie cutter approach to designing training programs and should instead focus on providing individualized training programs that help each athlete reach their training goals. While this may seem simplistic, it is important to note that many aspects of different training programs may be similar or even identical. text: Step 1: Needs Analysis The strength and conditioning professional’s initial task is to perform a needs analysis, a two-stage process that includes an evaluation of the requirements and characteristics of the sport and an assessment of the athlete. Evaluation of the Sport The first task in a needs analysis is to determine the unique characteristics of the sport, which includes the general physiological and biomechanical profile, common injuries and mechanisms of injury, and position-specific attributes. This information enables the strength and conditioning professional to design a program specific to those requirements and characteristics. Although this task can be approached in several ways, it should at least include consideration of the following attributes of the sport (50, 128): Body and limb movement patterns and muscular involvement (movement analysis) Strength, power, hypertrophy, and muscular endurance priorities (physiological analysis) Common sites for joint and muscle injury and causative factors (injury analysis), especially for non-contact injuries Other characteristics of a sport—such as cardiovascular endurance, speed, agility, and flexibility requirements—should also be evaluated. This chapter, however, focuses only on the physiological outcomes that specifically relate to resistance training program design: strength, power, hypertrophy, and muscular endurance. text: Alternatively, increased hypertrophy may be beneficial for force production, as well as for collision and contact-based sports (e.g., American football or rugby) as a protective mechanism against impacts, and to increase the athletes’ momentum (momentum = mass × velocity) to improve outcomes in collisions. For example, if any reduction in speed is disproportionately lower than the increase in muscle mass, the collision sport athlete will be able to generate greater momentum, likely making him or her more difficult to stop or tackle. In contrast, excessive hypertrophy may negatively affect the performance of endurance-based athletes due to the requirement to carry extra mass for longer durations (13). Despite being in the same sport (i.e., athletics) as a shot-put thrower, a distance athlete requires a substantial amount of cardiovascular and muscle endurance within his or her events while also being prone to different overuse injuries (e.g., stress fractures). Moreover, the amount of hypertrophy may be limited when considering weight-categorized sports such as weightlifting, powerlifting, and combat sports. Depending on the athlete’s body composition and body mass, there may only be a limited potential for increases in lean body mass to ensure he or she does not exceed the weight category. To yield pertinent and reliable data that can be used effectively to develop a resistance training program, the tests selected should be related to the athlete’s sport, consistent with the athlete’s level of skill, and realistically based on the equipment available. The result of the movement analysis discussed previously provides direction in selecting tests. Typically, major upper body exercises (e.g., bench press and shoulder press) and exercises that mimic jumping movements to varying degrees (e.g., power clean, squat, front squat) are used in testing batteries. Such assessments should not replace the assessment of jump performance but instead should be used to determine whether any substandard jump performances are due to poor strength levels. After testing is completed, the results should be compared with normative or descriptive data (if published data exist or at least to squad data in team sports) to determine the athlete’s strengths and weaknesses. Based on this evaluation and the needs analysis of the sport, a training program can be developed to improve deficiencies, maintain strengths, or further develop physiological qualities that will enable the athlete to better meet the demands of the sport. text: Step 2: Exercise Selection Exercise selection involves choosing exercises for a resistance training program. To make informed exercise selections, the strength and conditioning professional must understand the nature of various types of resistance training exercises, the movement and muscular requirements of the sport, the athlete’s exercise technique experience, the equipment available, and the amount of training time available. Figure 18.2 on page 528 displays exercise selection flow charts for lower body strength and power exercises. Exercise Type Although there are hundreds of resistance training exercises to select from when one is designing a program, most involve primary muscle groups or body areas and fall into categories based on their relative importance to the athlete’s sport. Core and Assistance Exercises Exercises can be classified as either core or assistance based on the size of the muscle areas involved and their level of contribution to a particular sport movement. Core exercises recruit one or more large muscle areas (i.e., chest, shoulder, back, hip, or thigh), involve two or more primary joints (multijoint exercises; e.g., split squat, bench press, bent-over row), and receive priority when one is selecting exercises because of their direct application to the sport and enhanced dynamic correspondence (i.e., transference of gym-based training to improved performance in athletic tasks). The exercises selected for a resistance training program that focus on conditioning for a particular sport need to be relevant to the activities of that sport in their body and limb movement patterns, joint ranges of motion, and muscles involved and muscle actions. The exercises should also create muscular balance to reduce risk of injury from disproportionate training. Thus, it is up to the strength and conditioning professional to understand how each exercise may affect muscular development and to prescribe exercises accordingly based on the needs of his or her athletes. Sport-Specific Exercises The more similar the training activity is to the actual sport movement, the greater the likelihood that there will be a positive transfer to that sport (i.e., dynamic correspondence) (160, 165). This is the specificity concept, sometimes confused with the SAID principle. Arguably the SAID principle is more important than movement specificity; strength and conditioning professionals need to be mindful of the specific physiological adaptations that are targeted during each phase of training. Table 18.3 provides examples of resistance training exercises that relate in varying degrees to the movement patterns of various sports. The strength and conditioning professional should find this table helpful when trying to identify sport-specific exercises to ensure dynamic correspondence. For example, the primary muscles involved in jumping for basketball are the hip and knee extensors. An athlete can train these muscles by performing the leg press or back squat, but which exercise is preferable? text: Step 3: Training Frequency Training frequency refers to the number of training sessions completed in a given time period. For a resistance training program, a common time period is one week. When determining training frequency, the strength and conditioning professional should consider the athlete’s training status, sport season, projected exercise loads, types of exercises, and other concurrent training or activities. When the weekly resistance training volume–load is equated, hypertrophic adaptations (142) and strength adaptations (34) are comparable irrespective of training frequency. Training Status The athlete’s level of preparedness for training, which was determined during the needs analysis (step 1), is an influential factor in determining training frequency because it affects the number of rest days needed between training sessions. Traditionally, three workouts per week are recommended for many athletes, because the intervening days allow sufficient recovery between sessions. As an athlete adapts to training and becomes better conditioned, it is appropriate to consider increasing the number of training days to four and, with additional training, maybe five, six, or seven (table 18.4), although this depends on the phase of the competitive cycle. The general guideline is to schedule training sessions to include at least one rest or recovery day—but not more than three—between sessions that stress the same muscle groups (77); however, this may also depend on the intens
