However, as mentioned previously, an emphasis on strength development in weaker individuals may result in the greatest improvements in performance (8, 26, 29, 30, 178). This is likely due to the fact that relative force production determines acceleration, with the duration over which the force is applied determining acceleration, based on the impulse–momentum theorem. Other Training Exercise frequency is also influenced by the overall amount of physical stress, so the strength and conditioning professional must consider the effects of all forms of exercise. If the athlete’s program already includes aerobic endurance (e.g., long, slow distance) or speed, agility, and power (e.g., sprinting, agility, speed– endurance, plyometric) training, sport skill practice, or any combination of these components, the frequency of resistance training may need to be reduced (32). Additionally, the effects of a physically demanding occupation may be relevant. Athletes who work in manual labor jobs, instruct or assist others in physical activities, or are on their feet all day may not be able to withstand the same training frequency as athletes who are less active outside of their sport-related pursuits. 1216

text: Power, Other Core, Then Assistance Exercises Power exercises such as weightlifting movements and their derivatives (e.g., snatch, hang power clean, jump shrug) and other ballistic exercises (e.g., jump squat or hexagonal barbell jump) should be performed first in a training session, followed by other non-power core exercises, and then assistance exercises. This is due to the large neuromuscular demand placed on the body by power exercises because they require greater levels of skill and are prone to fatigue (71). The literature also refers to this arrangement as multijoint exercises and then single-joint exercises or large muscle areas and then small muscle areas (151, 183). Athletes who become fatigued are prone to using poor technique and consequently are at higher risk of injury. The explosive movements and extensive muscular involvement of power exercises also result in substantial energy expenditure (138). This is another reason to have athletes perform such exercises first, while they are still metabolically fresh. If power exercises are not selected in step 2 (exercise selection), the recommended order of exercises is core exercises (ideally with the most demanding exercises first) and then assistance exercises. This is an important consideration because researchers have shown that greater maximal strength adaptations may be produced with the exercises programmed earlier in a training session (44, 152) while the latter exercises may be negatively affected due to the ac

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: used to improve cardiovascular endurance (58, 130), although to a lesser extent than conventional aerobic exercise training. “Push” and “Pull” Exercises (Alternated) Another method of improving efficiency of training when time is limited is to alternate pushing exercises (e.g., bench press, shoulder press, triceps extension) with pulling exercises (e.g., lat pulldown, bent-over row, biceps curl) (2). This push–pull arrangement ensures that the same muscle group will not be used in two exercises (or sets, in some cases) in succession, thus reducing fatigue in the involved muscles. This approach is similar to the programming of antagonistic supersets, described later. In contrast, arranging several pulling exercises (e.g., pull-up, seated row, hammer curl) one after the other, even with a rest period between each, will compromise the number of repetitions performed because the biceps brachii muscle (involved in all three exercises) will become less responsive due to fatigue. The same result would occur if several pushing exercises (e.g., incline bench press, shoulder press, triceps pushdown) were sequentially arranged (all three engage the triceps brachii) (150). There are also push–pull arrangements for the lower body—for example, back squat and front squat as “push” and stiff-legged deadlift and leg (knee) curl as “pull”—but the classification of some exercises as “push” or “pull” is not as clear (e.g., leg [knee] extension). However, in such examples strength and conditionin

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: Step 5: Training Load and Repetitions Load most simply refers to the amount of weight assigned to an exercise set and is often characterized as the most critical aspect of a resistance training program (50, 106, 162, 163). Terminology Used to Quantify and Qualify Mechanical Work Mechanical work can be defined as the product of force and displacement (sometimes referred to as distance). An athlete can perform (external) mechanical work via demands made on the body to generate (internal) metabolic energy. Thus, it is important to quantify the amount of mechanical work or degree of metabolic demand to plan variation in the training program and to avoid the exhaustion phase of Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome associated with overtraining (33, 148). A quantity measure for resistance training work is needed. Traditionally, at least in the sport of weightlifting, this work is called the load, and one can calculate it by multiplying each weight lifted by the number of times it is lifted and summing all such values over a training session. Volume–load is a proxy for work, because displacement and force production are not measured in applied settings. However, volume–load (90) is a better term than just load. This quantity is related to mechanical work and the associated metabolic energy demands and physiological stress and is distinguished from repetition-volume (i.e., the total number of repetitions; see Step 6: Volume for more explanation). Volume–load should be considered as sys

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: amount of work being performed by athletes within a training session may vary. For example, athletes who are 5 feet 6 inches (1.68 m) and 6 feet (1.83 m) in stature who perform the back squat exercise with the same load and to the same squat depth are performing different magnitudes of work based on the displacement of the barbell. Within this scenario, the taller athlete must move (displace) the external load a greater distance, which results in performing more work than the shorter athlete. When monitoring training load, load displacement can be accounted for by calculating volume–load displacement, which multiplies volume–load by the displacement of the exercise. Although strongly correlated to volume–load, researchers have indicated that volume–load displacement may provide a better indicator of an athlete’s overall workload totals (78). Thus, if strength and conditioning professionals have the time to measure the displacements of exercises for their athletes (using appropriate technology), greater insight into how athletes respond to various training phases may be provided. Note that the volume–load is not affected by the set and repetition scheme (e.g., 15 sets of 1 repetition, 5 sets of 3 repetitions, 3 sets of 5 repetitions, or 1 set of 15 repetitions). Various set and repetition schemes affect the true intensity value for resistance exercise and indicate the quality of work performed. text: Although %1RM–repetition tables provide helpful guidelines for assigning an athlete’s training loads, research to date does not support the widespread use of such tables for establishing training loads for every exercise assigned to athletes, for the following reasons: Table 18.8 assumes there is a linear association between the loads lifted and the repetitions performed; however, several studies have reported a curvilinear relationship (95, 99, 103). Resistance-trained athletes may be able to exceed the number of repetitions listed in the table at any given percentage of their 1RM, especially in lower body core exercises (74, 75, 120, 134). The number of repetitions that can be performed at a certain percentage of the 1RM is based on a single set. When an athlete performs multiple sets, the loads may need to be reduced so that the desired number of repetitions can be completed in all the sets. Despite the prevalence of 1RM research, athletes may not always perform the predicted number of repetitions at a specified percentage of a 1RM. For instance, researchers have shown that subjects were able to perform two or three times more repetitions than are listed in table 18.8 (74, 75, 134). A certain percentage of the 1RM assigned to a machine exercise can result in more repetitions at the same percentage of the 1RM than with a similar free weight exercise (74, 75). Exercises involving smaller muscle areas may not produce as many repetitions as seen in table 18.8, and exercises re

text: actual 1RM (directly tested), estimated 1RM from an xRM test (e.g., a 10RM), or xRM based on the number of repetitions planned for that exercise (the “goal” repetitions; e.g., 5 repetitions per set). Once the actual 1RM is measured or estimated, the athlete’s training load is calculated as a percentage of the 1RM. Alternatively, a xRM test may be performed based on goal repetitions, thereby eliminating computations or estimations. In many cases, the strength and conditioning professional will use a variety of testing options depending on the exercises selected and the athlete’s training background. A common strategy for testing sufficiently conditioned athletes is to conduct a 1RM test in several core exercises and use xRM testing for assistance exercises. Testing the 1RM To assign training loads based on a percentage of the 1RM, the strength and conditioning professional must first determine the athlete’s 1RM. This method of assessment is typically reserved for resistance-trained athletes who are classified as intermediate or advanced and have exercise technique experience in the exercises being tested; however, 1RM testing can be safely performed with youth (19), adolescents (49), inexperienced adults (24), and older adults (127). Individuals who are untrained, inexperienced, injured, or medically supervised may not be appropriate participants for 1RM testing. One-repetition maximum testing requires an adequate training status and lifting experience, because the assessment

chapterTitle: Program Design for Resistance Training
text: become very fatigued after several testing sets, resulting in a loss of proper exercise technique and an invalid test. A variety of procedures can be used to accurately determine a 1RM; one method is described in figure 18.8. Despite an orderly testing sequence, variations in training status and exercise type will affect the absolute load increases in sequential testing sets. For example, the gradual load increase for 1RM attempts for an athlete who can back squat 495 pounds (225 kg) may be 20 to 30 pounds (9-14 kg) per testing set. For a weaker athlete with a back squat 1RM of 100 pounds (45 kg), a 20- or 30-pound testing load increment is too aggressive and is not precise enough to yield an accurate 1RM value. To improve the appropriateness and accuracy of the sequential testing sets, figure 18.8 also includes relative percentages that can be used instead of the absolute load adjustments. Estimating a 1RM When maximal strength testing is not warranted, testing with a 3RM or 5RM load (and then estimating or predicting the 1RM) can be a suitable secondary option. This approach is appropriate for nearly all athletes, provided they can demonstrate the proper technique in the exercise tested. Core and assistance exercises can be selected for RM testing, but excessive warm-up and testing sets may fatigue the athlete and compromise the accuracy of the test. text: consistently training with low xRM resistances (i.e., heavy loads) for a few months before testing (14). xRM Testing Based on Goal Repetitions A third option for determining training loads requires the strength and conditioning professional to first decide on the number of repetitions (i.e., the goal repetitions) the athlete will perform in the actual program for the exercise being tested. For example, if the strength and conditioning professional decides that the athlete should perform 6 repetitions for the bench press exercise in the training program, the xRM testing protocol should have the athlete perform the exercise with a load that will result in 6 repetitions (6RM). Core and assistance exercises can be selected for xRM testing, but as previously mentioned, high-repetition testing sets can create significant fatigue and may compromise the accuracy of the tested xRM. This effect seems to be more problematic for exercises that involve multiple joints and large muscle areas due to their high metabolic demand (138, 185). Further, xRM testing (and subsequent load assignments) for assistance exercises should be at or above an 8RM to minimize the isolative stress on the involved joint and connective tissue (2, 46). In other words, even if an athlete is following a muscular strength training program that involves 2RM loads for the core exercises, the heaviest load the assistance exercises should be assigned is an 8RM. When implementing RPE and RIR, it is recommended to prescribe intensities in the form of ranges (e.g., RPE of 7-8 or RIR of 2-3) (176). Although relatively few studies exist, some have shown that load prescription based on RPE for 8 weeks (73) and RIR for 12 weeks (60) may lead to greater strength improvements compared to using percentages of 1RM. Beyond the initial weeks of training, previous training blocks may be used as starting points for upcoming blocks. For example, the heaviest loads used during a general strength block (e.g., 3 sets of 6 repetitions) may serve as the starting loads for an absolute strength block (e.g., 3 sets of 3 repetitions). Readers are directed to previous literature for more thorough information on SRB (162, 176). Once decided on, the training goal can be applied to determine specific load and repetition assignments via the RM continuum and the chosen loading method. Repetition Maximum Continuum Figure 18.10 represents how RM ranges have been historically associated with training goals. In general, relatively heavy loads should be used if the goal is maximal strength, whereas light loads should be used to develop muscular endurance. To state this another way, low xRMs appear to have the greatest effect on maximal strength and high xRMs seem to result in better muscular endurance improvements (65, 106, 141). In contrast to strength and muscular endurance, a spectrum of RM loads may be used to develop muscle hypertrophy. The same research group followed up this study with a meta-analysis that showed no difference in muscle hypertrophy changes following various training protocols performed to muscular failure using lighter (<60% 1RM) and heavier (>60% 1RM) loads (141). As greater muscle activation was shown during multiple heavier versus lighter (i.e., 80% vs. 30% 1RM) sets performed to failure (82), high-load, lower-repetition sets may be considered more efficient at producing hypertrophic adaptations and benefiting muscular strength due to the neural adaptations associated with this characteristic (1). Strength and conditioning professionals should also be cautious in prescribing multiple low-load sets to failure to mitigate potential injury (109). Percentage of the 1RM Despite the physiological blend of training effects, the specificity principle still dictates the dominant outcome that is attained and enhanced with a particular training load. The relationship between the percentage of the 1RM and the estimated number of repetitions that can be performed at that load (table 18.8, page 544) allows the strength and conditioning professional to assign a specific resistance to be used for an exercise in a training session. In other words, the training goal is attained when the athlete lifts a load of a certain percentage of the 1RM for a specific number of repetitions (table 18.11). text: Because speed- or power-related sport movements often begin from zero or near-zero velocities, slow-velocity strength gains have direct application to rapid force development and power production (1, 22). For these reasons, the load and repetition assignments for power training overlap the guidelines for strength training (table 18.11). Non-weightlifting, multijoint power exercises (e.g., jump squat, bench press throw, overhead press throw) and single-joint muscle action data reveal that peak power is generally reached with the lifting of very light loads—from body weight (0%) to 30% of the 1RM (27, 105, 154, 157, 174, 175). Performing some of these exercises (e.g., bench press throw and overhead press throw) in a Smith machine, for example, can help to address the safety issues. On the other end of the load continuum, data from multiple national- and world-class weightlifting and powerlifting championships clearly indicate that power output increases as the weight lifted decreases from 100% of the 1RM (i.e., the 1RM) to 90% of the 1RM (56). In fact, for the back squat and deadlift exercises, power output for a load at 90% of the 1RM may be twice as high as with the 1RM load due to a large decrease in the time required to complete the exercise with the lighter load (57). Even for the already “fast” power exercises (weightlifting-based movements), there is still a 5% to 10% increase in power output as the load decreases from the 1RM to 90% of the 1RM (57). text: To promote program specificity, particular load and repetition assignments are indicated for athletes training for single-effort power events (e.g., shot put, high jump, weightlifting) and for multiple-effort power events (e.g., basketball and volleyball). For example, single-effort-event athletes may be assigned sets of 1 or 2 repetitions using loads that equal 80% to 90% of the 1RM, especially on heavy training days. For sports with multiple maximum-power efforts (e.g., the frequent maximum vertical jumping motions of a volleyball blocker), 3 to 5 repetitions per set with loads at 75% to 85% of the 1RM may be most appropriate. However, strength and conditioning professionals should consider the training season that the athlete is currently in to ensure that fatigue is being appropriately managed. On the basis of the %1RM–repetition relationships shown in table 18.8 (page 544), the strength and conditioning professional may question the load assignments for power training in table 18.11. The %1RM loads may appear to be too low compared to the goal number of repetitions. For example, according to table 18.8, 3 to 5 repetitions are typically associated with loads 93% to 87% of the 1RM, not 75% to 85% of the 1RM or less as table 18.11 indicates. Power exercises cannot be maximally loaded at any repetition scheme, because the quality of the movement technique will decline before momentary muscle fatigue defines a true xRM set (71). text: strength as the goal (e.g., Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays). It would be difficult for the athlete to perform the same high-load, low-volume regimen— especially in the power and other core exercises—with only one or two days of rest between sessions. As noted previously, training to failure may not be necessary to promote the desired training adaptations (36, 63, 137, 191). One strategy to counterbalance the monotony associated with lifting heavy loads is to alter the loads (%1RMs) for the power and other core exercises so that only one training day each week (e.g., Monday) is a heavy day. These heavy-day loads are designed to be high but usually with 1 to 2 RIR to avoid training to failure. The loads for the other training days are reduced (intentionally) to avoid an excessive accumulation of fatigue after the heavy day while still maintaining sufficient training frequency and volume. In the example of the three-days-a-week program, Wednesday can still serve as another heavy training day (depending on the organization of workouts) (table 18.5, page 538), while Friday may serve as the light day of the week in which 80% of the loads lifted in the power and other core exercises on the heavy day (Monday) are performed with the same number of goal repetitions. Even if the athlete is able to perform more repetitions than the designated goal number, he or she should not do so. This approach can be used for any training frequency. text: training session. For example, a strength and conditioning professional assigns 3 sets of 6 repetitions in the bench press exercise, and the athlete performs all 6 repetitions in all sets. After several workout sessions (the specific number depends on many factors), the athlete can complete 8 repetitions in the third (last) set for two consecutive workouts. In the following training session, the load for that exercise should be increased. While the 2-for-2 rule may provide strength and conditioning professionals with a tool to progress load in novice athletes, this method may eventually promote training to failure because it does not account for exercise technique, the goals of a given training phase, or relative intensity. For example, if an athlete modifies his or her technique just to achieve additional repetitions, an increase in load may not be warranted until exercise technique becomes more stable. Moreover, programming that allows for additional repetitions to be performed (i.e., not to failure) may be by design (176). In this instance, strength and conditioning professionals may plan for athletes to perform additional repetitions beyond the amount prescribed (i.e., RIR) with the goal of providing an overload stimulus while managing fatigue. Thus, it is advised that the professionals understand the limitations of the 2-for- 2 rule when adjusting the load during training. text: Step 6: Volume Volume–load relates to the total amount of weight lifted in a training session, and a set is a group of repetitions sequentially performed before the athlete stops to rest. Repetition-volume is the total number of repetitions performed during a workout session, and volume–load is the total number of sets multiplied by the number of repetitions per set, then multiplied by the weight lifted per repetition. For example, the volume–load for 2 sets of 10 repetitions with 50 pounds (23 kg) would be expressed as 2 × 10 × 50 pounds or 1,000 pounds (454 kg). (If different sets are performed with different amounts of weight, the volumes per set are calculated and then added to obtain the total training session volume.) In running exercise, the common (rep) volume measure is distance. If an intensity value is known or measured (e.g., running pace, which relates to percent V̇ O2max), total metabolic energy cost (which is proportional to mechanical work done) can be calculated. This value is comparable to volume– load in resistance exercise. The same concepts are applicable to the number of foot or hand contacts (volume) in plyometric exercise (note that the intensity is not considered when counting contacts but should be considered carefully by the coach), the number of strokes (volume) in swimming or rowing, or the number of throws or jumps (volume) for various sport activities. Training Status The training status of athletes affects the volume they will be able to safely tolerate. It is appropriate for an athlete to perform only 1 or 2 sets as a beginner and to add sets as he or she becomes better trained. As the athlete adapts to a consistent and well-designed program, more sets can be added gradually to match the guidelines associated with the given training goal. Thus, it is important that strength and conditioning professionals understand that heavy loads (i.e., >80% 1RM) can be used to train muscle hypertrophy rather than only maximal strength characteristics. In fact, the use of heavier loads may target specific fibers and higher threshold motor units (i.e., type II) to a greater extent than lighter loads (82, 106, 158), which in turn may allow for greater force, rapid force, and power output adaptations in future training blocks (187). Thus, it has been suggested that using heavier loads to target hypertrophic adaptations may be more beneficial to strength and power athletes (53, 97). However, it is also important to adjust the number of sets and repetitions compared to traditional hypertrophy prescription; for example, strength and conditioning professionals could prescribe 10 sets of 3 repetitions when using heavier loads compared to the more traditional 3 sets of 10 repetitions typically prescribed when targeting hypertrophy. text: Step 7: Rest Periods The time dedicated to recovery between sets and exercises is called the rest period or inter-set rest. The length of the rest period between sets and exercises is highly dependent on the goal of training, the relative load lifted, and the athlete’s training status. (If the athlete is not in good physical condition, rest periods initially may need to be longer than typically assigned.) The amount of rest between sets is strongly related to load; the heavier the loads lifted, the longer the rest periods the athlete will need between sets to safely and successfully complete the prescribed subsequent sets and to promote higher quality training. For example, training for muscular strength with 4RM loads would likely require significantly longer rest periods between sets than training for muscular endurance in which lighter 15RM loads are lifted. Despite the relationship between training goals and the length of rest periods (e.g., long rest periods for muscular strength training programs), not all exercises in a resistance training program should be assigned the same rest periods. It is important that the strength and conditioning professional allocate rest periods based on the relative load lifted and the amount of muscle mass involved in each exercise. An example of this specificity is for an assistance exercise as part of a muscular strength training program. text: Muscular Endurance A muscular endurance training program has very short rest periods, often less than 30 seconds. This restriction of the recovery time is purposeful; only a minimal amount of rest is allowed when light loads are being lifted for many repetitions. This type of program is designed to meet the guideline of the specificity principle for muscular endurance (2). Short rest periods are characteristic of circuit training programs (58) in which it is common to alternate exercises and limit rest period lengths to 30 seconds or less. 1255

text: Conclusion Well-designed programs are based on the application of sound principles during each step of a process referred to as program design. The process begins with a needs analysis to determine the specific demands of the sport and the training status of the athlete. With this knowledge, appropriate exercises are selected, and training frequency is established. The order of exercises in the workout is considered next, followed by load assignments and training volume choices based on desired training outcomes. Deciding on the length of the rest periods is the last step leading to the design of a sport-specific resistance training program. Practically defined, plyometric exercise is a quick, powerful movement using a prestretch, or countermovement, that involves the stretch- shortening cycle (SSC) (64). Furthermore, plyometric exercises are typically classified as being either ballistic or rebounding. Ballistic exercises are those that minimally include contributions from the neuromuscular component of the SSC (e.g., squat jump, medicine ball overhead throw). In contrast, rebound exercises are those that require physiomechanical SSC contributions (e.g., drop jumps or repeat countermovement jumps). This classification is important because it determines the specific neuromuscular and mechanical demands of each exercise (37). The purpose of plyometric exercise is to increase the power of subsequent movements by using both the natural elastic components of muscle and tendon and the stretch reflex. To effectively use plyometrics as part of a training program, it is important to understand the mechanics and physiology of plyometric exercise, the principles of plyometric training program design, and the methods of safely and effectively performing specific plyometric exercises. 1261

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Plyometric Mechanics and Physiology Functional movements and athletic success depend on both the proper function of all active muscles and the velocity at which these muscular forces are used. The term used to define this force–velocity relationship is power. When properly implemented, plyometric training consistently improves an athlete’s ability to produce muscle force and power (34, 59). This enhancement affects the impulse an athlete can generate. Impulse, defined as the integral of force over time, directly influences an athlete’s performance by changing momentum. Specifically, an increased impulse leads to greater momentum, which allows athletes to accelerate and decelerate more effectively. These rapid changes in velocity are crucial performance qualities across a wide range of sports. These increases are best explained by two proposed models: mechanical and neurophysiological (64). Mechanical Model of Plyometric Exercise In the mechanical model, elastic energy in the musculotendinous components is increased with a rapid stretch and then stored (3, 16, 35). When this movement is immediately followed by a concentric muscle action, the stored elastic energy is released, increasing the total force production (3, 16, 35). Of the mechanical model’s many elements, it is the series elastic component (SEC) that is the workhorse of plyometric exercise. While the SEC includes some muscular components, it is the tendons that constitute the majority of the SEC. When the musculoten

text: FIGURE 19.1 Mechanical model of skeletal muscle function. The series elastic component (SEC), when stretched, stores elastic energy that increases the force produced. The contractile component (CC) (i.e., actin, myosin, and crossbridges) is the primary source of muscle force during concentric muscle action. The parallel elastic component (PEC) (i.e., epimysium, perimysium, endomysium, and sarcolemma) exerts a passive force with unstimulated muscle stretch. Adapted from Albert (1995). Neurophysiological Model of Plyometric Exercise The neurophysiological model involves the potentiation (change in the force–velocity characteristics of the muscle’s contractile components caused by stretch [25]) of the concentric muscle action by use of the stretch reflex (9-12). The stretch reflex is the body’s involuntary response to an external stimulus that stretches the muscles (31, 49). This reflexive component of plyometric exercise is primarily composed of muscle spindle activity. Muscle spindles are proprioceptive organs that are sensitive to the rate and magnitude of a stretch; when a quick stretch is detected, muscular activity reflexively increases (31, 49). During plyometric exercises, the muscle spindles are stimulated by a rapid stretch, causing a reflexive muscle action. The series elastic component (SEC) and parallel elastic component (PEC) are two elastic structures that can be stretched within the muscle during plyometric exercises. The SEC includes tendons and muscle fiber cro

text: collagenous structures (e.g., fascicular membranes), which provide stability and protection to musculature. This reflexive response potentiates, or increases, the activity in the agonist muscle, thereby increasing the force the muscle produces (9-12, 41). As in the mechanical model, if a concentric muscle action does not immediately follow a stretch (i.e., if there is too long a time between stretch and concentric action or movement over too large a range), the potentiating ability of the stretch reflex is negated. Enhancements in measurement techniques using force platforms (kinetic data), motion capture (kinematic data), and electromyography (motor unit activation) have demonstrated that the mechanical and neurophysiological models contribute to the increased production of force seen during plyometric exercise (3, 9- 12, 16, 35, 41). For example, Jarvis and colleagues (37) have reported that rebound activities elicit enhanced neurophysiological contributions when compared to ballistic activities and that increased mechanical outputs exhibited during high-impact plyometrics are largely the result of mechanical factors associated with potential energy production (i.e., mechanical contributions). Stretch-Shortening Cycle The stretch-shortening cycle (SSC) employs the energy storage capabilities of the SEC and stimulation of the stretch reflex to facilitate a maximal increase in muscle recruitment over a minimal amount of time. This is the time from the end of the eccentric phase to the initiation of the concentric muscle action. Research has shown that increasing time in the amortization phase results in increases in elastic energy lost in the bench press compared to no delay between eccentric and concentric phases (energy losses were 0.35 s = 25%, 0.9 s = 52%, 1 s = 55%, and 1.5 s = 70%) (66). Consider the countermovement vertical jump mentioned earlier. Once the countermovement has stopped, the amortization phase has begun. As soon as movement begins again, the amortization phase has ended. The concentric phase, phase III, is the body’s response to the eccentric and amortization phases. In this phase, the energy stored in the SEC during the eccentric phase either is used to increase the force of the subsequent movement or is dissipated as heat. This stored elastic energy increases the force produced during the concentric phase movement beyond that of an isolated concentric muscle action (15, 58). In addition, the alpha motor neurons stimulate the agonist muscle group, resulting in a reflexive concentric muscle action (i.e., the stretch reflex). The efficiency of these subsystems is essential to the proper performance of plyometric exercises. Again, visualize the vertical jump. text: illustrated by three different vertical jump tests: a static squat jump, a countermovement jump, and an approach jump with several steps. As the rate of stretch increases, an athlete’s absolute performance in these tests improves; the static squat jump results in the lowest jump height, and the approach jump results in the highest. The static squat jump requires the athlete to get into a squatting position (i.e., 90-degree hip flexion and 90-degree knee flexion) followed by a jump up. This jump does not use stored elastic energy and is too slow to allow potentiation from the stretch reflex because there is essentially no eccentric phase. The countermovement jump uses a rapid eccentric element (i.e., a partial squat) followed immediately by rapid concentric muscle activity (i.e., a jump up). The rapid eccentric phase allows the athlete to store and use elastic energy in the stretched musculotendinous unit and stimulates the stretch reflex, thereby potentiating muscle activity (7, 33). The approach (one- or two-step) jump uses an even quicker, more forceful eccentric phase than the countermovement jump; the increased rate of stretch during the eccentric phase allows a further increase in vertical jump height (4, 6, 8, 29). The type of ground contact (and, hence, the rate of stretch and duration of the amortization phase, which affects the return of elastic energy) is influenced by the technique used during rebound actions. text: characteristics. To this end, Schmidtbleicher (56) categorized plyometric activities as either slow SSC (>0.25 s) or fast SSC (<0.25 s), depending on their ground contact time. As well as enhancing nonvoluntary neuromuscular outputs, the SSC serves a protective function within the myotendinous structures of the musculoskeletal system. The Golgi tendon organ is encapsulated within the serial components of the myotendinous junction. This is a proprioceptive mechanism that detects the rate and magnitude of force being applied to the respective tendon and will cause an inverse stretch reflex to occur past a tensile threshold, which immediately inhibits the excitatory signal through the motor neuron to the motor unit. Progressive plyometric training serves to desensitize the Golgi tendon organ, thus increasing the excitability potential of the motor unit for increased performance gains. The SSC combines mechanical and neurophysiological mechanisms and is the basis of plyometric exercise. A rapid eccentric muscle action stimulates the stretch reflex and storage of elastic energy, which results in an increase in the force produced during the subsequent concentric action. 1268

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Program Design Plyometric exercise prescription is similar to resistance and aerobic exercise prescriptions—mode, intensity, frequency, duration, volume, density, technique development and progression, and a warm-up period must all be dynamic variables incorporated in the design of a sound plyometric training program. Unfortunately, there is minimal research demarcating optimal program variables for the design of plyometric exercise programs. Therefore, when prescribing plyometric exercise, strength and conditioning professionals must rely on the available research, practical experience, and the increasing availability of motion capture and force plate technology to guide decision making. Needs Analysis To properly design a plyometric training program, the strength and conditioning professional must analyze the needs of the athlete by evaluating his or her sport, sport position, anthropometry, and training status. Each sport and position has its own unique requirements; some requirements are unique because of the movements involved, while others have distinctive injury profiles and risks. The anthropometry of the athlete is important, because heavier athletes face exponentially higher loads in gravity-assisted exercises than athletes with a lower mass; therefore, athletes’ body weight and their strength relative to their body weight become important considerations. Further, each athlete possesses a unique training status; some may be new to training and have never performed p

text: Mode The mode of plyometric training is determined by the body region performing the given exercise. For example, a single-leg hop is a lower body rebounding plyometric exercise, while a two-hand kneeling medicine ball throw is an upper body exercise that is performed ballistically. Modes of plyometric exercise are discussed in the paragraphs that follow. Lower Body Plyometrics Lower body plyometrics are appropriate for virtually any athlete and any sport or rehabilitation context. Because most sports require athletes to produce a maximal amount of muscular force in a short amount of time, lower body plyometrics provide an ideal and highly variable training stimulus that positively transfers training benefits to a variety of sports. For example, sprinters require sagittal plane movements, whereas most other sports require combinations of sagittal plane, frontal plane, and occasional transverse plane movements to be successful in competition. Demand can differ within positions in each sport: A middle blocker in volleyball may require predominantly lateral and vertical movements, whereas an outside hitter may have an increased emphasis on horizontal into vertical movements. American football, baseball, soccer, and basketball athletes must make quick, powerful movements and changes of direction in all planes to compete successfully. A basketball center is an example of an athlete who would benefit greatly from a plyometric training program, because the center is required to jump

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: professional to consider that plyometric session design is not limited to actions purely in the sagittal plane, and the transition from one foot to two feet, two feet to one foot, one foot to the other, or one leg to the same leg are often as important for performance enhancement as two-footed actions. Aerobic endurance athletes can also benefit from participation in a plyometric training program, because repetitive efforts that have neurophysiological and mechanical properties to optimize movement efficiency improve running and cycling economy by allowing muscles to produce more force with less energy. The various lower body plyometric drills have differing intensity levels and directional movements. The types of lower body plyometric drills include singular and repetitive actions (e.g., bounds) using one foot (hop) or both feet (jump), which may be transitional, in-place, or involve objects such as a box (e.g., a box jump) or hurdle. See table 19.2 for a description of these drills. TABLE 19.2 Lower Body Plyometric Drills Type Description Hops Takeoff from one foot and landing on the same foot. Volume is either measured by distance traveled or number of foot contacts. This movement develops acceleration and deceleration capabilities in a single limb, with intensity defined by displacement velocity and volume defined by foot contacts. These drills may be singular (ballistic hop) that is in place or horizontal, or reactive (multiple repetitive actions for height or distance).

Depth jumps and depth hops Depth jumps and hops (“shock” actions) use gravity and the athlete’s weight to increase exercise intensity. The athlete assumes a position on a box, steps off, lands, and immediately transitions vertically, horizontally, laterally, or to another box. The height of the box determines the intensity of the action, and the volume is determined by the number of foot contacts. Repetitive jumps onto boxes or over barriers may be added in sequence. Upper Body Plyometrics Rapid, powerful upper body movements are requisites for several sports and activities, including baseball, softball, tennis, golf, and throws in track and field (i.e., the shot put, discus, and javelin). For example, an elite baseball pitcher routinely throws a baseball at 80 to 100 miles per hour (129-161 km/h). It is important to understand that to reach velocities of this magnitude, throwing actions have to be initiated with the legs and require hip–shoulder separation and high rotational velocities in the hip and thoracic spine (e.g., a baseball pitcher’s shoulder joint must move at more than 6,000 degrees per s) (23, 26, 27, 53). Plyometric training of the shoulder joint may not only increase pitching velocity, but it also may prevent injury to the shoulder and elbow joints. Exercises for the trunk may be performed ballistically provided that movement modifications are made. Specifically, the exercise movement must be shorter and quicker to allow stimulation and use of the stretch reflex. The relatively large range of motion and the time needed to complete the movement do not permit reflexive potentiation of the abdominal muscles. The exercises can be modified to decrease both the range of motion and time, thereby allowing the agonist muscles to be potentiated. Intensity Plyometric intensity refers to the stress placed on muscles, connective tissues, and joints during an exercise. It is primarily determined by the type of drill performed, technique used, and arrangement of equipment. text: Frequency Frequency refers to the number of plyometric training sessions per week, typically ranging from one to four. This frequency depends on the athletes’ sport, their experience with plyometric training, their overall training status, the volume and intensity of plyometrics within the broader resistance training program, and the time of year (e.g., off-season or in-season). For example, during the season, one session per week is appropriate for American football players, while two or three sessions per week are common for track and field athletes (2). During the off-season, plyometric training frequency may increase to two or three sessions per week for American football players and to three or four sessions per week for track and field athletes (2). As with other program variables, research on the optimal frequency for plyometric training is limited. Because the literature is sparse, strength and conditioning professionals often rely on practical experience when determining the frequency with which athletes train using plyometric exercise. Rather than concentrating on the frequency, many authors suggest relying more on the recovery time between plyometric training sessions (19). Forty-eight to 72 hours between plyometric sessions is a typical recovery time guideline for prescribing plyometrics (19); using these typical recovery times, athletes commonly perform two to three plyometric sessions per week. As with resistance training, recovery between workouts must be adequ

text: 10 seconds of rest between repetitions and 2 to 5 minutes between sets. The time between sets is determined by a proper work-to-rest ratio (i.e., 1:5 to 1:10) and is specific to the volume and type of drill being performed. Drills should not be thought of as aerobic endurance training but as power training. Plyometric training can induce fatigue and inflammatory responses that can significantly increase delayed onset of muscular soreness and may impair jumping performance for up to 72 hours after a session. While these effects are noticeable in power-related measurements, strength levels may remain unchanged (5, 18, 60). Given this prolonged recovery period, strength and conditioning professionals should carefully schedule plyometric sessions to allow adequate recovery time between workouts and before competitions. This approach helps ensure optimal performance and reduces the risk of overtraining or injury. Volume Plyometric volume is typically expressed as the number of repetitions and sets performed during a given training session (table 19.6). Lower body plyometric volume is normally given as the number of foot contacts (each time a foot, or the feet together, contact the surface) per workout (2, 19) but may also be expressed as distance, as with plyometric bounding. For example, an athlete beginning a plyometric training program may start with a bound for 30 yards (or meters) per repetition but may progress to 100 yards (or meters) per repetition for the same drill. Progression Plyometrics is a form of resistance training and thus must follow the principles of progressive overload, which is the systematic increase in training frequency, volume, and intensity in various combinations. In simplistic models, as intensity increases, volume decreases. This relationship, however, is variable depending on the athlete’s training status and the nature of the activity prescribed. For example, athlete A who has minimal plyometric experience and a low training status may do 3 sets of 10 repetitions of the pogo jump to specifically train the SSC in the gastrocnemius–soleus complex, but athlete B, who has a higher training age, may do the same drill with an emphasis on minimizing ground contact time, and elite athlete C may do the drill at the end of a warm-up to simply potentiate the neuromuscular system. Further, after the pogo jump, athlete A may do jumps over short hurdles, but athlete B may do the depth jump instead and perform 2 sets of 4 repetitions with a 24- inch (61 cm) box. Elite athlete C may also do the depth jump but at a higher volume and intensity, such as 4 sets of 8 repetitions using a 45-inch (114 cm) box. Other

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Program Length Research has yet to determine an optimal plyometric training program length. Currently, most programs range from 6 to 10 weeks (2, 34); however, vertical jump height improves as quickly as four weeks after the start of a plyometric training program (54). In general, plyometric training should be prescribed similarly to resistance training within a periodized plan. For those sports requiring quick, powerful movements, it is beneficial to perform plyometric exercises throughout the training cycle. The intensity and volume of the selected drills should vary with the training status of the athlete and the sport season. 1281

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Warm-Up As in any training program, a plyometric exercise session should begin with a specific warm-up that incorporates activation, mobilization, and potentiation of the neuromuscular and musculoskeletal system (refer to chapter 15 for movement preparation guidelines). The specific warm-up for plyometric training should consist of low-intensity, dynamic movements that increase in intensity as the warm-up progresses. Table 19.7 provides a list and explanation of examples of specific warm-up drills for plyometric training. Steps for Implementing a Plyometric Training Program 1. Evaluate the athlete, including the athlete’s sport and training history. 2. Establish sport-, position-, and athlete-specific goals. 3. Teach the athlete proper jumping, landing, and throwing technique. 4. Assign proper plyometric training program design variables, addressing intensity, frequency, recovery, and volume. 5. Properly progress the plyometric training program. 1282

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Age Considerations It is becoming more common for younger and older individuals to want to augment the training programs for their sport with plyometric exercise. When these exercises are applied appropriately, these populations can experience the same positive outcomes as other age groups, with minimal risk of injury, with appropriate consideration of prescription to technical competence and strength levels. Adolescents Although plyometrics commonly have been viewed as appropriate only for conditioning elite adult athletes, prepubescent and adolescent children may also benefit from training with plyometric and plyometric-like exercises. Besides providing the well- documented muscular power and bone strength adaptations, regular participation in an appropriately designed plyometric training program can better prepare young athletes for the demands of sport practice and competition (20) by enhancing neuromuscular control and performance. Research has yet to determine a universal age at which people are physically able to begin participating in a plyometric training program. An analysis of the body’s development provides some insight into the issue. Because the epiphyseal plates of the bones of prepubescent children have yet to close (39, 47), depth jumps and other high-intensity lower body drills are contraindicated (2, 36, 46). text: It is extremely important that plyometric exercise programs for children gradually progress from relatively simple drills to more complex drills. It is important to focus on the quality of the movements (e.g., proper body alignment and speed of movement) to develop techniques that will be essential for more advanced exercises. The current evidence suggests that a twice-weekly program for 8 to 10 weeks beginning at 50 to 60 jumps a session and increasing exercise load weekly results in the largest changes in running and jumping performance in young children (38). An alternative program for children who do not have the capability or tolerance for a twice- weekly program would be a low-intensity program for a longer duration (38). Under proper supervision and with an appropriate program, prepubescent and adolescent children may perform plyometric exercises. Depth jumps and high- intensity lower body plyometrics are contraindicated for this population. Masters Masters athletes find that they can maintain their physical capabilities late into life and are looking for additional training insights. When designing a plyometric training program for a masters athlete, the strength and conditioning professional needs to be specific in deciding on the goal of the program. Some primary issues to consider are strength levels (i.e., ensuring that age-related sarcopenia has not degraded muscle function) and any preexisting orthopedic conditions (e.g., osteoarthritis or any sort of surgical j

text: runner with a history of knee surgery such as partial meniscus removal or with significant joint degeneration should regard depth jumps and single-leg plyometric exercises as contraindicated and use other forms of plyometrics cautiously. After consideration of the predispositions related to the masters athlete’s physical condition, a plyometric program should be designed according to the same guidelines as outlined for adult athletes, with the following emphases: Intensity and volume should be carefully considered relative to the performance capacities of the individual. Cautions regarding decreased strength capacities, potential for degenerative joint conditions, and decreased recovery capacities associated with aging should be applied. It is important to note how the masters athlete feels after training; soreness may occur, but the program should be modified if chronic or excessive pain or discomfort is present. 1286

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Plyometrics and Other Forms of Exercise Plyometric exercise is only one part of an athlete’s overall training program. Many sports and activities use multiple energy systems or require other forms of exercise to properly prepare athletes for competition. Each energy system and sport-specific need must be included in a well-designed training program. Plyometric Exercise and Resistance Training A combination of plyometrics and resistance training during a training cycle should be structured to allow maximal efficiency and physical improvement. The following list and table 19.8 provide guidelines for developing a combined program: Combine lower body resistance training with upper body plyometrics, and upper body resistance training with lower body plyometrics. Performing heavy resistance training sessions and plyometric sessions on the same day is not usually recommended (17, 24). However, many athletes may benefit from complex training, a combination of resistance training and plyometric training within the same training session to enhance fast and slow force expression. If athletes perform this type of training, adequate recovery is needed between plyometrics and other high-intensity training. Plyometrics can comprise a stand-alone training session or be incorporated into a resistance training session. Incorporating plyometrics into a resistance training session may have neuromuscular recruitment benefits through facilitating postactivation potentiation during biomechanically

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Plyometric Exercise and Aerobic Exercise Many sports—such as basketball and soccer—have both an anaerobic (i.e., power) and an aerobic component. Therefore, multiple types of training must be combined to best prepare athletes for these types of sports. Because aerobic exercise may have an interfering effect on power production (17), it is advisable to perform plyometric exercise before aerobic endurance training. The program design variables do not change and should complement each other to most effectively prepare these athletes for competition. 1289

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Safety Considerations Plyometric exercise is not inherently dangerous; however, as with all modes of exercise, the risk of injury exists. Injuries can occur simply due to an accident, but they more typically occur when proper training procedures are violated and may be the result of an insufficient strength and conditioning base, inadequate warm-up, improper progression of lead-up drills, inappropriate volume or intensity for the phase of training, poor shoes or surface, or a simple lack of skill. The following sections identify and address these and other risk factors. Knowledge of risk factors can improve the safety of athletes performing plyometric exercise. Pretraining Evaluation of the Athlete To reduce the risk of injury and facilitate the performance of plyometric exercises, the athlete must understand proper plyometric technique and possess a sufficient base of strength, speed, and balance. In addition, the athlete must be sufficiently mature, both physically and psychologically, to participate in a plyometric training program. The following evaluative items can help determine whether an athlete meets these conditions. Technique Before adding any drill to an athlete’s plyometric program, the strength and conditioning professional must first demonstrate proper technique to the athlete and then coach and cue the athlete on proper technique to maximize the drill’s effectiveness and minimize the risk of injury. For lower body plyometrics, proper landing technique is essen

text: performing lower body plyometrics, it is essential that the knees are positioned over the toes. Inward movement of the knees—also termed dynamic valgus—is a significant risk factor for knee injuries of all types, including patellofemoral pain and tears or ruptures of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) (45). In addition to instructing an athlete on a proper body position while landing, the strength and conditioning professional must explain, coach, and cue the athlete to land with an active flat foot. In preparation for ground contact, the athlete’s ankles should be dorsiflexed (so that the toes are pulled back toward the knees). This means that the bottom of the foot is parallel to the ground as the athlete comes into landing. Immediately before landing, the athlete should be taught to aggressively plantarflex the ankle to “attack the ground with the foot.” This achieves two outcomes. First, the plantarflexion increases the tension in the gastrocnemius–soleus complex at ground contact, which increases the efficacy of the SSC and enhances the output power in the resulting jump. Second, the last-second adjustment in the angle of the foot, along with the increased muscle tension, means that the heels stay off the ground during the land–takeoff action. This enhances both anterior and vertical propulsion and is often coached as “the credit card rule,” meaning that enough of the foot should be in contact with the ground to achieve high impulses, but the strength and conditioning

Previous recommendations for lower body plyometrics stated that the athlete’s 1RM squat should be at least 1.5 times his or her body weight (17, 24, 36, 50, 63). However, many plyometric activities can be safely taught to athletes without such formalized levels of strength (figure 19.5). It is our recommendation that plyometrics be included for all athletes whose sports require running, landing, jumping, or cutting. As a prerequisite, teaching proper alignment and movement mechanics through the use of plyometric exercise has been shown repeatedly to decrease the athlete’s risk of injury during practices and games (50). Various authors have theorized that basic in-place jumps such as repeated pogo jumps and countermovement jumps require relatively low levels of strength; repeated hops and jumps may require a basic strength level equivalent to a back squat of 1 × body weight, bounding and depth jumps using a box 12 inches (30 cm) tall or shorter may have a back squat strength equivalent of 1.5 × body weight, and depth or box jumps with a box higher than 12 inches (30 cm) may require a back squat strength equivalent of 2 × body weight (58). 1292

text: FIGURE 19.3 Proper plyometric landing technique. (a) When learning to land and stop, the shoulders are in line with the knees, which helps place the center of gravity over the body’s base of support. The knees are over the toes; excessive inward (valgus) movement increases the risk of lower extremity injury; weight is evenly distributed through a flat foot to allow a balanced deceleration position. Learning to land and stop, decelerating body mass completely, is a precursor to learning to land and rebound (i.e., reaccelerate body mass). (b) Proper landing technique to facilitate reactionary rebound actions; the shoulders are in line with the knees, the ankles are stiff, and athlete contacts the ground with the midfoot and forefoot to enable a rebound acceleration to occur. Note the alignment of the hips, knees and toes, with the feet hip-width apart to optimize vertical or horizontal force (depending on the subsequent movement). Back squat equivalent strength is a descriptive term used to infer the necessary strength capacity required to tolerate the impact stress of the exercise so that it does not acutely overreach the athlete and become injurious. The back squat is illustrative due to the nature of its axial load on the total body, yet it is recognized that not every athlete measures maximal squat strength. text: Balance Balance is a lower body plyometric prerequisite that should not be overlooked. Balance is the maintenance of a position without movement for a given period of time. Many lower body plyometric drills require the athlete to move in nontraditional patterns or on a single leg. These types of drills necessitate a solid, stable base of support on which the athlete can safely and correctly perform the exercises. Three balance tests are provided in table 19.9, listed in order of difficulty; each test position must be held for 30 seconds (62). For example, an athlete beginning plyometric training for the first time would be required to stand on one leg for 30 seconds without falling. An experienced athlete beginning an advanced plyometric training program must maintain a single-leg half squat for 30 seconds without falling. Additionally, the surface on which the balance testing is performed should be the same as that used in the plyometric drills. 1294

Physical Characteristics Athletes who weigh more than 220 pounds (100 kg) may be at an increased risk for injury when performing plyometric exercises (50, 1296

text: 63). Greater weight (mass) increases the compressive force on joints during the exercises, thereby predisposing ankle, knee, and hip– pelvic complex joints to injury. Therefore, athletes weighing over 220 pounds (100 kg) should approach high-volume and high-intensity plyometric exercises and depth jumps from heights greater than 18 inches (46 cm) with caution (50, 63). As with other forms of exercise, an athlete’s joint structure and previous injuries must also be examined before he or she begins a plyometric training program. Previous injuries or abnormalities of the spine, lower extremities, or upper extremities may increase an athlete’s risk of injury during plyometric exercise. Specifically, athletes with a history of muscle strains, pathological joint laxity, or spinal dysfunction—including vertebral disk dysfunction or compression—should use caution when beginning a plyometric training program (28, 29, 36, 55). Ultimately, because the body composition, strength, and technical competency can differ between athletes who weigh the same, professional judgment always should be applied when considering plyometric prescription. Equipment and Facilities In addition to athletes’ fitness and health, the area and equipment used for plyometric drills may significantly affect their safety. Landing Surface To prevent injuries, the landing surface used for lower body plyometrics must possess adequate shock-absorbing properties. A grass field, suspended floor, or rubber mat is a good s

text: plyometrics, especially for those recovering from musculoskeletal injury, mini-trampolines, like thick exercise mats, are not effective for plyometric training of uninjured athletes because the amortization phase is extended while the athlete is in contact with the elastic surface. Training Area The amount of space needed depends on the drill. Most bounding and running drills require at least 30 yards (or meters) of straightaway, though some drills may require a straightaway of 100 yards (or meters). For most standing, box, and depth jumps, only a minimal surface area is needed, but the ceiling height must be at least 10 feet (3 m) to be adequate. Equipment Boxes used for box jumps and depth jumps must be sturdy and should have a nonslip top. Boxes should range in height from 6 to 42 inches (15-107 cm) and should have landing surfaces of at least 18 by 24 inches (46 × 61 cm) (19). The box should be constructed of sturdy wood (e.g., 3/4-inch [1.9 cm] plywood) or heavy-gauge metal that is covered in a protective covering to reduce the risk of injury if the athlete contacts the box. High density foam within a cubed framework with solid landing surfaces is also appropriate. To further reduce injury risk, there are several ways of making the landing surface nonslip such as adding nonslip treads, mixing sand into the paint used to cover the box, or affixing rubberized flooring to the top (19). Proper Footwear Athletes must use footwear with good ankle and foot support; good lateral

text: joint damage. Shoes with excessive cushioning may also interfere with the amortization phase process, and a shoe that has increased inbuilt pronation (such as a weightlifting shoe) may interfere with ground contact mechanics and therefore the safety and effectiveness of the exercise. Supervision In addition to the safety considerations already outlined, close monitoring of athletes is necessary to ensure proper technique. Plyometric exercise is not intrinsically dangerous when performed correctly, but as with other forms of training, poor technique may unnecessarily predispose an athlete to injury. Depth Jumping There is a limit to the maximal height at which a depth jump can be effectively and safely performed. A height of 48 inches (122 cm) would provide a significant overload on the muscles, but the resistance may be too great for many athletes to overcome while maintaining correct technique (47). Jumping from such a height increases the possibility of injury; furthermore, the amount of force to be overcome is so great that the amortization phase is extended and thus the purpose of the exercise is defeated. The recommended height for depth jumps ranges from 16 to 42 inches (41-107 cm), with 30 to 32 inches (76-81cm) being the norm (4, 21, 30, 43, 44, 48). The depth jump box height for athletes who weigh over 220 pounds (100 kg) should be 18 inches (46 cm) or less. 1299

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Conclusion The major goal of plyometric training is to rapidly apply force to provide an overload to the agonist muscles. Although it has been repeatedly shown that plyometric exercise increases muscular power for athletes in a formal training program (34, 53, 65, 67), research has yet to determine whether mechanical or neurophysiological adaptations account for the improvement. Plyometrics should be considered not an end in itself but part of an appropriately periodized program that includes strength, speed, endurance, and mobility training. Plyometrics requires an appropriate warm-up and should be preplanned to allow adequate recovery. After the athlete has begun a proper strength and conditioning program, plyometric training may be used to further develop impulses and positive transfer of training benefits.
