COMMON ERRORS Excessive flexion of the hip, knee, and ankle on landing, which unnecessarily increases the amortization phase and ground contact time Hopping with the weight too far forward in the foot, which reduces ground reaction forces and limits optimal force production to maximize flight distance 17 MULTIPLE BARRIER HOP 1326

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Intensity level: Medium to high Direction: Horizontal and vertical Equipment: Two to 10 barriers such as cones or hurdles Starting position: Facing the first barrier, get into a comfortable, single-leg upright stance with the contralateral hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement on the hopping leg. Bring the other leg behind the body. Upward movement: Explosively hop forward, driving from the hip, knee, and ankle over the first barrier as tall as possible, using necessary hip and knee flexion to clear the barrier. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing in the starting position, and immediately repeat the jump over the second barrier. Note: Intensity level of this exercise can be increased from medium to high by progressively increasing the height of the barrier (e.g., from a cone to a hurdle). Increasing the intensity of the hop may increase the ground contact time and the amortization phase. COMMON ERRORS Incorrect hurdle height or a less-than-maximal push from the ground to achieve full extension position when clearing the hurdle Inappropriate landing mechanics, which increases ground contact time between hurdles 1327

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 18 LATERAL BARRIER JUMP Intensity level: Medium Direction: Lateral and vertical Equipment: A barrier such as a cone or hurdle Starting position: With the barrier to one side, get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement. Upward movement: Leaning out of the countermovement in the direction of travel, use a powerful triple extension to jump over the barrier as tall as possible with both legs, using necessary hip and knee flexion to clear the barrier. (Note: The second photo shows the 1328

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: athlete clearing the hurdle too high relative to the hurdle height and with too much knee flexion.) Keep the hips and shoulder square and the knees and feet together without lateral deviation. Downward movement: Rotate over the hurdle so the lean is in the direction of the subsequent jump on landing. Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing on the opposite side of the barrier, and immediately repeat the jump to the starting side. (Note: The third photo does not show the athlete leaning back toward the starting side for the return jump.) Note: The intensity level of the lateral barrier hop can be increased from medium to high by progressively increasing the height of the barrier or by performing movement with one leg only (i.e., a hop), which is an excellent exercise for aiding direction change capacity in the athlete. By reversing the direction of movement, the ground contact time and the amortization phase of the movement are changed compared to movements in the same direction. This will be influenced further by the height of the hurdle. COMMON ERRORS Not maintaining a square hip and shoulder position, so the jump does not stay in the frontal plane Lack of preparatory lean in both takeoff (center of mass should lean in the direction of travel) and landing (orient the body so that it is leaning back toward the start for the return jump), which increases the ground contact time and reduces the effectiveness of the drill 1329

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 19 FOUR-HURDLE HOP Intensity level: High Direction: Lateral and vertical Equipment: Four hurdles: two pairs of hurdles. Each hurdle in the pair is separated by 12 inches (30 cm). Each pair is separated by 18 inches (46 cm). Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance on the right foot; the line of four hurdles will be to the left. The non-jumping leg is held in a stationary position with the hip and knee flexed during the exercise. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement. Movements: 1330

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 1. Lean in the direction of travel. 2. Explosively hop left over the first hurdle with the right foot, using both arms to assist. 3. Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing. 4. Land on the right foot, and immediately repeat the hop over the next hurdle. 5. Land on the right foot, and immediately repeat the hop over the next two hurdles. 6. Land on the left foot, and immediately hop right over the first hurdle with the left foot, using both arms to assist. 7. Land on the left foot, and immediately repeat the hop over the next three hurdles; finish by landing on the right foot. COMMON ERRORS Not reflecting subsequent takeoff direction in the body lean (i.e., the center of mass in the takeoff and the landing before direction change should reflect the direction of travel in the subsequent movement; failure to do so increases the ground contact time and reduces the effectiveness of the drill) Not increasing ground contact time for both the two- hurdle hop and the change of direction movement, meaning insufficient force is produced in the jump 1331

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 20 PROGRESSIVE LATERAL JUMP Intensity level: High Direction: Diagonally lateral and vertical Equipment: String tied at athlete’s eye level and loosely secured to the ground at a 45-degree angle to the ground Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance on one side of the string next to the anchor on the ground. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement. Movements: 1. Explosively jump diagonally (sideways and forward) over the string using both arms to assist the movement. 1332

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 2. Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing. 3. Land on the other side of the string, and immediately repeat the jump diagonally forward. Continue the jumping sequence over the string as it gets progressively higher. Note: As the string gets higher, the athlete will need a longer ground contact time and more hip and knee flexion to clear the string. Ensure that the anchor on the string enables the string to give way should the athlete make contact with it. COMMON ERRORS Changing the orientation of the hips (i.e., rotate in the transverse plane) during takeoff, which increases the ground contact time on the subsequent jump Not increasing ground contact time and hip and knee flexion through the sequence, meaning insufficient force is produced as the required jump height increases 1333

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Bounds 21 SKIP Intensity level: Low Direction: Horizontal and vertical 1334

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Starting position: One leg is lifted to approximately 90 degrees of hip and knee flexion with the ankle dorsiflexed. Arm action: Reciprocal (as one leg is lifted, the opposite arm is lifted) Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement on one leg. Upward movement: Drive up and forward on one leg. The opposite leg should remain in the starting flexed position until landing. Downward movement: Land in the starting position on the same leg. Immediately repeat the skip with the opposite leg. COMMON ERRORS Rotating at the hip and shoulders during the movement (which should be in the sagittal plane only), detracting from the velocity achieved Coordination errors in the reciprocal arm and leg action, which detract from the forward momentum achieved 1335

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 22 POWER SKIP Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical and horizontal Starting position: One leg is lifted to approximately 90 degrees of hip and knee flexion with the ankle dorsiflexed. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement on one leg. Upward movement: Drive up and forward on one leg. Move the flexed, non-jumping leg up and into greater hip and knee flexion while jumping. Both arms should be used to assist with the upward movement. Downward movement: Land in the starting position on the same leg. Immediately repeat the skip with the opposite leg. Note: Emphasis is on high-quality ground contact and leg drive as athletes determine the effectiveness of the skip. This movement should be more vertical and with a faster ground contact than the higher intensity linear bounding drills listed later in the chapter. COMMON ERRORS Not attacking the ground with significant intensity to accelerate the center of mass forward in subsequent takeoff; this influences the subsequent flight phases and landings Coordination errors in the double-arm action, which detracts from the forward momentum achieved 1336

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 23 LATERAL SKIP Intensity level: Medium Direction: Vertical and lateral Starting position: One leg is lifted to approximately 90 degrees of hip and knee flexion with the ankle dorsiflexed. This leg should be opposite to the direction of movement (i.e., if the skip is to the right, the left leg should be raised). Arm action: Reciprocal (as one leg is lifted, the opposite arm is lifted) Preparatory movement: Drive the lifted leg forcefully toward the ground and away from the direction of movement so that it contacts the ground outside of the base of support. Upward movement: The lateral drive of the downward leg will cause the body to move up and sideways away from the foot contact. As this happens, the other leg should flex at the hip and knee in flight. The drive leg typically takes a small adjustment step to aid stability and rhythm in the action. 1337

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Downward movement: Land in the starting position on the same leg. Immediately repeat the skip, continuing the lateral movement for a number of repetitions or over a given distance, then use the opposite leg. COMMON ERRORS Not contacting the ground with sufficient lateral distance from the hip to cause sideways momentum to occur Not controlling rotations at the hip and shoulders during the movement, which detracts from the lateral velocity achieved 1338

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 24 LINEAR BOUND Intensity level: Medium Direction: Horizontal and vertical Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart. Arm action: Single arm 1339

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Preparatory movement: Jog at a comfortable pace; begin the drill with the left foot forward. Upward movement: Push off with the left foot as it contacts the ground. During push-off, bring the right leg forward by flexing the thigh to a position approximately parallel with the ground and the knee at 90 degrees, with the ankle stiff and dorsiflexed. During this flight phase of the drill, reach forward with the left arm. Downward movement: Attack the ground with an active flat-foot contact. Land on the right leg, and immediately repeat the sequence on the opposite side. Note: A linear bound is an exaggeration of the running gait; the goal is to cover as great a distance as possible during each stride. COMMON ERRORS Not achieving sufficient horizontal velocity to initiate the driving action of the bound Not achieving sufficient height with the lead leg in the flight phase to attack the ground with enough force to accelerate the athlete forward Overreaching with the lead leg and then not driving down under the hips 1340

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 25 DOUBLE-ARM LINEAR BOUND Intensity level: Medium Direction: Horizontal and vertical Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Jog at a comfortable pace; begin the drill with the right foot forward. Upward movement: Push off with the right foot as it contacts the ground. During push-off, bring the left leg forward by flexing the thigh to a position approximately parallel with the ground, the knee at 90 degrees, and the ankle dorsiflexed. During this flight phase of the drill, reach forward with both arms. Sequence the arm swing so that they come forward from behind the body into landing, and forward from the hips to reach in front of the body during takeoff. Downward movement: Land with an active flat-foot on the left leg and immediately repeat the sequence on the opposite side. Note: A bound is an exaggeration of the running gait; the goal is to cover as great a distance as possible during each stride. COMMON ERRORS Not achieving sufficient horizontal velocity to initiate the driving action of the bound Coordination errors between arm and leg action; both arms should be forward as the athlete takes off and behind as the athlete lands Overreaching with the lead leg 1341

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Box Drills 26 DROP STEP TO LATERAL BOUND AND RETURN Intensity level: High Direction: Lateral and vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 6 to 18 inches (15-46 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. Arm action: None Preparatory movement: Step from the box with the right foot, ankles dorsiflexed. Downward movement: Land on the ground with active flat foot contact in the right foot. Upward movement: Immediately push up and sideways toward the left. Land on the left foot and immediately push back toward the 1342

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: right. Land on the right foot in front of the box and immediately stabilize the landing, with hips and knees aligned with toes. Note: The trunk orientation should change in the flight so that the athlete is leaning toward the intended direction of travel into the landing. COMMON ERRORS Not orienting the body in landing to facilitate optimal lateral takeoff Absorbing the landing force through excessive hip and knee flexion, prolonging the ground contact time Crossing the foot of the non-landing leg behind the landing leg 1343

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 27 SINGLE-LEG PUSH-OFF Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 6 to 18 inches (15-46 cm) high Starting position: Stand facing the plyometric box with one foot on the ground and one foot on the box. The heel of the foot on the box should be near the box’s closest edge. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Lift the front foot slightly so that it can be driven down into the box. Upward movement: Drive the front foot down into the box to cause an upward jumping action. Downward movement: Land with the same foot on the box; this foot should land just before the ground foot. Immediately repeat the movement. COMMON ERRORS Not orienting the body at takeoff to optimally generate vertical force Not creating sufficient vertical force with the front foot 1344

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 28 ALTERNATING-LEG PUSH-OFF Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 6 to 18 inches (15-46 cm) high Starting position: Stand facing the plyometric box with one foot on the ground and one foot on the box. The heel of the foot on the box should be near the box’s closest edge. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Lift the front foot slightly so that it can be driven down into the box. Upward movement: Drive the front foot down into the box to cause an upward jumping action. Downward movement: Land with the opposite foot on the box; this foot should land just before the ground foot. Immediately repeat the movement, reversing the feet each repetition. 1345

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: COMMON ERRORS Not creating sufficient vertical force to enable the switch of legs to occur above the box Asynchronous actions between the front leg and back leg, which means that the high knee position at the end of the jump does not occur at the point of maximum height or leg extension; this results in poor landing positions that prolong ground contact times for the next jump 29 LATERAL PUSH-OFF Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 10 to 18 inches (25-46 cm) high 1346

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Starting position: Stand to one side of the plyometric box with one foot on the ground and one foot on the box. The inside of the foot on the box should be near the box’s closest edge. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: None or slightly lift the foot off the box. Upward movement: Jump up using the foot on the box to push off. Downward movement: Land with the same foot on the box; this foot should land just before the ground foot. Immediately repeat the movement. COMMON ERRORS Not producing sufficient vertical force from the front foot Poor coordination or strength deficiencies, which means that peak height of the center of mass does not occur at the same time as maximal extension of the lower limbs and flexion in the shoulders 1347

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 30 REAR FOOT–ELEVATED MULTIDIRECTIONAL HOP Intensity level: Medium Direction: Vertical and lateral Equipment: Plyometric box, 6 to 18 inches (15-46 cm) high; mini- hurdle, 6 to 24 inches (15-61 cm) high Starting position: Start in a deep split squat position, with the rear foot elevated on a plyometric box (or equivalent). The foot on the ground should rest parallel to the mini-hurdle. Preparatory movement: None 1348

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Upward movement: Push off with the standing leg to rise vertically and sideways over the mini-hurdle. Keep the ankle dorsiflexed in preparation for an active flat-foot contact with the ground on landing. Downward movement: Land with the same foot on the opposite side of the hurdle. Immediately repeat the movement to the opposite side. COMMON ERRORS Not producing sufficient vertical force from the front foot to push out of the squat position and clear the hurdle with full extension in the hip and knee Absorbing too much of the landing impact into the hip and knee of the front leg, increasing ground contact time 1349

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 31 SIDE-TO-SIDE PUSH-OFF Intensity level: Medium Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 10 to 18 inches (25-46 cm) high Starting position: Stand to one side of the plyometric box with one foot on the ground and one foot on the box. The inside of the foot on the box should be near the box’s closest edge. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: None Upward movement: Jump up and over the box using the foot on the box to push off. Downward movement: Land with the opposite foot on the opposite side of the top of the box; this foot should land just before the ground foot. Immediately repeat the movement to the opposite side. COMMON ERRORS Not producing sufficient vertical force from the front foot Poor coordination or strength deficiencies, which mean that peak height of the center of mass does not occur at the same time as maximal extension of the lower limbs and flexion in the shoulders 1350

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 32 BOX JUMP Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical and slightly horizontal Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Facing the plyometric box, get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement. 1351

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Upward movement: Forcefully triple extend to jump onto the top of the box using both legs. Downward movement: Land on both feet in a half-squat position, step down from the box, and repeat. Note: The arm action contributes significantly to the upward momentum of this jump. By having athletes perform the movement with their hands on their hips, or their fingers interlocked behind the head and elbows pointing sideways, the lower body power required to perform the jump can be significantly increased. COMMON ERRORS Focusing on landing on the box and flexing hips and knees early, thus reducing vertical power; the aim should be to land on the box because of powerful extension into the ground, maximizing the forward and upward movement of the body Not coordinating arm actions with the forward movement of the body; powerful shoulder flexion should be simultaneous with the lower body jumping action 1352

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 33 BOX HOP Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical and slightly horizontal Equipment: Plyometric box, 6 to 42 inches (15-107 cm) high Starting position: Facing the plyometric box, get into a comfortable, upright stance on one foot. The non-jumping leg is held in a stationary position with the hip and knee flexed during the exercise. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement. Upward movement: Forcefully triple extend and hop onto the top of the box. Downward movement: Land on the same foot in a triple flexion position (hip, knee, and ankle flexed and stable), step down from the box, and repeat. Note: Although significant force may be required to hop onto boxes in excess of 30 inches (76 cm), this is a low-intensity drill because the athlete is accelerating against gravity and lands with less force than his or her body weight because of this. COMMON ERRORS Focusing on landing on the box and flexing hips and knees early, thus reducing vertical power; the aim should be to land on the box because of powerful extension into the ground, maximizing the forward and upward movement of the body Not coordinating arm actions with the forward movement of the body; powerful shoulder flexion should be simultaneous with the lower body jumping action 1353

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 34 LATERAL BOX JUMP Intensity level: Medium Direction: Vertical and slightly horizontal Equipment: Plyometric box, 6 to 42 inches (15-107 cm) high Starting position: Stand to one side of the plyometric box; get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement. Upward movement: Jump onto the top of the box using both legs. Downward movement: Land on both feet in a half-squat position and jump down, landing with an active flat-foot contact and optimal ground contact to enable the jump to be repeated in the opposite direction. Note: If the athlete steps down rather than jumps down from the box, the drill would be classified as a low-intensity ballistic exercise. Also, this drill can be made into a low-intensity ballistic drill by stepping down off the box and jumping up and laterally only. 1354

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: COMMON ERRORS Focusing on landing on the box and flexing hips and knees early, thus reducing vertical power; the aim should be to land on the box because of powerful extension into the ground (and flexion of the shoulders), maximizing the forward and upward movement of the body Not leaning into the jump; bringing the center of mass outside the base of support in the frontal plane will assist the lateral action of the jump 35 DROP FREEZE Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. 1355

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Arm action: None Preparatory movement: Step from the box. Downward movement: Land flat footed on the ground with both feet, quickly absorbing the impact on landing. Ensure the hips, knees, and toes align, with the trunk vertical. Step back onto the box and repeat. Note: This drill teaches joint alignment and landing mechanics and is often the first drill used in plyometric teaching and rehabilitation progressions. Also, this can also be performed as a single-leg landing drill. COMMON ERRORS Absorbing ground reaction forces while landing through hip and knee flexion, rather than landing and instantaneously holding position to develop load tolerance Losing the knee alignment with the toes when landing in a knee valgus position, potentially compromising the knee joint 1356

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Depth Jumps 36 DEPTH JUMP Intensity level: High Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. Arm action: Double arm 1357

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Preparatory movement: Step from the box. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles and land on the ground with an active flat-foot contact with both feet. Upward movement: On landing, immediately jump up as high as possible. Note: When stepping from the box, step straight out. Do not first jump up or lower the center of gravity while stepping down, because these adjustments will change the height from which the exercise is performed. The time on the ground should be kept to a minimum; there is an optimal relationship between ground contact time and resultant vertical force production. On landing, emphasis should be on jumping up, with minimal horizontal movement (less than what is shown in the third photo). COMMON ERRORS Absorbing ground reaction force as the athlete lands through hip and knee flexion, which increases the amortization phase and ground contact time; hips, knees, and ankles should be stiff when landing to optimize the ground contact time and rebound jump height Not dorsiflexing the ankle in preparation for ground contact; this negates the active flat-foot contact and increases ground contact time 1358

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 37 DEPTH JUMP TO BOX JUMP Intensity level: High Direction: Vertical and horizontal Equipment: Two plyometric boxes, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box, facing the second box; toes should be near the edge of the box. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Step from the box. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles in flight in preparation for an active flat-foot landing with both feet. Upward movement: On landing, immediately jump onto the second box. Note: When stepping from the box, step straight out. Do not first jump up or lower the center of gravity while stepping down, because these adjustments will change the height from which the exercise is performed. The time on the ground should be kept to a minimum; 1359

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: there is an optimal relationship between ground contact time and resultant vertical force production. Also, the distance between boxes depends on experience and ability; the greater the distance between boxes, the higher the intensity of the jump. Begin with the boxes placed 24 inches (61 cm) apart. COMMON ERRORS Absorbing ground reaction force as the athlete lands through hip and knee flexion, which increases the amortization phase and ground contact time; hips, knees, and ankles should be stiff when landing to optimize the ground contact time and rebound jump height Not dorsiflexing the ankle in preparation for ground contact; this negates active flat-foot contact and increases ground contact time 1360

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 38 DEPTH JUMP INTO DIRECTIONAL SPRINT Intensity level: High Direction: Vertical and lateral Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high; a partner Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. 1361

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Step from the box. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing with both feet. Have a partner point to the right or left just before landing. Upward movement: On landing, immediately sprint in the direction determined by the partner. Note: When stepping from the box, step straight out. Do not first jump up or lower the center of gravity while stepping down, because these adjustments will change the height from which the exercise is performed. The time on the ground should be kept to a minimum. COMMON ERRORS The athlete prioritizing the sprint over landing mechanics, leading to poor alignment on landing The partner signaling which direction to sprint too late for the athlete to prepare for landing and a reactionary sprint; body lean and weight distribution between the inside and outside of the feet are important considerations for successful sprints from landing 1362

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 39 DEPTH JUMP TO LONG JUMP Intensity level: High Direction: Vertical and horizontal Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Step from the box. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for a flat- foot landing on both feet. 1363

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Upward movement: On landing, immediately jump forward as far as possible with both feet. Note: When stepping from the box, step straight out. Do not first jump up or lower the center of gravity while stepping down, because these adjustments will change the height from which the exercise is performed. The time on the ground should be kept to a minimum; there is an optimal relationship between ground contact and resultant horizontal projection. COMMON ERRORS Not achieving an optimal forward-leaning angle through landing (i.e., too vertical and the ground contact time is increased or horizontal distance is lost, whereas leaning too far forward reduces the ground reaction force applied) Not pushing maximally into the ground to optimize the lower limb push for horizontal distance 1364

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 40 DEPTH JUMP TO 180-DEGREE TURN Intensity level: High Direction: Vertical and horizontal Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Step from the box. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing with both feet. Upward movement: On landing, immediately jump up as high as possible with both feet. While in the air, turn 180 degrees to land facing the opposite direction. Note: When stepping from the box, step straight out. Do not first jump up or lower the center of gravity while stepping down, because these adjustments will change the height from which the exercise is performed. The time on the ground should be kept to a minimum. COMMON ERRORS Not controlling the rotational component of the rebound takeoff, leading to poor joint alignment in the 180- degree landing Not achieving sufficient ground contact to enable a rebound flight time that is long enough for a full turn to be completed 1366

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 41 DEPTH HOP Intensity level: High Direction: Vertical Equipment: Plyometric box, 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart on the plyometric box; toes should be near the edge of the box. Arm action: Double arm Preparatory movement: Step from the box with one foot. Downward movement: Dorsiflex the ankles in preparation for an active flat-foot landing on one foot. Upward movement: On landing, immediately hop up as high as possible with the landing foot. The other leg should be actively flexed during the upward movement to contribute to vertical momentum. Note: When stepping from the box, step straight out. Do not first jump up or lower the center of gravity while stepping down, because these adjustments will change the height from which the exercise is 1367

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: performed. The time on the ground should be kept to a minimum; there is an optimal relationship between ground contact time and resultant vertical and horizontal force. This is a very advanced form of the depth jump and should be performed only by those with adequate experience, ability, and strength as demonstrated in other versions of the depth jump. COMMON ERRORS Absorbing ground reaction force as the athlete lands through hip and knee flexion, which increases the amortization phase and ground contact time; the hips, knees, and ankles should be stiff when landing to optimize the ground contact time and rebound hop height Not dorsiflexing the ankle in preparation for ground contact; this negates the active flat foot contact and increases ground contact time 1368

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: UPPER BODY PLYOMETRIC DRILLS Throws 42 CHEST PASS Intensity level: Low Direction: Forward Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 8 to 30 pounds (4- 14 kg); wall or partner Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart; face the wall or partner approximately 10 feet (3 m) away. Raise the ball to chest level with the elbows flexed. 1369

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement in the hips, knees, and ankles as well as the arms (i.e., cocking the arms by moving them slightly backward before the throw). Arm action: Extend the legs forcefully, and transfer the power to both arms, throwing the ball to the wall or partner by extending the elbows. When the wall or partner returns the ball, catch it, return to the starting position, and immediately repeat the movement. COMMON ERRORS Not initiating the movement from the legs, reducing the impulse to the ball Not coordinating or sequencing the transfer of power from the lower body to the upper body, reducing the impulse to the ball 1370

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 43 TWO-HAND OVERHEAD THROW Intensity level: Low Direction: Forward and down 1371

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 8 to 20 pounds (4- 9 kg); wall or partner Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart; face the wall or partner approximately 10 feet (3 m) away. Raise the ball overhead. Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement (i.e., cock the arms by moving them slightly backward before the throw). Arm action: Using both arms, throw the ball to the wall or partner, keeping the elbows extended. When the wall or partner returns the ball, catch the ball and immediately repeat the throw. The partners can also bounce the ball on the ground between them for a downward movement and a catch on the rebound. COMMON ERRORS Arching the back in the start position, increasing lumbar spine involvement (rather than hip flexion) in the throwing action Not coordinating or sequencing downward throwing action so the optimal horizontal distance is not achieved 1372

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 44 ROTATIONAL THROW Intensity level: Low Direction: Forward through frontal plane Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 8 to 35 pounds (4- 16 kg); wall Starting position: Start in a lunge stance. The front leg (with the hip, knee, and ankle aligned) should face the wall approximately 3 to 6 feet (1-2 m) away. The rear leg should be externally rotated at the hip so that the foot is flat on the ground and pointing approximately parallel to the wall. Hold the ball at waist height in front of the body. Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement so that the ball is brought back outside of the hip furthest from the wall and the 1373

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: weight is shifted to this hip. (A countermovement for plyometric throws requires cocking the arms—that is, moving the arms slightly backward before the actual throw.) Arm action: Initiate the movement with a rotational drive of the hips that continues through the trunk, bringing the ball across the body so that it gains momentum. Using both arms, complete the rotational arc of the ball so that it is released and thrown against the wall as it passes the front hip. Catch the rebound, and immediately repeat the movement. Note: This exercise can be made more of a hip-initiated movement by shifting the weight onto the rear foot and abducting the hip (frontal plane) to bring weight onto the rear foot; this variation may benefit baseball pitchers seeking more leg-driven throwing action. Golfers may find it beneficial to rotate the hip in the transverse plane (not move in the frontal plane). Both variations enable the rear hip to initiate the action and accelerate the trunk rotation. COMMON ERRORS Rotating from the lumbar spine and trunk rather than shifting weight to facilitate the hip drive Over-relying on the upper body to throw the ball compared to using the lower body and hip rotation to enable a speed multiplication effect through the trunk to achieve greater impulse on the ball 1374

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 45 SINGLE-ARM THROW Intensity level: Medium Direction: Forward Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 1 to 5 pounds (0.5- 2.3 kg); wall or partner Starting position: Get into a comfortable, upright stance with feet hip-width apart; face the wall or partner approximately 10 feet (3 m) away. Raise the ball in one hand to a position of 90 degrees of shoulder abduction and 90 degrees of elbow flexion, with the arm rotated so the forearm is perpendicular to the ground. Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement (i.e., cock the arm by moving it slightly backward before the throw). 1375

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Arm action: Using one arm, throw the ball to the wall or partner. When the wall or partner returns the ball, catch the ball and return to the starting position, allow the shoulder to externally rotate slightly, and immediately repeat the throw. Note: This drill may also be performed using a natural throwing motion. Performing the action from a half-kneeling position may help isolate the upper body action of the throwing motion. COMMON ERRORS Not achieving a stable throwing position due to lack of thoracic mobility and overcompensations through lumbar spine flexion Not throwing from the shoulder but rotating through the trunk (lumbar spine); this is likely to occur when the ball is too heavy for the athlete 1376

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Direction: Upward Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 5 to 40 pounds (2- 18 kg); partner; plyometric box 12 to 42 inches (30-107 cm) high Starting position: Lie supine on the ground with elbows extended and both shoulders in approximately 90 degrees of flexion; the head should be near the base of the box. The partner should be on the box with the medicine ball held above the athlete’s arms. Preparatory movement: None Arm action: When the partner drops the ball, catch it using both arms and immediately throw the ball back up to the partner. COMMON ERRORS Catching the ball too high and absorbing the impact force, increasing the amortization phase Releasing the medicine ball too early, reducing the potential vertical impulse to the ball 1378

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 47 HALF-KNEELING OVERHEAD MEDICINE BALL THROW FOR DISTANCE Intensity level: Low Direction: Forward Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 5 to 30 pounds (2- 14 kg); wall or partner 1379

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Starting position: Start in a half-kneeling position, with the kneeling knee directly under the hip of the supporting leg and the hip and knee of the stance leg flexed to approximately 90 degrees with the hip, knee, and toe aligned. The trunk should be upright, facing the wall or partner approximately 10 feet (3 m) away (not shown). Raise the ball above the head with the elbows extended. Preparatory movement: Begin with a countermovement in the trunk as well as the arms, cocking the arms (i.e., moving the arms slightly backward, from the shoulder, before the actual throw). Arm action: Using both arms, throw the ball to the wall or partner by flexing the trunk and extending the shoulders, maintaining a straight arm position. When the wall or partner returns the ball, return to the starting position, and immediately repeat the movement. COMMON ERRORS Overextending the trunk in the start position, detrimentally increasing the involvement of the lumbar spine Producing a cross-body throwing motion (either from not having the ball directly overhead or by finishing with the hands toward one hip); this produces trunk rotation, which may increase the distance but changes the exercise from an isolated sagittal plane movement 1380

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 48 SINGLE-ARM REVERSE THROW Intensity level: Low Direction: Backward Equipment: Small medicine or plyometric ball weighing 2 to 30 pounds (1-14 kg); partner Starting position: Start in a tall-kneeling position, with the kneeling knee directly under the hip and the trunk upright, facing away from a partner who is standing approximately 1 to 2 feet (30-61 cm) behind the athlete. The partner starts with the ball. The athlete starts with the throwing arm raised above the head with the elbow extended. Preparatory movement: The partner throws the ball over the athlete’s head so that its trajectory takes it an arm’s length in front of the athlete, traveling toward the opposite knee to the raised arm. Arm action: The athlete tracks the ball in a diagonal pattern with the throwing arm and catches it with an overhand grip before it hits the ground. Once caught, the athlete keeps the elbow extended while flexing the shoulder in the diagonal pattern, moving to a release 1381

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: point where the ball is thrown back to the partner when the elbow is fully extended. Immediately repeat the movement. Note: Because this exercise trains smaller muscle groups involved in scapular control, large increases in implement weight can make a big difference to the intensity of the action. COMMON ERRORS Using compensatory muscle recruitments to control the shoulder and throw the ball, compromising the objective of the drill Not catching the ball with sufficient arm extension to challenge the deceleration–reacceleration moments through the rotator cuff as a dynamic shoulder stabilizer 1382

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 49 VIKING THROW FOR HEIGHT Intensity level: Low Direction: Vertical Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 10 to 50 pounds (5-23 kg) Starting position: Start in an upright stance with the medicine ball held in straight arms in front of the middle of the body. Preparatory movement: Initiate a countermovement by performing a deep and rapid squat action, keeping the ball held in straight arms. Arm action: From the base of the countermovement, perform a rapid triple extension of the hips, knees, and ankles to drive the ball vertically. As the body rises, continue the upward momentum of the ball so that it is released and thrown as high as possible at the top of the triple extension. COMMON ERRORS Not optimizing leg extension and transferring power to the upper body, reducing the impulse to the medicine ball Releasing the ball too early (before full leg and trunk extension and shoulder flexion), reducing the impulse to the medicine ball 1384

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 50 MEDICINE BALL SLAM FROM SINGLE-LEG BALANCE Intensity level: Low Direction: Downward Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 10 to 30 pounds (5-14 kg) Starting position: Start in a single leg Romanian deadlift position, with the trunk parallel to the ground and the hips hinged and level with one leg extended straight behind the body. The stance foot should be flat on the ground with weight distributed toward the heel. The shoulders should be flexed so the straight arms are holding the medicine ball level with the head. Preparatory movement: Initiate a small countermovement by flexing the shoulders. 1385

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Arm action: Keeping the arms straight, slam the ball directly down into the ground, maintaining a stable trunk and hip position. Catch the rebound and repeat the movement, then repeat on the contralateral leg. Note: With the shoulder position, small increases in load can make a big impact on drill intensity. This drill also can be adapted to a chest- dominant pattern by starting with the ball held at the chest and slammed into the ground from there. COMMON ERRORS Not achieving a stable and balanced position at the hips to form a stable platform from which to throw the ball Hyperextending into the lumbar spine to achieve sufficient power to throw the ball to the ground rather than throwing from the shoulder 1386

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Plyometric Push-Ups 51 DEPTH PUSH-UP Intensity level: Medium Direction: Vertical Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball (or stable implement of similar height) Starting position: Lie in a push-up position, with the hands on the medicine ball and elbows extended. Preparatory movement: None 1387

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Downward movement: Quickly remove the hands from the medicine ball and drop down. Contact the ground with hands slightly wider than hip-width apart and elbows slightly flexed. Allow the chest to almost touch the medicine ball by letting the elbows flex. Upward movement: Immediately and explosively push up by fully extending the elbows. Quickly place the palms on the medicine ball and repeat the movement. Note: When the upper body is at maximal height during the upward movement, the hands should be higher than the medicine ball. COMMON ERRORS Not achieving sufficient tension in the arms to stop the downward movement of the chest, which collapses onto the medicine ball Not achieving sufficient bilateral vertical force to land with both hands onto the medicine ball in a balanced fashion 1388

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 52 LATERAL TRAVEL PUSH-UP Intensity level: High Direction: Lateral Equipment: Medicine ball or a stable implement of similar height Starting position: Get into a push-up position, with one hand on the medicine ball (elbow partially flexed) and one hand on the ground, elbow extended (not shown). Preparatory movement: None Downward movement: Keeping both hands in place, rapidly drop down into a push-up deep enough so that the chest is level with the top of the medicine ball (or lower). Drill movement: Immediately and explosively push up and sideways by fully extending the elbows. The trunk should move laterally across the medicine ball while quickly switching hands (the hand that was on the ground now lands on the medicine ball, and vice versa). Immediately on landing, repeat the movement in the opposite direction (alternate hands with each repetition). Note: When the upper body is at maximal height during the upward movement, both hands should be above the medicine ball. COMMON ERRORS Leading the vertical movement with the hips rather than pushing through the upper body Not achieving sufficient vertical height to travel across the ball (which should not move) 1389

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Trunk Plyometrics 53 45-DEGREE SIT-UP Intensity level: Medium Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 5 to 30 pounds (2- 14 kg); a partner 1390

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Starting position: Sit on the ground with the trunk at an approximately 45-degree angle. The partner should be in front with the medicine ball. Preparatory movement: The partner throws the ball to the athlete’s outstretched hands. Drill action: Once the partner throws the ball, the athlete catches it using both arms with minimal trunk extension and immediately returns the ball to the partner. Note: The force used to return the ball to the partner should come predominantly from the abdominal muscles. COMMON ERRORS Extending at the hips to absorb the force of the ball, increasing the amortization phase and reducing the efficacy of the exercise Not keeping the foot in contact with the ground, reducing the stable base from which to exert force 1391

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 54 SEATED ROTATIONAL MEDICINE BALL THROW Intensity level: Medium Equipment: Medicine or plyometric ball weighing 5 to 30 pounds (2- 14 kg); a wall or partner Starting position: Sit on the ground with the trunk at an approximately 45-degree angle. The partner should stand to the side with the medicine ball. Preparatory movement: The partner throws the ball to the athlete’s outstretched hands. Drill action: Once the partner throws the ball, the athlete should track it across the body and catch it using both arms with minimal 1392

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: trunk extension. The rotation of the trunk should be decelerated and then rotated in the opposite direction to immediately return the ball to the partner. Note: The force used to return the ball to the partner should come predominantly from the abdominal muscles and trunk rotation. COMMON ERRORS Not rotating sufficiently to optimize the SSC within the trunk musculature Not keeping the foot in contact with the ground, reducing the stable base from which to exert force 1393

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: 55 LEG PUSHDOWN Intensity level: High Equipment: A partner Starting position: Lie on the ground with slightly flexed knees and the hips flexed to 90 degrees (not shown). The hands should hold the partner’s ankles for stability (shown). 1394

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training
text: Preparatory movement: Brace the core. Breathe in and pull the ribs down toward the hips to tighten the core musculature to prevent the lumbar spine from going into forced extension during the movement. Drill action: The athlete raises the legs toward the partner’s outstretched hands, and the partner briefly grasps the athlete’s lower legs before forcefully pushing the athlete’s legs down toward the ground. Before the legs reach the ground, the athlete decelerates and ultimately stops the downward movement before flexing the hips to return to the starting position to reset for the next repetition. Immediately repeat the movement. Note: Intensity may be increased by using greater force of the downward push or by altering the direction of the push so that the leg action is not purely in the sagittal plane. COMMON ERRORS Lowering the legs without waiting for the partner to push them to the ground, reducing the eccentric load of the exercise Not controlling the lumbopelvic position and extending the spine as the legs are lowered, increasing the pressure on the lower back musculature 1395

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: CHAPTER 20 PROGRAM DESIGN AND TECHNIQUE FOR SPEED AND AGILITY TRAINING Thomas Dos’Santos, PhD, and Paul A. Jones, PhD The authors would like to acknowledge the significant contributions of Brad H. DeWeese, Sophia Nimphius, and Steven S. Plisk to this chapter. After completing this chapter, you will be able to describe the underlying biomechanical constructs of sprint, change-of-direction, maneuverability, and agility performance; apply fundamental biomechanical movement principles to the coaching of locomotion modes and techniques; analyze the abilities and skills needed to perform specific movement tasks; effectively monitor the development of sprint, change-of- direction, and agility abilities; apply evidence-based methods for developing speed, change of direction, and agility; and design and implement training programs to maximize athletic performance. 1398

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: This chapter addresses the development of speed, change-of- direction, and agility abilities. Although the term speed is often used when an athlete displays one or all of these aspects of physical performance, it is critical to understand that athlete development requires various underpinning physical capacities and skills as a result of differing biomechanical requirements. These three important aspects of physical performance can be defined as follows: Speed. The skills and abilities needed to achieve high movement velocities Change of direction. The skills and abilities needed to explosively change movement direction, velocities, or modes Agility. The skills and abilities needed to change direction, velocity, or mode in response to a stimulus The ability to outrun and maneuver the competition is a hallmark of most athletic endeavors. Further, the ability to change direction rapidly during an activity can mute the effect of an opponent’s speed or provide both physical and tactical advantages on the field of play. Although it may seem that these scenarios all involve the “speed” of an athlete, this perceived speed may be a result of one quality or a combination of the three qualities just listed. Within sport, high- speed human locomotion can be categorized as linear or multidirectional. Generating high speeds linearly, more commonly referred to as sprinting, is the underlying requirement for success in many track and field events as well as open-field running in game- based

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: and they are limited only by their physical capacity to perform this activity (e.g., a route, play, or predetermined pattern). The physical capacity to change direction while decelerating and then reaccelerating, sometimes using a different mode of travel, is change-of-direction (COD) ability, whereas agility requires the use of perceptual-cognitive ability in combination with change-of- direction ability. This highlights the similar and contrasting qualities of speed, change of direction, and agility. For example, acceleration is a part of change-of-direction ability and agility, but additional aspects such as deceleration ability and mode of movement differentiate the training for speed from the training for change of direction and agility. The physical capacity to change direction may be a component of agility (i.e., action capacity), but the perceptual-cognitive component influences the physical demands of agility. Therefore, while reading this chapter, one should understand that although these qualities overlap some, differing physical, technical, or perceptual-cognitive development is required to improve each of these aspects of physical performance. When athletes are sprinting or changing direction, their performance is a function of physical capacity and technical proficiency. While biomechanical and metabolic efficiency underpin performance in aerobic sport, effective application of force (net impulse) limits speed, change of direction, and agility. Simply put, an at

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: velocities. In addition to the force application associated with acceleration and attainment of velocity in sprinting, COD ability requires effective application of force to decelerate, deflect the center of mass, and then reaccelerate in another direction. Further still, agility performance is considered a function of the athlete’s ability not only to change direction but also specifically to change direction in response to a stimulus (4) such as a defender or ball; this is known as perception–action coupling. For this reason, strength and conditioning professionals must be aware of their training choices regarding the development of physical characteristics that assist in promoting speed, COD, and agility on both the track and the field. Speed requires the ability to accelerate and reach maximal velocity, whereas agility performance requires the use of perceptual- cognitive ability in combination with the ability to decelerate and then reaccelerate in an intended direction. 1401

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Speed and Agility Mechanics To execute movement techniques, athletes must apply force—the product of mass and acceleration. Due to the limited available time to produce force during most athletic activities, two variables describe force relative to the time available to produce force: Rate of force development (RFD)—The development of maximal force in minimal time, typically used as an indicator of explosive strength (3). Impulse—The product of the generated force and the time required for its production, which is measured as the area under the force–time curve. According to the impulse– momentum relationship, net impulse dictates the magnitude of change of momentum of an object. Because mass remains constant in most sporting scenarios, increases in net impulse are therefore proportionate to changes in velocity. Physics of Sprinting, Change of Direction, and Agility Force represents the interaction of two physical objects. Force is a vector quantity, meaning that it has both magnitude (size) and direction. Traditionally, force is described as a push or a pull exerted on one object by another, which prevents both objects from occupying the same space. This movement of mass changes an object’s velocity, causing acceleration. Within the strength and conditioning profession, velocity and speed are often used interchangeably. For a proper discussion on sprint and agility performance, these terms need to be separated. Speed is a scalar quantity, which means that it describes only h

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Acceleration refers to the rate at which an object’s velocity changes over time. Once a force acts on a physical object, the mass will change direction and leave the space it was occupying. Acceleration of the object will continue if external forces continue to change velocity. In practical settings, deceleration replaces negative acceleration in describing a change from higher to lower velocity. Rate of Force Development Within the sporting context, the ability to produce force rapidly is arguably a more desirable trait than maximal force production given the time constraints associated with most high-intensity actions (100). While the ability to generate high levels of maximal force has been shown to improve performance in jump height and other athletic measures, most competitive scenarios do not occur within a time frame that allows an athlete to generate maximal forces (27). Specifically, the generation of maximal contraction force takes at least 300 milliseconds, while many sport activities consume 0 to 200 milliseconds (figure 20.1) (1). For this reason, in sport settings where success is restricted to timing of movement, RFD is a more useful measure of an athlete’s impulsive ability (5). RFD can be described as the change in force divided by the change in time (100). 1403

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: FIGURE 20.1 Force as a function of time, indicating maximum strength, rate of force development (RFD), and force at 0.2 seconds for untrained (solid blue line), heavy resistance–trained (dashed yellow line), and explosive-ballistic–trained (dotted black line) subjects. Impulse is the change in momentum resulting from a force, measured as the product of force and time (represented by the area under each curve), and is increased by improving RFD. When functional movements are performed, force is typically applied very briefly—often for 0.1 to 0.2 seconds—whereas absolute maximum force development may require 0.6 to 0.8 seconds. Komi, “Changes in Electrical and Mechanical Behavior of Leg Extensor Muscle During Heavy Resistance Strength Training,” Acta Physiologica Scandinavic 125 (1985): 573-585; and K. Häkkinen, P.V. Komi, and M. Alen, “Effect of Explosive Type Strength Training on Isometric Force- and Relaxation Time, Electromyographic and Muscle Fibre Characteristics of Leg Extensor Muscles,” Acta Physiologica Scandinavica 125 (1985): 587-600. The ability to accelerate a mass depends on a change in velocity resulting from the application of an external force. Therefore, from a practical standpoint, an athlete wishing to achieve higher acceleration capabilities should apply forces at a greater rate and orient force in the optimal direction (84). Impulse For an object to change its position, forces must be applied (to

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: the running surface over a period of time (i.e., impulse) in the stance phase of sprinting (figure 20.2) or in the plant phase of changing direction. The length of time athletes are in this stance or plant phase is termed their ground contact time. The product of the time the force is applied to the ground and the amount of force applied is termed impulse and can be graphically represented as the area under a force–time curve. Changes in impulse result in changes of the athlete’s momentum and therefore the ability to either accelerate or decelerate, thus underpinning human locomotion. FIGURE 20.2 Sprint ground reaction force and impulse during the (a) acceleration phase and (b) maximal-velocity phase. Wb = body weight. Figure 20.2 demonstrates how the vertical and horizontal forces differ in magnitude when the acceleration phase (figure 20.7 on page 645) is compared to the maximal-velocity phase (figure 20.8 on page 646), which reflects the two different body positions used to produce force through maximal extension. Further, these two diagrams demonstrate the concept of impulse (represented as the area under the force–time curve) during the braking phase, indicated by a negative horizontal force, or during the propulsive phase that occurs where there is a positive horizontal force. These two phases of impulse are indicated by the vertical dotted line. It 1405

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: should be noted that during maximal-velocity phases, production of force is asymmetrical and the RFD is very high, resulting in much shorter ground contact times in comparison to the acceleration phase. Momentum is defined as the product between the mass of an object and the velocity of movement. During a sprint, an athlete’s body mass remains constant. Thus, given the same time frame, the only way to achieve a greater impulse is to generate greater net force. This increase in net impulse leads to an increase in momentum or a decrease in momentum, depending on whether the athlete is intending to accelerate or reaccelerate or decelerate before a COD or as an isolated action. In other words, a change in impulse results in a change in momentum and is the cause of an object’s movement. Within human locomotion, the magnitude of the force coupled with the length of time the force is produced during an individual step is paramount to success. Changes in these forces can increase or decrease the athlete’s momentum. For this reason, training should focus on developing impulse—the area under the force–time curve— in addition to RFD. Power has not been discussed here because it is derived from force and velocity. Therefore, power is considered a mechanical construct and, practically speaking, it can be more useful to directly measure the characteristics that determine power production (e.g., force and velocity), because measurement of power alone does not give insight into the performan

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: create a positive change in velocity. Within a short sprint, force is the effort needed to accelerate an athlete up to his or her highest achievable speeds, which are largely determined by physiological factors. These forces or efforts are produced rapidly, with time constraints that are shorter than the time needed for maximal voluntary force production. For this reason, rate of force production may be a more important factor for sprinting success. Moreover, since sprinting success is largely dependent on the production of forces within a short amount of time, impulse is an important underlying factor. Practical Implications for Change of Direction and Agility In addition to the requirement for acceleration, the production of braking forces over certain periods of time, or foot contacts, termed braking impulse, should be considered during COD, deceleration, and agility maneuvers. The amount of impulse required to change momentum effectively and efficiently is a direct reflection of the physical requirements for COD. For example, as the angle of directional change required typically increases or the entry velocity into the COD increases, so does the impulse required to change momentum and deflect the center of mass; therefore, it is physically more demanding to perform such activities. Further, the time restraints placed on a performer due to the perceptual-cognitive aspects of agility can influence the physical demands by limiting the time available to produce the required f

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Neurophysiological Basis for Speed Sprinting, agility, and COD are all dynamic displays of force production in the athletic setting. Because strength and conditioning professionals are often asked to assist in the development of these competitively advantageous qualities, an overview of how these force measures are produced during movement is warranted. Nervous System Neuromuscular function is vital to sprint performance because the activity and the interaction of the central nervous system with the muscles ultimately influence the rate and strength of muscle contraction. Research has shown that the combination of strength, plyometric, and sprint training produces several adaptations within the neuromuscular system that may contribute to improved sprint performance. Resistance training enhances neural drive, the rate and amplitude of impulses being sent from the nervous system to the target muscles (1). Increases in neural drive, which are indicative of an increase in the rate at which action potentials occur, are related to increases in both muscular force production and the rate of force production. Similarly, plyometric training demonstrates increases in excitability of high-threshold motor neurons. Increased excitability ultimately enhances neural drive to the muscle. Taken together, increases in neural drive may contribute to increases in the athlete’s RFD and impulse generation. Stretch-Shortening Cycle Many functional tasks begin with preparatory countermovements invol

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: a rapid transition from an eccentric action to a concentric action occurs. Therefore, SSC actions are particularly prevalent in sports involving running, jumping, directional changes, and other explosive changes in velocity; thus reactive strength development is a highly important quality to develop in training programs and can be a distinct capability that is independent of maximal strength in elite athletes (45, 55, 56, 82, 83, 91, 98, 112). SSC actions exploit intrinsic muscle–tendon behavior as well as the force and length reflex feedback to the nervous system (3, 4, 10, 18, 33). Acutely, SSC actions tend to increase mechanical efficiency and impulse via elastic energy recovery, whereas chronically, they upregulate muscle stiffness and enhance neuromuscular activation (45, 55, 56, 82, 83). Training activities aimed at improving SSC performance should fulfill two criteria (47, 82, 83, 91, 98): They should involve skillful, multijoint movements that transmit forces through the kinetic chain and exploit elastic– reflexive mechanisms. To manage fatigue and emphasize work quality and technique, they should be structured around brief work bouts or clusters separated by frequent rest pauses. In practice, a combination of progressive plyometric and heavy resistance methods can accomplish these objectives (i.e., complex or contrast training). Spring–Mass Model Exposure to strength and speed training may be linked to a rise in the preactivation of the musculature used in sprinting

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: model (SMM). The SMM (figure 20.3) is a mathematical model that depicts sprinting as a type of human locomotion in which the displacement of a body mass is the aftereffect from energy produced and is delivered through the collective coiling and extension of spring-like actions within muscle architecture (11, 29, 37, 39). During a complete running cycle, one spring compresses and propels the sprinter’s body forward. Simultaneously, the other spring swings forward in preparation for ground contact. FIGURE 20.3 A simple spring–mass model relative to the ground reaction force during the stance phase of a sprint. During the stance phase, the model demonstrates how the leg (represented as a spring) is uncompressed at initial contact and then is compressed (represented by the change in length of the spring) during midstance or as vertical ground reaction force increases. Reprinted by permission from K.P. Clark and P.G. Weyand, “Are Running Speeds Maximized With Simple-Spring Stance Mechanics?” Journal of Applied Physiology 117, no. 6 (2014): 605. Within an upright sprint, compression of the spring begins at foot strike, resulting in horizontal braking forces. This sudden and brief deceleration assists in propelling the swing leg forward in preparation for the subsequent step. As the center of mass moves ahead of the foot, the sprinter is in midstance. Within the SMM, the spring is compressed to the lowest point, which coincides with a lowered center of mass at midstance. Finally, th

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: the push-off segment of the stance phase as the return of energy through the extension of the coiled spring. This resultant energy and return of force projects the sprinter forward. While the SMM provides a conceptual framework for highlighting the actions involved in upright high-speed running, recent investigations suggest that the model’s ability to describe the stance phase of elite sprinters is limited. As illustrated in figure 20.2 on page 640, during the maximal-velocity phase, elite sprinters tend to deviate from a classic SMM by producing much of their vertical force in the first half of a ground contact. In contrast, most non-elite sprinters, such as those involved in many team or field-based sports, display stance phases that are described by the SMM (24), where the vertical force curve is more symmetrical, as shown in figure 20.3. As such, the SMM should be used as a means to describe the relationship between the SSC, muscle stiffness, and sprinting. In fact, as stride frequency increases at a given running speed, one of the most important features of the leg spring is an increase in muscle stiffness (39). Because sprinting requires an athlete to move at high speeds, strength and conditioning professionals should emphasize the prescription of exercises that have been shown to increase neural drive while overloading musculature of the hip, knee, and ankle regions involved in the SSC. In the context of COD, as the intended angle of direction change (i.e., deflection of center of mass) increases, the ground contact time of the main execution plant foot typically increases, attributed to the greater braking force, negative work (i.e., knee flexion), and deceleration demands associated when having to reduce momentum with sharper directional changes (36). As a result, this prolongs the contact time to increase braking impulse to reduce momentum along the original direction followed by propulsive impulse to enable acceleration toward the new intended direction of travel. In view of this, COD actions <45 degrees generally can be considered fast SSC activities, whereas direction changes >45 degrees generally can be considered slower SSC activities, though this depends on entry velocity and an athlete’s physical capacity (36). 1412

This is the point in a COD movement that represents the transition between the deceleration step and the acceleration step and is the main step in achieving deflection of the center of mass. Body positioning and the ability to maintain strong trunk positions during the deceleration of momentum and reorientation of the body to run in a new direction are critical for performance. Since effective braking is an important part of agility performance (83, 84), neuromuscular development with respect to high-velocity and high-force eccentric muscle actions should be considered, for two reasons. First, the adaptations or motor unit recruitment pathways called on during an eccentric muscle action are different than those called on during concentric contractions (38). Secondly, the adaptations to eccentric training appear to be specific to the velocity of eccentric loading (74). In addition, training athletes for effective agility performance requires knowledge of perceptual- cognitive demands over and above the neurophysiological requirements for changing direction. Not only are the perceptual- cognitive demands on athletes related to their abilities in the areas of visual search scanning, anticipation, decision making, and reaction 1413
