Further, neurophysiological requirements of agility performance extend beyond physical requirements to perceptual-cognitive requirements that are specific to the tactical situation. 1414

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Running Speed Sprinting is a series of coupled flight and support phases, known as strides (e.g., right foot contact to next right foot contact, essentially comprised of two steps—right to left, left to right), orchestrated in an attempt to displace the athlete’s body down the track at maximal acceleration or velocity (or both), usually over brief distances and durations. Sprinting has been described as rapid, unpaced, maximal- effort running of 15 seconds or less (78). However, the classic definition of sprint speed concerns the relationship between step length (distance between the toe and heel of two consecutive footsteps) and step frequency (or rate; number of steps per second) (63). For clarity, one stride is equal to two steps (right to left, then left to right). Based on this understanding, sprint speed can be increased by an increase in step length or an increase in step frequency (figure 20.5). Although these changes in performance variables are logical, the underlying component to maximizing step length and step frequency is related to rapid force production. FIGURE 20.5 Step length–frequency interaction as a function of running velocity. Adapted from Dillman (1975). 1415

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: The differences between elite and novice sprinters can be traced to a single component. Much of the current literature on sprinting (17, 105, 106) suggests that the amount of vertical force applied to the ground during the stance phase at top speed may be the most critical component to improving top speed. In addition, these greater forces must be applied to the ground in the shortest period possible. Application of force is needed to displace a mass. In sprinting, step length represents the displacement of mass. Elite male sprinters achieve a step length of 2.70 m (8.9 ft), whereas novice sprinters display a step length of 2.56 m (8.4 ft) at maximum velocity (figure 20.6a) (62). Since contact with the ground is needed to continue force production and subsequent alterations in velocity, increasing the step frequency theoretically would maximize the time available to produce force. Elite male sprinters demonstrate step frequency near 4.63 steps per second compared to novice sprinters, who produce a lesser step frequency of 4.43 steps per second (figure 20.6b) (62). In other words, elite sprinters need less ground contact time with each step to exert the effort needed to displace their mass due to their ability to create greater impulses. Thus, these faster sprinters also spend more time in the air. Interestingly, elite sprinters display times to reposition the swing leg that are similar to those of their slower counterparts (62, 106). 1416

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: FIGURE 20.6 Step length (a) and step rate (b) in sprinters with varying qualifications. Data from Mann (2011). Although the time required for staging the subsequent ground contact is similar between elite and novice sprinters, elite sprinters are able to propel themselves farther down the track due to properly directed vertical forces. Mann (62) suggests that these vertical forces are better directed toward the track due to an optimized knee height at maximal flexion of the recovering leg. This higher knee position provides a greater time period for force production and subsequent ground clearance (i.e., range of motion force movement principle). This technical advantage may be further evidence for why elite sprinters tend to produce most of their force within the first half of the stance phase. Additionally, faster sprinters are able to achieve higher velocities through the continuous application of high forces in a short stance phase, which results in longer steps or steps occurring at a higher rate. Within the elite setting (e.g., 100 m world championship finalists), this results in male sprinters achieving velocities between 11.0 meters per second and 12.5 meters per second (24.6-28.0 mph) (46). Conversely, team sport athletes generally achieve maximum velocities of approximately 8.0 to 9.5 meters per second (17.9-21.3 mph) (25). While force production is arguably the limiting 1417

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: factor, technical efficiency and properly designed training also limit sprint speed. Sprint speed is determined by an athlete’s step length and step frequency; more successful sprinters tend to have longer step lengths as a result of properly directed forces into the ground while also demonstrating a more frequent step rate. These findings suggest that RFD and proper biomechanics are two of the primary limiting factors influencing sprint performance. Sprinting Technique Guidelines Linear sprinting is composed of a series of subtasks that can be divided into the start, acceleration (figure 20.7), and top speed (figure 20.8). While these phases of a sprint are technically distinct, they all require the athlete to volitionally move the lower limbs at maximal speeds through a series of stance and flight phases. The stance phase can be broken down further into a braking period followed by a propulsive period. In contrast, the flight phase consists of the recovery and ground preparation (i.e., late swing) segments of the swing leg. 1418

Technical Errors and Coaching Table 20.1 highlights many common sprinting errors as well as possible causes and coaching corrections. Quite often, these errors are the result of the misapplication of forces due to improper coaching cues, insufficient mobility, or disruption to an athlete’s normal gait caused by external interference. For instance, an athlete may demonstrate overstriding due to a coaching drill (such as reaching to successively longer marks along the track to gain speed) or the belief that acutely increasing step length will allow one to catch up to a competitor in a race. Regardless of the reason, the aim of strength and conditioning professionals should be to promote an athlete’s speed through the proper transmission of forces into the ground that will optimize the athlete’s gait cycle. text: Methods of Developing Speed From a practical standpoint, the demonstration of maximal speed is the result of well-organized programming that organically develops and matures the required skill sets within the athlete. This organic approach to sprint training results from a schema of development that is based on the emphasis and de-emphasis of certain qualities, such as acceleration and maximum velocity, within each training phase. Furthermore, the training plan should coordinate these singular qualities through phasic progression. A well-constructed training plan highlights specific components that will assist in fully maximizing an athlete’s movement potential. Sprinting Although a variety of training stimuli are important for the optimization of athletic performance, it can be argued that no exercise improves running velocity more than maximum-velocity sprinting (i.e., primary methods). An athlete’s sprint prowess depends on the generation of high forces in short time periods (62, 105). Neurological adaptations resulting from long-term training plans that emphasize maximal strength and movement velocity improve both RFD and impulse generation (1, 100). In the strength and conditioning setting, weightlifting movements and jump training are prescribed to develop RFD and impulse at varying loads, because these movements use the SSC (i.e., tertiary methods). Similarly, upright sprinting uses the SSC, defining it as a plyometric movement. Chronic exposure to movements eliciting

text: neurophysiological adaptations from previous practices would bolster subsequent training. In an effort to either enhance the force required or target potential neuromuscular adaptations for sprinting improvement, resisted and assisted sprint training techniques are often employed (i.e., secondary methods). The proposed benefits, potential drawbacks, and coaching considerations are outlined in table 20.2. Strength As noted throughout the chapter, sprint speed is underpinned by an athlete’s ability to produce large forces within brief time periods. These forces must be large enough to support the body weight in the presence of gravity and displace the body through an increase in velocity (62). Thus, many strength and conditioning professionals are aware of the importance of resistance training in the development of a sprint-based athlete. Central to the discussion of resistance training is how best to transfer newly developed strength qualities from the weight room to the track or field (109). The transfer of strength improvements to sprinting may require an emphasis on the specificity of training (i.e., dynamic correspondence and coordinative overload). This transfer of training effect deals with the degree of performance adaptation and may result from the similarities between the movement patterns, peak force, RFD, acceleration, and velocity patterns of an exercise and the sporting environment (98). While training for maximal strength may be beneficial, training should emphas

text: snatch, and mid-thigh pulls may enhance sprint performance through physiological adaptations such as muscular stiffness, enhanced RFD, and coactivation of the musculature surrounding the hips and knees (6, 26, 32). Mobility While not a kinetic variable, soft tissue manipulation is a commonly used practice in the development of speed athletes. Strength and conditioning professionals and athletic trainers rely on tools such as stretching, chiropractic care, massage, and myofascial release to achieve optimal mobility within the dynamic state. Mobility is the freedom of an athlete’s limb to move through a desired range of motion, whereas flexibility is a joint’s total range of motion. With an understanding that positional characteristics are among several limiting factors in performance, strength and conditioning professionals should ensure that proper postural integrity is in place before the onset of practice or competition. text: Agility Performance and Change-of- Direction Ability In both field and court sports, there is a substantial number of preplanned COD movements as well as changes in direction in response to the ball, the game, teammates, or opponents. In sports such as baseball, softball, American football, and basketball, athletes decide before commencement of movement on the path they will run. Such patterns often including a quick or sudden COD—for example, exploding into a sprint out of a shuffle off a base or running a route before receipt of a ball. However, many sports also include rapid COD in response to teammates, opponents, or tactical situations (i.e., external stimuli). Such responses can occur in an offensive or a defensive scenario, and the physical movement and perceptual-cognitive aspects of such performances impose different demands on the athlete. Therefore, one should thoroughly understand the factors associated with agility performance from a physical standpoint (COD ability) and in combination with the perceptual-cognitive aspects (agility). Athletes improve COD ability through development of several physical factors and technical skills during a variety of speeds and modes of movement. The development of agility also requires improving perceptual-cognitive abilities in relation to the demands of the sport. Factors Affecting Change of Direction and Perceptual-Cognitive Ability It is becoming increasingly clear that the ground contact time and GRF during the plant phase (

COD and agility movements performed at shallow cutting angles (less than 75 degrees) and associated with shorter ground contact times (less than 250 ms) (94) benefit from training similar to speed training with regard to the physical demands but still require additional perceptual-cognitive training. On the other hand, when a COD involves a more aggressive cutting angle (equal to or greater than 75 degrees), the length of ground contact time can often exceed 250 milliseconds (8, 48, 64, 36) due to the greater braking requirements. Therefore, one should consider increasing emphasis on eccentric strength for braking and maximal strength alongside the concentric impulsiveness required for propulsion during the reacceleration. Additionally, due to the eccentric–concentric coupling during the plant phase of directional changes, reactive strength development is also a key training priority (36). The test used for assessment of agility performance has an impact on perceived agility ability of the athlete. A plethora of tests are used to assess “agility,” but tests without a reactive aspect should be considered COD tests, and a test that includes a reactive stimulus is now by definition a test of agility for most sports. Further, the requirements of the test may result in assessment of factors other than COD ability or perceptual-cognitive requirements. Therefore, one must be informed about and critical regarding a test used to assess “agility” or “change-of-direction ability.” For example, if the Illinois agility test, often performed with soccer athletes (91), was used after preseason training, improvements in performance may be due to improved metabolic capacity and not necessarily improved COD ability. This is attributed to the length of the Illinois test, which imposes a higher metabolic demand than shorter tests and thus is more representative of maneuverability. However, it should be noted that even similar-length tests such as the traditional 5-0-5 test, the modified 5-0-5 test (the 5-0-5 without the initial 10 m run-up), and the L-run used on the same athletes 1440

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: have only a moderate relationship (41), indicating they are not all assessing the same type of COD ability or the same underpinning physical requirements. This becomes more apparent when one realizes that some tests require a rapid COD while others require multiple COD. Tests with multiple COD often require more bending around an object or cone while maintaining as much velocity as possible, in comparison to a sharp COD that demands a rapid deceleration (e.g., 5-0-5 test). Therefore, tests such as the Illinois agility or L-run that require a bend to maintain velocity instead of an aggressive COD could be considered tests of maneuverability (69). With this said, table 20.3 gives examples of COD and agility tests and drills that address different physical requirements within the realm of “agility.” One should consider the aspect most important to the given sport when determining COD and agility abilities and consider testing and monitoring various types of COD abilities and perceptual-cognitive abilities required during true agility tests. Furthermore, tests such as the traditional 5-0-5 may be influenced by an athlete’s linear running speed (70, 81); thus, to isolate COD ability, the COD deficit (5-0-5 test time—10 m linear sprint time) could be determined (70, 71). Therefore, it may be beneficial to choose different tests that measure this ability under a high-velocity braking requirement; with multiple COD; or, as will be discussed, in reaction to a scenario, opponent, or stimulus. Another consideration regarding COD ability is the orientation of the body leading into the deceleration, through the transition phase as the athlete comes to a stop, and then the positioning as he or she subsequently reaccelerates out of the COD. Therefore, the positioning of the trunk influences the performance of the COD. As such, it is a combination of the ability to decelerate (high braking impulse), reorient the body to face or partially face the direction of intended travel, and then reaccelerate (high propulsive impulse) over short contact times that truly determines COD ability. Additionally, the ability to perform the COD requires the athlete to have the physical capacity to produce high and rapid magnitudes of force, tolerate the high loads associated with braking, and adopt favorable postures that are associated with braking and propulsion (22, 35). Considering the requirements for rapidly changing momentum, increased muscle mass in combination with decreased body fat (i.e., improving functional mass) has been regarded as a predictor of COD performance when assessed by the T-test in elite basketball players (23). Other anthropometrics and their relationship to COD ability are not discussed here, because aspects such as height and

Because the ability to decelerate, hold body position, and then reaccelerate is important in COD tasks as described by the kinetic and kinematic requirements of faster COD and agility performances, it is clear that a well-rounded approach to strength development involving dynamic, isometric, and in particular eccentric strength capacities is needed for the development of better COD performances (51, 97), with training methods that span the entire load–velocity and force–velocity curve (42) across multiple lower-limb and trunk segments (35). In contrast to sprint development, it is recommended that athletes undergo training that allows for the neuromuscular system to effectively adapt to the rate of loading required during the braking phase, with the understanding that the neuromuscular requirements for braking capacity must be specifically trained using low- and high-velocity eccentric muscle actions (38) such as those during drop landings, landing from a loaded jump, or the catch phase of a power clean or power snatch, in addition to supramaximal eccentrics that particularly load the knee extensors. All of these place different eccentric loading demands on the hips, knees, and ankles (67). However, general drills to help improve these skills are discussed in the section on methods of developing agility. Technical Guidelines and Coaching In comparison to sprinting, COD and agility have a large degree of freedom due to the multitude of movements that occur during a COD. Further, agility performance as restricted or determined by opponents or other tactical restraints and scenarios cannot be trained through the use of a single technique, with evidence to suggest we should be creating within- and between-skill variability and a flexible coordinative approach (35). Nevertheless, the following are some technical guidelines and coaching suggestions. Visual Focus When changing direction in response to an opponent (either offensive or defensive), the athlete should visually scan the environment and opponent while focusing on the shoulders, trunk, and hip. Following the anticipation of the event, unless deception is intended, the athlete should quickly redirect attention to a new area to help lead the transition of the body. Body Position During Braking and Reacceleration Control the trunk leading into the deceleration (decrease large amounts of trunk motion) (80). When decelerating, posterior trunk lean may assist in orienting the force vector posteriorly. Through the stance phase, reorient the trunk and hips toward the direction of intend

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: strong alignment of the ankle, knee, and hip to the trunk and shoulders. Enter and exit changes in direction with a lower center of mass to increase stability and to enable a manipulation of the base of support relative to the center of mass (89). Leg Action Ensure that the athlete can effectively dissipate or tolerate the eccentric braking loads through an effective range of motion at the hip, knee, and ankle (i.e., co-triple flexion) and avoid a stiff-legged braking style (92, 94). Emphasize a firm base of support for effective push-off and manipulation of base of support relative to center of mass (i.e., wide lateral foot plant when cutting, large anterior foot placement when turning) while pushing the ground away in order to enhance performance (i.e., rapid simultaneous triple extension of ankle, knee, and hip), especially while learning in closed drills. External focus of attention—through instructions to concentrate on the ground instead of a body part—has been shown to improve COD performance (76). Arm Action Powerful arm actions should be used to facilitate leg drive. Ensure that the action of the arms is not counterproductive (i.e., does not cause a decrease in speed or efficiency), particularly during transitioning between difficult COD (e.g., from a backpedal to a sprint), while keeping the arms close to the body to reduce the moment of inertia and to increase the total body rotation velocities when changing direction (35). text: COD); this leads to the actualization phase that involves a sport skill or sprint to a position. For example, a corner back, when tracking a wide receiver, may perform a backpedal (transition), before performing a directional change (initiation) into a sprint and then intercepting an underthrown pass (actualization). While the success of this play or other expressions of agility manifest in the actualization phase, the preceding phases are just as important and require good technical execution. Backpedaling (rearward locomotion with periods of double limb support and one foot in contact with the ground between contralateral foot strikes) or backward running (rearward locomotion involving single-leg support throughout foot–ground contact and both feet simultaneously in the air between foot strikes) (101) may be performed to displace an athlete rearward while maintaining a forward visual gaze of an opponent or ball, such as in basketball, soccer, rugby, and football. The frequency and importance of differing transitional movements may be sport dependent, and more research is required in specific sports to develop this understanding (12, 21). Nevertheless, practitioners should develop their athletes’ ability to perform a variety of transitional movements (e.g., lateral shuffle, backpedal, crossover running) and to perform sprints from these transitional movements to develop athletes’ movement solutions and all-around physical literacy. Flex the back knee to approximately 90 degrees and the hips to around 60 degrees. The front foot should be flat (firm base of support), while the rear foot heel should be raised. Distribute weight toward the balls of both feet. Keep the back flat. Lean the torso, with the shoulders over the front knee. The head is up looking forward (or toward the opponent; visual scanning). Relax the arms and hang them straight ahead of the hips. First Step 1449

text: To initiate movement, drive off the back leg by extending the back leg knee and hip with the center of mass (COM) moving behind center of pressure at toe-off. Using a low heel recovery, the front leg moves back behind the rear leg and makes subsequent ground contact underneath the hips. Each foot contact should be toe to heel (never heel first). Keep hips low to increase stability. Maintain a forward trunk lean. Keep the head up and looking forward (or toward an opponent). Involve a relaxed contralateral arm movement to match the timing and amplitude of the leg movement. The range of motion at the shoulder should be small. text: Foot Position Foot contact is on the balls of the feet. Feet are placed perpendicular to movement (parallel or slight hip external rotation). Feet stay close to the ground. Foot placement is wider than the knees; increased width increases stability and lowers COM. The feet should not cross. (In a diagonal or faster shuffle, the feet may cross using a crossover step to help with the directional change or provide extra propulsion to increase velocity [21].) Leg Action Take short steps, driving more from the leg farthest (i.e., pushing the medial aspect of foot) from the intended direction of travel (i.e., COM moves medially relative to center of pressure at toe-off), with the other leg acting as a pivot, allowing the COM to travel medially and assist the shuffle step (COM is now over center of pressure). Leg action is close to the ground in preparation for ground contact. COM Travel COM is projected medially or laterally, with minimal vertical projection and oscillation. The legs remain in a loaded athletic position and the trunk remains vertical. 1451

Training Goals The three goals to enhance agility performance through training are to develop the physical qualities to allow athletes to adopt the required postures and positions for a range of different agility movements performed in the sport as well as enhance braking and propulsion of such tasks (action capacity); to develop movement efficiency and competency of range of agility movements pertinent to the athlete’s sport, and to enhance perceptual-cognitive ability in various situations and tactical scenarios (35). 1453

text: Methods of Developing Agility As discussed throughout the chapter, a multifactorial approach is warranted to develop both the physical and the perceptual-cognitive aspects required for continual improvement in agility performance. Therefore, one should consider a plan that addresses underpinning physical capacities using various strength development strategies, technical competence in a closed-skill environment with movement- specific actions (COD ability), and improvement of perceptual- cognitive capacity through agility drills and inherent aspects of skills practice (58). Strength Similar to aspects of strength development for speed, strength development for agility should emphasize relative strength and a variety of speed–strength qualities along the force–velocity spectrum. However, additional development of the eccentric strength of the athlete due to the large braking forces during deceleration and COD actions within expressions of agility should be considered. This means that training exercises can include a spectrum of load– velocity profiles in the weight room (42) as well as a variety of load– velocity profile activities in the field, such as squat jumps, countermovement jumps, and drop jumps of various heights in combination with the COD and agility drills themselves. The multifactorial nature of agility warrants a well-rounded approach to strength development that spans the load– and force–velocity curve. Perceptual-Cognitive Ability During years of skills training (within the sport), athletes continually enhance visual scanning, pattern recognition, and knowledge of the situation, while in drills used to improve agility (outside of skills practice) they primarily focus on improving anticipation, decision- making time, and accuracy. text: Program Design Program design involves planning at several levels, each with its own set of considerations: microcycles (short term), mesocycles (medium term), and macrocycles (long term). The process is referred to as periodization. Periodization is the strategic manipulation of an athlete’s preparedness through the employment of sequenced training phases defined by cycles and stages of workload (see chapter 22). These planned workloads are varied to facilitate the integration of planned programming tactics that will harmonize the relationship between training-induced fatigue and accommodation (30). Furthermore, the periodization process is guided by information collected during the athlete monitoring process. Specifically, as an athlete progresses through a training phase, consistent information acquired through various monitoring strategies helps to show how the athlete is responding to the training stimulus in the short term and how the athlete should be further developed in the long term—that is, how the original training program should be modified to reflect responses to the training. At each level of training plan development, strength and conditioning professionals must manipulate certain variables. While these are useful in characterizing the training agenda as well as quantifying workloads, strength and conditioning professionals should keep in mind that each variable must be considered individually, and they should regard how it affects the collective system. text: Speed Development Strategies The planning process for speed development is similar to that used by strength and conditioning professionals in the weight room. Specifically, planning tactics should be periodized in a manner that addresses the physical and psychological components of sprinting through emphasis and de-emphasis on particular qualities in a phasic manner. An athlete’s capability to sprint can be improved through the incorporation of training periods that are designed to fully maximize and saturate a fitness quality, which may bolster the effects of future training agendas. To enhance speed, a practitioner should consider the relationship between human locomotion and force production. Throughout this chapter the authors have pointed to a link between sprint success and certain physiological phenomena. Elite sprinters produce large amounts of force within a short amount of time. This high level of force allows the sprinter to produce longer step lengths at a faster rate. This display of movement on the track reflects enhanced neuromuscular factors—namely, maximal strength, RFD, and impulse. These variables are the product of well-designed training protocols that aim to enhance qualities such as the hypertrophy of task-specific motor units, firing frequency, rate coding, and muscle– tendon stiffness. An option for speed development is provided in table 20.7, demonstrating how sequenced phases of training may seamlessly develop sprint potential through the maturation

text: phase of a sprint. Later, the athlete bridges into longer sprint work that aims to enhance top speed through upright running mechanics. The concept behind this proposed model is that an athlete may see greater improvements in top speed if force production can occur at the ideal rate and moment through an investment in acceleration development and optimization (62). An alternative approach for track sprinters (100-200 m) may involve sequencing training from general to specific preparation starting with an aerobic foundation to developing anaerobic capacity (short speed–endurance), to speed– endurance (long speed–endurance) culminating in speed (inclusive of acceleration and maximum velocity) before the main competition (14, 46). text: Wild and colleagues (107) examined the first three steps during initial acceleration and observed that sprinters achieved greater step velocities and greater normalized average horizontal external power, and they displayed greater normalized step length and flight length, greater normalized touchdown distance (i.e., foot impact under or behind COM), and greater toe-off distance (i.e., effective push-off behind COM) compared to rugby forwards and backs. Conversely, rugby backs displayed slightly shorter contact times and slightly greater step rates compared to sprinters. From a kinetics perspective for later acceleration at matched velocities (step 8-12 for sprinters and 9-20 for soccer), while no differences were observed in the initial 20% of the stance phase between sprinters and soccer athletes, sprinters produced greater anterior–posterior force across most of the propulsive phase and greater net forces over similar contact times, thus resulting in greater relative net impulse (25). As such, the sprinters achieved greater average horizontal external power, which allowed them to accelerate beyond the velocity plateau of the soccer athletes. It should be noted that the spatiotemporal, kinematic, and kinetic differences observed could be partially attributed to sprinters accelerating from a four-point position using blocks and performed on a rubber surface while wearing spikes. text: Monitoring Sprint Ability The longstanding method of assessing an athlete’s speed ability has typically involved a test of maximal-effort linear sprinting. Much of the time, the maximal-effort sprint test is carried out over a distance, such as 40 yards (37 m), that is believed to be relevant to the athlete’s sport. While time to completion is an effective tool to evaluate changes in sprint performance, these tests do not fully address the minute changes regarding an athlete’s progression toward race or field readiness. In addition, testing error in the form of hand timing and various start tactics confound the interpretation of testing results. As a result, strength and conditioning professionals may consider the adoption of additional monitoring tools as part of their battery of assessments. One such method of evaluation comes from the assistance of high-speed cameras or optical timing systems that use interruptions of infrared light to capture data from an athlete’s collective foot strike (15). This technology provides strength and conditioning professionals with additional insight into the sprint capabilities of the athlete, such as technique and movement strategies (16). Additionally, technology that permits the quantification of instantaneous speed is also advantageous for insights into speed at specific distances, time to achieve specific speeds, peak speed, acceleration, and τ (acceleration time constant). text: Agility Development Strategies The development of agility is best achieved using a periodized programming method. Random programming or the development of agility using only sport-specific methods such as small-sided games has not been found to be as effective (13). Although agility is a constant element on the field of play or during skills practices, it is recommended that agility development begin with the use of COD drills (preplanned) and progress in difficulty through increases in the physical demands; this is followed by the addition of drills involving perceptual-cognitive stress or what are typically termed agility drills (60, 110). In line with this recommendation, the development of agility should start with a needs analysis based on assessment of the athlete’s COD ability and agility. The agility test should specifically evaluate perceptual-cognitive ability, as previously described in table 20.3 on page 655. Further, depending on the additional movement requirements of the sport, one may also choose to use a test that is more dependent on maneuverability. The following is an example of steps for determining the appropriate tests, analyzing the results, and using them to program agility development of an athlete. Because agility performance is underpinned by multiple factors, one should target the largest window of opportunity through direct assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of the athlete. Step 1. text: Conclusion Speed, change of direction, and agility are well-established measures of athletic prowess in most sporting contexts. For this reason, strength and conditioning professionals should be aware of how these abilities are established and modified through training plan design and execution. These components of athletic movement and game play are underpinned by task-specific force application. This task-specific force production must be large enough to stabilize the athlete’s body weight in the presence of gravity, displace the athlete from one point to another, and continue moving the athlete at high velocities. Running speed is associated with the relationship between step length and rate. Sprinting is a near-maximum to maximum run that is defined by large rates of force developed within a short stance time. Better sprinters spend more time in the air as a result of increased step lengths that occur at faster rates than those of their slower counterparts and are better able to produce larger net forces that are oriented optimally for effective acceleration and top speed. Agility encompasses the skills and abilities needed to explosively change movement direction, velocities, or modes in response to a stimulus. Both sprinting and agility use the SSC and greater neuromuscular efficiency compared to slower movements. However, agility includes perceptual-cognitive demands such as visual search scanning, decision making, anticipation, and reaction times that make it a separa

Starting Position Begin the exercise in a tall stance with the torso directly above the hips, knees, and ankles (stacked joints). 1484

text: Movement Phase Initiate movement by pushing off one limb through the ankle, achieving a small flight phase. For the subsequent foot ground contact, the ankle should be in a neutral position and make contact on the forefoot under the hips or center of mass. During ground contact there should be minimal knee and ankle flexion. The athlete should be cued to “punch the ground” with the limb, emphasizing short, stiff ground contacts with each ground contact. The trunk should remain upright with a slight lean and hips extended (little to no flexion during ground contact). The contralateral arm range of movement will be small, but the speed of the arm movement should match the rate of foot contacts. Technique Tips Ensure an upright trunk and avoid leaning back. Make sure the athlete drives vertically with each foot contact, emphasizing a stiff strategy landing on the forefoot with the ankle in a neutral position. Ensure the arm movement is timed with the leg movement and will be of a low amplitude. Avoid excessive hip flexion, resulting in excessive foot contact ahead of the COM, with the aim for foot contact as close as possible to under the COM. 1485

text: 2 A-SKIP The A-skip is a commonly prescribed sprint drill to develop the correct leg recovery mechanics for maximum-velocity sprint running. Starting Position Begin the exercise in a tall stance with the torso directly above the hips, knees, and ankles (stacked joints). Movement Phase Initiate movement by lifting one leg to a flexed knee position in which the top of the thigh is near parallel. The foot of the lifted leg (swing leg) should be approximately at knee height of the stance leg, with the heel pulled up under the buttocks and the ankle dorsiflexed. This will result in the appearance of a figure four at the legs. The swing leg will always accord with this description. Begin the first skip by driving the swing leg down to the ground through an active foot, established through slight dorsiflexion. Lift the big toe up to establish appropriate dorsiflexion. 1486

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Complete the drive down of the swing leg through the forefoot until near–triple extension of the new stance leg occurs. The fore- to mid-foot of the new stance leg should land under the hips, maintaining the appearance of stacked joints. At the initiation of contact, the opposing leg should pop up rapidly to create a swing leg. The force generated from the active push down should coincide with a skipping motion that will result in a horizontal displacement of the body down the track. Technique Tips Maintain a tall posture with relaxed shoulders through the entire duration. The arms should move at the same rate as the legs, with minimal to no pausing of arm action between cycles. Regression and Progression A regression of the drill includes an A-march, which involves the same movements but at a slower pace to establish the correct leg recovery mechanics. If athletes struggle coordinating the contralateral arm movement, the hands can be placed on the hips initially. To progress from the A-skip, a running form emphasizes the leg recovery action with the thighs reaching parallel with the ground. 1487

text: 3 B-SKIP The B-skip is a commonly prescribed sprint drill to develop the correct leg recovery and subsequent touchdown mechanics for maximum-velocity sprint running. Starting Position 1488

The foot of the lifted leg (swing leg) should be approximately at knee height of the stance leg, with the heel pulled up under the buttocks and the ankle dorsiflexed. This will result in the appearance of a figure four at the legs. The swing leg will always accord with this description. Begin the first skip by aggressively driving the swing leg down to the ground through an active foot, established through slight dorsiflexion. Lift the big toe up to establish appropriate dorsiflexion. (The main difference between the A- and B-skip is the more aggressive driving down of the swing leg to emphasize correct touchdown mechanics and increased angular velocities.) Complete the drive down of the swing leg through the forefoot until near–triple extension of the new stance leg occurs. The fore- to mid-foot of the new stance leg should land under the hips, maintaining the appearance of stacked joints. At the initiation of contact, the opposing leg should pop up rapidly to create a swing leg. The force generated from the active push down should coincide with a skipping motion that will result in a horizontal displacement of the body down the track. text: 4 SWITCHES Switches emphasize rapid limb switching and path of movement of the feet that resemble the more linear path of movement associated with accelerative sprinting. Starting Position 1491

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Stand on one leg with one leg flexed 90 degrees at the hip and knee to ensure the thigh is parallel with the ground. The ankle is neutral or dorsiflexed, which emphasizes front-side mechanics and a positive shin angle. The contralateral arm is held with the elbow flexed to <90 degrees and with the hand around the height of the chin. The foot of the standing leg is flat on the ground, and the ipsilateral arm is relaxed by the side of the body. The trunk is upright with the head up and eyes looking forward. Movement Phase While maintaining an upright trunk with the head up, the athlete simultaneously drives the standing leg up and the flexed leg down, emphasizing rapid switching of the limbs. The contralateral arm movement matches the speed of the leg movement. The landing of the previously flexed limb on the ground and the standing limb to the flexed position should occur at the same time. Pause in this position (initial position) before repeating for a desired number of repetitions. Technique Tips Ensure an upright trunk and head with no leaning back or excessive lumbar flexion. Emphasize rapid leg and arm switching, avoiding excessively high thigh and knee lifts (>90 degrees). Progressions Rather than perform with a pause between repetitions, this drill can progress to performing repeatedly for a desired number of repetitions on the spot (e.g., 2 or 3) before pausing. text: foot contact should be with the ankle in a neutral position and may begin heel to toe with each foot contact. The drill will involve a low knee lift but will become larger with progressions. The foot contact will also progress to forefoot contact with these progressions. The trunk leans forward slightly with the head up and eyes looking forward. The athlete adopts a contralateral arm movement at a lower amplitude of maximal sprint running, but the timing and range of motion should match the timing and range of motion of the legs. Technique Tips Emphasize the circular recovery motion of the foot. Maintain a slight trunk lean with head up and eyes looking forward. Ensure the contralateral arm movement matches the timing and range of motion of the leg action. Regressions and Progressions If the athlete initially struggles with the ankle dribble, he or she could lower the intensity to a walking pace and work on the circular path of movement of the foot over the opposing ankle using a heel–toe contact. text: 6 STRAIGHT-LEG BOUND This drill emphasizes rapid retraction of the lower limb, offering similarity to the desired touchdown leg mechanics of maximum- velocity sprinting and increasing hip angular velocity and foot touchdown velocity. Starting Position Stand with the feet hip-width apart and the head and trunk upright. Movement Phase After an initial upward and forward hop from one limb, while maintaining a straight limb (extended knee and neutral ankle position), drive the opposite hip forward and then rapidly retract the limb to make ground contact on the forefoot before rebounding and repeating with the opposite limb. Emphasize the rapid retraction of the limb in preparation for ground contact, and ensure that ground contact times remain short and, ideally, under the hips. The trunk should be maintained in an upright position (must avoid leaning back), with the head up and eyes looking forward. 1495

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: The athlete should adopt a contralateral limb movement that matches the timing and range of motion of the limbs. Technique Tips Maintain an upright trunk without leaning back. Emphasize rapid, forceful retraction of the limb toward ground contact, and ensure that ground contacts are short and under the hips. Adopt a contralateral arm movement that matches the timing and range of motion of the lower limbs. Regressions and Progressions If the athlete initially struggles with the straight-leg bound, the athlete could lower the intensity by reducing the hip flexion range of motion and speed of retraction, and gradually and progressively build up the speed and range of motion. Trunk stability and lumbopelvic control can be challenged with overhead variations of straight-leg bounds, and straight-leg bounds can be transitioned or blended into normal upright running with the aim that previous straight-leg bounds will transfer to increased hip angular velocities, limb retraction, and active touchdowns with high velocities (i.e., 20-yard straight leg build up into flying 20-yard sprint). 1496

text: 7 SPRINT RESISTANCE: INCLINE FOR ACCELERATION Incline sprinting is a type of resisted sprinting that is prescribed to promote physical and technical improvements within the acceleration phase of a sprint. Alternative approaches to using an incline include using weighted sleds. Starting Position 1497

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Begin in the correct starting position (commonly called a crouched start). First, split the stance position by placing the dominant leg forward and dropping the back or swing leg by one to two foot lengths. The length of split between the drive and swing leg is largely determined by the compromise between the (a) ability to generate sufficient forces needed to overcome a lower center of gravity and (b) comfort. In addition, the feet should be split in such a manner that the front and back legs are in line with the pelvis, so that no unnecessary twisting of the hips occurs. Once the split stance has been established, drop the back knee straight down so that the shank (shin) is nearer (more parallel) to the ground. This aids in promoting the proper driving position needed to begin acceleration. With a tall and rigid torso, raise the arm that is opposite to the front or drive leg to a position near or slightly above the forehead. The hand should be spaced approximately 6 to 8 inches (15-20 cm) away from the forehead. The rear arm (opposite to the rear or swing leg) should be pulled back to a point at which the hand is near the lateral aspect of the buttocks with an elbow angle that may range from 100 degrees to 120 degrees. This position allows for the arm action to assist in producing sufficient propulsive forces to overcome static inertia. On completion of setup, lean the entire body forward so that 60% of the body weight is on the front leg. Avoid breaking at the waist during

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: The back leg should also assist in force production but will leave the ground earlier due to the starting stance position. Arm action should be synchronous with leg action. Technique Tips Cue the athlete to maximize accelerative mechanics through a low heel recovery of the rear or swing leg. This should be staged through the proper setup of the crouched starting position described earlier. Coach the athlete to continue aggressively pushing against the ground alongside an arm swing that may be cued to emphasize a hand that is pulled down and back. Arm action often parallels movements of the legs. The torso should remain tall and tight with the head in a neutral position. The torso and head are in line and will rise at the same rate as the hips gradually rise. Agility Drills 8 DECELERATION DRILL The deceleration drill requires the athlete to reduce horizontal momentum (negative acceleration) across a series of foot contacts as an isolated agility action or prior to a COD maneuver (35). 1499

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training
text: Task The athlete initiates a linear acceleration from a two-point static position and sprints to a predetermined distance (i.e., 5, 10, or 20 yards or meters) before braking and decelerating over a series of steps as rapidly as possible. Progressions and Regressions Tasks can begin submaximally, preplanned, and over smaller approach distances and thus velocity before increasing intent and increasing approach distances and subsequent velocities, and momentum. Deceleration drills can be further developed through the use of generic and sport-specific stimuli. For example, the “Stop at the Lights” game is a game-based agility drill in which the athletes must react to the green (accelerate) and red (decelerate) signals from the coach. Athletes race to the end and are disqualified if they are unable to stop on command. Additionally, drills can be further developed through the use of auditory stimuli (i.e., “stop”) and partner or opponent stimuli. Variations Practitioners can vary the initiation positions and planes of motion (two-point, three-point, falling, false step, amplitude jump, crossover cut, pivot, torso rotation, drop step, pop steps) and develop a range of different deceleration actions to improve movement solutions. Deceleration positions include the following: Bilateral (athletic ready position) Split position Transverse (jockey position) Lateral deceleration position Diagonal (crossover) 1500

text: 9 Y AGILITY DRILL The Y agility drill requires the athlete to plant his or her foot laterally opposite to the direction of travel to create a propulsive impulse into the new intended direction (35). Cutting is the key movement with this drill. Task The athlete initiates a linear acceleration from a two-point static position and sprints linearly to a predetermined distance (e.g., 5 yards or meters) and then performs a side-step cutting action 45 degrees to the left or right and accelerates a further 5 yards or meters (or alternative distance). 1501

text: Progressions and Regressions Tasks can begin submaximal, preplanned, and applied over smaller approach distances and, therefore, involve lower approach velocities. The drill can then be progressed by performing it maximally or by increasing the approach distances, which would lead to greater approach velocities and 1502

For example, the drill can be adapted whereby the athletes must react to auditory or visual stimuli when approaching the turning area, such as a color cone or auditory command (i.e., left or right). Moreover, the tasks can be further developed by incorporating a sport-specific stimuli such as an opponent and alternating between leading (attacking) and following (defending) through the use of mirror drills. The athlete positions the plant foot on the same side (ipsilateral) of the new direction (or sometimes medially across the pelvic midline) and then crosses the opposite leg (contralateral) in front of the body for the new step in the new direction, accelerating in the same direction of the push-off leg (35). Split step cut. The athlete performs a small jump (amplitude jump) before push-off, landing with both feet greater than or equal to shoulder-width apart (not shown; it would come after the second photo), and then, on landing, the contralateral limb is used for push-off into the intended direction of travel (35). 1504

text: Progressions and Regressions Multiplanar acceleration initiations to decelerations can be further developed using generic and sport-specific stimuli. For example, multiplanar acceleration initiation box drills can be progressed whereby the athletes must react to an auditory or visual stimulus when initiating their acceleration, such as a color cone or auditory command (e.g., left, right, forward, rear left, rear right) (figure a). The tasks can be further developed by incorporating a sport-specific stimuli such as an opponent and alternating between leading (attacking) and following (defending) through the use of mirror drills whereby the defender has to mirror and copy the initiation movement and direction of travel (figure b). 1507

text: 11 EVASION DRILL Task Using a 10 × 10-yard (or -meter) box, the purpose of this open drill from an attacking perspective is to create space, take space, create separation, evade an opponent, and penetrate defensive lines accurately and efficiently and entering a specific end zone (e.g., 1v1 evasive drill with two gates). A range of different COD actions, deceleration actions, or simply linear or curvilinear speed actions could be performed to achieve the objective. Conversely, from a defensive perspective, the aim is to prevent the attacker from penetrating the defensive line and entering the end zones, limiting space for the attacker, potentially making a tag, or delaying the opponent. The defender is encouraged to identify kinematic and postural cues and anticipate and react to the opponent. 1508

text: Progressions and Regressions A range of different mechanical and perceptual-cognitive factors can be manipulated within agility drills, which can create variation, new learning environments, and problems to solve while also influencing the task complexity and cognitive loading, which are summarized in table 20.7 (page 666). For example, the pitch dimensions could be expanded (figure a), which can increase the entry and exit velocities and momentums with a variation in end zones for the attacker to target. To increase game representativeness, the addition of static mannequins or defenders can further replicate the chaotic environments that are often encountered in sports such as American football (figure b). Finally, most multidirectional sports have multiple attackers and defenders; thus, to increase specificity, 2v2 small- sided games (and other configurations) also can be used to work on attacking and defensive transitions, organization, and communication (figure c). 1509

Sharp, PhD The authors would like to acknowledge the significant contributions of Benjamin H. Reuter, J. Jay Dawes, and Patrick S. Hagerman to this chapter. After completing this chapter, you will be able to discuss the factors related to aerobic endurance performance; select the mode of aerobic endurance training; set aerobic endurance training frequency based on training status, sport season, and recovery requirements; assign aerobic endurance training duration and understand its interaction with training intensity; assign aerobic endurance exercise intensity and understand the various methods used to monitor intensity; describe the various types of aerobic endurance programs; 1512

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: apply the program design variables based on the sport season; and address the issues of cross-training, detraining, tapering, concurrent training, heat acclimation, and altitude when designing an aerobic endurance training program. This chapter discusses the general principles of program design as they apply to aerobic endurance training and a stepwise approach to designing a safe and effective program. Improvements in aerobic endurance performance can be derived only when sound principles are applied during training. While some of the fundamental mechanisms responsible for inducing adaptations during training are undefined, it is clear that in order to adapt, the various systems and tissues of the body must be challenged by an exercise stimulus (e.g., specificity and overload). The physiological systems that are not involved during the training session or not stressed sufficiently by exercise will not adapt to the training program (5, 85). Training specificity refers to the distinct adaptations to the physiological systems that arise from the training program. Moreover, a training effect is limited to the physiological systems used and overloaded during training (140, 142). To improve aerobic endurance performance, training programs must be designed to enhance the function of the respiratory, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and nervous systems. For a training adaptation to occur, a physiological system must be stressed at a level beyond which it is presently accustomed (105

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Successful performance in aerobic endurance competitions involving running, cycling, and swimming depends on athletes’ ability to cover a fixed distance in the shortest time possible. This requires athletes to be in peak physical and psychological condition for the competition. To reach this level of performance, athletes must consistently train hard, yet intelligently, to maximize the physiological adaptations derived from training while avoiding injury and overtraining. A commonly observed trend with aerobic endurance athletes is to adopt and embrace the training practices of highly successful or well-known athletes. Although this strategy may be effective for a few, most aerobic endurance athletes would likely be better served by constructing their own training regimen based on a good working knowledge of sound training principles and an understanding of their own individualized physical limitations and needs. Another common belief is that greater overload via longer duration, higher intensity, and greater frequency is required to improve performance. However, training smarter by identifying physiological, biomechanical, and performance strengths and weaknesses (e.g., poor leg strength, muscle imbalances, low heat tolerance) and working to consolidate strengths while correcting weaknesses, has greater opportunities to improve performance outcomes with lower risk of injuries. An extension of this principle is applying the minimum effective dose (MED) (132, 133). MED was ori

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: and athletes have also come to understand the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) or maximum effective dose (133). This can be considered the maximum training workload that provides measurable benefits to the athlete. However, as discussed earlier, while still providing benefits, the side effects of MTD training stress (e.g., tissue microtrauma and fatigue) are also relatively high, and the risk–reward balance must be strongly considered. This chapter is designed to provide the strength and conditioning professional with a good working knowledge of the scientific principles of aerobic endurance training and conditioning. Specifically, this chapter includes information about the factors related to performance, aerobic endurance training program design variables, and various types of training programs. Additional discussion focuses on sport season training and special issues related to aerobic endurance training including concurrent training (i.e., combining resistance and aerobic endurance training in one training program) and heat acclimation. Because it would be exhaustive to summarize all the relevant information about training for all possible aerobic endurance sports, only foundational aerobic endurance training topics are presented, with specific examples as they relate to running, cycling, and swimming. 1515

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Factors Related to Aerobic Endurance Performance When designing aerobic endurance training programs, it is important to understand those factors that influence and play a significant role in successful aerobic endurance performance. This allows for the development of sound training programs while minimizing unnecessary training that may lead to counterproductive adaptations, fatigue, injury, or overtraining. Maximal Aerobic Capacity As the duration of the aerobic endurance event increases, so does the proportion of the total energy demand that must be met by aerobic metabolism. Therefore, high maximal aerobic capacity (V̇O2max) is necessary for success in aerobic endurance events (87). A high correlation has been shown to exist between V̇ O2max and performance in aerobic endurance events (2, 3, 134, 87). Consequently, aerobic endurance training programs should be designed, in part, to improve V̇ O2max. However, although a high V̇ O2max is important for successful performance, other factors may be equally or even more important. These factors include a high lactate threshold, good exercise economy, high efficiency in using fat as a fuel source, and a high percentage of type I muscle fibers. For well-trained aerobic endurance athletes, improving V̇ O2max may benefit performance only up to a certain point, especially since these individuals typically already possess excellent aerobic capacity. Consequently, the ability to sustain higher velocities during competition and training

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: ventilatory threshold, hydrogen ion buffering, use of fat as a fuel source, and improved exercise economy (76). Lactate Threshold In aerobic endurance events, the best competitor among athletes with similar V̇ O2max values is typically the person who can sustain aerobic energy production at the highest percentage of his or her V̇ O2max without accumulating large amounts of lactic acid in the muscle and blood (74). Although numerous terms have been used to refer to this phenomenon, lactate threshold (LT) is the one most commonly employed in the literature. Lactate threshold is that speed of movement or percentage of V̇ O2max at which a specific blood lactate concentration is observed (i.e., 4 mmol/L of blood) or the point at which blood lactate concentration begins to increase above resting levels (136). Several studies have shown that an athlete’s LT appears to be a better indicator of his or her aerobic endurance performance than V̇ O2max (7, 113). The maximal lactate steady state (MLSS) is another term that often appears in the aerobic endurance training literature. The MLSS is defined as the exercise intensity at which maximal lactate production is equal to maximal lactate clearance within the body (14). MLSS is an indicator of the transition from heavy to severe exercise intensity (70). In other words, while lactate production increases at the onset of exercise in the heavy exercise intensity domain, it plateaus and can be maintained at a steady state at this elevated lev

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Exercise Economy A measure of the energy cost of activity at a given exercise velocity is referred to as exercise economy. Athletes with a high exercise economy expend less energy during exercise to maintain a given exercise velocity (e.g., running speed). Several investigators have suggested that exercise economy is an important factor in successful performance in running events (71), with better performers also having a slightly shorter stride length and greater stride frequency compared to less successful performers (106). During cycling, exercise economy can be affected by body mass size, cycling velocity, and aerodynamic positioning (7, 41, 42). For cyclists, an increase in body mass and cycling velocity as well as an inefficient body position generate greater wind resistance, resulting in a decrease in exercise economy. It has been demonstrated that elite swimmers are much more economical than non-elite swimmers (6) and use less oxygen at any given swimming velocity. The most profound impact on exercise economy during swimming can be observed when swimming technique becomes more efficient. As improvements in stroke mechanics occur, energy demand for a given swimming velocity is reduced (146). Training to improve exercise economy is critical for aerobic endurance athletes. An improvement in exercise economy can enhance maximal aerobic capacity (V̇ O2max) and lactate threshold. 1518

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Designing an Aerobic Endurance Program An effective aerobic endurance training program must include an exercise prescription specifically developed for the individual athlete based on his or her individual strengths and weaknesses, goals, and sport. This requires manipulation of the primary program design variables. The sidebar lists the design variables as steps 1 through 5. Unfortunately, strength and conditional professionals and athletes often use the training practices or programs of current successful strength and conditional professionals or athletes in their sport. This does not carefully consider the strengths and weaknesses of the athlete and may lead to development of an ineffective or potentially harmful training program. The optimal development of a safe and effective training program is to have the factors related to aerobic endurance performance evaluated and then use that information to generate a training program specific to the athlete. For example, an athlete with poor exercise economy should place a greater emphasis on training to improve exercise economy compared to other factors that are known strengths. This might include HIIT with a focus on technique, as well as using long rest periods. Conversely, athletes who need to increase LT might consider performing more high- intensity training with shorter rest periods. Aerobic Training Program Design Variables Step 1: Exercise mode Step 2: Training frequency Step 3: Training intensity Step 4: Exercise durati

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Training programs for female athletes do not have to be different from those used to train male athletes; evidence indicates that males and females respond similarly to training programs (12, 78). Refer to chapter 8 for a discussion on sex-related differences and their implications for exercise. Step 1: Exercise Mode Exercise mode refers to the specific activity performed by the athlete: cycling, running, swimming, and so on. When training to improve aerobic endurance performance, the athlete should select activities that mimic as closely as possible the movement pattern employed in competition. This will cause positive adaptations in specific physiological systems and tissues of the body related to those used during competition. For example, the recruitment of specific muscle fibers and the adaptation of the energy systems within those fibers must be challenged during aerobic endurance training. Selecting the appropriate exercise mode during training ensures that the systems used in competition are challenged to improve. Note that the more specific the training mode is to the sport, the greater the improvement in performance is likely to be experienced. For an athlete involved in multiple aerobic endurance sports, or one who is interested in a general aerobic endurance fitness program, cross-training or participation in multiple aerobic endurance activities may be warranted (47). Step 2: Training Frequency Training frequency refers to the number of training sessions conducte

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: training frequency, with lesser-trained athletes requiring more recovery days at the beginning of a training period than more highly trained athletes. The sport phase or season that the athlete is currently in can also influence training frequency; an off-season program may include three to four training days per week, but training frequency may progress to daily workouts (or even multiple workouts per day for triathletes and highly competitive distance runners) in the preseason. Additionally, fewer training sessions may be required to maintain an achieved level of physiological function or performance than to attain that level initially (128). Appropriate training frequency is important for the aerobic endurance athlete, because too much training may increase the risk of injury, illness, or overtraining (i.e., maximum tolerable dose). While some evidence shows a positive relationship between exercise frequency and increased injury rates (63), these studies used active individuals in a wide age range, not only young and healthy athletes, as subjects. Additional research has shown injuries are multifactorial and there is insufficient evidence definitively associating injuries with increases or high levels of training frequency, volume, or other training factors (44). Conversely, too little training will not result in positive adaptations to the various systems of the body (i.e., below the minimum effective dose). Research has shown that it is necessary to train more than twice

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: may further increase glycogen resynthesis via an increase in the transcription and transcription rate of certain genes responsible for training adaptations. However, the researchers cautioned that these results should not necessarily be used by strength and conditioning professionals and practitioners to guide practice, because low glycogen concentrations may reduce the period of time an athlete is able to train and may increase risk of overtraining. This is one reason why it is important to monitor the effects of the training load on athletes. Further, strength and conditioning professionals and athletes need to understand that adaptation takes place during periods of rest, and undertaking more frequent training can affect the recovery process and, ultimately, the level of adaptation. Recovery from individual training sessions is essential if the athlete is to derive maximum benefits from the subsequent training session. Exercise performance has been shown to improve following relative rest from difficult training sessions (16). Obtaining sufficient rest, becoming rehydrated, and restoring fuel sources are critical issues for the athlete during recovery. Physical and mental relaxation and avoidance of strenuous physical activity are particularly important following days of high-intensity or long-duration training. Postexercise ingestion of adequate fluids and electrolytes is important for replacing those lost during training. If the training session was especially long or in

text: they do not actually use them (19). Research has further elucidated that elite athletes are more likely to use all forms of recovery, except cold water immersion, than lower tiered well-trained athletes (13). The use of or lack of use of different strategies has been found to be related to coach and athlete awareness of the effectiveness of such strategies (13). Further, the majority of athlete information and recommendations about recovery strategies comes from coaches and fellow athletes rather than peer-reviewed scientific publications (19). Therefore, to maximize recovery, and aid performance, it is important that coaches and athletes are educated and up to date on the types of recovery strategies that have been shown in multiple scientific publications to be effective, available, and best suited to athletes in training and competition. With regards to recovery and training, the term recovery run/ride/swim, which is often used by aerobic endurance athletes to reflect an easy run, ride, or swim after competition, or a training session during the training cycle, must be clarified. Typically, a recovery session would fall under the banner of active recovery, which relates to low-intensity physical activities designed to facilitate recovery from the metabolic responses of exercise fatigue (72). Step 3: Training Intensity Central to causing training adaptations in the body is the interaction of training intensity and duration. Generally, the higher the exercise intensity, the shorter the exercise duration. Adaptations in the body are specific to the intensity, or effort expended during a training session. High-intensity aerobic exercise increases cardiovascular and respiratory function and allows for improved oxygen delivery to the working muscles (105). Increasing exercise intensity may also benefit skeletal muscle adaptations by affecting muscle fiber recruitment (85). As exercise intensity is increased, greater recruitment of

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: intensity that is too low does not stress the body’s systems and induce the desired physiological adaptations, whereas an intensity that is too high results in excessive fatigue and a premature end to the training session. In either instance, the training session will be poor and ineffective. The most accurate methods for regulating exercise intensity are to monitor oxygen consumption during exercise to determine its percentage of V̇ O2max and to periodically measure blood lactate concentration to determine the relationship to LT. If V̇ O2max monitoring is not available, exercise prescriptions can use heart rate, ratings of perceived exertion, metabolic equivalents (in clinical populations), or exercise velocity to monitor exercise intensity. Power-measuring devices are also frequently used by elite and top- level amateur competitors, especially in cycling. Heart Rate Heart rate is likely the most frequently used method for prescribing aerobic exercise intensity. The reason is the close relationship between heart rate and oxygen consumption, especially when the intensity is between 50% and 90% of functional capacity (V̇ O2max), also called heart rate reserve (HRR). HRR is the difference between an athlete’s maximal heart rate and their resting heart rate (24). The most common means of regulating intensity using this method is to determine the specific heart rate associated with the desired percentage of V̇ O2max or the heart rate associated with the LT. As aerobic power (V̇ O2max), LT, MLSS, and exercise economy improve, the prescribed absolute intensity will be a lower relative intensity, resulting in a lower stress and stimulus. As such, corresponding adjustments must be made to increase training intensity to maintain a stimulus that will elicit continuing and sustainable adaptations. To provide accurate information on the magnitude of these improvements in aerobic fitness, and to inform subsequent adjustments in training intensity, it is important to test athletes regularly in each of these factors. Refer to chapters 13 and 14 for information on selecting, administering, and scoring appropriate validated field and laboratory tests. Additionally, using estimations of exercise intensity via estimated maximal heart rate equations provides no information about the intensity associated with the LT. Without some knowledge of an athlete’s LT, achieved from field or laboratory testing, a highly effective aerobic endurance training program cannot be developed. One metabolic equivalent (MET) is equal to 3.5 ml · kg−1 · min−1 of oxygen consumption and is considered the amount of oxygen required by the body at rest (3). Metabolic equivalent values have been determined for a variety of physical activities; an activity with a MET value of 10.0 requires 10 times the oxygen uptake that is required by an individual at rest. Assigning MET values as part of an aerobic exercise prescription requires the strength and conditioning professional to know (or estimate) an athlete’s maximal oxygen 1529

text: uptake to be able to calculate an exercise MET level. However, the use of METs in exercise prescription is typically limited to clinical populations. Intensity Measuring Technology Previously due to cost, power devices for cycling such as power measuring cranks and hubs to monitor exercise intensity were mostly only used by professionals and top-level amateurs. Research has supported their use from the perspective of demonstrating that they provide valid and reliable power measurement (49). However, due to the advancements in technology, it is common to see athletes of all levels using technology to monitor exercise intensity. This technology ranges from smart watches to running stride power meters to power measuring cranks. Each technology has its own reasons for being selected. For example, using power measuring cranks in cycling has an advantage over other measures because metabolic rate is closely related to mechanical power production (30). Also, using power as an intensity measure allows reproducible intensity efforts regardless of environmental conditions, which may influence other measures of intensity such as heart rate and velocity (30). Irrespective of the technology selected to monitor power, speed, or similar variables, they should have training zones allocated to them that reflect the athlete’s training status. Technology also extends to advanced indoor trainers such as treadmills, rowers, and ski and cycle ergometers. Due to the large variety of technological d

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: professionals must understand what each variable actually reflects, how to interpret it, and how it may change with respect to the training prescribed. Similarly, while an athlete may be familiar with technology, it does not mean they are used to the specific device measuring their performance, and as such, a familiarization period may be required. For example, it can feel foreign to run on a treadmill (active, passive, or Alter-G) when one has not done so before. As such, coaching cues need to be developed and provided to the athlete to ensure he or she transitions successfully to the new technology or device. It also should be noted that variances in technology between indoor and outdoor equipment or differences in performance between exercising indoors versus outdoors exist and can produce differing results (90). For example, it has been shown that running inside on a treadmill at slower speeds can feel easier and produce a lower exercise heart rate than running outside at higher submaximal speeds (90). Aerobic endurance performance was also found to be superior outside compared to when performed indoors. The researchers suggest this may be related to a potential fear of falling from the treadmill at higher speeds and the potential build-up of heat due to the absence of air flow around the body when running indoors.
