Step 4: Exercise Duration Exercise duration refers to the length of time of the training session. The duration of a training session is often influenced by the exercise intensity: the longer the exercise duration, the lower the exercise intensity. For example, exercise that is conducted at an intensity above the maximal lactate steady state (e.g., 85% of V̇ O2max) will have a relatively short duration (20-30 min) because the accumulation of lactate within the muscle will contribute to fatigue. Conversely, exercise that is performed at a much lower intensity (e.g., 70% of V̇ O2max) may be performed for several hours before the athlete experiences fatigue. 1532

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: The duration of a training session is often influenced by the exercise intensity; the longer the exercise duration, the lower the exercise intensity. Step 5: Exercise Progression Once athletes begin an aerobic endurance exercise program, they need to continue training to either maintain or advance their aerobic fitness level. However, research indicates that aerobic fitness does not decrease for up to five weeks when frequency decreases to as few as two times per week as long as training intensity is maintained (126). Increasing aerobic endurance fitness requires program progression, which initially involves increasing the frequency, intensity, and duration of exercise. Typically, for the general population, it is recommended that from week to week within a longer-term training plan, exercise frequency, intensity, or duration should not increase more than 10% each week to avoid overtraining or injury (57). While 10% may not seem like a significant increase, when these increases and their associated adaptations are added over a longer period of months and years, the adaptations and performance improvements are substantial and achieved while minimizing the risks of injury and overtraining. However, for athletes preparing for long-distance events, and especially those starting from a low fitness level, it may be necessary to adjust this guideline for a small number of weeks within the larger training plan. It should be noted that if an increase in training volume above 10% is im

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: However, to only increase the remaining extensive endurance session of 32 miles by 10% would only result in an increase of about 3 miles or, assuming they ride at an average of 18 miles per hour, an increase of 10 minutes, from 1 hour 46 minutes to 1 hour 56 minutes. Instead, given the low impact and intensity of exercise and the time involved, the duration of this extensive endurance ride may reasonably and safely be extended by 15 to 20 minutes (i.e., about 6 miles), which would equate to an increase of approximately 20%. But, as stated previously, this increase above the recommended 10% should be done cautiously, with injury and overtraining monitoring systems implemented, and only for a short period of time with an appropriate increase in recovery time and techniques reflective of the increased stress on the body. This type of planned increase in training frequency, intensity, or duration may be referred to as short- term functional overreaching. An important point regarding training duration progression is that it is often recommended to use predicted time to set the duration of a training session rather than distance. This is because training time factors in the effects of terrain and environmental conditions, whereas distance does not. For example, if an athlete runs 10 miles over a flat course in 1 hour and 10 minutes, and then runs a hilly 11-mile course the following week in a much slower time of 1 hour and 58 minutes, even though the prescribed distance only increa

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: further adaptations, a greater reliance on manipulating training intensity exists. Note that as the athlete’s level of fitness changes over the course of the sport seasons, training intensity levels (e.g., heart rate range for a given training zone) must be adjusted. Similarly, as the training environment changes (e.g., from cool to hot and humid), RPE charts may be particularly helpful for monitoring intensity in addition to heart rate, which will be elevated by the increased physiologic demands induced by the environmental conditions. In conjunction with these points, progression of training frequency, intensity, and duration, along with recovery, should be monitored at all times to ensure appropriate periods of loading and unloading are applied, and signs or symptoms of overreaching or overtraining are detected early. More detailed information on these topics can be found in chapter 24. 1535

Each type incorporates the five design variables and results in regimens created for specific outcomes. Sample training programs for each type of aerobic endurance training are included after the sections that follow. chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Extensive Endurance Training Many aerobic endurance coaches and athletes over the years have used the term long, slow distance (LSD) or high-volume training to reflect training for a long period of time at a slow pace. However, this term can give the wrong impression of what an athlete is actually trying to achieve—that is, to extend their aerobic endurance capabilities, not just exercise slowly for a long duration. Hence, the term extensive endurance training is a more appropriate term and the one used in this text. Irrespective of the term used, a common factor with extensive endurance training is that the training distance should be greater than race distance, or the duration should be at least as long as 30 minutes to 2 hours (98). However, as the race distance increases, it is not practical to complete an extensive endurance training session greater than the race distance. For example, because of the level of fatigue and tissue damage, it is not recommended for athletes to run 26 miles (42 km) or greater in training before running a marathon. What the athlete relies on in this situation is a combination of his or her extensive endurance runs plus the accumulation of the training volume over the weeks of training before the event. The length of an extensive endurance session will vary according to the training status of the athlete, where the athlete is in the program, the mode of exercise (e.g., cycling vs. running), as well as the duration of the aerobic endurance event

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: exercise, with the athlete able to talk without undue respiratory distress, or at a speed that the athlete feels they could run indefinitely. In general, increases in duration are prioritized when programming extensive endurance training sessions into a training program. It is important to not substantially increase the speed of the extensive endurance sessions in combination with increases in session duration, for as speed increases the stress of the session also increases, which in turn lengthens the posttraining recovery time and therefore can also increase the risk of overtraining or injury. The physiological benefits derived from extensive endurance training primarily include enhanced cardiovascular and thermoregulatory function, improved mitochondrial energy production and oxidative capacity of skeletal muscle, and increased use of fat as a fuel (15, 20, 64, 75, 83, 85, 96, 104, 136, 140, 142). These changes are likely to improve the LT intensity by enhancing the body’s ability to clear lactate. Chronic use of this type of training also causes a change in the metabolic characteristics of the involved muscles (27) and an eventual shift of type IIx fibers to type I fibers (103, 124). The increase in fat use also causes a sparing of the body’s limited muscle glycogen reserves (60, 64, 69, 136). The intensity during extensive endurance training is lower than the intensity used during competition. However, extensive endurance training does not stimulate the neurological patt

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: types of speed training (59). This ensures the athlete is not only more aerobically efficient and has muscular endurance but also has race speed capabilities. It is also worth noting that extensive endurance sessions provide athletes with mental strength and stamina by experiencing extended periods of time exercising, which they will encounter on race day. Pace/Tempo Training Pace/tempo training employs an intensity at or slightly higher than race competition intensity. The intensity corresponds approximately to the maximal lactate steady state; therefore, this type of training is also often called threshold training or aerobic– anaerobic interval training (98). There are two ways to conduct pace/tempo training: steady and intermittent (98). Steady pace/tempo training is continuous training conducted at an intensity equal to the maximal lactate steady state for durations of approximately 20 to 30 minutes. The purpose of pace/tempo training is to stress the athlete at a specific intensity and improve energy production from both oxidative and nonoxidative metabolism. Intermittent pace/tempo training is also referred to as tempo intervals, cruise intervals, or threshold training (98). During intermittent pace/tempo training, the intensity is the same as for a steady-threshold workout, but the training session consists of a series of shorter intervals with brief recovery periods between work intervals. During pace/tempo training, it is important to avoid exercising at a higher in

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: this type of training include improved running economy and increased LT and MLSS. Interval Training Interval training involves exercise at intensities close to V̇ O2max. The work intervals should last between 3 and 5 minutes, although they can be as short as 30 seconds (3). The rest intervals for 3- to 5-minute work intervals should be equal to the work interval, thereby keeping the work-to-rest ratio (W:R) at 1:1. Interval training permits the athlete to train at intensities close to V̇ O2max for a greater amount of time than would be possible in a single exercise session at a continuous high intensity. This type of training should not be performed until a firm base of aerobic endurance training has been attained (74). Interval training is very stressful on the athlete and should be used sparingly. The benefits derived from interval training include an increased V̇ O2max and enhanced anaerobic metabolism. High-Intensity Interval Training High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a form of training that uses repeated high-intensity exercise bouts above MLSS or critical V̇ O2 interspersed with brief recovery periods (76). One high-intensity interval training protocol is Tabata training. This methodology requires athletes to train at an intensity high enough to result in exhaustion after 7 to 8 repetitions of 20 seconds of work with 10 seconds rest between exercise periods (129). HIIT has been shown to provide a number of benefits to aerobic endurance performance in recreation

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: exercise economy (48, 53), which have both been strongly associated with aerobic endurance performance. In cases where improvements in aerobic endurance performance or factors associated with this performance are similar from HIIT and traditional low-intensity aerobic training, HIIT provides an advantage by taking significantly less time to complete (23). According to Buchheit and Laursen (22), for an optimal stimulus it is necessary for athletes to spend a total of several minutes within the HIIT session above 90% of the V̇ O2max. Both short (<45 s) and long (2- to 4-min) HIIT intervals can be used to elicit different training responses. For example, shorter intervals with higher intensity may elicit positive changes in neuromuscular power and exercise economy, and as the work duration for a single exercise bout is increased, the energy contribution from fast glycolysis will likely increase along with blood lactate levels, which may stimulate improvements in lactate metabolism. In performing HIIT, the appropriate amount of rest between repetitions is critical. If the relief intervals are too short, the athlete will be unable to put forth a quality effort on subsequent exercise bouts and also will be at a greater risk for injury. If the rest periods are too long, many of the benefits experienced from challenging the glycolytic energy system will likely diminish. An example of an appropriate work-to-rest ratio for long-interval HIIT training is ≥2 to 3 minutes at or above 90%

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: apply this basic format to cycling and swimming by simply combining extensive endurance training, pace/tempo training, and interval training. A Fartlek training workout challenges all systems of the body and may help reduce the boredom and monotony associated with daily training. This type of training is likely to enhance V̇ O2max, increase the LT, and improve exercise economy and fuel use. The various types of training induce different physiological responses. Ideally, a sound program would incorporate all types of training into the athlete’s weekly, monthly, or yearly training schedule. 1542

text: However, for beginner athletes who start with a very low training volume, it may be safe and logical to increase by more than 10%. For example, an athlete who is new to running may run 1 mile (1.6 km) three times in their first week. By following the 10% recommendation, the following week would realize an increase of only a total of 0.3 miles (0.5 km), whereas the athlete should logically be able to absorb more than this—in this case, an additional 0.5 miles (0.8 km) on two separate days (i.e., a total of 1 mile [1.6 km] or 33% increase). Similarly, cyclists, by the nature of the volume of training they engage in as well as the low-impact nature of their sport, may be able to safely increase their volume by more than 10%. For example, a beginner cyclist may complete an average of 25 miles (40 km) in a week. The recommendation would mean the following week they would increase their volume by a total of 1.25 to 2.5 miles (2-4 km). If this athlete is training at an average speed of 10 miles per hour (16 km/h), this volume would equate to an additional 7.5 to 15 minutes, which in both absolute and relative terms is small. However, it is also important to consider that training is progressed across many weeks in a training program, and even small changes on a week-to-week basis will eventually add up to substantial increases in volume or intensity. Therefore, while an initial increase in volume of >10% may be advisable in some, continued increases across a training program of more

text: In-Season (Competition) The in-season training program needs to be designed to include competition or race days in the training schedule. Low-intensity and short-duration training days should precede scheduled competitions so that the athlete is fully recovered and rested. The types of training employed during the in-season are based on the continued goal of improving weaknesses and maintaining strengths of the athlete. Sample Training Program for a 5 Kilometer (3.1 Mile) Collegiate Cross- Country Runner During the In-Season Phase Sunday Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Rest or easy run 60 min aerobic run 45-min Fartlek run of hard/easy work on hills and flats 20 min pace/tempo run 30 min aerobic run with race pace pickups 20 min aerobic run with race pace pickups Competition Comments Frequency. Because Fartlek and tempo runs are stressful, no more than two in total should occur during the week. Duration. The total distance or duration of the training portion of the session (i.e., the sum of the interval work bouts) should approach the competition distance as the athlete becomes more highly trained. chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Postseason (Active Rest) During the postseason, the main focus should be on recovering from the previous competitive season. Low training duration and intensity are typical for this active rest phase, but enough overall exercise or activity should be performed to maintain a sufficient level of cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and lean body mass. During the postseason, the aerobic endurance athlete should focus on rehabilitating injuries incurred during the competitive season and improving the strength of weak or underconditioned muscle groups. A sound year-round aerobic endurance training program should be divided into sport seasons with specific goals and objectives designed to improve performance gradually and progressively. 1550

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Special Issues Related to Aerobic Endurance Training In addition to the program design variables, it is important to consider other related issues when developing an aerobic endurance training program. These include cross-training, detraining, tapering, and supplemental resistance training. The strength and conditioning professional should contemplate these issues when adapting the types of aerobic endurance training programs to an individual athlete or developing an aerobic endurance program based on the sport season. Cross-Training Cross-training is a mode of training that can be used to maintain general conditioning in athletes during periods of reduced training due to injury or during recovery from a training cycle (96). Cross- training may reduce the likelihood of overuse injuries because it distributes the physical stress of training to muscle groups different from those used during training (122). Multiple-event athletes also use cross-training to maximize performance in swimming, cycling, and running. The benefits derived from cross-training include adaptations of the respiratory, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems (88, 122). It seems reasonable to expect that cross-training would maintain some level of conditioning in single-event athletes who perform another mode of training (e.g., runners who perform cycling or swimming). To be effective in maintaining V̇ O2max, cross- training must be equal in intensity and duration to the athlete’s primary mode of exerci

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: program, injury, or illness. In the absence of an appropriate training stimulus, the athlete experiences a loss of the physiological adaptations brought about by training. It has been demonstrated that most of the physiological adaptations attained with training regress rapidly toward pretraining levels when the training stimulus is removed (5, 102). To avoid some of the effects of detraining, the use of other training modes may be beneficial; however, cross- training may only attenuate some of the loss of physiological adaptation normally seen during complete cessation of training. Aerobic endurance athletes can minimize the effects of detraining by continuing to use their primary mode of exercise at reduced frequency and intensity, if possible (136). Tapering Tapering is an important component of the training program as aerobic endurance athletes prepare for major competition. Tapering involves the systematic reduction of training duration and intensity, combined with an increased emphasis on technique work and nutritional intervention. The objective of tapering the training regimen is to attain peak performance at the time of competition. While the duration of the taper depends on numerous factors, a typical tapering period may last between 7 and 28 days (91). Although most of the available research on tapering has been conducted on swimmers (95, 126, 131), the use of tapering is not limited to these aerobic endurance athletes. Research among runners and cyclists has shown

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: the duration of the taper. In contrast, a step taper is typified by an abrupt and considerable reduction (normally ≥50%) in training volume that is maintained throughout the duration of the taper without fluctuation. The progressive taper uses a combination of the linear and step tapering models. This model is associated with a rapid 10% to 15% immediate reduction in training volume, with smaller, more gradual reductions in volume at each tier. Training volume is systematically reduced while intensity and frequency are maintained. Concurrent Aerobic Endurance Training and Resistance Training Resistance training is an important but often overlooked factor in improving performance in aerobic endurance athletes. This may be due to misconceptions that resistance training may increase an athlete’s nonfunctional muscle mass and thereby decrease performance, or the potential interference phenomenon that may occur when resistance and aerobic endurance training sessions are completed within a training program (i.e., concurrent training) (35). However, apart from the well-known benefits that resistance training can provide athletes, such as reducing muscle imbalances, assistance with preventing overuse injuries, and recovery from injuries (122), numerous research investigations (25, 32, 45, 82, 84, 109, 114, 119, 127, 135), meta-analyses, and systematic review articles (1, 4, 10, 11, 17, 31, 37, 38, 65, 80, 89, 116, 143) have demonstrated that it can also improve performance (e.g., tim

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: both heavy resistance training and explosive or plyometric training have been found to be effective training methods to concurrently train with aerobic endurance training to improve running economy (10, 31). Improvements in running economy and performance following heavy resistance training and plyometric training are primarily related to an increase in strength of the muscles used during running thereby reducing the relative intensity of the load of the exercising muscles (43). Plyometric training, which uses the stretch-shortening cycle, not only improves the storage and elastic energy properties of the exercising muscles but assists them to work more efficiently (86). It is important to note that maximal strength training has been found to produce greater benefits than submaximal strength training or maximal power training, with submaximal strength training producing the least gains of all other methods (10). It is also worth highlighting that no signs of overtraining (1) or significant increases in body mass (1, 17), maximal oxygen uptake (17), or blood lactate markers (17) have been associated with the aerobic performance improvements for the majority of concurrent training studies. However, not all concurrent training studies (143) have resulted in improvements in aerobic endurance performance measures. The differences between studies is often due to the choice of resistance training exercises (e.g., high vs. low intensity, explosive or plyometric) (80), characteristics

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: hence neuromuscular stimulus experienced with free weights compared to machine-based or single-joint exercises (17). For those studies involving running, the benefit may also be related to the greater transference from the resistance training environment to the running movement due to the biomechanical similarity between the two (17). High-velocity movements including plyometric exercises such as hops, bounds, jumps, drop jumps, and squat jumps have shown to have a positive impact on aerobic endurance performance measures (31, 38). For more information, refer to chapters 18 and 19 for program design and technique details. Training Intensity and Frequency A common finding of concurrent training research for improving aerobic endurance performance is the use of heavy resistance training or plyometric training by athletes two or three times per week (10, 17) or a combination of both (4, 31, 38). However, to reduce the impact of a resistance training session on a subsequent aerobic endurance training session (i.e., residual fatigue, muscle soreness, and physiological disturbance), the volume should be reduced to limit the potential carryover of fatigue caused by the resistance training session (35). That is, keep the loads high (e.g., ≥90% of 1RM or ≤4RM) (38) but the weekly volume low (31). It is also worth noting that strength developed during a preparatory phase has been found to be maintained for up to 12 weeks with just one resistance training session per week thereafter (11

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: recovery period between training sessions, the greater the level of fatigue carried from one training session to the next (33, 110). In conjunction, there is an increase in the physiological cost of the next training session and a reduction in training performance, which may result in lower adaptations (32). Some posttraining fatigue is necessary for stimulating training adaptations, but it is simultaneously necessary to maximize recovery between training sessions, particularly if on the same day. To achieve this, manipulation of concurrent training variables such as sequence of training, training intensities, volumes, and frequency as well as the recovery period between training sessions can be adjusted (11, 34, 110). However, because athletes respond differently to training stimuli and recovery techniques, it is important to monitor athletes’ recovery via measures such as heart rate, task completion times, RPE, blood lactate, power output, and the like (35). Training Sequence The order in which resistance and aerobic endurance training sessions are completed may affect adaptations because the acute physiological responses for resistance and aerobic endurance training are distinct to each form of training (34) and may influence the quality and quantity of training sessions completed on the same day. Findings have been mixed on the effects of concurrent training sequence on strength and V̇ O2max (25, 32, 45, 46). As a general guide, however, the training sequence should be va

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: benefiting similarly in terms of performance from undertaking a concurrent training program (10). However, the difference in muscle action types (eccentric vs. concentric) may create a greater level of muscle damage from some modes compared to others (e.g., running vs. cycling) (143), particularly if large distances are involved. Therefore, in concurrent training programs that involve running, a greater recovery period may be needed when completed in the hours before or following a resistance training session. This concept may be especially important for athletes undertaking more than one aerobic endurance discipline, such as triathletes (35). Athlete Training Status The training status of athletes has been suggested to be an important variable to consider when undertaking concurrent training (11). While the majority of findings indicate that concurrent training can benefit aerobic endurance performance of athletes of different levels across different aerobic endurance disciplines (10), the responses may be different. For example, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that following a concurrent training program, trained or highly trained aerobic endurance athletes did not demonstrate any impairments to improvements in V̇ O2max; however, untrained individuals did (65). Consequently, for aerobic endurance athletes who have minimal resistance training experience or for lesser trained aerobic endurance athletes, it may be necessary to allow greater recovery times between t

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Altitude Altitude is classified into several categories, ranging from sea level (>500 m [1,640 ft]) to low (>500-2,000 m [1,640-6,562 ft]), moderate (>2,000-3,000 m [6,562-9,843 ft]), high (>3,000-5,500 m [6,562-18,045 ft]), and extreme (>5,500 m [>18,045 ft]) (39). While the percentage of oxygen is the same at different altitudes (94), the atmospheric pressure drops, causing a reduction in partial pressure (PO2), which acts as the driving force for gas exchange in the lungs (39, 94). This leads to a cascade of physiological responses to compensate for the reduction in PO2. Subsequently, aerobic endurance performance decrements upon acute altitude exposure may begin to occur at altitudes as low as 700 meters (2,297 ft) (145). Acclimatization to altitude may occur between 12 and 14 days at moderate altitudes up to 2,300 meters (7,546 ft); however, it has been found that this process may take up to several months (145). According to Wyatt (145), recommendations for optimizing performance at altitude vary dramatically, from arriving immediately before competition (24-48 hr) to 12 weeks of altitude exposure. Many elite and sub-elite athletes train at altitude to produce an ergogenic effect. In order to experience a benefit from this type of training, it has been reported that an athlete must receive a hypoxic dose of training ≥12 hours per day for a minimum of three weeks at moderate altitude (approximately 2,100-2,500 m [6,890-8,202 ft]) (66, 145). Live high, train low (LHTL) is

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Heat Acclimation It is well documented that aerobic endurance performances are influenced by hot environments (55, 99, 100). Consequently, undertaking training or competition in hot environments before an athlete has acclimatized results in greater thermoregulatory and cardiovascular strain, fatigue, increased perception of effort, and a negative impact on performance (52) via elevated core and skin temperatures, increased sweating, and loss of electrolytes. To avoid these negative effects, athletes are advised to acclimatize prior to competition in warm to hot conditions. Adaptations to heat acclimation protocols include an increase in plasma volume and thereby an increase in blood volume, an improvement in skin blood flow sensitivity, earlier onset of sweating at a lower core body temperature combined with an increase in sweat rate and evaporative cooling, and a reduction in gastrointestinal distress (51, 101). These changes, along with many others, help provide cardiovascular stability, lower core and skin temperatures, and a reduced exercise heart rate. A more detailed description of the adaptations to training in the heat can be found in chapter 6 (see the section Heat Acclimatization). Heat Acclimation Protocols An athlete can adapt naturally to a hot environment by either living and training in hot ambient conditions over a long period of time (i.e., heat acclimatization) or training in an artificially hot indoor environment (i.e., heat acclimation) (108). Heat acclima

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: or multiday events as well as those of a lesser training status undertake longer protocols to ensure appropriate levels of heat adaptation (107). The frequency of heat exposure is important because adaptations occur more rapidly with days of consecutive exposure; however, if over a 10- to 14-day protocol, one to three days of heat exposure are missed, it is unlikely that these missed days will significantly affect heat acclimation adaptations (107). It is important to note that twice-daily heat exposure is no more effective than once-daily for physiological, perceptual, or performance adaptations (141). For a heat acclimation protocol to be effective, an increase in core and skin temperatures and sweat rate is required (101, 108). To achieve this, it is generally recommended that athletes aim for 60 minutes of heat exposure (108) and a maximum of 90 minutes, although 120 minutes has been shown to be effective (115, 144). It should be noted that it may take time to build up to these exposure times over the heat acclimation protocol period as determined by the intensity of the training sessions as well as the athlete’s heat tolerance. Measures of training intensity such as heart rate and performance times may be misleading in the short term until the athlete heat acclimatizes (54). A more appropriate alternative may be a scalar method such as perceived exertion (54). However, markers that an athlete is positively adapting are a lower heart rate and core temperature for a given

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: be implemented when working with heat acclimation protocols. For example, always begin well hydrated, maintain hydration, ensure cooling equipment is available (e.g., cold-water immersion bath or ice vests), and signs and symptoms of exertional heat illness should be well known to athletes and staff and be posted. For more information, readers are directed to Pryor and colleagues (107). To determine individual athlete adaptation and decay rates, heat acclimatization protocols should be practiced months before competition in the heat (9), and athletes should also undertake a practice heat event in similar conditions to those they expect to perform in on competition day (9). It is recommended that the environment have a wet-bulb globe temperature >30 °C (>86 °F) to provide the necessary stress to elicit heat adaptations in core body temperature as well as induce a higher sweat response (28). A reduction in training duration or intensity followed by a progressive increase over the protocol period may be required compared to the usual training load, on the initial introduction of a heat acclimation protocol (107). In addition, it may be necessary to use a combination of exercise and passive heat exposure (e.g., sauna or hot-water immersion) sessions as the athlete commences and progresses through the heat acclimation process to enable integration with the athlete’s training schedule (54). chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Conclusion Training to improve aerobic endurance performance requires a well- developed and scientifically based program. The training program should be developed in conjunction with periodic performance assessment and should be structured to enhance the strengths and improve the weaknesses of the athlete. A combination of a variety of the training types described in this chapter should be used so that all physiological systems involved in successful performance are overloaded and challenged to respond with positive adaptations. Training programs should be developed far enough in advance and with enough structure to ensure enhancement of performance but with enough flexibility to avoid overuse injuries and overtraining. Although other forms of training can be employed to avoid boredom and overtraining, activity-specific training results in the best adaptations to training and ultimately the most improvement in performance. AEROBIC ENDURANCE TRAINING EXERCISES The following section discusses some basic technique considerations for performance of aerobic endurance training. General guidelines for both common aerobic training machines and nonmachine activities are provided. These exercise instructions are largely adapted from Beck (8). 1 Treadmill 713 2 Stationary Bike 714 3 Rowing Machine 715 4 Stair Stepper 716 5 Elliptical Trainer 717 1562

text: 6 Walking (Gait) 718 7 Running (Gait) 718 8 Freestyle Swimming 719 Aerobic Endurance Training Exercises 1 TREADMILL Starting Position Begin by attaching the security clip to the clothing where it will not interfere with the action of the lower or upper limbs. Straddle the belt by placing the feet on the right and left platform. Read the instructions on the console of the treadmill to gain an understanding of how to adjust the speed and incline of the specific treadmill being used. Turn on the machine and adjust the speed of the belt so it is at the desired warm-up speed. Movement Phase While holding the handrails, allow one leg to swing freely, and using a pawing action, strike the treadmill with the mid-foot. Once comfortable with the speed of the belt, begin walking or running on the treadmill. Run or walk, keeping toward the front portion of the machine while remaining in the center of the treadmill deck. Release the hands from the handrails and adjust the speed and incline until the desired training level is attained. Avoid holding on to the console or front handrails or leaning backward while walking or running. Keep the head up and eyes focused forward to avoid looking down at the console for extended periods of time. 1563

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Ending Position Reduce the speed of the treadmill and perform a 3- to 5-minute cooldown to prevent blood pooling in the lower extremities and improve venous return to the heart. Step onto the platforms on either side of the belt and turn the machine off. COMMON ERRORS Continually holding the handrails—holding the handrails beyond the initial entry phase interrupts posture and stride mechanics and limits core activation; after the initial entry phase use a natural walking or running stride pattern with an upright posture and free moving arm swing, as if walking or running outside Looking continuously down at the console, which affects stride mechanics and posture and can cause neck discomfort; keep the eyes focused forward, with short glances to the console as needed to monitor display information 2 STATIONARY BIKE Starting Position Begin by adjusting the seat height so the knee of the extended leg is slightly flexed (25-30 degrees) at the bottom of the pedal stroke. The foot of the down leg should be flat and parallel to the floor with the balls of the feet in contact with the pedals. Adjust the seat so the knee is over the center of the pedal on the extended leg and the hips do not rock back and forth during pedaling. While maintaining a neutral spine position, lean slightly forward at the hips. 1564

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Adjust the handlebars so that when the arms are extended at a downward angle the elbows are slightly flexed. Ideally, the lower arm and torso will form an angle of approximately 90 degrees. Movement Phase Begin pedaling while keeping the balls of the feet in contact with the pedals throughout the duration of the exercise. Maintain a neutral spine posture and do not round the shoulders. With bullhorn handlebars, a variety of hand positions may be used. These include pronated, palms-facing-downward grip, allowing a more upright posture; neutral palms-facing grip on the sides of the handlebars, encouraging a greater forward lean; and racing position, with the forearms resting on the handlebars, creating maximum forward lean. Ending Position Slow down until the pedals have come to a complete stop, and then step off the bike. COMMON ERRORS If pedaling using the toes only and not the balls of the feet or moving laterally in the seat, the seat is too high. If the knees come above the height of the hips at the top of the pedaling stroke, the seat is too low. If struggling to reach the handlebars, the seat may be too far back or the handlebars too low. Correct seat and handlebar height ensures maintenance of power output throughout the pedaling stroke. 1565

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Proper seat height adjustment: (a) leg straight with knee locked and heel on pedal; (b) knee slightly flexed with ball of foot on pedal; (c) with the pedal at 12 o’clock, the knee is about even with the hips and approximately parallel with the floor 3 ROWING MACHINE Starting Position (Start) Keep the back upright, not rounded, with a slight forward lean from the hips. Hold the head upright while looking straight ahead. Extend the arms in front of the body and grab the rower handle while flexing the hips and knees until the shins are approximately vertical. Movement Phase (Drive) Extend the knees first followed by the hips before using the arms to pull the handle toward the abdomen just below the rib cage. As the knees near their end range of motion, tilt the upper body backward by extending the hips before pulling with the arms to complete the movement. Adjust the air vent to increase (more air admitted) or decrease (less air admitted) the resistance provided. 1566

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Ending Position (Finish) The knees should be fully extended with the torso leaning slightly backward. Arms are flexed at the elbows and the handle is at the abdomen just below the rib cage. Recovery is the movement from the finish position back to the start in the reverse order of drive phase events—that is, extension of the arms first before flexion at the hips (to move the upper body forward), then flexion of the knees back to the start position. COMMON ERRORS Using arms and legs at the same time or pulling only with arms—the legs provide the majority of the power in the drive phase; the drive phase sequence is knees, hips, then arms. The handle going up and over the knees on the way back or the chain hitting the machine in a whipping motion, which is often due to the recovery sequence being out of sync; the recovery sequence is the opposite of the drive phase, so arms, hips then knees 1567

Movement Phase Begin stepping, using the handrails for support. While maintaining an upright posture and with the legs providing the force, take deep (4- to 8-in. [10-20 cm]) steps. Keep the hips level and centered on the machine to avoid swaying from side to side or step to step. Do not allow the steps to contact the floor or the upper-limit stop of the machine. text: 5 ELLIPTICAL TRAINER Starting Position Facing the center console of the elliptical, place one foot on each pedal. While standing upright and looking forward, grasp the handrails with the torso upright and evenly balanced directly over the hips, head held high, and shoulders relaxed (but not rounded). Movement Phase Begin pedaling forward, moving the arms and legs in a reciprocating fashion. The feet should remain in full contact with the pedals throughout the duration of the exercise unless the design of the 1570

text: machine causes the rear heel to lift. The knees should not be allowed to come forward past the toes when in the flexed position. Hold onto the handrails in order to maintain balance. If handrail holding is unnecessary, it is a good idea to release the hold on the handrails and pump the arms similarly to the way they move in walking or running. The incline of the elliptical may be increased to more closely simulate a running motion or reduced to replicate a walking motion. Performing this exercise with a forward motion may place greater emphasis on the quadriceps; performing it with a backward motion may increase the stress on the hamstrings and gluteals. Ending Position Slow down until the machine has come to a complete stop, then step off the pedals. COMMON ERRORS Lifting the heels and applying too much pressure via the forefoot; use the whole pedal to distribute pressure when applying force to the pedals Leaning on the handrails, which disengages the core muscles and affects movement phase execution; if necessary to hold on for balance, ensure an upright posture is always maintained and the core is engaged, and avoid placing hands too low on the handrails, which can cause a forward lean 1571

text: 6 WALKING (GAIT) Body Position Hold the head upright with the eyes looking straight ahead. Relax the shoulders, and do not allow them to round. Position the upper body directly over the hips while keeping the ear, shoulder, and hip aligned. Foot Strike The heel should strike the ground first, followed by a gentle rolling heel-to-ball action, allowing the weight to be spread over the foot. The weight should transfer from the outer side of the heel and continue to shift forward and slightly inward toward the middle of the ball of the foot at push-off. Stride 1572

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Without rolling the pelvis (unless racewalking), allow the hips to move freely to increase stride length. Lift the knees and engage the hips and gluteals in the movement. Arm Action The arms should swing forward and backward in a reciprocating fashion with the lower body (i.e., when the left arm is forward, the right leg is extended, and vice versa). The shoulders should be relaxed, allowing the arms to swing freely. At faster walking speeds, the actions should be as follows: The arms should be flexed at the elbows and maintained at 90 degrees with arm movement originating at the shoulders. The arms and hands should swing backward and forward, not crossing the midline of the body, in order to create forward propulsion. The hands should stay relaxed, with the hand coming up to the level of the chest at the nipple line on the forward swing and the hip bone at the side of the body on the backward swing. Note: Racewalkers must increase hip rotation with each stride to create a pelvic roll. This enables them to increase stride length while keeping one foot in contact with the ground at all times per the rules of the sport. 7 RUNNING (GAIT) Body Position Hold the head upright with the eyes looking straight ahead. Relax the shoulders, but do not allow them to round. Position the upper body during running with an approximately 2- to 4-degree lean from the heels to the athlete’s head while keeping the ear, shoulder, and hip aligned. 1573

chapterTitle: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance and Metabolic Training
text: Foot Strike The foot should strike the ground slightly in front of or directly below the athlete’s center of gravity (i.e., hips), which may be a heel, mid-, or forefoot strike, followed by a gentle rolling heel- to-ball action, allowing the weight to be spread over the foot during the foot contact phase. The weight will likely transfer from the outer side of the heel and continue to shift. Stride Without rolling the pelvis (unless racewalking), allow the hips to move freely to increase stride length. Lift the knees and engage the hips and gluteals in the movement. With each running step, the foot should land approximately under the hips to avoid braking and minimize contact time with the ground. Arm Action The arms should swing forward and backward in a reciprocating motion with the lower body (i.e., when the left arm is forward, the right leg is extended, and vice versa). The shoulders should be relaxed, allowing the arms to swing freely. The arms and hands should swing backward and forward from the shoulder, not crossing the midline of the body, in order to create forward propulsion. Arm action of ±20-degree oscillation of the hands is acceptable and may improve running economy (91a). 8 FREESTYLE SWIMMING Swimming performance is a combination of swimming-specific fitness and technique. Less-than-optimal swimming technique can significantly and negatively affect an athlete’s performance due to 1574

text: CHAPTER 22 PERIODIZATION G. Gregory Haff, PhD The author would like to acknowledge the significant contributions of Dan Wathen, Thomas R. Baechle, and Roger W. Earle to this chapter. After completing this chapter, you will be able to understand the central concepts that underpin the periodization of training; appreciate the value, role, and application of periodization in strength and conditioning programs; describe the four periods of the traditional periodization model; describe the two phases of the preparatory period of the traditional periodization model; relate the four sport seasons to the four periods of the traditional periodization model; and apply the program design variables to create a periodized strength training program. The ability to guide the training process and implement programming strategies that enhance the athlete’s potential for achieving the highest level of performance at targeted time points is largely affected by the long- and short-term programming strategies implemented by the strength and conditioning professional (69). The process of organizing these programming strategies is generally referred to as periodization. The basic concepts associated with periodization can be traced to ancient philosophers and physicians, such as Galen (also known as Clausius Aelius Galenus), who presented the first description of the application of periodized strength training methods, and Lucius Flavius Philostratus, who presented a structured pre-Olympic training

Later on, American sport scientists Michael H. Stone, Harold O’Bryant, and John Garhammer adapted the concepts of the early periodization theorists with special application to strength and power athletes (89, 91). While the concepts that underpin our understanding of periodization are well established and are well accepted, confusion still exists in both the scientific (1, 2, 54, 79) and practical (25) literature about what periodization is and how it is used to guide the training process. At the center of this confusion is the fact that the terms periodization and programming are often used interchangeably within the literature (20, 35, 37, 88). While periodization and programming are interrelated, they represent different management levels of the training process (35, 38). Specifically, periodization serves as the macro-management level of the training process, while programming allows for the micro-management of the process (38). Conceptually, periodization serves as a method for organizing deliberate practice by providing the scaffold from which programming decisions are made (60). The objectives targeted by the periodized plan are then aligned with training cycles (e.g., micro-, meso-, and macrocycles, and annual and multiyear cycles) (73) and individualized programs are constructed. text: Central Concepts Related to Periodization A successful training program allows for management of the adaptive and recovery responses to specific interventions that are delivered in a structured way (41). The ultimate success of any training program centers on its ability to induce specific physiological adaptations and translate those adaptations into increases in performance. At the center of this process is the ability to manage the adaptive response, handle accumulated fatigue, and capitalize on the aftereffects established from the various training factors encountered. The strength of a periodized training plan lies in its ability to sequence and structure the training interventions in order to manage all of these factors and peak performance at appropriate time points (35, 37, 38, 41). Ultimately, peak performance can be optimized only for short periods of time (7-14 days), and the average time it can be maintained is inversely related to the average intensity of the training plan (35, 36). In order to elucidate how periodized training models can manage these factors, three basic mechanistic theories have been established: the general adaptation syndrome (GAS), stimulus–fatigue– recovery–adaptation theory, and the fitness–fatigue paradigm (35, 38, 41). Periodization is the logical and systematic process of sequencing and integrating training interventions in order to manage the training process and to increase the potential of achieving peak performance at appropriate ti

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: resistance phase, when it adapts to the stimulus and returns to a normal functional capacity. If the training stress is appropriately structured and not excessive, these adaptive responses can result in specific biochemical, structural, and mechanical adjustments that further elevate the athlete’s performance capacity, resulting in what is termed supercompensation (91). An additional factor that modulates the stress response to training is the athlete’s psychological and emotional state (95, 96). If the athlete has chronic elevations in psychological and emotional stress, the magnitude of the fatigue response will be increased during the alarm phase and the time course for recovery will be lengthened, resulting in an elongation of the resistance phase, ultimately resulting in a delayed supercompensation response (38). As such, the strength and conditioning professional must not only monitor the training loads the athlete is exposed to but must also consider the athlete’s current psychological and emotional state when manipulating training loads within the periodized training plan. In this regard, the integration of a comprehensive monitoring program can provide additional information that allows that strength and conditioning professional to better manage the athlete’s exposure to training stress and increase the potential for appropriate elevations in performance. If, however, the stress persists (either physical or psychoemotional) for an extended period of time, the athlet

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: accumulates and the longer the delay before complete recovery and adaption can occur. As the athlete recovers from and adapts to the training stimuli, fatigue dissipates, and preparedness and performance increase. If no new training stimulus is introduced, a state of involution or detraining (i.e., a reduced overall capacity, to below the current baseline) is observed. In contrast, if a new training stimulus is introduced, the process is repeated. This basic pattern is present whenever an athlete is exposed to a training exercise, session, day, or cycle within a periodized training plan. It should be noted that while recovery is an important part of the training process, it is not always necessary to reach a state of complete recovery before engaging in a new bout or session of training (72). The manipulation of workloads and training intensities through use of light and heavy sessions or days of training can be used to modulate fatigue and recovery responses (8, 26, 88) while allowing for fitness to be either increased or maintained. Conceptually, this theory serves as the foundation for sequential periodization models in that these models allow for the manipulation of various training factors to modulate the athlete’s overall fatigue levels, rate of recovery, and adaptive response to the training stimuli. text: Fitness–Fatigue Paradigm Generally, a summation of the two primary training aftereffects (i.e., fitness and fatigue) occurs in response to training interventions that influence the athlete’s level of preparedness (15, 38, 107). In 1995, Zatsiorsky (106) presented the classic explanation of these relationships as the two-factor model, more commonly referred to as the fitness–fatigue paradigm (figure 22.4). Ultimately, every training bout, session, or cycle creates both fatigue and fitness aftereffects, which summate to create a state of preparedness (15, 106). When training loads are the highest, fitness becomes elevated, but because of the high training loads, a concomitant increase in fatigue occurs. When fitness and fatigue are summed in this case, the level of fatigue results in a reduction in preparedness. On the other hand, when training workloads are low, little fatigue occurs and minimal fitness is developed, resulting in a low level of preparedness. Thus, the sequencing of training loads becomes important in that it allows for training workloads to be varied in a systematic manner. An important thing to remember is that fatigue dissipates at a rate two-thirds faster than fitness, thus allowing preparedness to become elevated if appropriate training strategies are used to retain fitness while reducing fatigue (35, 38, 41). chapterTitle: Periodization
text: Models of Periodization While the scientific and coaching literature presents numerous models of periodization, all models can be classified under three general models (figure 22.5). Parallel Training Models The parallel training models, as shown in figure 22.5, involve targeting all training factors simultaneously within one training session, training day, series of training days, or a microcycle (33, 35, 37, 38). Sometimes this approach is referred to as the concurrent or complex parallel approach (4). This planning approach aligns with the early stages of most long-term athlete development models (61, 62) where youth athletes are exposed to multilateral training strategies. Additionally, this approach works well with novice and developmental athletes (38). A major concern with parallel models is that as the athlete develops his or her total training load (i.e., volume or load, time dedicated to training, etc.) must be continually increased (35) and may exceed his or her training tolerance (51). As such, this model may not be the best option when working with intermediate to elite athletes, who require greater training variation and stimulus to continue to stimulate adaptation and elevate performance (16, 35, 37, 38). With these athletes it may be warranted to implement different planning strategies (i.e., emphasis or parallel models) to optimize the training process (38). Emphasis Training Models Emphasis training models, as shown in figure 22.5, contain aspects of both parallel and sequential models of periodization (35, 37, 38). Similar to parallel models, multiple training factors are targeted simultaneously but with varying degrees of emphasis over time (38). Over time the degree of focus on the individual training is shifted in a sequential manner that aligns with the periodized training plan. Generally, when this model is implemented the training emphasis is rotated every two weeks to optimize performance capacity (108). When varying the emphasis some training factors will be undertaken with training loads that stimulate adaptations, while some training factors are undertaken with training loads that are used to maintain the athlete’s current state (38, 108). Additionally, some training factors will be targeted with a minimal training dose, which would result in a degree of detraining. This training model is ideally suited for intermediate to advanced athletes who compete in individual or team sports and have congested competitive schedules (38). chapterTitle: Periodization
text: Periodization Hierarchy Ultimately, periodization is simply a means of organizing the planning of the training process so that it is partitioned into specific time periods (table 22.2) (36, 37, 41). The multiyear training plan covers the most time but is the least detailed plan within a periodized training structure. For example, it may involve the basic progression of a college soccer player from her freshman to senior year and contain key developmental goals that are targeted within each year of training. This multiyear training structure is then subdivided into more detailed individual annual training plans that are developed based on the athlete’s progression through the various stages or benchmarks forecasted across the multiyear training plan. In sports that have only one competitive season, such as American football, an annual training plan would be represented as a macrocycle. However, in a sport such as college track and field, the annual plan would be divided into two macrocycles because of the indoor and outdoor seasons typical of this college sport. Alternatively, if a high school athlete competes in American football in the fall, basketball in the winter, and track and field in the spring, the annual plan would be subdivided into three macrocycles. Typically, the macrocycle lasts several months up to a year, depending on the sport or the number of sports participated in within the year. text: Periodization Periods The overall variation and structure of the program design variables within each individual meso- and microcycle are constructed based on the periods included in the macrocycle or annual training plan (35, 36, 38). Across these periods of the training plan, the volume and intensity of the training and conditioning program generally receive the greatest attention, but the time spent acquiring and perfecting sport-specific technique must also be considered when one is constructing the overall periodized training plan (77). Ultimately, periodized training plans systematically shift training foci from general nonspecific activities of high volume and low intensity toward activities of lower volume and higher intensities over a period of many weeks or months to help reduce the potential for overtraining while optimizing performance capacities. The basic sequencing of periodized training programs and how training progresses through the various phases for specified training targets are very similar to the sequencing and evolution of learning academic concepts. For example, in academics we start with simple concepts and skills that progress to more complex concepts; that is, we develop simple skills to provide a sound foundation for learning more complex items. Ultimately, the periods within a periodized training plan serve as the pathway for developing foundational physical, psychological, and performance attributes into more complex sport- specific targets. Advanced athletes tend to train closer to their abilities and have smaller adaptation windows. Therefore, these athletes require greater training variation as well as higher volumes and intensities to allow them to continue to experience appropriate training stimuli (77). For example, Zatsiorsky and colleagues (107) demonstrate that a stimulating load for a novice athlete would be a maintenance load at best for advanced athletes. To address this issue, the shift from higher- volume to higher-intensity training can occur earlier in the preparatory phase, with higher overall training volumes as compared to those in the base model presented in figure 22.6. Preparatory Period In outlining a periodized training plan, the starting point is usually the preparatory period. This period occurs when there are no competitions, and technical, tactical, or sport-specific work is limited.

Based on the model presented in figure 22.6, the conditioning activities would begin with relatively low intensities and high volumes: long, slow distance running or swimming; low-intensity plyometrics; and high-repetition resistance training with light to moderate resistances. Traditionally, the preparatory period is subdivided into general and specific phases. The general preparatory phase typically occurs during the early part of the period and often targets the development of a general physical base (38, 69). This early part of the preparatory period includes high training volumes, low training intensities, and a larger variety of training means that are structured to develop general motor abilities and skills (49, 65). The specific preparatory phase occurs after the completion of the general preparatory phase and involves a shift in training focus. From the training base that has been established, this phase expands the athlete’s training base through an increased emphasis on sport- specific training activities that prepare the athlete for the competitive period (18, 69). During the preparatory period, resistance training phases can be created to depict more refined differences in training intensity and volume. In order, these are the hypertrophy (or strength–endurance) phase and the basic strength phase (89, 91). Basic Strength Phase In the later portion of the preparatory period, during the specific preparatory phase, the primary aim of the basic strength phase is to increase the strength of the muscles that are essential to the primary sport movements (12-14). For example, the sprinter’s running program would progress to include interval sprints of a moderate distance and more complex and specialized plyometric drills. The resistance training program also becomes more specific to the sport (e.g., squat, power clean, Bulgarian squat) and involves heavier loads performed at lower volumes than in the hypertrophy or strength–endurance phase (table 22.3). As with the hypertrophy or strength–endurance phase, daily variations in training load facilitate recovery (35, 38). The basic strength phase involves higher intensity (80%-95% of the 1RM) and moderate to high volumes (2 to 6 sets of 2 to 6 repetitions). First Transition Period As originally described by Stone and colleagues (89-91), the first transition period is a link between the preparatory and competitive periods. Classically, the resistance training in this period focuses on the development of strength and power as noted in Stone, O’Bryant, and Garhammer’s (89) seminal paper on the periodization of strength training. The central aim of this period is to shift the training focus toward the elevation of strength and its translation into power development (89, 90). In order to maximize this process and fa

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: facilitated with a load of 80% of the 1RM with power cleans performed from the hang (55) or floor (17), while a load of 50% to 70% of the 1RM may be used with the bench press throw when the aim is to maximize power development (55). Ultimately, to address both strength and power development, a mixed training approach is warranted in which heavy- and low-load training is used to optimize both attributes (44). The strength/power phase involves low to very high loads (30%-95% of the 1RM, depending on the exercise) and low volumes (2 to 5 sets for 2 to 5 repetitions). Competitive Period The central training target during the competitive period is preparing the athlete for competition by further increasing strength and power via additional increases in training intensity while decreasing volume. This process can be a delicate balancing act, because adequate volume and intensity of training are needed to maintain competitive preparedness, and reductions in volume, intensity, or both are needed to optimize performance. To understand this conundrum, consider the fitness–fatigue paradigm presented earlier. If training workloads (volume or intensity) are reduced too much, fatigue will be reduced, but there will be a concomitant decrease in overall fitness that results in a reduction in competitive preparedness. Also during this period, time spent practicing sport-specific skills and tactics increases dramatically, and a proportional decrease occurs in time spent performing physical con

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: strength and power while managing the fatigue associated with a frequent competition schedule. Generally, a maintenance program is marked by moderate- to high-intensity training (e.g., 85%-93% 1RM) at low to moderate volumes. At the microcycle level, the training loads are modulated based on the training, travel, and competitive schedule. Careful monitoring of the athlete’s performance capacity and recovery is critical during the team-sport athlete’s competitive period. The competitive period includes peaking and maintenance. For peaking, athletes use very high to low intensities (50% to ≥93% of the 1RM) and very low volume (1 to 3 sets of 1 to 3 repetitions) for one to two weeks. For maintenance, athletes modulate training between moderate and high intensities (85%-93% of the 1RM) with moderate volumes (about 2 to 5 sets of 3 to 6 repetitions). Second Transition Period (Active Rest) Between the competitive season and the next annual training plan or the preparatory period of a macrocycle, a second transition period is often used to create a linkage (89). This period is sometimes referred to as an active rest or restoration period and generally lasts for one to four weeks (38). It is important to note that if active rest is extended for a prolonged duration, athletes will require a much longer preparatory period to regain their performance capacities (39). Therefore, it is generally recommended that the second transition period last no longer than four weeks unless an athlete

text: Applying Sport Seasons to the Periodization Periods In practical terms, periodization involves a logical, systematic variation and integration of training to direct the training responses while managing fatigue and optimizing performance in accordance with the seasonal demands of the sport and athletes. Based on the competitive season, the overall annual plan or macrocycle is structured to sequentially develop specific attributes required by the athlete. To avoid monotony, staleness, and overtraining potential, the training program must involve structured variation of key training variables (e.g., volume, intensity, training frequency, training foci, exercise selection) (41). Classically, most intercollegiate and professional sports have an annual schedule that includes an off-season, preseason, in-season, and postseason. These seasons are easy to relate to the periods in a periodized training model (figure 22.7). Off-Season The off-season should be considered the preparatory period; it typically lasts from the end of the postseason to the beginning of the preseason, which can be about six weeks before the first major competition (although this varies greatly). This preparatory period is subdivided into general and specific preparatory phases that are broken down into mesocycles; these interlink to prepare the athlete for the subsequent competitive season. For example, the athlete may complete several rotations of mesocycles that focus on hypertrophy/strength endurance and ba

Preseason After the completion of the off-season, the preseason is used to lead into the first major competition. The first transition period is often undertaken at this time with a focus on the strength/power phase of resistance training. This time is used to prepare the athlete for the subsequent competitive period. It is very important to note that the preseason is not the time to build the foundational physical capacities needed for the sport; this should occur primarily in the off-season. The preseason is designed to capitalize on the off-season and elevate the athlete’s performance capacity during the competitive period. In-Season The competitive, or in-season, period contains all the contests scheduled for the given year, including any tournament games. Most sports have a long season that requires multiple mesocycles arranged around key contests. Thus, a long competitive season (12-16+ weeks) presents unique programming challenges—in these situations, three- or four-week mesocycle blocks that unload the athlete in the last microcycle to allow for fatigue reduction and performance supercompensation before critical c

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: intensity and volume are increased or decreased to maintain physical capacities while reducing fatigue and elevating preparedness before the competitive engagements. During the in-season, monitoring activities are used to make strategic decisions about how to vary training loads to more precisely prescribe training to align with the athlete’s current state (11). Postseason After the final contest, the postseason or second transition period provides the athlete with a relative or active rest before the beginning of the next year’s off- season or preparatory period. It is important to remember that the longer the postseason, the greater the chance for detraining, which results in an increased need for a longer general preparatory phase during the next off-season (38). 1603

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: Undulating Versus Linear Periodization Models For better or worse, contemporary periodization literature has adopted the terms linear and nonlinear when referring to periodization models. However, it should be noted that a central tenet of periodization is the removal of linearity from training (35, 38, 45, 51, 65, 72, 88). In fact, when developing his original model of periodization Matveyev used Yakovlev’s concept of supercompensation (104, 105) as the basis for the need for training to be applied in a nonlinear and rhythmic manner (59, 103). Matveyev (65) noted that removing linearity from the training process and implementing appropriate training load variations provides a superior method of training. Often the traditional resistance training model is falsely referred to as linear due to the gradual and progressive mesocycle increases in intensity over time (7, 51, 77). However, a closer look at the traditional model as described by Stone, O’Bryant, and Garhammer (89, 91) and within the literature (51) shows that the traditional model contains nonlinear variation in training intensity and volume-load at the microcycle level and throughout the mesocycle. Regardless of this, the nonlinear periodization model has been introduced in the strength and conditioning industry (2, 58, 79). Alternatively, this model is sometimes described as an undulating or daily undulating periodization model because it involves larger daily (i.e., within the microcycle) fluctuations in the load a

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: Some research studies suggest that the daily undulating model is more effective than the traditional model (21, 57, 67, 68, 79), although other evidence suggests that no difference exists between these models (2, 10, 31, 78, 100, 101) or that traditional models are superior (47, 48, 74, 75, 101). Proponents of the daily undulating model suggest that one of its strengths is the absence of accumulated neural fatigue caused by extended, ever-increasing training intensities common to the traditional model (56). Conversely, proponents of the traditional model suggest that the overall high volume-loads of training in the undulating model result in greater peripheral fatigue and increased risk of injury because of the high levels of metabolic fatigue this type of programming can stimulate (74, 75). Additionally, examination of the stimulus–fatigue–recovery– adaptation theory (figure 22.3) and the fatigue–fitness paradigm (figure 22.4) indicates that the daily undulating model has the potential to decrease athlete preparedness because of accumulated fatigue that occurs with higher volume- load training sessions. Some authors suggest that, based on the GAS, this response may actually increase the potential for overtraining with higher-level athletes (35, 94) and result in an increased injury risk for athletes using this model in conjunction with their sport-based training. 1605

text: Example of an Annual Training Plan A sample approach to designing a full annual training plan (i.e., macrocycle for sports with one competitive season) spanning all four sport seasons is presented in figure 22.8. The annual plan example provided in this chapter defines a macrocycle that lasts from May 1 until April 28. This macrocycle is subdivided into four seasons: off-season (May 1-August 20), preseason (August 21-November 5), in-season (November 6-April 14), and postseason (begins on April 15). Since there is only one competitive season in this annual training plan a single macrocycle structure has been used. This macrocycle is then subdivided into 14 mesocycles, which range in length between two and four weeks. Note: The primary focus of this sample annual training plan is to explain how to subdivide the annual plan and to design the resistance training component. Although other modes of training are described briefly (e.g., plyometrics, anaerobic conditioning, aerobic endurance) and can be easily incorporated into the annual plan, this example is not intended to illustrate every aspect of a strength and conditioning program for basketball. For more information on how to structure an annual training plan, consult NSCA’s Guide to Program Design (41). text: In-Season After an unloading week following the preseason, the athlete is ready to begin the competitive period of training. The in-season period lasts approximately 22 weeks, spanning a time period from November until April (including a four-week tournament period, although it could last longer). The goals for the in-season are to maintain and possibly improve strength, power, flexibility, and anaerobic conditioning. The time constraints of games, skill and strategy practice, and travel result in a lower volume of off-court training activities. Due to multiple games each week, resistance training may be limited to 30 minutes, one to three times per week, consisting of an undulating regimen of varying volume-loads and relative intensities. Power and basketball-specific nonpower core exercises predominate, with assistance exercises added for balance. See the sample in- season program near the end of this chapter. Plyometric sessions should be alternated with resistance training and conducted once or twice weekly, depending on the number of games. On days when no resistance training is scheduled, 15 to 20 minutes of various short sprint intervals could be performed once or twice weekly during practice. Speed, agility, and other running conditioning can be incorporated into practice time, and flexibility training can be part of the practice and game warm-up and cool-down. text: Reviewing the Annual Plan Example For any periodization model to function optimally, the sport coach and the strength and conditioning professional must plan the program together to share goals and strategies. This is a critical issue in that working together allows all the training factors that the athlete will engage in to be integrated so as to better manage the training stress and modulate fatigue and recovery. Without the cooperation of all involved professionals, optimal performance cannot be fully achieved. The example in this chapter is a representation of only one periodization model that could be used to structure training for a sample athlete. Other athletes or sports may require subtle to radical variations in the structure presented here. It is important to remember that a multitude of periodization models can be adapted to meet the needs of the various athletes and sports. 1609

chapterTitle: Periodization
text: Conclusion Periodization is a process through which the athlete’s training is logically and systematically organized to optimize preparedness and increase performance potential for the most important competitions. The annual training plan (year of training) is divided into macrocycles that contain preparatory, competitive, and transition periods. Each period is subdivided into mesocycles that target specific phases of development: hypertrophy/strength endurance, basic strength, or strength/power. Transitions are used to link mesocycles or macrocycles and provide the athlete with an unloading period that enhances recovery. The overall structure of the macrocycle, mesocycle, and individual microcycles is dictated by the individual sport’s competitive season and demands.
