chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: CHAPTER 24 OVERREACHING, OVERTRAINING, AND RECOVERY Andrew C. Fry, PhD, and Bradley C. Nindl, PhD After completing this chapter, you will be able to define and differentiate overtraining and overreaching; understand the difference between the process of overtraining and the result of the overtraining syndrome; recognize contributing factors to overtraining and overreaching; understand the role of allostatic loading; realize that not all decreases in performance are due to overtraining; know the physical performances most sensitive to overtraining and overreaching; appreciate the physiological, biomechanical, and psychological responses and adaptations to overtraining and overreaching; learn about potential strategies for avoiding performance decrements due to overtraining; and understand how functional overreaching can be a beneficial part of an appropriately designed training program. 1679

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Training for optimum performance is familiar territory for athletes, as it is for most people. Attaining one’s performance potential often requires advanced training methods that include phases (i.e., cycles or blocks) of high training volumes and intensities (see chapter 22). While these training phases can be effective for long-term performance enhancement, they also run the risk of creating a training stimulus that is greater than the recovery capabilities of the individual. When this happens, it is called overtraining (OT), and it contributes to the resulting overtraining syndrome (OTS). The problem of overtraining was recognized as far back as 1866 (101), but the topic of overtraining has received much attention in the scientific literature in recent years, and it is readily apparent that this is a complex and often confusing phenomenon (13, 38, 40, 43, 61, 65, 72, 74, 80, 88, 89, 104, 107, 135, 137, 139). Furthermore, the issue of overtraining is a problem in areas other than sport, such as with tactical (i.e., military) personnel (134). A common finding in many reviews and position stands is that more research must be performed to understand more fully what overtraining and overreaching (OR) is, how it affects the individual, and what measures can be taken to avoid this problem. In the present chapter we will examine the known causes and results of the various stress responses as they apply primarily to strength and conditioning programs for high performance and will p

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Periodization and the General Adaptation Syndrome When the total training program is correctly designed and implemented, the individual can adapt and improve. This can closely align with Selye’s general adaptation syndrome (GAS; figure 24.1) (117). In the GAS paradigm as applied to any biological system, a stress creates an initial alarm phase, followed by a resistance phase, and ultimately adaptation. If the stress is too great, the system is unable to successfully resist the stressor and the biological system dies. In the context of an athlete and a well- designed strength and conditioning program, this sequence initially produces decreases in performance, followed by performance recovery, and eventually performance improvements. This assumes that the training program permits the athlete to resist the stress; otherwise, persistent decreases in performance occur. These performance decrements can be either long term due to overtraining, or short term due to overreaching (see the Overreaching Defined section later in the chapter) (93, 108, 125, 126). Therein lies the problem for the strength and conditioning professional: how to create the proper overload (i.e., training stress) and how to correctly adjust the training load to permit the athlete to recover and attain enhanced performance. When done correctly, this process can be part of a well-designed periodized program (see chapter 22). It must be remembered that both the GAS and the concept of periodization are paradigms, o

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: be acknowledged that our understanding of overtraining and overreaching is far from complete (88, 89, 135) and requires much more study. The goal of this chapter is to help the practitioner and athlete avoid unintended long-term decreases in performance, which are exactly the opposite of the intended training goal. FIGURE 24.1 Relationship between the general adaptation syndrome paradigm and stages of overtraining and overreaching. Adapted by permission from V.M. Zatsiorsky, W.J. Kraemer, and A.C. Fry, Science and Practice of Strength Training, 3rd ed. (Human Kinetics, 2021), 180. One of the biggest challenges when training an individual or a team is how to get the most from training. If working with athletes training for maximum performance, this means implementing a training program that will optimize performance for their sport. If working in a tactical environment (e.g., military, law enforcement, fire fighter, first responder), the goal again is to optimize performance for the tasks to be performed. Even for those in the general population who are hoping to optimize their health and fitness, it is sometimes desirable to get the maximum effects from the training program to satisfy their needs. In each of these scenarios, the person designing the training program will most likely not be satisfied with mediocre results but is rather seeking to obtain 1682

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: the best results possible despite potential limitations encountered. These limitations can include a number of factors such as those listed in figure 24.2. Figure 24.2 Possible limiting factors when designing an optimal strength and conditioning program. Time available Equipment and facilities available Sport-specific training Sport governing body regulations Prior training history Travel and time zones Competition density Injury and physical limitations Menstrual cycle Age Job Family demands and schedule Recreational activities In an effort to maximize the training effect, it may be necessary to include blocks of training that highly tax the individual in an attempt to attain the greatest training response possible. Examples of this can include the high-volume general preparation phases found in many strength and conditioning programs (see chapter 18 for more details). When implemented correctly, the resulting longer- term training effect can be quite substantial. But a problem arises when these phases of training have too high a volume or intensity and are beyond the recovery capacity of the individual or team, which can give way to overtraining. But what exactly is overtraining? What are the lesser forms of overtraining, referred to as overreaching? And how do these differ from a stressful but well- designed training block? Although the term overtraining is commonly 1683

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: used in the sport coaching and strength and conditioning professions, we must first define exactly what we are talking about. 1684

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Overtraining and Overreaching A number of definitions of overtraining and overreaching can be found in the literature; however, in many cases the definitions are vague or extremely general. Some may think the concept of overtraining is a relatively new topic. However, as previously mentioned, though not in the context of sport performance, the issue was recognized as early as 1866 concerning general physical effort. It was stated that “the exertion shall not exceed the powers of recruitment; and … the recruitment shall be facilitated by adequate diet and rest” (101). Additionally, much of the overtraining literature is based on the seminal work of Hans Selye’s GAS (117), which is also discussed in chapter 22. In the 1980s and 1990s, sport scientists and sports medicine clinicians began to recognize the problems of overtraining in sport and began to study and evaluate this challenge as described in several reviews (13, 38, 72, 74, 80, 104, 126, 129, 139). The following things had become clear: Not all forms of overtraining are identical (72, 129). Not all types of performance decrements are the same (33, 34, 80, 104). The contributing factors are variable (13, 38, 72, 80, 104, 126, 129, 139). Figure 24.3 illustrates the training continuum from no training to optimum training, which can include stressful training to various overtraining scenarios. What should be abundantly clear in this figure is that different sports (i.e., training goals) present different types of overtraini

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: contributing to overtraining for these same three athletes, and the performance impairments and physiological responses, are also different (13, 33, 34, 38, 72, 80, 104, 126, 138, 139). Overtraining Defined Due to the emergence of numerous attempts to define and understand overtraining (64, 71), a joint task force on the topic was convened by the combined efforts of the European College of Sports Science (ECSS) and the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) (88). The result was their position statement titled “Preventions, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome” that presented a consensus definition of overtraining and overreaching, as well as what was scientifically known about these problems at the time. This was followed in 2013 by an updated position stand summarizing what had been learned subsequent to 2006 (89). The consensus of this working group was to adopt the following definition of overtraining: An accumulation of training and/or non-training stress resulting in long-term decrement in performance capacity with or without related physiological and psychological signs and symptoms of maladaptation in which restoration of performance capacity may take several weeks or months (88, p. 2). 1686

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: FIGURE 24.3 Training continuum resulting in overtraining for numerous forms of exercise and training. RE = resistance exercise; OT = overtraining; OR = overreaching. Adapted by permission from V.M. Zatsiorsky, W.J. Kraemer, and A.C. Fry, Science and Practice of Strength Training, 3rd ed. (Human Kinetics, 2021), 179. As can be seen in this definition, this is a serious condition for the athlete from which recovery can take a long time, and it greatly interferes or halts the competition training program. Since this definition was proposed, more recent working groups have added their definitions to the literature, as well as concerns with the state of the overtraining research (65, 135) that have helped illustrate the challenges of understanding this phenomenon. An important aspect of this definition that was also clarified in these position stands is that overtraining is actually the process (e.g., excessively high volumes and intensities of training) that then can result in an overtraining syndrome (i.e., the collection of symptoms and performance impairments) (figure 24.4) (88, 89). To be overtrained, one actually has the OTS and the required long-term performance impairments (i.e., weeks to months or longer). Performance impairments are necessary for overtraining to have occurred. However, we will see that not all performance impairments are alike. 1687

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: FIGURE 24.4 Overtraining is the process, and the overtraining syndrome is the result. In all instances, performance impairment of some type will be one of the results. Overtraining is the process that can result in an overtraining syndrome. Overtraining Syndrome Defined When the ECSS-ACSM Task Force defined overtraining (88, 89), they specifically stated that the OTS was a combination of “related physiological and psychological signs and symptoms of maladaptation,” some of which may not be part of the training program. As such, the use of the term syndrome indicates the complex nature of the condition and the fact that the symptoms are associated with each other. 1688

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: A major challenge to understanding overtraining and its causes and effects are the numerous different terms found in the literature. This is one reason several groups have developed position stands (88, 89) and consensus statements (65) that include suggested terminology. Likewise, many symptoms of an overtraining syndrome can vary between individuals and between different types of training. However, it is important to note that in all cases, performance is impaired in some manner. Figure 24.5 lists a number of the terms used in the literature for overtraining and its effects. Figure 24.5 Terminology commonly used for overtraining, the overtraining syndrome, and related topics. Overtraining Overreaching Functional overreaching Nonfunctional overreaching Overtraining syndrome Stagnation Overworked Overstressed Burnout Overfatigued Excessive fatigue Imbalance of work and recovery Underrecovered Failure to adapt Stressful training syndrome Unexplained underperformance Underperformance Staleness Maladaptation Chronic fatigue Adapted by permission from V.M. Zatsiorsky, W.J. Kraemer, and A.C. Fry, Science and Practice of Strength Training, 3rd ed. (Human Kinetics, 2021), 178. 1689

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Research on the OTS sometimes identifies two types of OTS related to the autonomic nervous system, specifically the sympathetic overtraining syndrome (sometimes referred to as SOTS) and the parasympathetic overtraining syndrome (sometimes referred to as POTS) (126). First presented by Israel in 1976 (61), these syndromes were named based on how the autonomic nervous system responded to the training stresses. Parasympathetic Overtraining Syndrome Initially named the Addisonoid syndrome since it is often accompanied by decreased concentrations of the stress hormone cortisol, this condition is characterized by the predominance of parasympathetic activity. In general, the parasympathetic overtraining syndrome is most often found in aerobic endurance athletes where very large training volumes are common. Diagnosing parasympathetic overtraining syndrome in aerobic endurance athletes can be tricky since decreased resting heart rate (HRrest) is typically a sign of beneficial cardiovascular adaptations to a training program (e.g., decreased resting HR). However, in this case, the decreased HR in already highly trained individuals is due to a parasympathetic overtraining syndrome and the prerequisite training program. It should be noted that the parasympathetic overtraining syndrome does not cause the performance impairments, but rather is a collection of symptoms typically resulting from the huge training volumes often used by aerobic endurance athletes. Some of the classic studies of

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: training (78, 80). At times, this has been called adrenal exhaustion due to the inability of the adrenal glands to produce adequate concentrations of epinephrine. Sympathetic Overtraining Syndrome For a number of years, the existence of a sympathetic overtraining syndrome was hypothetical, until it was shown in a group of resistance exercise overtrained subjects (36). It had been hypothesized that a sympathetic overtraining syndrome would occur before development of a parasympathetic overtraining syndrome, but enhanced sympathetic activity had never been previously shown in response to an OT stimulus. The primary characteristic of sympathetic overtraining syndrome is an increased epinephrine response to exercise and training (36, 37, 38, 40, 41, 139). Eventually, the elevated catecholamines result in a down- regulation of their primary receptor in skeletal muscle, β-2 receptors (41, 124). This is believed to be an important part of the sympathetic overtraining syndrome and the accompanying impaired contractility of skeletal muscle in this condition. Overreaching Defined A lesser form of stressful training than overtraining is called overreaching (OR) and is defined as follows: An accumulation of training and/or non-training stress resulting in short-term decrement in performance capacity with or without related physiological and psychological signs and symptoms of maladaptation in which restoration of performance capacity may take from several days to several weeks (88, 89).

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: stagnated performances have been considered a type of overtraining (13), this is difficult to differentiate from good training programs since all seriously trained individuals experience periodic plateaus in performance. However, if stagnation occurs due to an inappropriate training load (33), adjustments must be made. FIGURE 24.6 Different types of performance impairment due to an overtraining syndrome. Being overreached or overtrained results in decreased performance. The primary differences include the recovery times, whether performance is ultimately enhanced, and the magnitude of other symptoms that occur. Functional Overreaching Many training programs purposely include micro- or mesocycles of greater training volumes or intensities as part of the long-term plan. Examples of these include preseason training camps for many sports that include two or three training sessions a day or general preparation training blocks in the strength and conditioning program. When properly prescribed, these can be very effective training 1692

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: methods that prepare the athlete for later performance gains (88, 89, 106, 126). The short-term effect is decrements in performance, but recovery can be attained within days or weeks and can result in a supercompensation effect. As such, and although stressful to the athlete, functional overreaching (FOR) can be beneficial provided appropriate recovery is allowed. It should be noted that functional overreaching is a commonly used training strategy by many successful coaches. Figure 24.1 on page 778 illustrates how functional overreaching can fit into the GAS paradigm. Nonfunctional Overreaching On the other hand, nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) is somewhat similar to functional overreaching with two very important differences. First, the short-term accumulated fatigue is greater, and, second, the recovery takes longer (88, 89, 126). In the case of NFOR, the individual does not experience any supercompensation and is only able to return to his or her baseline performance levels (see figure 24.1 on page 778) (88, 89, 93, 108, 125, 126). As the name implies, this type of training does not serve any useful function since no performance benefits result, and the athlete has been unnecessarily stressed. Overtraining and Overreaching Share Properties With Other Conditions A number of other problematic conditions share symptoms and characteristics with OT and OTS. For example, similarities between OT and the OTS with clinical depression (4, 5), post-traumatic stress disorder (6), an

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: trained professionals need to be involved, but the strength and conditioning professional must be able to recognize when help of this type is needed. 1694

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Overtraining Continuum All the different types and severities of overtraining and overreaching can collectively make an overtraining continuum (figure 24.7). Although some overlap may exist between each of the categories, this continuum illustrates how each successive level becomes more serious for the athlete and requires longer and more intense recovery. FIGURE 24.7 The overreaching/overtraining continuum. SOTS = sympathetic overtraining syndrome; POTS = parasympathetic overtraining syndrome. It should be apparent now that not all forms of overtraining are identical (28, 126, 129), and the resulting OTS is not a simple problem with simple solutions. Indeed, it has been repeatedly reported that many factors contribute to this problem, and whether it is due to training for aerobic endurance sports (28, 46) or resistance exercise (37, 43), it is extremely complex (46, 49, 84, 88, 89, 139) and multidisciplinary (75, 107). The net result is that there are many risk factors for overtraining (110, 139) that must be recognized to avoid this problem. As evidenced by some who believe there is no evidence of fatigue accumulation from resistance exercise (63), much more research is needed (48, 135). It is highly likely that understanding this complexity will require novel and emerging research methods and approaches such as advanced statistical 1695

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: modeling and work in the field of -omics (e.g., proteomics and genomics) (4, 30). 1696

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Factors Contributing to Overreaching and Overtraining The first step in understanding overtraining and overreaching is identifying the balance between stress and recovery (53). Stress from a strength and conditioning program must be countered with adequate recovery to permit long-term progression (figure 24.8). The inability to adequately recover will undoubtedly result in an overtraining scenario. Likewise, an inadequate training load will likely produce suboptimal performance. The challenge for the strength and conditioning professional is to find the appropriate balance to maximize the long-term performance adaptations. FIGURE 24.8 Although many factors can contribute to poor performance, overtraining, as the name implies, is due to excessive training, inadequate recovery, or both. Training Factors Since we are focusing on overtraining and overreaching in the strength and conditioning context, the first and most obvious contributing factors are found in the strength and conditioning program in question. A quick review of the numerous variables in the resistance exercise program illustrates the many ways the program can be adjusted to the needs of the individual being trained (139; see chapter 18). In general, the volume of training (e.g., total repetitions, volume-load, mechanical work, metabolic work, frequency of training) and the intensity of training (e.g., relative intensity [%RM], absolute intensity [kg], perceptions of effort) are 1697

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: important variables when determining the training stress (figure 24.9). Excessive amounts of either training volume or intensity can combine to produce an overtraining stimulus. Monitoring the characteristics of the training program may be one of the most important methods for prescribing load. Additionally, the long-term periodized training program also must be correctly applied. Even though a periodized program can be effective (see chapter 22), it can also be incorrectly designed, resulting in overtraining. Additionally, an appropriately designed training taper can also enhance performance testing (96). Another training error is a lack of variation in the training load (126), which can be quantified by calculating the coefficient of variation (%CV; SD/ x–) for the training load (29, 82, 139). Finally, the most important part of an athlete’s training stress is the sport-specific training and practices, not to mention the stresses of competition. FIGURE 24.9 Excessive levels of training volume and intensity can contribute to overtraining. Allostatic Load Often overlooked aspects of an overtraining syndrome are contributing factors outside the training hall or the competition arena. These are many and varied, and in the context of overtraining they have been termed the allostatic load (86, 107). Collectively, the cumulative causes of stress (i.e., antecedents) produce the various stress responses (i.e., allostatic load) (71, 86). The allostatic load is created by various ante

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: produce adverse responses of the body that are part of the stress responses. To better understand the stress, various algorithms have been created to help make sense of all the antecedents that contribute to this problem (21). In this stress model, if the allostatic load is too great, illness or disease can result. A simple description of the allostatic load is the wear and tear on the body (103). The concept of allostatic load was originally presented in 1993 (86) and is a central concept for the study of how humans respond and adapt to stresses (71). If we now apply the concept of allostatic loads to overtraining syndrome, we see that the totality of stresses to the body include primary factors that are part of the training and recovery process and secondary factors that also contribute to the overtraining syndrome but are not part of training and competition. Collectively, the allostatic load can create a large stress that must be considered by the strength and conditioning professional when planning training programs to avoid overtraining. Figure 24.10 illustrates how these secondary factors can contribute to an overtraining syndrome. One important note is that these secondary factors that can contribute to the overtraining syndrome can also be caused by an overtraining syndrome. The challenge is to determine if these factors exist outside the training program and add to the overtraining stress or if they are created by overtraining. Many factors have been identified as p

text: FIGURE 24.10 Allostatic load includes all contributing factors to overtraining and overtraining syndrome (OTS). Solid lines notate required factors or direct causes. Dashed lines show contributing factors, not direct causes. 1700

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Underperformance and Its Relation to Overtraining and Overreaching Despite the name of this chapter, all discussions regarding overtraining and overreaching must start with the concept of underperformance. Although all our efforts may go to creating training programs to optimize performance, achieving excellence can be very elusive. Seldom are all components of the training and competition processes in complete synchrony. The job of a strength and conditioning professional is to help navigate the athlete through the many hurdles standing in the way of achieving absolute peak performance. Although few, if any, may ever attain that level of performance perfection, the task of the strength and conditioning professional is to develop, prescribe, and apply the type of training program that gives the athlete the best opportunity to reach that goal. Therefore, it is not only necessary to know how to develop the appropriately challenging training program required to reach this level of performance but also to understand what is happening when performance is less than expected (i.e., underperformance). We will see that even though overtraining and overreaching can be contributors to underperformance, many other factors can contribute as well. Many may be beyond our control, but recognizing possible contributing factors will permit the strength and conditioning professional to determine what appropriate measures can be taken to help the athlete when, despite all the effort, he or she c

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Performance-Related Variables Affected by Overtraining and Overreaching Up to this point we have discussed what contributes to overtraining and overreaching, but at some point, the strength and conditioning professional needs to know how and when performance is affected (figure 24.14). To better understand performance decrements due to overtraining, a number of studies have been performed both in the laboratory and in the field (32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 39, 41, 42, 76, 99, 100, 108, 133). One of the problems with this line of research is the difficulty in creating an overtraining syndrome in the laboratory, and when data are taken from actual athletes who have overtrained, the lack of study control makes interpreting the data difficult. Regardless, table 24.1 lists a number of performance measures that have been shown to be adversely affected by overtraining or are believed to be vulnerable to overtraining (18, 33, 35, 36, 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 50, 52, 78, 105, 106, 124, 139). The wide range of performances that can be affected makes understanding the practical implications of overtraining challenging. In general, when overtraining in the weight room, speed (e.g., sprinting) is most sensitive to overtraining and decreases before most other variables. This is closely followed by decreases in power (force × velocity), with maximal strength consistently being one of the last performances to decrease. chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Physiological Mechanisms Associated With Overreaching and Overtraining As discussed earlier, not all forms of overtraining and the resulting overtraining syndrome are identical. Furthermore, the symptoms and physiological responses can also be quite different depending on the individual and the characteristics of the training program. However, a number of physiological systems have either been shown or theorized to be affected by overtraining. It should be noted that although these mechanisms can be the result of an overtraining stimulus, it is also possible that if these conditions are preexisting, they can also contribute to an overtraining syndrome and be considered part of the allostatic load. Understanding the underlying physiology can, in some cases, provide insight on preventive strategies to help minimize the risk of developing overtraining syndrome and the accompanying impairments in performance. Table 24.2 provides example references for each of the proposed mechanisms, as well as the strength of the data supporting each. 1706

chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Assessment of Overreaching and Overtraining Ideally, a carefully designed athlete monitoring program is developed to determine the training and recovery capabilities of each individual. Qualities of the tests included in this program must be specific to the training being performed or the physiological system involved (i.e., valid), reliable (i.e., capable of providing consistent results), sensitive to the training and competition stimulus, and easy to incorporate into the regular athlete monitoring program. Furthermore, those administering the tests must precisely follow correct protocols and must ensure that each person performing the tests provides a maximal effort. If the tests are not administered correctly, the data acquired will be meaningless. Once the tests are performed, an efficient data management system must be used to help best interpret the results rapidly and correctly. Rapid turnaround of test results is important to permit adjustments in the training program when needed. text: Recovery Methods and Strategies Once overtraining or overreaching has occurred and the individual has developed an overtraining syndrome, the most important next step is developing a recovery plan. An important consideration is that overtraining often has a complex and sometimes slow onset and is not rapidly reversed. Table 24.4 lists some of the essential or suggested measures that must be taken when overtraining occurs. Training Factors for Recovery Once overtraining occurs and overtraining syndrome has developed, the first thing that must be done is a careful revision of the training program. A rapid decrease in the training volume, intensity, or both is typically warranted. When overreaching has occurred, training cessation has permitted performance to return to original levels in as little as one week (36, 37, 87, 88, 111, 139). When more serious levels of overtraining have occurred, recovery can take as long as four weeks after high-intensity resistance exercise (35) or months to a year after high-volume distance running (78). In each case, training volume or intensity was immediately decreased or removed. It may not always be practical or desirable to cease training, depending on each individual case. Although it has been suggested that one week of resistance training cessation does not benefit strength and hypertrophy gains, the training did not incorporate training similar to overtraining or overreaching (22). text: Overtraining Considerations Not all types of overtraining are identical. Strength is well-protected. Speed and power may be more sensitive to overtraining. Psychological variables may be effective markers. Hormonal variables indicate stress, not OT. Orthopedic problems present different OTS. Autonomic nervous system activity responds rapidly to OT. Muscle fiber maladaptation can follow. Overtraining Avoidance Strategies Use active and passive recovery methods during training. Allow one or more days of routine training abstinence to enhance recovery. Rest days are critical. Limit excessively long training sessions and too many sessions in a day. Exercise caution with excessive training volumes and large increases in training volume (>30% increases). Prior exposure to stressful training enhances training stress tolerance. Variation in the training stimulus is critical, and use of periodized training is important. Avoid excessive training to failure. Coordinate resistance exercise with other stressors (e.g., sport training and other conditioning). Incorporate recovery strategies (e.g., sleep, diet, mental skills). Appropriate diet for training (e.g., adequate Kcal, protein ingestion, glycogen repletion, sufficient vitamins and minerals, adequate fluid intake). Dietary supplements may help (e.g., recovery drinks, protein and carbohydrate supplements, creatine, oral ATP). Monitor outside stressors. Monitor internal and external training loads. chapterTitle: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery
text: Conclusion The occurrence of overtraining or nonfunctional overreaching can be devastating to those athletes training for high performance. Not only does it mean they are not able to perform as planned, but it can also mean that training and performance are impaired for an extended period of time. While those who are seriously training may want to push themselves as much as possible, they must be careful not to pass the threshold so that overtraining occurs. Due to the complex nature of this problem, it can result in the maladaptation of many physiological systems (figure 24.17). Conversely, preexisting problems in any of these physiological systems can also contribute to an overtraining syndrome. Overall, we have discussed in this chapter how everything revolves around the impaired performances caused by improper training (figure 24.18). However, it is clear that many factors can contribute to this problem. Knowledge of the causes and effects of overtraining and how to avoid it and recover from it are valuable tools for every successful strength and conditioning professional. 1722

Organizing the construction and design of a strength and conditioning facility requires a well-thought-out plan created by a committee of experienced professionals. This chapter provides information on the different phases of planning a new facility, along with details about facility design, organization, and equipment maintenance. The chapter also outlines the phases of construction or remodeling of a facility. The design should account for the needs of various stakeholders (e.g., athletes, staff, administrators) for the layout to be most efficient. 1728

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: General Aspects of New Facility Design Building a new facility takes significant time and planning. One of the first things to do is assemble a committee of professionals. The committee should consist of a builder, architect, designers, lawyers, financial departments, and people who will be involved in using the facility. At least one strength and conditioning professional, or other expert who will be working in the facility, should be included in the committee to provide a perspective that will help maximize the utility and safety of the space. This committee will assist with the facility design as well as consider economic factors of opening a new facility. One of the main challenges in designing a strength and conditioning facility is tailoring the facility to the intended audience. Figure 25.1 outlines the four phases of designing a new facility, along with the main objectives for each phase. FIGURE 25.1 Phases and objectives of designing a new facility. Predesign Phase The predesign phase is the first step in building a new facility. This phase should consist of a needs analysis, a feasibility study, and master plan formation. At the end of the predesign phase, a reputable architect should be hired—likely through a bid process— and begin developing a blueprint for the facility. The needs analysis is the step when the designers and experts collaborate to determine the needs of the strength and conditioning program (10). Examples of questions are “How much open space do 17

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: you need?” and “What equipment needs to fit into the allotted space?” The needs analysis should be consistent with the specific programming needs of the strength and conditioning and athletic departments. For example, if a strength and conditioning professional regularly incorporates jump testing on force plates during weight room sessions, an area needs to be set aside for that activity. For those serving on the design committee, the needs analysis should convey an effective environment to properly implement the intended program. While site, budget, construction, and other limitations may require a certain level of flexibility as the project progresses, safety considerations for facility users should not be jeopardized (2-7, 9-17, 19-22). The second part of the predesign phase is called a feasibility study. This process should analyze strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (known as a SWOT analysis) (10). The goal of the feasibility study is to ensure that the financial investment will yield a viable and sustainable return. The feasibility study should also evaluate the location, strengths and weaknesses of any proposed ideas, and the growth potential for strength and conditioning and related programs within the department. The potential opportunities and competition threats also need to be considered. This includes market evaluation to identify the best opportunity to train athletes most efficiently, as well as analyzing the target market and growth potential of

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: the success of the facility both in the near term and in the future. The operational plan should also include staff development and a plan for the hiring process. Hiring an architect is the final step of the predesign phase. Selecting an architect is crucial for meeting administration and department goals. It is important to select from a list of architects who have a positive reputation based on previous work. If possible, it is best to choose an architect who has had previous experience in the strength and conditioning industry. The architect will likely be hired through a bid process, meaning that the architect who is hired is often the one who submits the lowest price. Bid plans require efficient use of resources so that the money is spent on what is most useful for the users of the facility. Design Phase The design phase is the second phase in the process of building a new facility. In the design phase, ideas from the committee come together with regard to the structure and design elements of the facility. It is extremely important to plan around the flow of the facility while adhering to all relevant regulations and codes. Federal, state, and city codes are often highly specific about aspects of the design. City planning departments can provide the local guidelines and applicable codes for constructing a facility. The first step in the design phase is finalizing the design committee. To reiterate, the committee should include strength and conditioning and other athletic

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: access for people will have the greatest effect on the function and safety of the facility when multiple groups of athletes are present at the same time. The flow of traffic should also allow coaches or supervisors to have a clear view of the entire floor. The locations of any structural pillars, columns, or other obstructions must be considered in the planning of equipment spaces to account for traffic flow and access to emergency exits. Construction Phase The construction phase is the period of time from the beginning of building the facility until completion. This is usually the longest phase of the process. During construction, the committee needs to continually refer to the master plan to ensure that the project is on track with regard to the established goals and design. Keeping the project on track in relation to the deadline must also become a priority. Delays in construction can add significant financial strain. Having access to legal counsel is beneficial to making sure that construction deadlines are met and extra expenses and legal action are avoided. Preoperation Phase The preoperation phase consists of the final steps before the facility can open. These steps include finishing the interior decor (note that appearance can greatly enhance the experience of users), aesthetic considerations to support athlete recruiting or membership enrollment, and hiring a staff of qualified professionals. The staff should have at least the minimum required certifications and educ

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: knowledgeable, loyal, and trustworthy employees is crucial to running a successful strength and conditioning program. During the preoperation phase, it is important to include a plan for staff development as well. This could vary from semiannual workshops to weekly staff meetings. During the preoperation phase it is vital to create a plan that will make opening the facility easy. For example, duties such as cleaning and maintenance should be delegated to the staff on a weekly basis. This is easier to do when a cleaning and maintenance schedule has been created and is followed as soon as the facility is operating. Also during preoperation, a plan for administrative and clerical duties should be created to organize work related to matters such as liability insurance, scheduling, and budgeting. Details, such as choosing a scheduling software package, installing an athlete management system, and delegating clerical duties, should be accounted for before the facility opens. 1733

text: Existing Strength and Conditioning Facilities Modifying an existing strength and conditioning facility is similar to designing a new facility, without the process of building from the ground up. A design committee can also be formed for renovating an existing facility, but members such as a builder and architect may not be necessary. An existing facility may also use different hiring processes. Sometimes strength and conditioning professionals continue to work in the same facility regardless of a change of ownership or management. However, there should still be a focus on standards, education, professionalism, and staff development. Figure 25.2 outlines the main steps in modifying an existing facility. FIGURE 25.2 Steps in modifying an existing facility. The strength and conditioning professional should assess existing equipment based on the current and future needs of everyone who uses the facility. 1734

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Satellite Training Facilities It has become common in recent years for college and professional sport organizations to add alternative and sport-specific satellite training facilities to accommodate the needs of growing strength and conditioning departments. Other examples of this include providing a strength and conditioning facility for visiting team use, as is mandated by some professional sport leagues, or designing a studio space for individualized or small group training sessions. Special attention should be given when planning satellite training facilities, especially if existing, dated, or nontraining spaces are being converted for strength and conditioning use. Satellite training facilities may benefit from smaller pieces of equipment based on the size of the space available (e.g., half rack vs. full rack). In small facilities, it can be beneficial to install multipurpose pieces of equipment rather than equipment with a single function (9). A satellite training facility that does not have dedicated walkways separating the equipment areas should be set up with equipment bolted and secured around the perimeter. The center of the room should remain open for transitions between training stations while allowing unimpeded access to emergency exits. As a rule, equipment and safety spacing should never be compromised due to limited space. text: Outdoor Training Spaces Weight room adjacent or satellite outdoor training spaces have become more common in geographically moderate climates. In addition, the global COVID-19 pandemic created increased awareness among strength and conditioning professionals for the benefit of social distancing, including the use of open-air outdoor training spaces for enhanced ventilation (15). There are also scenarios when scheduling or programming can be improved by having strength and conditioning equipment available near sport or practice facilities that do not have a dedicated weight room space. While environmental factors, like weather, must always be considered for athlete safety, this section provides recommendations for the safe use of strength and conditioning equipment in outdoor training areas. Outdoor training spaces may include multipurpose training lockers or pods and be located next to a game or practice field (e.g., grass or artificial turf) or in proximity to the weight room (e.g., via garage door access). Outdoor training spaces may be for seasonal or year- round use depending on climate. Important considerations include ensuring adequate space for strength and conditioning activity to be performed safely and that standards for equipment, safety spacing, and walkways are clear. Outdoor training surfaces must offer proper traction for athletic activity and should not be wet or damp from recent storms. Ground surface temperatures should also be considered to avoid injury due

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Assessing Athletic Program Needs One of the more important considerations in building a strength and conditioning facility is the needs and requirements of the athletes and athletic program. The number of athletes, coaching philosophies, athlete ages and experience levels, schedules and availability, and equipment factors can affect the design of the facility (12). When it is time to evaluate such needs, the facility designers should be able to answer these questions: How many athletes will use the facility? This is an important consideration because the facility size will be greatly influenced by the number of athletes using the facility at the same time (i.e., at peak usage) and the total number who use it per day, week, and season. The number of athletes will also affect the scheduling and flow of the facility if two or more groups are training simultaneously. Based on regulations such as fire codes or other occupational health and safety regulations, the city planning departments will specify the maximum room capacity. In addition to the number of athletes training, it is also essential to consider staffing and supervision. The number of athletes being trained simultaneously will affect the number of strength and conditioning professionals required to safely and effectively monitor the training session (16). What are the training goals for the athletes, coaches, and administration? Training goals will directly affect equipment selection for the facility. For example, if a

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: and platforms are more space efficient compared to bench or incline bench press setups that serve only one purpose. What are the demographics of the athletes? The demographics of the users are important when determining the equipment needs of the facility. Are the users primarily older, younger, male, female, middle school, high school, college, or professional? A facility with primarily older populations may not need as much free weight equipment as it does machines. In a collegiate or team environment, use of the equipment may be more efficient if it is grouped into sections so that multiple groups can work out simultaneously without interference. What will the training experience of the athletes be like? Answering this question will help the strength and conditioning professional devise training plans, which in turn will dictate the equipment needed. Training will vary according to the experience of the athlete. Athletes with no previous resistance training experience may do more bodyweight exercises than advanced athletes, who may do more weightlifting. It is also important to assess whether needs will change over time and whether equipment requirements will vary depending on the season. How will training sessions be scheduled? The scheduling of athletes or groups is one of the more difficult aspects of running a facility. The number of people on staff, the layout, and the design of the facility can all be affected by the training schedule. If more than one group will be

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: What technology is needed to administer training as intended? Planning for technology is important to account for the continued growth of the program. A strong Wi-Fi or Bluetooth connection may be required if the intent is to deliver strength and conditioning programs using technology devices, such as tablets, TV monitors, or cell phone apps. Ensuring access to a strong cellular signal can provide an additional layer of safety in case of an emergency. Additionally, exercise testing and monitoring equipment may require dedicated space to be operated during training sessions and stored securely between uses. This includes specific exercise testing devices, athlete monitoring sensors, and accessories that may require special cleaning, charging, and maintenance. What equipment needs to be repaired or modified? No equipment in a facility should have issues such as holes, cuts, or missing pieces. If a cable is frayed or damaged, discontinue using the cable column until the cable is replaced. All existing equipment should be repaired or replaced if broken. Existing equipment should be repaired promptly or should be sold to provide funds for new equipment. In some cases, a piece of equipment is in good repair but needs an accessory for an upgrade. For example, cable columns may require new attachments to be fully functional. Once all of these questions are answered, the process of designing the facility will be much easier. chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Designing the Strength and Conditioning Facility Before arranging and positioning equipment, one must consider the design of the strength and conditioning facility, whether new or existing. The strength and conditioning professional should pay particular attention to facility location and access, structural and functional considerations, environmental factors, and safety and supervision. Location The strength and conditioning facility ideally should be located on the ground floor away from offices and classrooms. This will prevent interruptions elsewhere in the building that are caused by dropped weights, music, or other noises common to strength and conditioning facilities. If the facility is not located on the ground floor, the floor must be stable enough to support heavy equipment and equipment that is dropped. The load-bearing capacity should be at least 100 foot-pounds per square foot (4.8 kN/m2) (7). Supervision Location An office area for supervision should be in a central location with a clear line of sight and windows or mirrors providing the opportunity to look out and see everyone, including individuals and groups entering or exiting the room. One option is to place the office at an elevation over the floor of the weight room for better viewing. Access Every facility should be accessible to people with disabilities, with either a ramp or a wheelchair lift for any change in height exceeding 0.5 inches (1.3 cm). A ramp should run 12 inches for every 1-inch rise (30.5

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: help prevent anyone from falling. Another option for persons with disabilities is a mechanical lift or an elevator. Every facility should have at least one phone that is accessible to persons in wheelchairs. This complies with the Americans With Disabilities Act (3); it also provides safety in the event of an emergency if the only person who can help is in a wheelchair. The phone should be close to the entrance of the facility or near the office area so that a supervisor can call emergency services as soon as possible following an accident (2). The ADA also requires that light switches, water fountains, fire extinguishers, and automated external defibrillator (AED) devices are reachable and that safety signage is viewable by persons in wheelchairs (3). A weight room should also have double or garage doors so that large equipment and machines can be moved in and out. However, if the hallway or access point is too narrow, the size of the doors will not make a difference (14), because an outside wall will have to be removed temporarily when moving or installing equipment. Ceiling Height The ceiling should be high enough to accommodate any jumping or explosive activities. This includes the height of the athlete plus the space required for box jumps, vertical jumps, and weightlifting exercises. A recommended height is 12 to 14 feet (3.7-4.3 m), which should give enough clearance to allow athletes to comfortably perform most activities (14, 18). Certain exercises, such as overhead

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Flooring Several types of flooring options are available for a strength and conditioning facility. The most common option is some type of rubber flooring and an antimicrobial carpet. Another option is indoor turf, which can be useful if the strength and conditioning professional plans to have athletes perform dynamic warm-up, plyometric, agility, or conditioning exercises. Turf is also a good surface for ground-based movements and sled pushes that require a more field-like surface than typical gym flooring. Rubber flooring is available in rolls, tile inserts, and mats and is considered a premier option because it protects the subfloor from heavy weights and provides durable cushioning. Rubber flooring can also be easier to clean than carpet and is generally more durable and long-lasting within a facility. As a general rule for safety, floor surfaces in physical activity areas should be slip-resistant to minimize the risk of exercise and fall-related injuries (2). For facilities designed to train athletes for weightlifting competitions, platforms should have a middle portion made of wood and outer sections made of rubber, in alignment with competition rules. Especially in high-traffic strength and conditioning facilities, inlaid platforms are a safer alternative to raised platforms because they are flush with the floor and do not present a tripping hazard. Lighting Strength and conditioning facilities have special lighting needs to keep athletes safe and focused on training. K

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: The distribution of light throughout the facility is important to avoid shadowy areas or excessive glare. Glare from direct overhead lighting is especially a concern for users lying on horizontal benches or exercise mats (18). Windows can help make a facility feel more open and modern, and mirrors may enhance the amount of light that comes in by reflecting it to spots in the room without natural light (2). Light-emitting diode (LED) lights are a popular choice because of their extended life span and energy efficiency (2). Lights with color temperatures between 4,000° and 5,000° Kelvin are considered best for strength and conditioning facilities because they resemble daylight, provide optimal visibility for enhanced safety, and can have an energizing effect. Finally, adjustable lighting controls, automated on-and-off settings, and motion sensors also can be considered to reduce power consumption, energy costs, and maintenance (11). Room Temperature, Humidity, and Ventilation A strength and conditioning facility needs to maintain a comfortable training temperature. The heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system should have the capability to heat and cool individual sections of the facility. Most sources indicate that between 68 °F and 78 °F (20-26 °C) is an appropriate temperature range, with many suggesting an optimal range of 68 °F to 74 °F (20-23 °C) (2, 5, 18). If the facility is too hot or too cold, the athletes and staff may be uncomfortable and the quality

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: that any adjacent pool or spa areas are equipped with negative exhaust air flow helps to prevent moisture and chlorine odor from escaping into other areas of the training facility (2). Ventilation and circulation are primary concerns with regard to facility design and the HVAC system. The HVAC system, a fresh air exchange system, and ceiling or box fans should provide necessary ventilation and circulation that are in accordance with ANSI/ASHRAE 62.1 requirements for health clubs and weight rooms (6). Air systems must provide air circulation at proper levels according to the needs of specific equipment areas and occupant loads (6). For example, aerobic training areas require a higher circulation rate than resistance training spaces (2). Room air should be exchanged a minimum of 8 to 10 times per hour—optimally 12 to 15 times per hour to prevent odors and stagnant air (5). If fans are used, a general guideline is two to four fans for every 1,200 square feet (111 m2). Fans help keep the air from feeling stagnant and muggy, which makes for a better training environment. Sound Systems and Noise Control While not essential, many facilities have sound systems that help create a motivating training environment conducive to hard work. The two main considerations for installing a sound system are speaker volume and placement. The sound volume should be less than 90 decibels so that athletes can hear instructions and coaching cues (2). To avoid damage, speakers should be elevated above

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: yoga or dance classes, sound-absorbing material should be used in the floors and walls to prevent music from reaching others in the facility. Absorbent rubber flooring can be used to reduce noise caused by people jumping, running, or dropping things. Electrical Service and Devices A strength and conditioning facility typically requires more outlets than other buildings. Some outlets may require relatively higher voltage for more powerful equipment, such as stair climbers, elliptical trainers, and treadmills. The electrical service also needs to be properly grounded to protect the system from lightning strikes or power surges. Ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets are also necessary to ensure safety in the event of an electrical short (1). With the increase of technology now being used in weight rooms, the placement of wall, floor, and elevated power outlets should be considered to limit future issues with devices and power cords once the facility becomes operational. Specifically, power cords should never extend into exercise areas, safety spacing, walkways, or spotter areas. In addition, any equipment and device charging stations should be in an office or storage area away from weight room traffic. If televisions will be used in the facility, the use of elevated outlets and secured wall or ceiling mounts are recommended. Planning ahead for the use of technology is valuable, especially if the intent is to use television monitors or overhead projectors to communicate

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Mirrors should be placed at least 6 inches (15 cm) away from any equipment (e.g., behind a rack of dumbbells) and a minimum of 20 inches (51 cm) above the floor (4). The purpose of the height guideline is to ensure that weights do not roll, bounce, or slide into the bottom of the mirror and cause the glass to break. The standard weight plate is 18 inches (46 cm) in diameter, giving mirrors a 2-inch (5 cm) clearance if the plate is dropped near the mirror or leaned against the wall behind the mirror (14). Bumper railings or padding may be useful for places that require added protection from damage, such as walls and mirrors. Railings are also used in dance and yoga studios so people can hold on for balance when necessary. Balance railings should be installed securely with safety in mind and checked regularly before any weight-bearing activity. The choice of material and beam structure used for constructing walls (e.g., drywall or cinder block) should be considered for properly securing balance railings and other wall attachments. Also, strength and conditioning professionals who plan to program medicine ball throws into a wall should make sure to use a solid wall, such as cinder block, to prevent damage. Hydration and Nutrition Spaces in the Weight Room Drinking fountains and water bottle refill stations are important additions to a strength and conditioning facility. They should be located away from the training area and should not interrupt traffic flow. Water stations and n

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: have policies and recommendations to avoid food poisoning and food contamination. (See Standard 9.1 in the NSCA Strength and Conditioning Professional Standards and Guidelines for additional detail on the responsibility of strength and conditioning professionals related to supplements, ergogenic aids, and drugs [16].) Locker and Changing Room Access Access to locker rooms is a good benefit within a facility. At minimum, having a shower located somewhere in the building ensures that cleaning up after a workout will be convenient. Good hygiene is important for preventing the spread of infections and disease. Although not everyone will use the showers or lockers, having them available for on-the-go athletes may boost morale and give them another reason to work hard during a workout. Storage Spaces A strength and conditioning facility should have a dedicated storage space to keep items such as extra equipment, cleaning supplies, facility maintenance tools, or broken equipment. A larger facility with more equipment requires more storage space than a small facility. Depending on the layout of the facility, or if it has multiple floors, multiple storage areas may be best to avoid excessive clutter or injury from equipment not being used. For example, an athlete or strength and conditioning professional may injure his or her fingers while racking and storing weights on a plate tree in a space that is too narrow and filled with unnecessary equipment accessories. Additional areas to wa

text: extinguisher, AED, CPR equipment, and a stocked first aid kit. Additional details about emergency policies and action plans are presented in chapter 26. Other areas to consider related to storage include determining where athletes will store personal items, such as coats, backpacks, and water bottles, during training sessions. If no locker room is available at the facility, designating an area for personal item storage is important to avoid clutter. The use of cube storage, shelving, or other functional storage solutions can help maintain organizational flow of the weight room. 1750

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Arranging Equipment in the Strength and Conditioning Facility It is essential to consider spacing requirements when arranging equipment in the strength and conditioning facility. A floor plan can be drawn to help with visualizing how to arrange equipment, especially since each type of equipment and mode of exercise comes with its own safety and efficiency recommendations. Equipment Placement Equipment should be grouped into sections such as a stretching and warm-up area, agility and plyometrics, free weights, aerobic area, and resistance machines. Ideally, free weights and racks should be organized along the wall, and there should be walkways between the free weights and machines (1). Racks and machines also can be placed in rows with the back of the equipment facing each other. This allows for improved flow through the weight room, preventing congestion and maximizing usage space. Using line of sight as a guideline, shorter equipment is better placed in the middle of the room so that strength and conditioning professionals and staff can easily see across the facility. Planning ahead and organizing the equipment so it can be used as a circuit or exercise pairing will also help with traffic flow. Tall machines should be bolted to the floor, a column, or the wall to prevent tipping over. Cardiovascular machines should be in their own section and should be lined up and organized such that the treadmills, elliptical trainers, stair climbers, ski trainers, rowers, and bikes are gr

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: from the walkway to minimize the chances of someone tripping over it or on associated electrical cords. Racks, barbells, and dumbbells should have a minimum of 3 feet (0.9 m) of space between equipment to allow for movement without danger to the athlete or spotter. If a spotter or multiple spotters are needed (e.g., on a rack), providing additional space may be required. Traffic Flow Traffic flow is heavily influenced by equipment placement. Many facilities are one big room, and walkways can be created via arrangement of the equipment. As mentioned, most racks or machines are best placed lined up in a row running the length of the facility. This usually creates two or three main walkways that should be 5 to 7 feet (1.5-2.1 m) wide (2, 3, 13). For safety, all individuals in the training facility should have clear access to an exit at all times. Ensuring proper equipment and walkway spacing is important for allowing clearance to move freely throughout the facility and for ADA-required wheelchair access (3, 13). Weight Room Pillars and Building Structures When placing equipment in facilities that contain supporting structure, such as weight room pillars, columns, or other weight room obstructions, logistical planning for training sessions and safety factors should be prioritized. Due to the large size of many strength and conditioning facilities, the inclusion of weight-supporting and other building structures may be unavoidable. Strategically placing training equipment with con

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: and equipment guidelines in this chapter around building structures will improve the functionality and traffic flow of the facility. Safety, function, and traffic flow are top priorities when deciding on the placement of equipment in a facility. Stretching and Warm-Up Area A stretching and warm-up area is an open area with soft tissue instruments, mats, or elastic bands. This area may include foam rollers and other tissue rolling tools (e.g., PVC pipes, and lacrosse, tennis, golf, or softball balls) and jump ropes. Mats can be used so that athletes do not have to lie on a hard floor, but this is not necessary. Circuit Training Area A circuit training area is typically a space with machines lined up or grouped together to make it easy for people to switch from one machine to the next. Grouping the machines can be done in several ways. Examples of different groupings include upper body and lower body, pushing actions and pulling actions, and various body part groupings. In many facilities, injured athletes use the circuit machines to exercise the body parts that are still healthy. Ease of access between machines should be kept in mind so that injured athletes can move freely. Stationary circuit training machines should be at least 30 inches (76 cm) (3), preferably 36 inches (91 cm), away from each other to provide a wide enough area and some extra space for safety. Safety spacing in the weight room is generally referred to as a safety cushion. Free Weights Free weight equipment

chapterTitle: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization
text: Since most activities with a kettlebell are dynamic and require space to complete a variety of movements, this section should be large enough to accommodate both the exercises being performed and the number of athletes using the space simultaneously. Weightlifting Area A weightlifting area generally contains racks with platforms or a platform standing alone. It could also be an open area where weightlifting is performed without a platform. This is typically done on a rubber floor with a concrete foundation. To keep things organized, weight trees or racks and bar holders can be used when the equipment is not in use. Racks and platforms should have enough room between them that if someone were to fall, people nearby would not be injured. Weightlifting racks should be bolted to the floor to ensure that they do not move when in use. If a rack is portable, it should be moved to a designated storage area when not in use. Exercise and Performance Testing Spaces Exercise testing equipment should be in their own section or dedicated space. Exercise testing spaces are where equipment is grouped together for exercise testing sessions. This equipment may consist of force plates, isometric mid-thigh pulling racks, exercise testing bikes and treadmills, testing and monitoring device charging stations, and associated computer equipment. Ensuring a consistent location for exercise testing within the training facility is optimal for ensuring the validity and reliability of exercise testing. I

Additional considerations should be made for the placement of clocks and television monitors that contain pertinent information to ensure optimal visibility throughout the training session. Aerobic Area The aerobic area is where the cardiovascular training equipment is grouped together. This equipment consists of stationary bicycles, stair climbers, elliptical trainers, treadmills, rowers, and so on. A general guideline is to allocate approximately 40 to 60 square feet (3.7-5.6 m2) of floor space per piece of equipment (2). Specific floor space requirements for aerobic equipment and the recommended space between pieces of equipment are provided in table 25.1. These requirements outline the amount of space needed for each piece of equipment, along with the required amount of space to allow for room to move and prevent accidents caused by falling into equipment. Within aerobic training areas it is important that there is adequate spacing around and behind all continuous-motion exercise equipment (e.g., treadmills, elliptical trainers, bikes, ski trainers, and rowers) (2). These surfaces also can be used to implement warm-up and dynamic movement programs with athletes. text: Suspension Training Equipment Suspension training equipment refers to commercially available ring, handle, or strap setups (8). They are most often used for bodyweight training focusing on upper body, lower body, and core. The straps of a suspension training unit can be anchored independent of each other (e.g., gymnastics ring) or connected by a common anchor (e.g., eyelet and carabiner). Specific usage should be in accordance with setup and loading guidelines determined by the equipment manufacturer. Safe and effective suspension training requires a stable attachment point, level nonskid flooring, open space free of obstacles, and handles that are easy to grip (e.g., not worn or slippery) (8). Because suspension training equipment must be attached to a fixed structure (e.g., load-bearing wall mount, bolted rack, or rig frame), it is suggested that the strength and conditioning professional regularly checks the integrity of the anchor point before each use. Ideally, the anchor point should be between 7 to 9 feet (2.1-2.7 m) above the floor. Further, suspension training equipment should not be mounted in or near doorways to prevent blocking emergency exits and hindering access to storage areas, cleaning closets, locker rooms, and restrooms. All accessories used to mount suspension training equipment should be load bearing. text: Maintaining and Cleaning Surfaces and Equipment Surfaces in the strength and conditioning facility should be cleaned, sanitized, and disinfected consistently to ensure that the equipment is safe and functional. Proper maintenance will reduce cost in the long run, because cleaning supplies are cheaper than replacing padding, flooring, exercise mats, and so on. Microbes will begin to grow if the surfaces are not wiped down with a germicidal cleaner. Equipment and surfaces that are used more often and have a greater chance of developing bacterial growth (e.g., padding and vinyl), should be cleaned daily or every other day. It is important that any germicidal cleaner used in the strength facility have the ability to prevent the spread of germs, including bacteria, viruses, parasites, and fungi, and illness, such as the flu, COVID-19, HIV, hepatitis, and ringworm (or other infectious rashes). After cleaning surfaces and equipment to remove any dirt and debris, the CDC recommends sanitizing and disinfecting surfaces with an EPA- registered disinfecting product to eliminate and inactivate germs to reduce the spread of illness (20). For laundry items, such as cleaning rags and gym towels, use detergent and the hottest available water setting, and dry items completely. Nonabsorbent floors should be regularly mopped for removal of dust and grime buildup. text: Conclusion Designing a strength and conditioning facility is an extensive process that involves a significant amount of planning. The process begins with the formation of a committee that will contribute to the design and construction of the facility. The next step involves assessing the specific needs of the strength and conditioning department. This is the phase in which the number and experience level of athletes being trained, preferences from strength and conditioning professionals and staff, scheduling, and equipment needs should be determined. After these determinations have been made, the process of designing the facility and arranging the equipment can begin. Care should be taken and guidelines followed in arranging and spacing equipment to optimize safety, function, and traffic flow. After the design process is complete, the facility and the equipment must be properly maintained and cared for to ensure safe training and protect financial investments. Regular maintenance and cleaning of equipment and surfaces are vital for the longevity of the facility, in addition to health and safety. Cleaning and maintenance should focus the most on high-traffic areas and equipment that is used more often. This will help to prevent the spread of infections and disease among the facility users as well as promote proper hygiene and maintain the appearance of the environment. chapterTitle: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues
text: properly schedule the strength and conditioning facility, along with formulating guidelines on seasonal planning and staff-to- athlete ratios. The strength and conditioning profession continues to evolve. Typically, a practitioner’s knowledge and skill development involves competencies in exercise science, administration, management, teaching, and coaching (30). With student-athlete safety and welfare at the forefront, developing a policies and procedures manual provides a blueprint for implementing safe and effective programs and services. Policies are essentially a facility’s rules and regulations; they reflect the goals and objectives of the program. Procedures describe how policies are met or carried out. It is necessary to examine program goals and objectives, because they are the basis on which policies and procedures are created. Additionally, specific policies and procedures should include elements that protect the program and its employees from a risk of litigation; issues such as guidelines for supervision and instruction, facility administration, and emergency action planning and response should be included. The goal of this chapter is to identify areas of risk exposure and means of increasing safety, as well as to guide the strength and conditioning professional in providing and enhancing the quality of services and programs. 1776
